Apex Legends is one of the greatest battle royale games ever created. Since its release in 2019, it has captured the attention of millions of players around the world. Developed by Respawn Entertainment, Apex Legends offers an exciting combination of fast-paced action, teamwork, strategy and unique characters. What makes the game so special is that it is not just another battle royale where players simply run around and shoot each other. Instead, it creates an experience where every match feels different, every decision matters, and every victory feels rewarding. From its amazing movement mechanics to its memorable characters and competitive gameplay, there are countless reasons why Apex Legends is such a fantastic game.

One of the biggest reasons Apex Legends is so great is its movement system. Unlike many other battle royale games, Apex Legends allows players to move around the map quickly and smoothly. Sliding down hills, climbing walls, jumping across buildings and escaping dangerous situations makes the gameplay incredibly enjoyable. The movement mechanics give players the freedom to approach fights in different ways and make every battle exciting. Learning how to move effectively can take time, but once players understand the mechanics, the game becomes even more satisfying. There is nothing better than successfully escaping a difficult fight using clever movement or outplaying an opponent with a perfectly timed slide and jump.

Another reason Apex Legends stands out is its huge variety of unique Legends. Each character has their own personality, abilities and playstyle, meaning that players can find a character that suits them. For example, Wraith is excellent for players who enjoy moving quickly and escaping dangerous situations, while Gibraltar is perfect for players who prefer protecting their teammates. Pathfinder allows players to travel across the map using his grappling hook, while Bloodhound helps the team locate enemies. These different abilities make the game more interesting because every team can have a different strategy. The characters also have entertaining personalities, interesting backgrounds and memorable voice lines that make the Apex Legends universe feel alive.

Teamwork is another major part of what makes Apex Legends such an incredible game. Unlike games where players can easily succeed on their own, Apex Legends encourages players to work together. Communicating with teammates, sharing equipment, reviving fallen players and planning attacks are all important parts of winning. The ping system is especially impressive because it allows players to communicate without needing a microphone. Players can mark enemies, point out useful equipment and suggest locations with just a few clicks. This makes teamwork easier and creates a more welcoming experience for people who might not want to use voice chat. Winning a match with friends after working together as a team is one of the most satisfying feelings the game can offer.

The weapons in Apex Legends also deserve recognition. The game includes a wide selection of guns, each with different strengths, weaknesses and firing styles. Whether someone prefers using an assault rifle, shotgun, sniper rifle or submachine gun, there is something for everyone. Weapons such as the R-301 Carbine, Peacekeeper and Wingman have become favourites among many players because of their unique designs and satisfying gameplay. Learning how to control recoil, aim accurately and choose the right weapon for different situations adds another layer of skill to the game. The weapon variety also means that players must constantly adapt depending on what equipment they find during a match.

Furthermore, Apex Legends has some incredibly well-designed maps. Locations such as World's Edge, King's Canyon and Olympus each provide different environments and opportunities for players. Some areas encourage intense close-range fights, while others are better suited to long-distance battles and strategic positioning. The maps contain interesting buildings, hidden areas, open spaces and different routes that players can use to their advantage. Over time, map changes and new locations help keep the experience fresh. Exploring these environments and discovering new strategies makes every match feel like a different adventure.

Another fantastic feature of Apex Legends is its competitive nature. The ranked system gives players something to work towards and allows them to test their abilities against opponents of similar skill levels. Climbing through the ranks requires patience, practice, communication and determination. Every match provides an opportunity to improve, whether that means getting better at aiming, learning when to attack or understanding when it is smarter to retreat. Although ranked matches can sometimes be frustrating, achieving a new rank after hours of hard work makes the experience worthwhile. The competitive scene also gives talented players an opportunity to showcase their skills through tournaments and professional esports competitions.

Apex Legends is also an enjoyable game because of its constantly changing content. New seasons introduce different updates, balance changes, events and sometimes entirely new Legends. These updates give players reasons to return and experience something different. The developers have continued to expand the game since its release, helping it remain an important part of the battle royale genre. Seasonal events and cosmetic items also allow players to customise their experience and show off their favourite characters. While not every update is perfect, the ongoing development helps keep the game interesting.

Of course, one of the best things about Apex Legends is the unforgettable moments it creates. Whether it is winning a match with only a few seconds remaining, getting an incredible squad wipe, reviving a teammate at the perfect moment or defeating an entire team against overwhelming odds, the game constantly creates exciting memories. These moments are what keep players coming back. Even when a match ends in defeat, there is usually something to learn or improve before the next game. Playing with friends makes these experiences even better because every victory, mistake and hilarious moment becomes something to remember.

In conclusion, Apex Legends is an outstanding game because of its incredible movement, unique characters, exciting weapons, detailed maps, competitive gameplay and emphasis on teamwork. It offers an experience that is difficult to find in other battle royale games. Although it can sometimes be challenging and frustrating, these difficulties make winning even more rewarding. The combination of skill, strategy and teamwork ensures that no two matches are exactly the same. Whether someone is a casual player looking to have fun with friends or a competitive player trying to reach the highest rank, Apex Legends has something to offer. Its exciting gameplay and unforgettable moments are what make it such a brilliant game and one of the best battle royale experiences available.

Apex Legends used to be the gold standard for movement shooters, but at this point, it’s impossible to recommend.

I am suprised that this game is still going 7 years after release. Like, I haven't met anyone mention this game just casually and yet this game is the 25th most played game on Steam! I played Apex Legends AGES ago, back when they still had gold armor and helmets. So when this game started appearing on my Instagram showing clips of people clutching the most unclutable fights, pulling some random bullshit movement tech that just breaks everyones ankles, or rizzing up japanese baddies? I knew I had to redownload and give this game a proper go!

It was quite suprising for me when I got into my first game back as a lot of things had been added or changed/reworked so I did have to spend some time learning new mechanics, but they were explained pretty well and or pretty simple to use. I remember struggling on the mantle boost but after a few games I had it down to a T and felt pretty good whenever I was able to hit it. So was I able to hit some crazy clips? YES SIR!! I've had a few clutch moments and let me tell you the dopamine high was immaculate, I swear my brain shortcircuited at least once during my time playing this game due to how crazy these fights get. I didn't really get much movement tech down but what I was able to achieve was pretty fun, and I wasn't able to rizz up any japanese baddies, so no tsundere girlfriend for me. But that doesn't matter that much.

I think Apex Legends does a pretty good job at achivements, as a majority of them insentivise you to give each Legend a proper go, and the rest are just unlocked naturally through playing the game. Which was great, as I didn't feel like I was doing a chore and instead was enjoying the game. The only achievement I had to go out of my way for was [b] Decked Out [/b] which is a lot harder to get due to gold armour and helment not existing anymore, but after that? It was just smooth sailing. I felt like I gave every Legend a good chance and got to try a variety of diffrent weapons to see what I liked/didn't like. Speaking of weapons, the gunplay in this game is so satisfying. Each weapon sounds so crisp and you can feel the feedback of each bullet hitting your target. The sound effects are also really good too and you can easily tell what is happening (sometimes) during a fight. My personal favourite weapons are the R-301 Carbine, Volt, Prowler, EVA-8 Auto, Peacekeeper and Triple Take. Each of these weapons both sound good and feel good to hit someone with.

Apex Legends was definitely a suprisingly fun experience for me, from wiping out squads solo to winning games, no matter what happens you will definitely have a good time. The acheivements although quite boring in nature, were pretty much perfect and to me, felt like an obligation to try out each Legend at least once. I even got a heirloom too! Which was the last thing I was expecting to get while playing this game LMAO. So I do think that I was able to experience everything that this game has to offer and I wouldn't mind playing this game again sometime. On a small note, I won the last game that I played as I hit level 50 which feels like the perfect end to my journey for now. Great game, great gunplay, great movement, no tsundere girlfriend.

This title used to be spectacular around the release period, and for the first year-ish of support, it seemed like they had something that could really stand up to Fortnite.

Around the time of the Loba update, cracks started to show, and I fear it's only gotten worse since then.  The game feels like the developers are sort of directionless... with the worst feature creep I've ever seen in a live-service title, bloated UI/UX, and a storefront tab that's dishearteningly massive.

Playlists are split in 4-5 different directions, and getting a successful match takes a bit of time... which wouldn't be a problem if the TTK wasn't so low.  At first, this trait of the game was what drew me to it, but now it only serves to FRUSTRATE, as the game bombards you with post-match info, several click-through boxes, and multiple button presses to just RETURN TO THE LOBBY.  Oh my god, please, just let me go back to re-queuing solo as fast as possible.

In a match itself, it's a cluster of things /happening/, constantly.  You have EVO Harvesters.  You have upgrade stations.  A ton of different ways to gear up... but all this does is confuse me and make me feel lost.

The skill floor is very high, too.  This wouldn't really be an issue if the game tracked MMR in a reasonable way, but it's still using statistical data from when I was playing it actively in 2019-2021.  It's been five years.  It's still matching me in a rank far beyond what I'm capable of now.  Trying to re-enter it is an exercise in utter frustration.

Due to these factors, getting +2 friends together to /try/ and play it is impossible.  Nobody wants to come back to it.  Even as they fix broken systems and other bugs, it feels like the game is desperate for your money & your attention.

I can only see myself coming back if they reduced the amount of systems bloat.

Apex is the kind of thing where you start thinking about it and then realize that thinking about it is basically the same as not thinking about it, because every time you try to pin down what makes it what it is, you end up circling back to the fact that it’s Apex, which is of course defined by being Apex in the first place. People will tell you it’s about the movement or the abilities or the way the matches feel, but then you notice that the movement only matters because of the abilities, and the abilities only matter because of how the matches feel, and the matches only feel the way they do because of the movement, so really you’re just describing a closed loop that keeps returning to itself without ever landing anywhere new.You could say the same thing about the characters, or the map, or the weapons, or the ranked system, but saying that is already just restating the previous sentence in slightly different words, which is itself just another way of pointing out that any attempt to isolate one aspect immediately collapses back into the others. And once you notice that, you start wondering whether the real subject of the review is even Apex or whether it’s the act of trying to review Apex, which of course brings you right back to the beginning where you were already trying to figure out what Apex is by talking about it.In the end—though “end” is probably the wrong word since nothing has actually concluded—you’re left with the same observation you started with: Apex is Apex, and any further description is just another lap around the same circle.

APEX LEGENDS: A Masterclass in Digital Masochism
Overall Rating: 11/10 Movement Mechanics | -4/10 Audio Engine | 0/10 Mental Sanity

Recommended For: People who enjoy getting super-glide tap-strafed on by a sweat who hasn't seen sunlight since Season 4.

The Core Experience
You boot up the game. You click "Play." You drop out of the dropship feeling like an absolute titan.

Three seconds after hitting the ground, you land on a single White Sniper Stock and a Syringe, while the Horizon who landed next to you somehow opens a single bin and instantly finds a Gold Armor, a Havoc, and a full stack of ammo.

Before you can even ping "I need a weapon," you hear the deafening, soul-crushing sound of an Octane main who has injected enough Stim into his system to legally qualify as a biological hazard, flying through the air at Mach 3, spraying a R-99 straight into your optic nerve.

The Four Pillars of Apex Misery
1. The Audio Engine (Or Lack Thereof)
Respawn’s audio mixing is a scientific miracle. You can hear a Gibraltar opening a Phoenix Kit from three miles away across World’s Edge, but a 250-pound Pathfinder in full metal armor can sprint up behind you, tap-dance on your skull, and execution-finish your teammate without producing a single decibel of footstep audio.

2. The Third Party Chain Reaction
You survive a brutal 3v3 fight. You have 4 HP remaining. You’re clutching your chest, armor swapping off a death box like your life depends on it.

Crack.

That was the sound of a third squad opening fire from a cliff 200 meters away with Charge Rifles and Longbows. And just as you process that, squad #4 jump-pads over the mountain, squad #5 evac-towers directly onto your head, and squad #6 is snickering in a bush waiting for everyone to finish bleeding out.

3. The Matchmaking Magic
Are you a casual player who plays three hours a week after work?

Congratulations! The SBMM algorithm has decided you belong in the exact same lobby as a 3-stack Predator squad with 100,000 kills on Wraith, matching heirlooms, and cross-hairs permanently etched into their retinas. Enjoy being absolute trade fodder for their next YouTube highlight reel.

4. Loot RNG & The "Mozambique Here" Trauma
Land hot. Open three bins.

Bin 1: Shield Battery, Light Ammo, Grey Helmet.

Bin 2: Ultimate Accelerant, Shotgun Ammo.

Bin 3: Mozambique.

Meanwhile, the guy who landed at the exact same building gets a Peacekeeper, full purple shields, and a dream.

Final Verdict
Apex Legends is the only game where you can spend 15 minutes loot-simulating, running across an entire continent, finally find one fight, get vaporized in 0.4 seconds by a tap-strafing crackhead, alt-F4 in sheer fury, and then immediately re-queue 10 seconds later because the movement mechanics feel too damn good.

It is an abusive relationship wrapped in butter-smooth sliding and grapple physics.

Will I play it tonight? Yes.

Will I regret it? Before the first drop even lands.

[b]Overall, I'd recommend it.[b] Apex is still a blast when it gets things right. Just be prepared for a few headaches along the way.

Apex Legends is an incredibly fun and fast-paced battle royale that delivers some of the most satisfying movement and gunplay in the genre. However, despite its strengths, there are a few issues that prevent it from being truly outstanding.

🔫 Gameplay & Combat

One of the greatest strengths of Apex Legends is its gameplay.

The movement feels incredibly fluid, allowing players to slide, climb, reposition, and engage in intense firefights with impressive freedom.

Gunplay is responsive and rewarding, and mastering different weapons adds a satisfying learning curve.

Every encounter requires quick thinking, good positioning, and teamwork, making victories feel genuinely earned.

🦸 Legends & Abilities

The variety of playable Legends is another major highlight.

Each character brings unique abilities and tactical possibilities, allowing players to experiment with different playstyles.

Whether you prefer aggressive combat, defensive strategies, reconnaissance, or supporting your teammates, there's a Legend that fits your approach.

Finding the right combination of abilities within a squad can completely change how a match unfolds.

🤝 Multiplayer & Teamwork

Apex Legends truly shines when played with friends.

Communication, coordination, and teamwork are essential, especially during intense battles where a single decision can determine the outcome.

However, playing with random teammates can sometimes be frustrating. Poor communication, players leaving matches, and uncoordinated decisions can negatively affect the experience.

⚠️ Areas for Improvement

Despite its excellent gameplay, Apex Legends isn't without problems.

Matchmaking can occasionally feel unbalanced, particularly when less experienced players are matched against highly skilled opponents.

Server issues, occasional bugs, and frustrating encounters can also interrupt what would otherwise be an excellent experience.

Additionally, the competitive nature of the game can sometimes make casual sessions feel unnecessarily stressful.

🎯 Overall Experience

When everything works as intended, Apex Legends is fantastic.

The combination of fast movement, satisfying combat, unique characters, and tactical teamwork creates an experience that few battle royale games can match.

Unfortunately, its inconsistencies sometimes make it difficult to enjoy every session equally.

🏁 Final Thoughts

Apex Legends is a great multiplayer shooter with outstanding movement mechanics, exciting combat, and plenty of strategic depth.

It offers countless hours of entertainment, especially when playing with friends.

While matchmaking frustrations and occasional technical problems hold it back, the core gameplay remains incredibly enjoyable.

A great battle royale that could be even better with a few improvements.

Recommended!

Open Steam
Go to your Library

Scroll down to Launch Options
Paste this exactly:

cmd /c "set OPENSSL_ia32cap=:~0x20000000 && %command%"

Honestly no clue, because if it was for optimization.. well then they somehow made it only worse, it's honestly surprising how the most difficult part of this game is figuring out which settings my pc can safely start the game for it to run smoothly at 165 fps or at the very least 60fps, without looking at characters made of 100 or smh polygons. which is surprising considering 7 years ago I had a pc that was already 10yrs old by that time and was capable of running the game pretty smoothly

[h1]👍 Recommended – 300+ Hours Later, I'm Still Playing[/h1]

After [b]300+ hours[/b], I can confidently say that [b]Paladins[/b] is one of the most enjoyable hero shooters I've ever played. It has its own identity thanks to the [i]Loadout[/i] and [i]Card[/i] system, allowing you to customize champions around your own playstyle instead of everyone using the exact same build.

[hr][/hr]

[h2]My Favorite Champions[/h2]

• [b]Ruckus[/b] – An aggressive frontline champion that's incredibly fun once you learn how to dive the enemy backline and create chaos.

• [b]Seris[/b] – One of the most satisfying support champions in the game. Great healing, excellent survivability, and the ability to completely turn a team fight around.

[hr][/hr]

[h2]Performance[/h2]

One of my favorite things about Paladins is how well it performs. Even if you have an [b]older PC or a low-end GPU[/b], the game runs surprisingly well while still looking good. It's refreshing to see a competitive multiplayer game that doesn't require expensive hardware just to enjoy smooth gameplay.

[hr][/hr]

[h2]The Good[/h2]

• [b]Free-to-play[/b] without feeling impossible to enjoy.
• Huge variety of unique champions.
• Deep customization with cards and talents.
• Fast-paced and rewarding gameplay.
• Excellent performance on lower-end hardware.

[hr][/hr]

[h2]The Not So Good[/h2]

No game is perfect.

Sometimes the matchmaking can feel uneven, and every now and then you'll run into bugs or balance issues. They can be frustrating, but they haven't stopped me from coming back for hundreds of hours.

[hr][/hr]

[h2]Final Thoughts[/h2]

If you're looking for a hero shooter that's easy to get into, offers plenty of replayability, and runs well on almost any PC, [b]Paladins is absolutely worth playing.[/b]

After more than [b]300 hours[/b], I'm still queueing up for "just one more match."

[b]Rating: 9/10[/b] 👍

I'll preface my review by stating that like few handful of people, I've played since the open beta around late 2016-2017. Unlike a majority of people however, I've played paladins since then on almost all platforms it has ever been available on, not because I love paladins that much even though I do but because it was what I could access it on during those periods. Collectively over the years, my total amount of playtime hours are closer to 7-8k hours

I say that to say despite everything, and I mean everything this game has gone through, there is no worse state that paladins has been in, more than now.

This game has a very recent specific bug unlike anything I've ever experienced, and have tolerated and still struggle to tolerate today. 

 After you, your team and the opposing team have successfully locked in your champions for a match and have been queued onto loading screen, they is a slight chance (say a 30% chance) you will be reverted back to the champion selection page, which renders you unable to do literally anything but force close the game. 

Unlike many, if you decided to launch paladins again and be placed back into the loading screen for the ongoing match that is probably already a "lost cause", there is another say 30%  chance you will be reverted back to the homescreen which (you guessed it) is glitched and also renders you unable to do anything but force close the game for the second time. 

I personally have experienced this "bug" numerous of times, and for others that join the match normally, if you notice your teammate has disconnected literally as soon as the map loads, they probably had this bug. I personally have had to close and re-launch paladins three times because of this bug, and by that point your match has already ended, or you're currently down 0:3 with teammates that have either willingly left or have had this bug happen to them and simply refused to re-launch paladins again.

Literally today, what lead me to make this review, was having my entire team, all five of us had this "bug", and only me (after to 2 restarts) and another rejoined the losing match.

I don't see anyone talking about this "bug" in the reviews, but genuinely unless you have unlimited patience or a genuine appreciation for what paladins is despite the bugs, toxic playerbase and the mandatory steamrolls you will experience either because people don't play their class roles properly or utilize in-game mechanics like items effectively then, for your own sanity.

Stay Away From This Game. 

I uninstalled this game very recently literally because our sole healer, purposely left mid match after we were up 2:0. For literally 0 reason. He did not return, but my teammates out of frustration left alongside him not too long after.

I reinstalled this game because personally the fun experiences of the champions outweigh all of the negative experiences.

Leaving games mid match, shit talking teammates during steamrolls, purposely afk-ing teammates because they are weak minded and believe they'll lose eitherway, hell some people throw matches just to spite other players. All of these things are normalized in Paladins.

I wouldn't recommend this to anyone, and I regret falling in love with this abused, mistreated abandonware, and the toxic negative playerbase that is a direct result of the treatment it received.

One of the most notable features of "Paladins" is its card system, which allows players to customize their champions in real-time. This level of personalization ensures that no two players will have the same strategy, encouraging creativity and adaptability. Whether you prefer dealing damage, supporting teammates, or controlling the battlefield, there's a champion and build that will fit your preferred playstyle.

The gameplay is fast-paced and engaging, with a strong emphasis on objective-based modes that require teamwork and communication. Coordinating with your team to capture points or push payloads adds a layer of strategic depth that keeps matches exciting. The thrill of victory, especially when executed through well-planned strategies, makes every win truly rewarding.

"Paladins" also thrives on its community, with regular updates, new champions, and events that keep the experience fresh and engaging. The developers actively listen to player feedback, ensuring that the game evolves alongside its player base.

In summary, "Paladins: Champions of the Realm" stands out as a dynamic, visually captivating team shooter that emphasizes strategy, creativity, and collaboration. With its rich roster of champions and ever-expanding universe, it's a must-play for anyone who enjoys competitive gameplay in a fantastical setting. Whether you're a seasoned player or new to the genre, "Paladins" promises an exciting and unforgettable gaming experience.

Paladins is one of those games that people constantly compare to Overwatch, but honestly, it does enough things differently to stand on its own.
At its core, it’s a fast-paced hero shooter with tanks, supports, flankers, and damage dealers, but the loadout and card systems give it much more customization than most games in the genre. Being able to modify abilities and playstyles for each champion makes matches feel more flexible and creative.

The game also deserves credit for having a huge roster of champions, many of which feel genuinely unique. Some characters are simple and beginner-friendly, while others are complete chaos once mastered. Finding a champion that clicks with your playstyle is easy.

When Paladins is working properly, it’s honestly extremely fun. Matches are fast, abilities are flashy, and team fights can become absolute madness in the best possible way.

The good:
- Large and diverse champion roster
- Loadout/card system adds customization
- Gameplay is fast and satisfying
- Easy to get into
- Many champions feel unique
- Matches usually move quickly
- Good variety of playstyles
- Free-to-play without being completely unbearable
- Crossplay support is nice
- Some champions are ridiculously fun to master

The bad:
- Bugs and technical issues have always been a problem
- Matchmaking can feel awful sometimes
- Balance changes are inconsistent
- Hit registration occasionally feels questionable
- UI can feel messy and outdated
- Some champions become extremely annoying to fight
- Ranked mode can be frustrating
- Servers can be unstable

Even though this game is in maintenance mode, I can still honestly recommend playing the game itself. It's genuinely one of the best FPS games and among the best hero shooters I've ever played. Balance is better than Overwatch, a game I very much enjoyed prior to the switch to Overwatch 2, a lot of influence is taken from Team Fortress 2, a game I'm a huge fan of, teamwork is crucial but not as difficult to carry out as in Overwatch, the characters are all fun to play and it has some of the most unique Heroes I've ever seen in a Hero Shooter, the Cards system allows for customization that keeps both the competition and the game itself fresh, the world of Paladins itself is vibrant and fun when it isn't eerie, and just about every game mode is fun and well-balanced. 

Really, my only complaints with this game outside of it not getting updates (again, HiRez, give this game another shot, it deserves it and it's got tons of fans who want the game to keep getting updates and improvements) are with it's monetization system. The prices for Crystals are...kind of absurd, to say the least, and Crystals are the in-game currency. As of now, I wouldn't give this game any more since it's unclear what it's current state is (give the game more love and new updates, HiRez), but i the past, unless you really want a select few skins or only really play a few Champions, you're often better off just getting the Battle Passes (which themselves are often a bit overpriced) and getting the available skins from that by winning battles and leveling up instead, and maybe getting the deal of the day pack. 

Other than that, this game's incredible. I just hope the game is given another chance to shine like it  deserves. The game in it's current state isn't a total loss, but there are more bugs and cheaters than there used to be. This could all be fixed with a few updates and more moderation, but that's only if HIRez listens to the fans. And if there's enough fans asking for the game to get new content and some much-needed bug anti-cheat fixes.

P.S: Shoutouts to my fellow Mal'Damba and Maeve mains out there!

've return've returned to Paladins after almost 5 years. I used to play it because I couldn't afford Overwatch. Now, I'm here purely out of nostalgia, and honestly, it's a mistake.

The game looks  like it hasn't been updated in the past five years. The animations are wooden, the technical aspects are clunky, and there are frequent glitches and a sense of a cheap Chinese clone. Hi-Rez has failed to address these issues over the years.

However, the most disappointing aspect is not the outdated graphics. The game is riddled with bots and cheaters. In regular matches, there can be as many as 3-4 bots per team, and the situation is even worse in ranked matches. You find yourself in a team with three empty accounts that just run around the spawn or AFK, while the opposing team consists of players with aimbots and wallhacks. The game has become a sad circus.

Over the years, the game's mechanics have also lost their soul. The constant reworks of champions, the removal of features, the reduction of maps, and the use of render maps instead of proper art suggest that the game has lost its direction and is simply trying to survive.

Paladins now feels like an abandoned project that Hi-Rez is barely managing. Pitifully. It used to be a really fun and heartfelt alternative to Overwatch, but now it's more of a sad reminder of how a good idea can die from indifference and poor management.

I've been playing this game (non-consistently) since it's birth, around 2016. It was a blast to be able to play a hero shooter on such an awful laptop, and I think that's the main thing to point out about this game, it can basically run in any computer or laptop. I remember being so excited about playing an Overwatch similar, in those days the game was truly great. No unnecessary in-game transactions, you could buy regular lootboxes with gold (regular coin of the game), and the lootboxes had a chance to give you rare skins. As someone who didn't had money to spend in games, that was such a breath of fresh air.

The strategy factor also made me have tons of fun, Paladins working fairly different from other hero shooters and FPSs from it's time. It might be the nostalgia talking, but I think that, at it's prime, this game might've been one of the most entertaining things around.

The first change that didn't please me was the fact that you couldn't buy lootboxes with gold anymore, you needed to acquire the payed coin of the game (crystals). Although it didn't present any threat to the gameplay, I was extremely disappointed, since the only way to acquire crystals at the time was through daily rewards or buying it with real money. It was sad to see that I wouldn't be able to acquire something that should be accessible for all players, but whatever, I went on playing.

The game went through other bad changes (I will forever hate elixir), decisions that made it a pay to win for a while. And then I took my first hiatus. Year after year I tried to come back to this game, only to see it get worse and worse. I was never really a fan of battle passes, specially the ones you need to pay for.

It's very sad to me, to see the potential of this game being wasted in such a way. I've came back recently to get all the achievements, and I had as much fun as I had years ago. If only this game got the treatment it deserved...

Through this review, I want to register my love and passion for this game, I'll never regret the hours spent on it, and while this game is still running, I recommend you to give it a chance. It doesn't get updates, and it's probably just a matter of time until the servers are shut down, but I still think that the experience is worth it. Don't let this chance go to waste, play it while we still have time.

The most fun hero shooter on the market, to me at least (Not counting TF2 as a hero shooter for this). It's a shame that HiRez over-extended and abandoned this game during their cost-saving measures of gutting everything that's not Smite 2. With a few small balance changes and a decent marketing push for a revival update this game could truly be something great again. Even if Hi-Rez would probably just fuck it up again. 
It's a 5v5 hero shooter where you make loadouts from a perk deck selection with a surprising amount of variety, letting you set up varied builds for the same characters, then buy moba items as the game progresses to add further layers to this. Has some really fun character designs that are quite unique to it, Like Yaggorath, a tank that can deploy incredibly fast but has to root in turret mode to do most of her damage, letting you do comical flank plays with one of the tankiest units in the game. The artstyle is very good, the VA is great, the only part that sucks is the music (which is a shame). The maps are varied enough in design and there's a decent amount of gamemode variety where you'll need to know how to play a few characters, but it adds to the charm with how maps can hinder or help specific team comps. The most common game-mode and IIRC the "main" mode of this game, Siege, is also an interesting design, being a central control point that turns into a payload for whoever wins the cap. You get 1pt for capping and 1pt for delivering, but also gain 1pt for stopping a defense, first to 4 wins and you can't win with a defense. Pretty interesting and would love to see a similar mode brought to something like TF2. 

Io has to be my favorite healer I've ever played in one of these games. A totem healer with decent damage that's also a strong healer on her own, but is made to synergize with her wolf spirit heal totem, and has a strong escape tool with a big backwards leap. You can build her for air control for funny aiming tricks, vibing alongside your wolf, doing damage to keep your healing resource filled, many things really.  She's also got an incredibly cute design and great VA. Definitely a design I'd borrow if I ever made a game like this myself. She's a 10/10 and I'm sad she's relegated to a dying game like this. 

However, this game is in maintenance mode. You'll only really get queues in NA and you can't expect the matches to be remotely balanced skill-wise. I love this game a ton, but I'd caution buying it for that reason. I'd say try the game via the F2P option and then if you like the flow of it buy the deluxe/$60 edition, as that gets you most of the characters, but know this game is a museum piece at best that'll never get another update, and at worst a game on borrowed time.

Veteran's Rating: ⭐️⭐️⭐️⭐️☆ (4/5) – “I’ve been playing since Day 1. I hate it. It’s my favorite game.”
⚔️ Gameplay: Unrivaled Build Freedom

Let’s be honest, if we’re still here after all these years, it’s for one specific reason: the card and item system. Unlike Overwatch, where heroes are set in stone, Paladins lets us break the rules.

    Want to play Grover as a makeshift sniper from across the map? Go for it.

    Want a flank-heavy Pip who barely heals anyone? Completely doable (much to your team's despair).
    This strategic depth, and the ability to counter-build the enemy composition mid-match, is what gives the game its unique DNA and infinite replayability.

📜 Nostalgia: A Long Journey... For Better and For Worse

Playing since the beginning means remembering the blessed (or chaotic) era of massive maps, Survival mode, and above all... the dark days of "Cards Unbound" (Patch OB64). We survived the worst pay-to-win system Evil Mojo could throw at us, and forcing the devs to roll it back remains one of the community's finest hours.

We’ve watched the roster grow from a dozen champions to over fifty. We’ve seen graphic overhauls, map reworks, and the release of champions with absolutely wild kits (looking at you, Yagorath and release-state Kasumi).
🐛 The Flaws: "Paladins: The Game of Bugs"

You can't write an honest review without addressing the elephant in the room: the game's code is held together by duct tape and dark magic.

    Servers that randomly decide to strike in the middle of a Ranked match.

    Textures glitching out, sound cutting off (the classic Viktor ultimate audio looping forever).

    Loading screen crashes that leave you praying you won't log back in to find a bot that already bought the worst possible items from the shop.

Evil Mojo does what it can, but it's clear the engine (Unreal Engine 3) is showing its age, carrying the weight of years of accumulated mechanics.
👥 Community and Matchmaking: The Rollercoaster

Paladins matchmaking is a mystical experience. You either get a hyper-coordinated esports squad, or a last-pick teammate who refuses to tank and locks in a third flank without saying a word in chat. The toxicity is there, as it is in any competitive shooter, but it has a certain "homegrown" flavor we’ve come to accept.
🏆 The Veteran Verdict

Paladins is a survivor. People have predicted its death against genre giants at least a dozen times, yet it's still here, standing strong with a dedicated fanbase.

If we're still queueing up after all this time, it's not out of spite—it's because its gunplay, longer and more rewarding TTK (Time to Kill), and deep gameplay customization have absolutely no equivalent on the market.

We'll keep complaining about the bugs and raging at champion balance, but we all know we're queueing up again tonight. VVGG to all the Realm veterans!

I’m giving this a thumbs up out of respect for the memories, but if you actually want to play with a community larger than a moderately sized high school cafeteria, just go play literally anything else. It’s a nice relic, but the world has moved on, and so should you.

While there are occasional balance issues and some overpowered champions, the developers regularly patch the game, which helps maintain a fair experience.

Paladins can feel a little overwhelming at first due to the number of champions and cards, but once you get a handle on the mechanics, it’s a fun, fast-paced shooter with plenty of depth for those willing to invest time.

I’ve spent some time with this game and honestly, it surprised me in a way I didn’t fully expect. I don’t want to sound dramatic, but there’s something oddly satisfying about how everything fits together — not in some perfect, polished “advertisement” way, but more like a game that knows exactly what it wants to be and just… goes for it.

The first thing I noticed is the atmosphere. Every part of the game — the visuals, the sound, the pacing — kind of blends into this feeling that you’re actually inside its world, even if you’re just casually playing. I know that sounds a bit cliché, but it’s true. Sometimes it’s chaotic, sometimes slow, sometimes you’re just wandering around thinking “ok, what now?” but that’s honestly part of the charm. The game doesn’t try to rush you unless it actually needs to.

Gameplay-wise, it has this mix of familiar elements and small twists that keep things from feeling stale. Nothing groundbreaking, maybe, but it all works together in a way that feels natural. There were moments when I thought “yeah, I’ve seen this in other games,” but then the game throws in tiny details or unexpected interactions that make it stand out just enough. It’s the kind of thing you only notice after a few hours, when you start connecting the dots.

Performance has been mostly fine. A little rough spot here and there, but honestly, show me a game these days that doesn’t have something weird happening once in a while. Nothing game-breaking on my end, at least. You can clearly tell the developers put effort into this, even if a few edges are still a bit sharp. Again — part of the charm.

What I really appreciate is that the game gives you space to play the way you want. Some people will rush through every objective, others will take their time exploring or messing around, and both approaches actually feel valid. I like games that don’t punish you for not following some “correct” path.

Overall, I’d say this is one of those titles that grows on you the longer you play. It doesn’t try too hard to impress in the first five minutes — instead it slowly builds its identity, layer by layer, until you suddenly realize you’ve been playing way longer than you planned. If you’re looking for something that balances comfort with challenge, familiar mechanics with fresh touches, and a world that’s just fun to be in, then I genuinely think this one is worth giving a shot.

Would I recommend it?
Yeah, I would — maybe not to everyone, because no game is for everyone, but definitely to anyone who likes getting lost in a game for a bit and discovering things at their own pace.

After sinking over 450 hours into Paladins, I can confidently say this is one of the most enjoyable hero shooters you can get—especially for free.

Is Paladins perfect? No. The matchmaking can be hit-or-miss, and balance patches sometimes feel like they were decided by throwing darts at a board. But when the gameplay clicks it’s genuinely some of the most fun I’ve had in a shooter.

For anyone wondering if Paladins is worth trying or returning to:
Yes. Absolutely.

It’s chaotic, stylish, surprisingly strategic, and still manages to be addictive after hundreds of hours. If you’re willing to embrace its quirks, you’ll find a game with a ton of depth and replayability.

450 hours later, and I’m still not done.

Way too often, my team gets paired against players who are obviously way more skilled or ranked much higher, turning matches into totally one sided stomps. It’s super demotivating when you realize that winning or losing feels out of your hands not because of how well you or your team plays, but simply because the matchmaking threw together teams of wildly different levels. Frankly, I want my effort and skill to matter, not just luck or who got stacked on my team.
Recent matchmaking changes have only made things worse. Matches feel even less fair than before, with the system regularly putting beginners against top-tier veterans, or grouping talent in ways that just don’t make sense. Sometimes I feel like the queue cares more about filling spots quickly than about actually creating competitive, fun games. All this randomness means I rarely enjoy ranked anymore, since I don’t get consistent, challenging matches with players on my level.
Honestly, unless the developers address the core of these matchmaking and balance problems pairing teams based on actual performance and skill rather than random chance I just don’t see myself having fun in ranked mode anymore. Competitive play needs to be fair, and right now, it’s just not

[h1]Team Fortress 2 – Nine Mercenaries, Zero Brain Cells, and a Lifetime of Memories.[/h1]
[b]20/10 – Some Games You Play. Others You Grow Up With.[/b]

Before battle passes became a religion and every multiplayer game needed a f*cking digital shopping mall, there was Team Fortress.
I started with the original Team Fortress, but TF2 became something much bigger.

Across two Steam accounts / on my first I forgot everything to log in, I've probably spent over 2,000 hours playing it.
My first friends on Skype, classmates, endless evenings of laughter, ridiculous strategies and unforgettable moments.

[b]This wasn't just my favourite multiplayer game. It was part of my childhood.[/b]

[h2]Nine Idiots. Infinite Personality.[/h2]
What made TF2 special wasn't just its brilliant class-based gameplay.
It was the characters.

Nine completely insane mercenaries, each with a unique personality, playstyle and sense of humour.
I spent most of my time playing Spy, Engineer and Sniper.

Disguising myself, stabbing unsuspecting enemies, building defensive positions and making somebody regret standing perfectly still.

And when strategy went out the window?
[b]HEAVY AND MEDIC. YEEEEHAW, MOTHERFUCKERS![/b]

Payload was fantastic. Every class had a purpose, teamwork mattered, and even the most ridiculous strategies could somehow work.

[h2]Valve Actually Gave This Game a Soul[/h2]
I didn't just play TF2. I followed its entire universe.
The comics, the animated shorts, the characters and their stories.

I watched every new cinematic like it was Christmas.
Meet the Team was legendary, but Expiration Date was something else.
Scout desperately trying to impress Miss Pauling, Engineer attempting to maintain some sanity, and Soldier being told not to teleport bread. Naturally, he teleported bread. [b]FOR THREE FUCKING DAYS.[/b]
That scene still reminds me of working with certain colleagues.

TF2 had something many modern multiplayer games desperately lack: genuine personality.
Even Miss Pauling, with her glasses, sharp humour and ability to tolerate Scout's stupidity, became one of my favourite characters.
Looking at my relationship today, I sometimes wonder whether my girlfriend deserves a medal for putting up with me. :-D

[h2]Mann vs. Machine – Three Christmases at Once[/h2]
When Mann vs. Machine arrived, I was absolutely ecstatic.

Cooperating against waves of robots, upgrading weapons, coordinating defenses and fighting enormous mechanical monstrosities?
[b]SIGN ME THE FUCK UP.[/b]

As an Engineer, I loved preparing everything perfectly.
Sentry? Ready. Dispenser? Ready. Teleporter? Ready.
Team? Apparently incapable of surviving a two-minute bathroom break.
[b]I GO TO TAKE A PISS AND THE ENTIRE DEFENSE COLLAPSES. WHAT THE F*CK?![/b]
Beautiful memories.

[h2]350 Items and an Economy I Actually Enjoyed[/h2]
TF2 was also the first game where I filled my inventory with more than 350 items.
Weapons, cosmetics, taunts, trading and collecting.
And I genuinely enjoyed it.

Unlike modern games where monetisation often feels like the main attraction, TF2 already had incredible gameplay underneath its economy.
Trading was something I did because I loved the game, not because the game needed me to spend money to feel worthwhile.

The community made everything even better.

[h2]An Old Legend Deserves More Love[/h2]
Of course, not everything stayed perfect.
The massive updates became less frequent, and the game's long-running problems with bots and cheaters damaged its reputation.
Valve has taken action against these problems, but I still wish TF2 received the same attention and ambition it enjoyed during its golden years.

[b]The game isn't dead. But it deserves more love from the company that created it.[/b]

And yet, none of that can erase what TF2 gave me.

[h2]Final Verdict – Thank You for Growing Up With Me[/h2]
Eventually, my friends moved on.
One of my old classmates changed schools. We grew older, discovered other games and followed different paths.

I fell deeper into RTS games and the Warhammer universe.
And slowly, without even realising it, I stopped playing TF2.
Sometimes I still look at it in my Steam library and think: [b]Maybe just one more match.[/b]
But I know it wouldn't be quite the same.

The maps are still there. The characters are still there. The memories are still there.
The people and the time we shared are what made it special.

[b]Team Fortress 2 wasn't just a game I played. It was a game I grew up with.[/b]

[b]20/10 – Thank you for the laughter, the friendships, the memories and over 2,000 hours of absolute madness.[/b]
[b]And Soldier...[/b] [b]STOP. TELEPORTING. BREAD.[/b]

For years, I struggled with depression. Every morning I would wake up, stare at the ceiling, and wonder what the point of it all was. I had no motivation, no friends, no goals, and no reason to continue. Food tasted bland, music sounded empty, and even the sun seemed to have given up on me.

Then, on a cold Tuesday evening, I discovered Team Fortress 2.

At first, I was skeptical. But the moment I loaded into my first match and got headshot by a sniper named "Obama Gaming" from across the map, something inside me changed.

I started smiling again. I started laughing. I started feeling emotions I hadn't felt in years. I met wonderful people, like a 43-year-old Russian man who exclusively plays Heavy and screams slurs into his microphone. I learned the meaning of friendship when a Medic Ubercharged me for 8 seconds before abandoning me to die.

I now wake up every morning with a purpose. I rush to my computer, boot up TF2, and spend the next 6 hours getting killed by a furry Pyro main with 12,000 hours.

My depression is gone, but my sanity is hanging on by a thread. I have developed a crippling gambling addiction to Mann Co. Supply Crates and I haven't seen sunlight since the Jungle Inferno update.

Would I recommend this game?

Absolutely.

Team Fortress 2 is one of the greatest multiplayer games ever created, and I genuinely believe gaming peaked when Valve decided to put nine mentally unstable mercenaries on a battlefield and give them absolutely zero adult supervision. 💀🔥

This game is genuinely timeless. It's been around for years, and somehow it still manages to be more entertaining than a ridiculous number of modern multiplayer games. You have nine completely different classes, each with their own weapons, abilities, personalities, and playstyles, and somehow every single match turns into the most chaotic experience imaginable.

I downloaded this game expecting a normal team-based shooter. Instead, I found a community where people communicate exclusively through voice commands, dance in the middle of combat, build relationships with enemy spies, and occasionally spend an entire match staring at a wall because someone found a funny exploit.

And honestly? That's gaming at its finest. 😂

Let's talk about the classes.

The Scout is what happens when someone gives a caffeinated squirrel a shotgun and tells it to solve military conflicts. This little menace runs around at 300 miles per hour, double-jumps over everything, and somehow manages to miss every shot despite being close enough to smell your character's breakfast.

Then he kills you with one hit and starts laughing.

I hate him. I respect him. I want to be him.

The Soldier is a walking American military recruitment advertisement with absolutely no understanding of personal safety. This man fires rockets at people, launches himself into the atmosphere using explosions, and screams like he's trying to wake up the entire continent. His entire strategy is basically, "IF IT MOVES, FIRE A ROCKET AT IT."

And somehow, it works.

The Pyro is genuinely terrifying. Nobody knows what's happening inside that gas mask, and frankly, I'm not sure humanity is ready to find out. You turn a corner and suddenly you're on fire, your screen is full of flames, and a mysterious creature is running toward you while making noises that sound like a broken vacuum cleaner.

Psychological horror has nothing on this lunatic. 💀

The Demoman is an alcoholic Scottish cyclops who has somehow been trusted with enough explosives to level a small country. He can turn a doorway into a minefield, launch himself across the map, and delete your entire team before anyone realizes what happened.

He's either the most dangerous player in the lobby or someone who accidentally blows himself up trying to jump over a fence. There is no in-between.

The Heavy is a giant Russian man whose entire personality revolves around his minigun, sandwiches, and making everyone within a five-mile radius reconsider their life choices. Hearing that minigun spin up is basically the game's version of a natural disaster warning.

And the sandwich mechanic? Absolutely incredible. Imagine being a heavily armed soldier in the middle of a war and stopping everything because you're hungry.

Priorities. 🥪

The Engineer is proof that the most dangerous person on the battlefield is the guy who knows how to use a toolbox. While everyone else is busy shooting each other, this man builds a miniature industrial complex in the corner of the map and turns it into a fortress guarded by an automated turret.

You can bring an entire army to his position, and somehow his little machine will still be standing there deleting people like it's getting paid per kill.

The Medic is a doctor who apparently graduated from a medical school that doesn't believe in patient consent, ethical procedures, or basic human decency. This man can heal you, make you temporarily invincible, and then casually discuss medical experiments that would get every hospital on Earth shut down.

And somehow, he's still the most important person on the team.

Everyone loves the Medic until he heals somebody else. Then suddenly the entire team has a medical emergency.

The Sniper is a professional people-watcher who spends his entire day sitting in a corner of the map, drinking jarate, and removing people's heads from distances that should be physically impossible.

You can be having the best match of your life, dominating the enemy team, feeling completely unstoppable, and then suddenly your screen goes black because some guy named "HeadshotEnjoyer" clicked on your forehead from another postal code.

Absolutely humbling.

And finally, the Spy. The most paranoid-inducing class in the entire game. Once you start suspecting that everyone on your team might actually be an enemy Spy, you can never go back to normal life.

Your Medic? Probably a Spy.

Your Engineer? Definitely a Spy.

Your own reflection? Better check it with a melee weapon just to be safe.

This man disguises himself as your teammates, sneaks behind your lines, and turns an otherwise peaceful match into a full-blown trust crisis. You don't even need enemies anymore. You become suspicious of your own coworkers.

And the best part? Sometimes the Spy isn't even doing anything useful. He's just standing in the corner wearing your name and watching you panic.

THE GAMEPLAY IS ABSOLUTE CINEMA. 🎬🔥

Every match feels different because the classes interact in so many entertaining ways. You can coordinate with your team, pull off ridiculous plays, defend objectives, or spend an entire match trying to kill one particularly annoying Engineer who has built a turret in the most inconvenient location imaginable.

The weapons add even more variety, and the customization gives you plenty of ways to experiment with different loadouts. Some weapons completely change how a class plays, which means there's always something new to learn.

And the taunts? GENIUS.

There is nothing more disrespectful than getting absolutely destroyed by an enemy, respawning, returning to the battlefield, and discovering that the person who killed you is now dancing over your corpse.

You don't even feel angry anymore. You just sit there questioning how your life reached this point.

Meanwhile, the community is an entire ecosystem of chaos. You've got competitive players hitting impossible shots, casual players doing whatever they feel like, friendly Heavies handing out sandwiches, and people who have apparently dedicated their entire existence to becoming the world's most annoying Spy.

And somehow, it all works.

The art style has also aged incredibly well. The character designs are iconic, the animations are full of personality, and the visual style gives the game a unique identity that doesn't depend on realistic graphics or constantly chasing the latest technology.

The voice lines alone are legendary. Every character has so much personality that even after hundreds of matches, you can still find yourself laughing at the same ridiculous interactions.

And let's be honest: TF2 has more personality in one voice line than some modern games have in their entire campaigns. 💀

What makes Team Fortress 2 truly special, though, is that it doesn't take itself too seriously. It can be competitive, strategic, ridiculous, hilarious, and completely unhinged all at the same time. You can spend one match playing seriously and coordinating with your team, then spend the next one participating in a conga line while the entire server watches.

Few games manage to create that kind of freedom and community-driven fun.

Is it perfect? No. There are frustrations, balance issues, and other problems that come with a game that's been around for so long. But the core gameplay is so strong, and the characters are so memorable, that there's still a reason to come back.

10/10. Team Fortress 2 is an absolute classic that proves you don't need photorealistic graphics, a battle pass every five minutes, or a cinematic universe to make an unforgettable multiplayer game.

You just need nine mercenaries, two teams, a briefcase, and enough explosives to make the Geneva Convention burst into flames.

This is no longer a matter of individual balance decisions. It's a pattern of systematically destroying the game's identity. Blizzard takes heroes with unique mechanics, playstyles and dedicated communities, then strips away what makes them special in the name of making the game more comfortable for casual players.

Wrecking Ball is a perfect example. Players spent years mastering his movement, momentum and grapple mechanics. Blizzard erased a fundamental part of his skill expression in a random midweek patch, then explicitly refused to reverse it. Sombra has also been repeatedly redesigned and stripped of the unconventional gameplay that made her unique.

The philosophy behind these decisions is embarrassing: rather than encouraging players to develop awareness, learn matchups or adapt to different threats, Blizzard removes whatever might inconvenience them. Apparently, even looking behind you is too much to ask.

Overwatch was once a game where heroes felt like entirely different games within the same game. Now its developers seem obsessed with turning everything into the same predictable, sanitized shooter. Unique mechanics are liabilities. High skill ceilings are problems. Dedicated players are expendable. The only thing that matters is making the experience as frictionless as possible for people who barely engage with it.

This is how you kill a game's identity: not in one catastrophic update, but through years of compromises that make everything progressively less interesting.

Don't spend hundreds of hours mastering a hero. Don't build your enjoyment around a unique mechanic. Don't get attached to a playstyle. Blizzard might decide tomorrow that it's unhealthy for the game and delete the very thing you loved, then tell you it's an intentional design decision.

There are plenty of games that respect their players' time and mastery. Overwatch, under this leadership, increasingly feels like a game designed to make sure nobody has to master anything at all.

TLDR; this game has tons of problems, but in the recent year+, I think, it deserved the right to be recommended to try.

Now, let's dive deeper.

There's a lot of hate and whining around Overwatch. A lot of it is absolutely deserved, some of it is (at least) barely reasonable. I can name at least 10-12 problems that exist in the game: hero balance, horribly designed maps, matchmaking system, "I have joined a QP game 3 seconds before the loss, thanks", hero skin bias, no PVP yet, overly priced re-colored skins, toxic community, boring battle passes, useless in-game events that consist of default "play N games" challenges, inability to change Battle.net account while playing Steam version...

All of them, and more, makes the experience barely bearable sometimes, it is true.

I still recommend this game, at least at this point. In recent year+ the game has been genuinely improving, a lot of user feedback keeps being addressed, map reworks are great, new heroes are fun to play (for the most part), lots of new lore drops, ESports scene is getting louder, Blizzcon is BACK, new mechanics (perks, sub roles, additional standard kit abilities and passives). Hero reworks have also gotten better, Hog and Sombra are good examples. The single best game feature IMO is the ability to turn off both text and voice chats. Such a gamechanger.

Stadium mode is VERY fun, such a playground for a silly "Brig tank" or "flying Rein" build. IMO it is the best mode for fun party play. It's a bit sad that this mode doesn't get supported outside of regular balance patches.

I also have to mention that often the user feedback is not addressed as people expect it to, a lot of genuinely exciting ideas transition to mediocre decisions. During the seasonal dev stream we hear of lot "right and positive vibes" just to get frustrated by the final implementation. Sometimes it feels like OW team doesn't play the game and throws the changes randomly, despite saying "we're looking to hear your feedback" nonstop.

But I still like this game a lot. I learned to live with its cons, while enjoying by pros.

I think you should at least try this game.

[b]Damage:[/b] A Tracer jumped in, did a little blink, and killed my entire team. I would like to say I was angry. I was mostly impressed. I was also dead.

[b]Teamwork: 10/10.[/b] Every game, my team works together as one. One of us goes left, one goes right, one stands on the payload doing nothing, and one is still in the spawn room asking "who's healing?" The answer is me. It is always me.

[b]Communication:[/b] The game has a very handy ping system. I have used it to say "enemy here," "I need healing," and "please stop." Nobody has responded to any of them. I have now started pinging the floor to see if it will back me up.

[b]Ultimates:[/b] You charge them up, you wait, you pick the perfect moment, and you use them. Nothing happens. You have just used it into a Sleep Dart. The enemy Ana had her entire team's ultimate cooldowns in her pocket.

[b]Linux:[/b] The game runs perfectly on Linux, which was a great surprise. The launcher does not, which was not. I did not expect anything else. I installed a game and it worked. I have never been more suspicious of anything.

[b]Mental health:[/b] Stable. I can now stay calm while four strangers explain what I did wrong in chat. I have also learned that "gg" means "go next" and that "go next" means "I want to leave this match." Both are very relatable.

[b]Value: 10/10.[/b] For the price of free, I got a bunch of new heroes, a very confident Genji main in my head, and a Steam library entry that is lying about my life.

TL;DR: Poor matchmaking (at least in quickplay), poor balancing, some heroes are very poorly designed (e.g., JPC and Sierra) or end up poorly designed due to reworks that come from listening to the wrong people, they still prioritize 5v5 over 6v6, boring lore, unoriginal events, and half the roster is annoying to play against.

MATCHMAKING:
You either play with people on your team who are half-awake in quickplay or spend your time with sweats in ranked. Every match that is not a landslide victory for your side (which I don't like either) is just a measure of how much nonsense you have to deal with before you can start having actual fun. Good luck if you're trying to learn a new hero in 6v6 open queue, as you'll most likely be flexing roles in nearly EVERY MATCH in the hopes of not ending up with 5 DPS and 1 healer.

BALANCING:
Developers go out of their way to ensure that every new hero will dominate the season they're released in. I don't recall a single new hero that didn't require multiple nerfs after release.

Cycle: new hero releases -> is overpowered -> is left purposefully overpowered for weeks or months to foster a new community around it for future skin sales -> is finally nerfed after waves of complaints -> by then, there are already enough people who have put the time into this new hero, which will increase skin sales -> rinse and repeat when next season comes.

HERO DESIGN:
I actively refuse to play any heroes in this game that use auto-aim. The fact that players of this game consider heroes with auto-aim to be completely valid is just beyond annoying. You should be expected to aim in an FPS.

Even worse, developers actively kowtow to the lowest common denominator when it comes to reworks. An example of this is when enough players complained about getting one-shot by Roadhog (usually due to their poor positioning or game sense) that he got neutered in his recent rework, yet they remain mysteriously silent about Widowmaker and Hanzo. Both Widowmaker and Hanzo can put so much pressure on entire swathes of maps because of their ability to one-shot most heroes without putting themselves in any danger by getting close to you. Will they be reworked? Of course not.

This approach resulted in ruining the enjoyment I had for my two favorite heroes - Roadhog and Pharah. New Pharah feels like there's a boulder attached to her, which results in you doing big jumps before plummeting rather than being the queen of the skies. New Roadhog is nothing more than a neutered pig that is an ult battery for enemies. You're on copium if you think new Roadhog has any lethality to him.

5v5 VS 6v6:
Why are you still prioritizing 5v5 over 6v6? Why is there no 6v6 role queue by now? Why are you depriving the community of the much needed resources for 6v6 to the point that some YouTubers are on so much copium that they keep looking for any obscure snippets of Overwatch developers dropping offhand comments in interviews about 6v6?

LORE:
I just don't find the lore to be interesting. I will give kudos to the developers for at least trying to develop the world of Overwatch, though. I just have no interest in being part of the Overwatch world.

EVENTS:
The variety of crossovers is great and impressive. However, the actual events themselves just tell you to play the game as one usually would to get rewards. Boring. Encourage players to play in new ways or with new heroes in order to get the rewards instead.

I have been playing Overwatch since 2019 and have at least a thousand hours between OW 1 and 2. At its peak this game was probably the best multi-player hero-shooter on the market, and by far the most fun I have ever had in a video game. However, through many updates and downgrades over the last 5 years it has deteriorated tremendously in several ways, including the now-extreme toxicity of the regular player-base, the oversized character roster, and the progression system. 
I will give the devs credit for stepping up their game when Marvel Rivals was released as they somehow managed to bring overwatch back from its near-death experience with the perk system. But at this point I have to give it a negative review because it just isnt the game I knew and loved 5 years ago. 
Overwatch 2 was a cash-grab project which was a mistake that nearly ruined the player-base and was a terrible let-down for nearly every excited player, and ended up being, for all intensive purposes, the end of the golden age of the game. At this point in its development the company is not adding anything really meaningful to the game, only adding to the already over-full roster, re-creating old maps that nobody had any issue with in the first place, and making new mercy skins with every single new skin bundle. The micro-transactions have gotten out of hand imo, with most good skins being basically out of reach for the normal player who doesn't want to spend real money for a cosmetic. That was also one of the beauties of OW1, that every cosmetic was accessible and one only needed to put in the time in order to get every cosmetic in the game, including the new skins whenever they were released. While OW2 does still have some of this in existence, it is so much more difficult and less accessible for the average player.
Anyway the final point is that this game just isnt really fun anymore. most of the characters are unbalanced with some being terrible and some just being better, causing the same 20 characters to be cycled through in every game. The players are toxic most of the time, and the majority of them are not good at the game either. Nobody plays the tank role but it is always blamed for lost games, and healers cannot ever find good dps players in competitive. All in all everything that made OW different from other action games has been lost to time, and thus it is no longer the fun and interesting game that it used to be.

Honestly, one of the least rewarding games I've played in a long time.

You can put everything into a competitive match, play your role properly, and still lose 30% of your rank because your team couldn't pull together. It genuinely feels like you're being punished for things completely outside of your control. There's very little incentive to keep playing when all that effort can be wiped out by one bad match.

You've got Roadhog, who can absorb up an absolutely ridiculous amount of damage, heal himself through it, and hook you from what feels like another postcode. Completely unbalanced.

The matchmaking is probably my biggest issue, though. The amount of people creating new accounts just to stomp bronze and silver players is ridiculous. You'll have genuine new or lower-ranked players trying to learn the game, only to get absolutely demolished by someone who clearly has hundreds of hours behind them. How is anyone supposed to improve when the matchmaking is that inconsistent?

I don't mind losing when the other team genuinely plays better. That's part of any competitive game. But when you're constantly dealing with unbalanced matches, frustrating character abilities, and a ranking system that makes your individual effort feel completely irrelevant, it becomes difficult to justify playing.

Overwatch 1
- Had general chat, making the game feel more social.
- The Tab screen showed gold, silver, and bronze medals for player contributions.
- Let players see which teammates were queued together as a premade group.
- Used a visible Skill Rating number, so progress toward the next rank was clearer.
- Had beautiful player borders and stars that showed your level and gave players a reason to keep leveling up.
- Focused on skill and teamplay, giving players the satisfaction and freedom to play the heroes they wanted.
- DPS felt impactful: accurate headshots could quickly secure kills and reward aim.
- Tanks felt killable rather than unstoppable.
- The 6v6 format created more team depth, roles, and coordinated gameplay.
- The maps were more interesting and cool, and made the whole team work together around the objective.
- Events gave players a real chance to earn skins just by playing.
- Players could earn three free loot boxes each week, making cosmetics feel accessible and rewarding.
- Was a paid game, which made it feel like a complete product with clearer value.
- Felt more focused on gameplay, competitive systems, rewards, and community features.
- Under Jeff Kaplan’s leadership, the game had a clearer player-focused vision and stronger community connection.
- Continued to be supported until it was discontinued and replaced by OW2.
- OW1 had more than 200,000 active players before 2022.
- OW1 i had all skins
- 32 seasons of rank competitive overwatch and hours saved
- OW1 fixed most bugs

Overwatch 2
- Removed general chat.
- Removed the medal system from the Tab screen, replacing it with a scoreboard.
- Does not show which teammates are in a premade group.
- Splits ranks into five divisions, such as Diamond 5 through Diamond 1, making the climb feel longer and less direct.
- Removed player borders, level stars, and the visible leveling system, taking away a meaningful reason to keep playing and progressing.
- Feels too focused on overpowered characters and the meta, reducing the freedom and satisfaction of playing whichever hero you want.
- Tanks have so much health, mitigation, and self-sustain that they can feel immortal—even when DPS players consistently land headshots.
- This makes many matches feel like prolonged shield-and-tank battles, where aim has less impact than simply wearing down a tank.
- The 5v5 format feels pointless and lower quality, with less team depth and less satisfying coordination than 6v6.
- The maps are too open, so players go in random directions and do not follow the objective or work together as a team.
- Event cosmetics are much more tied to the shop, premium passes, or currencies, so earning a skin through normal play feels less common and less rewarding.
- Some cosmetic bundles are priced at around €40, which feels excessive—especially for flashy, overdesigned skins that used to be obtainable through gameplay.
- Its free-to-play model makes the shop, Battle Pass, and paid cosmetics feel central to the experience.
- Its priorities can feel split between character lore and promotional messaging, while gameplay balance, meaningful rewards, and social features receive too little attention.
- Under new leadership, the game feels less coherent and more monetization-focused; for shortime players, it has lost much of its original identity.
- The balance feels so broken that many streamers and creators have moved on to other games instead of continuing to support OW2.
- It feels too different and less polished to deserve the name Overwatch 2.

 I was initially drawn to overwatch as a game with genuinely fun and unique characters. Though recently it seems as though the devs are more focused on dumbing down the game and stripping away aspects from characters that make them more fun.

The most recent "bug" fix for Wrecking Ball's grapple retract is a perfect example of this. Ball has always been a character that rewards effort and truly has a limitless skill ceiling with his movement mechanics. Skyballs, double/triple boops, angelic grapple refund, blenders, slingshots and all his other movement techs are what make him a unique and rewarding character to put time into and master.

By effectively rewriting his physics engine with this newest change you are essentially removing wrecking ball's identity and ruining his gameloop. For a character who's entire identity revolves around his momentum and mobility it certainly is an interesting decision to take that aspec away from him. 

Ball is not strong by any means, his win rate is in the negatives and his pick rate is abysmal. If the devs thought he was too punishing they should have just nerfed his numbers, not his core gameplay loop. This sets a awful precedent for other skill-expressive characters; even if you put years into learning a character and all their niche techs it ultimately means nothing, as the OW devs will change fundamental aspects of your character without even a days notice.

And, if it was intended as a nerf just state it. Hiding it smack dab in the bug section as a little bullet note only shows that either they didn't think of the ramifications of this change or that they simply did not care, and instead chose to hide it.
