Across PS4, Xbox Series X, and PC, I’ve logged roughly 600 hours into Destiny 2. I haven’t played every season or expansion; like many adult gamers with real-world responsibilities, my playtime dropped off whenever the checklist grind started demanding life-consuming commitment.

But when Destiny 2 hits its stride, practically nothing else in gaming can match it.

Running the Leviathan Raid for the first time remains one of my all-time favorite gaming memories:

- S-tier gunplay and movement

- Clever raid puzzles and tight encounters

- Genuinely meaningful co-op communication

- Rewarding buildcrafting, lore, and secrets tucked into every corner

- Challenging but fair mechanics that respect player coordination

(And on a co-op wishlist note: while I know the entire universe is tuned around the sacred 3-player fireteam, expending it to 4-players would be incredible for balancing friend groups without forcing someone to sit out.)

Ultimately, it’s the treadmill grind that made me walk away, and it’s the exact same wall keeping me away. When the pinnacle of Destiny 2—optimizing stat distributions and hunting down essential build-defining Exotics—requires a massive, multi-week ramp-up just to catch up, the barrier to entry feels insurmountable.

Whether Bungie can rekindle that design philosophy in D2 with un-vaulted content or channel it into an eventual Destiny 3, my biggest plea is simple: stop designing the game exclusively for players with 200 hours of free time every month.

Design for the player who has 30 to 50 hours a month to give. It is completely fine if players reach a natural stopping point between content drops. It's OK for people to replay content simply because they love playing it—not because they're forced into an optimal chore loop just to hit the power cap and access end-game activities. Quality beats artificial engagement metrics every time—a game shouldn't have to feel like a full-time job just to be fun.

The new-player experience in Destiny 2 is unnecessarily confusing. My quest log is packed with campaigns, tutorials, dungeon quests, and PvP objectives, with very little explanation of what order makes sense. There's a genuinely great game here. I just wish getting to it didn't require outside guides and constant research just to understand what content I can actually play.

Unvaulting content is a step in the right direction, but that content never should have been vaulted in the first place. Spending another year or more restoring previously removed content is a burden Bungie created for itself. While restoring that content is the right thing to do, imagine if those resources could instead be invested in building a fresh Destiny experience.

Destiny has come a long way from its original grind-heavy design, but the franchise is over a decade old, and Destiny 2's age is increasingly noticeable. The underlying progression systems need a serious overhaul.

Take item rarity, for example. Anything below Legendary (purple) is practically worthless once you're established. Why even have multiple rarity tiers if most of them serve no meaningful purpose? This is where a deeper crafting system could completely change the experience. Let players invest in lower-tier equipment, upgrade its rarity, manipulate stat distributions, and work toward desirable perk combinations. Give us meaningful progression beyond simply dismantling hundreds of useless drops.

Games like Diablo and Path of Exile have already demonstrated how engaging itemization and crafting can be. Bungie doesn't need to reinvent the wheel, just take inspiration from systems that already work and adapt them to Destiny's identity.

Ultimately, Destiny needs more than another content refresh. It needs a modern foundation, improved UI, better onboarding, meaningful loot progression, and substantial quality-of-life improvements. The gunplay and universe are still fantastic. I'd love to see Bungie build a genuinely fresh experience around those strengths rather than continually patching an aging game.

**There's a great future for Destiny, but I think it's time to build toward it instead of constantly rebuilding the past.**

Wuthering Waves has lost its identity, and it's getting worse with every update.

I genuinely loved what Wuthering Waves was trying to be when it first launched. It had an interesting post-apocalyptic setting, a darker atmosphere, engaging combat mechanics, and a world that felt mysterious and dangerous. There was so much potential here. Unfortunately, I feel like Kuro Games has slowly abandoned many of the things that made this game special in the first place.

The story has become repetitive and predictable. Instead of focusing on Rover's past, the mysteries of the world, and meaningful worldbuilding, almost every update revolves around introducing and promoting the newest limited character. The formula rarely changes: Rover saves the day, develops a close relationship with the new character, and then the story moves on to the next banner. Characters who should remain important are pushed aside, and the overarching narrative barely progresses. The cinematic presentation is still impressive, but good presentation cannot compensate for repetitive writing.

The game has also lost much of its post-apocalyptic identity. What initially felt like a ruined, dangerous world has gradually turned into a collection of increasingly colorful and cheerful environments. There is nothing inherently wrong with beautiful locations, but the original atmosphere was one of the main reasons I started playing. I miss the darker tone, the sense of danger, and the feeling of exploring a world struggling to survive.

The lack of meaningful male characters is another disappointment. The playable roster is increasingly dominated by female characters, while male characters often feel like an afterthought. I understand that gacha games have their target audiences, but a believable world needs variety, and its characters deserve meaningful roles regardless of gender.

Exploration has become ridiculously easy and increasingly restrictive. Puzzles rarely require much thought, and newer areas often feel disconnected from the rest of the world. For a game marketed as open-world, having so many separate regions and instances is disappointing. On top of that, locking exploration and character progression materials behind lengthy story quests makes the experience unnecessarily frustrating, especially for new or returning players.

Combat is slowly losing its depth. One of Wuthering Waves' greatest strengths was its fast-paced, skill-based combat and the freedom offered by quickswap mechanics. Unfortunately, newer characters increasingly rely on simplified rotations and restrictive mechanics that discourage switching between characters. Not every character needs to be difficult, but there should be room for both accessible and mechanically demanding playstyles.

Powercreep and monetization are becoming increasingly concerning. Older characters continue to fall behind newer releases, yet Kuro Games rarely provides meaningful improvements to keep them competitive. Instead of strengthening existing characters or making their reruns more accessible (SHOREKEEPER WHERE ARE U), the game increasingly encourages players to chase newer and stronger units. Some recent character designs and progression systems also raise concerns about important abilities being locked behind additional copies.

And perhaps the most frustrating part is that these changes are happening gradually. Individually, they may seem insignificant, but together they are slowly changing the game into something very different from what originally attracted me.

I don't hate Wuthering Waves. I still think it has some of the best visuals, animations, and combat foundations in the gacha genre. But that's exactly why its current direction is so disappointing.

A game can be generous with free pulls and still make decisions that are bad for its players. Kuro Games deserves praise when it does something right, but it also deserves criticism when it moves in the wrong direction.

Wuthering Waves doesn't need more flashy characters designed primarily to sell banners. It needs stronger writing, meaningful worldbuilding, challenging exploration, more diverse characters, and a combat system that rewards creativity rather than restricting it.

I want the Wuthering Waves that made me fall in love with the game, not a progressively simplified character-selling machine.

Until Kuro Games seriously reconsiders its direction, I cannot recommend it.

Thought I'd leave a review whilst everything regarding the launcher is going on:

- I play a good number of these style of games, and enjoy them still (including WuWa). If a neutral review option FINALLY existed on Steam, that's what I'd put here. That said, I would always tell people to be careful of the gacha genre if they struggle with spending habits, or getting upset over things such as one or the other similar games being marginally more/less generous

- WuWa is still fun for me personally, but honestly after a few years it's the most likely game I'd personally drop for Silver Palace. The original draws for this game were the obvious ones. Being extremely marginally more generous, something I have ALWAYS pointed out just about ANY competitor to Genshin HAS to be. Anything else would almost certainly sink, since it's trying to draw from that same playerbase pool. The graphics, being on a different engine also look fantastic, and I'd argue except for Silver Palace (which hasn't released yet as of writing this) I'd argue is probably still the best in the genre right now if your device can handle it.

- Story has NEVER been WuWa's strong point. There are great quests like the Fleurdelys and Phrolova patch stories, but from the very start it's been more flashes of great storytelling rather than consistency. Every gacha game has to sell its current patch banners, but WuWa is one of the most egregious for making me think "Where tf has THIS character been, and where is EVERYONE else?!"

- The most baffling thing to me is the inconsistency with WuWa's quality of life changes. Some changes, like the un-upgraded echo/artifact stacking are so fantastic I wish every game did it. But for every great QOL WuWa has, it has something so remarkably stupidly annoying it's crazy. Notifications for this type of game are always persistent, but WuWa is WAY worse than any of the Hoyoverse competitors. EVERY SINGLE month you get a notification you must clear for EVERY pack they update. BP is pushed way harder as well. Despite the "Dev's Listen" narrative, we get things such as Shorekeeper (One of the primary sustains people want on top of being an extremely popular character) not re-running for over a year EXCEPT for a "hey you wanna spend 200$ for her?" event. Which they have NO problem doing multiple times in quick succession. Same as I said above, don't be fooled Kuro is FAR from being a "generous" dev. People who played PGR know. There is a certain small but vocal subset of the community that is honestly more rabid about things like that to the degree that I'd argue WuWa gets a worse rap because of them than even Genshin ever did. I don't generally interact with gacha game communities, but WuWa and Genshin are the only ones that have ever gotten so bad friends that won't touch the genre know about it.

- I work/study in IT and Cybersecurity, but I'm not knowledgeable enough (yet) to completely weigh in on the security concerns regarding the launcher update. HOWEVER, it's another incredibly stupid move. Why have a Steam client that was requested for multiple years if you are going to make the Steam client now open the original client completely defeating the ENTIRE point? No, it's not more than an extra click. Yes, it will forever be annoying for devs to do this and will never seem necessary.... because it isn't. If they can't implement the pre-download or differing resource packs on Steam, it's definitely telling. Because it's doable, but the "Dev's Listen" Devs apparently can't or won't sink the money into doing so. Making everyone COMPLETELY redownload the game was also certainly.... a choice, and I say this as someone with a REALLY solid ISP because of my career path.

- Long rambling review aside, play the game if you enjoy it. Drop it if you don't.

I have played since Day 1 and have spent around £500+ on it (not including the monthly's Lunite Subscription + BP). Writing a negative review and saying goodbye genuinely saddens me, because beneath it's problems Wuthering Waves is a game I still believe has exceptionally good bones.

Wuthering Waves is visually beautiful. It's environments, character models and animations are among the best I have seen in this genre, and exploring it's world can be genuinely captivating. The combat is fluid and satisfying, the overall tone feels more mature than many similar games, and it's best characters and stories have stayed with me. I have taken countless screenshots and made many lovely memories here. There is a great deal about this game that I sincerely love, which is precisely why leaving is so difficult.

Unfortunately, the experience surrounding that beautiful core has gradually taken a toll on me.

The constant cycle of daily tasks, stamina, limited events and time sensitive rewards creates an exhausting amount of FOMO. I began logging in every day not because I was excited to play, but because missing resources felt unacceptable. Even when I wasn’t enjoying a particular story chapter, I sometimes felt forced to progress through it because limited events and their rewards were locked behind the current story.

Rather than allowing me to enjoy the world at my own pace, the game increasingly felt like a list of obligations. I fell several story patches behind while still logging in every day, spending my stamina and completing the routine. Opening the game began to feel heavy and demoralising rather than exciting.

The gacha system made that pressure worse. I have pulled every character released so far, as well as several signature weapons. Wuthering Waves does give players a reasonable number of free pulls, and I appreciate that, but characters are released so frequently and sometimes several desirable characters appear across closely grouped banners that it remains extremely difficult for a free to play player to obtain what they want.

Eventually, spending stops feeling like an optional way to support a game and starts feeling like the expected solution to an intentionally created shortage. Once you have maintained a complete collection, every new character feels like another financial commitment required to prevent that collection from becoming incomplete. I accept responsibility for my own spending, but I also have to acknowledge that these systems are carefully designed to create exactly this pressure.

Another longstanding disappointment is the extreme imbalance in how the game serves different parts of it's audience. I am an adult straight woman, and I have no objection to beautiful, revealing or fanservice heavy female characters. The issue is that comparable attention is rarely given to the male side of the roster.

Female characters are overwhelmingly more numerous and frequently receive revealing designs, intimate marketing and overt fanservice intended for the male gaze. Male characters are released far less often, with considerably less equivalent fanservice. Women spend money on games and characters too, yet it often feels as though players attracted to men are treated as a secondary audience expected to remain satisfied with occasional scraps.

This imbalance is particularly frustrating because the male characters Wuthering Waves does create can be wonderfully designed and written. The potential is clearly there. I kept hoping Kuro would develop the game in a more balanced direction and demonstrate that it could be different from other major gacha companies. Instead, over time, it's decisions have made it feel increasingly similar to the companies and practices I had hoped it might improve upon. That has left me feeling genuinely let down.

The new Steam launcher arrangement is not the primary reason I am leaving, but it became the final catalyst. I moved to Steam specifically to avoid an additional launcher and to benefit from Steam’s simpler, faster downloading and updating process (also to be able to take screenshots). Steam now launches Kuro’s launcher, which then manages the game itself, and existing players have been required to reinstall the full client.

I understand the stated benefits of selectable resource packages and future pre downloads, but forcing a launcher inside another launcher removes much of the convenience that made the Steam version appealing. It feels like another decision made without sufficient regard for the experience of existing players.

Ultimately, however, this review is not really about a launcher. It is about a beautiful game that gradually became unhealthy for me to continue playing.

I have tried to ignore these feelings for a long time because I love the world and characters, have played since launch and have invested substantial time and money. But continuing simply because I have already invested so much would only allow that investment to keep demanding more from me. The money I spent paid for the enjoyment and memories I already had, it should not obligate me to remain indefinitely.

Other games have recently reminded me how refreshing it feels to play because I want to, progress at my own pace and choose my activities without a constant fear of falling behind. Returning to Wuthering Waves after that feels like returning to a heavy list of chores and financial temptations.

For some people, taking a casual break or ignoring the daily systems may be possible. I know myself well enough to recognise that the FOMO prevents me from maintaining that kind of relationship with a gacha game. For my own mental wellbeing, I need to make a clean break.

So, as a Day 1 player who genuinely loves much of what Wuthering Waves is, I am sadly saying goodbye. I do not regret the wonderful characters, scenery, stories or memories. I only wish the game surrounding them had respected my time, mental space and part of the audience more equally.

There is an extraordinary game buried beneath the FOMO, relentless monetisation and one sided character direction. I sincerely hope Kuro eventually allows more of that game to shine♡

I've first heard of this game through the advertisement in App Store, and the fact that it was created and developed by Kuro Games since 2022, the same developers as Punishing Gray Raven, made me interested enough to download and give it a try. Well, what can I say, I have expected the game to be a hack-n'-slash title, but it also surprised me when they added the open-world aspect into it.

Of course, I sat through it rough patches during the 1.x and even the beginning of 2.x era, where it was constantly overshadowed with the fame of Genshin. What surprised me the most is that Kuro was really attentive and supportive to players - they constantly changed, optimized, and improved their game every day. It's not a perfect game, and not really a perfect customer service for those who have appealed in my experience, but I can see the dedication that they have put into their game. From the breathtaking scenes of the open-world, the flexible exploration methods, the awesome combat that made it stand out of other open-world titles, to its cinematic scenes in story with great worldbuilding, this game had proved me wrong in every patch that Kuro couldn't have done better. 

Of course, there was still rough patches here and then. Like I said, the game isn't perfect, and I understand this is a live-service product that developers have to constantly satisfy the playerbases, namely the CN ones. The story has significantly changed for the better during the Rinascita era, and probably a few notable ones in Lahai-Roi like 3.1, probably the best quest in WuWa to this day where the parents-daughter dynamics brought a fresh change from the previous patches, but there were still a few unpolished ones. SPOILER ALERT for the part below!

2.6 is pretty generic plot about Rover trying to save Iuno from her existence being erased to fight against the Dark Tide, while the romantic element was more predetermined and Rover got the Mary Sue title for doing all the stuff, despite the credit belonged to Iuno herself. 2.8 kicked off as a filler patch as we knew about Chisa (the potential girl, whatever you called her) who was struggling inside a deadlock she couldn't solve for 20 years in Ashinohara, a non-existent Tokyo-style city affected by the Lament... until Rover came to help. Both of this story fell into the same mistake of letting Rover took all the credit and then leave the sidekicks ignored and no further character building. I understood that unlike Genshin Impact, the story in Wuthering Waves focused more on Rover and their resolve to recover their memories, and save the Solaris-III on the brink of destruction from the Lament. However, these stories could have done better to avoid the snoozefest heroism they have applied. Then there's also 3.6, a recent patch revolving Qingxiao and a new villiain, Muyu. It was a disappointing patch since Muyu was dumbed down to a premature death without any satisfying pay-off. He had an interesting, high-potential premise that could have driven major narrative shake-ups or deeper character development, but it seemed like they focused mostly on Qingxiao and her sales that this was not catered carefully. I know some people would like this kind of plot, but honestly, Kuro could have done better to spice up the story of 3.6 and probably 3.7, which was the story directly related to Hsin and her internal battles for the Sentinel title, as he held the direct threat against her.

The open-world aspect in this game sometimes also feels bland, given that there were many blank spaces in the big maps and there were no extra contents after the missions and the collectibles are done, but there are still a few places where you could sit back and enjoy the beautiful scenes. The optimization... yeah, I know this has been voiced by many players, up from 1.0 until now. I would give them props to this matter, because with the change in programming language from JavaScript to C#, the game runs much smoother in my side. I could barely run on 30FPS on this device before 3.5, but now it went to a whooping 45FPS and sometimes 50-55 with Medium settings - that goes to say Kuro had gone to great extents optimizing this game.

As for the community... I would say most of us are chill and are ready to give you tips and great community contents, leave alone the tribalists who constantly looked down on other games and even this one. So, if you meet good ones, make sure to treat them as your friends, too!

All in all, I could not recommend this game enough if your device isn't good enough for it (despite Kuro had tried optimizing it) or you just dont like gacha games in general, but it's a title I would definitely recommend to anyone. My tip is to go through the 1.x stories real quick, then start at 2.x, it would pretty much worth your time and wait.

This ended up being a lot longer than I expected.

[h1] Positives [/h1]

To get the positives out of the way, visually the map and locations are beautiful. Pretty much nothing bad I could say on the visuals at all.

The combat is flashy and pretty fun, a lot of the character kits are very well made and feel quite satisfying to use. The character progression can be fun. It's the pretty standard numbers go up type of gearing but I thought the echoes system was a nice enough spin on it by giving the gear a purpose beyond just being a stat stick. 

The sound design for the characters is also amazing, Zani's especially I thought added so much weight to her attacks that really sold the character's gameplay for me.

[h1] The Rest [/h1]

I really did try to like it, between Steam and the original launcher I probably have at least 150 hours, yet all the good things I can say about the game are dragged through the mud by what is probably one of the worst stories I've sat through in recent years.

Pretty much every main story arc follows the same formula of:

Quest starts -> Immediately introduced to the new character they're trying to sell you this time -> Said character immediately becomes best pals with the MC -> Spend a few hours getting lore dumps of constant monologues and obtuse amounts of terminology -> Discover the main female character of the arc has some tragic backstory -> Big cinematic fight with the MC and the new character, usually having the MC rescuing said character ->  End with a cheery hour long epilogue of all the new people praising the ground the MC walks on -> Right when you think the chapter is over we cut to the evil group going "just as I envisioned" for the 10th time

I wish I was exaggerating but every time I heard "It gets better at Chapter X" I'd reach that point, then hear "Ok but Chapter Y though", with the aforementioned formula being nearly completely accurate each time I would reach where it supposedly "got good" until I just gave up.

[h1] Characterization [/h1]

The moment a character's chapter is over, unless they get a companion quest (Which they stopped making over a year ago now) there's little to no chance you'll see that character again in anything but filler events. One example for this is one of my favourite characters visually being Calcharo. 

Calcharo released in version 1.0, meaning they were present as a playable character since the very start of the game. It took almost a year and a half for him to appear in the main story, and even then it was for a maybe minute long cutscene. 

This happens to most characters, once we move out of their region its very rare we see them again which made any attachment I had to the characters completely pointless, since the game has zero intention of including them again when they can just give a new character a tragic backstory and repeat their old formula.

It makes them feel like cardboard cutouts rather than actual characters. One of the few positives the gacha format has is that its story is told over a long period of time, meaning you have ample opportunity to flesh out characters, have them return, interact with the world, do ANYTHING that isn't just praising the MC and vanishing once they've went backstage at the end of their chapters.

A character becomes interesting through meaningful interactions, through seeing them as a part of the world, interacting with it and with other characters in a believable manner. 

Wuthering Waves completely ignores this and has the bulk of its character writing spent on talking to the bland, nod along with everything MC we play as. This forces most characters into being one note, because they literally only have one character to show their personality to, with that character refusing to bounce back anything but the mildest of conversation points, leading to what is basically a one sided conversation full of exposition and monologues, the complete opposite of actual dialogue.

[h1] Storytelling [/h1]

The storytelling is also dreadful, it's the epitome of tell, don't show. So many times you'll be blasted with information about something unique to the region we're in for that chapter through a slideshow, only for these concepts to be immediately ignored or resolved just a few hours of playtime later so the MC can have a cool moment before moving on to the next set piece. It makes the world feel hollow.

I'm sure if I sifted through all the collectibles I'd understand some components of the world more but the onus of explaining these things coherently should fall on the game and their presentation, not on the player reading collectible documents on the ground.

I'll give an example below.

Tethys story spoilers:

[spoiler] [h1] Tethys [/h1]

[h2] What is the Tethys System? [/h2]

In very simple terms it's a supercomputer that uses data of disasters in the world to predict when future disasters are coming a few days in advance.

[h2] What role does it have in the story? [/h2]

We head over to the island it's located at, meet our female character for the patch named Shorekeeper who (of course) has a connection with the MC so that they can be praised.

It's then discovered the reason the system is able to predict these disasters is because it simulates them inside of itself, effectively causing constant suffering to the constructs inside of it to get sufficient data for its predictions.

The MC tries finding a different solution, finding out the System needs a core that can experience emotions as a replacement, with the only options available being the MC and Shorekeeper. Shorekeeper then decides to sacrifice herself to restore the system. (Fair enough, it sets up for what could be some good moments and establishes that there's actual stakes)

...except we can't have that as it would deviate from our formula, and so of course the MC jumps in to save her, having a big boss fight against the system.

The system outright says it needs a core of some kind to sustain itself, as it's foreseen that the world is pretty much destined to be destroyed or massively reshaped in the future without it, which the MC ignores and keeps going, their plan being and I quote "Tethys and the Black Shores (The group/island involved) will find another way." 

(??? it cant be understated how crucial the Tethys System is to the Black Shores, it's the core of everything they operate from which is a major part of why Shorekeeper chose to sacrifice herself. To say "eh they'll figure it out" is just...)

You'd expect some form of consequence. "oh the system broke since it has no core so now the organization is crippled / goes under". Or maybe "oh they're now on borrowed time and need to find a solution in x timeframe before the system runs out of power." Anything to show some form of consequence to this. And what we get is... after rescuing Shorekeeper she tells us "oh we swapped out the core with a calmer one so no more bad stuff it's working fine you can get going". This isn't even out of context the literal quote is:

MC: “How’s the Tethys System now?”
Shorekeeper: "After being fixed, it’s executing the master command given at its creation. The core computational unit has now been replaced by a special frequency that shares similar properties as the Lament. But this one is… more harmonious and mild."

...WHAT?? as far as I can tell this second core was never explained nor mentioned a single time as an option when we were about to sacrifice Shorekeeper herself?? We're never told where it came from, how it works, nothing. [/spoiler]

[h1] Conclusion [/h1]

The game is pretty, the character animations and sound design are great. The storytelling is abysmal, the characters feel one note and hollow. The story serves as a collection of set pieces to sell the next banner character without a connecting through-line.

I'd be surprised if someone read through all of this honestly but thanks if you did.

Title: New players: DO NOT download this on Steam. Get it from the official site instead.

If you are thinking about downloading Wuthering Waves on Steam, stop. You still have a choice. Don't make the same mistake we did.

In Version 3.8, Kuro changed the Steam version so it no longer uses Steam to download and update the game. You have to download Steam, then download Kuro's Official Launcher inside Steam, then download the game again inside that launcher.

Yes, you read that right. Two launchers to play one game.

For new players, this is the worst possible deal:

1. You will waste double the time and bandwidth.
You are not just downloading the game once. Steam players were forced to completely uninstall the old package and reinstall everything through the new launcher. If you start on Steam now, you are starting on the broken, complicated path for no reason.

2. You will waste RAM for nothing.
Steam is already heavy. Its WebHelper processes alone can eat hundreds of MB. Now you have to keep Steam running AND Kuro's launcher running, just to start the game. On 8GB / 12GB RAM PCs or low-end laptops, that is memory you need for the game itself.

If you download from the official site, you only need ONE launcher. No Steam overhead, no double launcher, no extra background processes.

3. You get none of the benefits in 3.8.
Kuro says this change is for tiered downloads (UHD / HD / SD) and pre-download. But pre-download will not even work until Version 4.0. So Steam players get all the pain of reinstalling in 3.8, and none of the payoff.

4. Steam Deck / Linux players, stay away.
This is now a Windows-first launcher running inside Steam through Proton. If you are on Deck, expect more launch failures and more troubleshooting. This change was not made with you in mind.

I chose Steam because I wanted a simple Steam experience: click Play, Steam updates, done. That version no longer exists. What is left is the official launcher, but with Steam still eating resources in the background.

If you actually want to play this game, do yourself a favor: skip Steam, go to the official Wuthering Waves website, and download the official launcher directly. Same game, same account, same progress, but without the double-launcher mess.

Do not start your Wuthering Waves journey on Steam in 3.8.

One of the Best Games I've Ever Played, but There's a Catch

Having played Wuthering Waves for six months now, I can safely say that it's one of the best games I've ever tried. It's also my first gacha game, and it probably won't be my last. If you've never played a gacha game before, this review is for you.

You know those games that you wish you could experience for the first time again? Wuthering Waves is one of those games, but perhaps for different reasons than you might think.

When you first begin, it feels like a huge single-player open-world game with fun and surprisingly deep combat mechanics, an interesting story, and great characters. There's so much to explore, and learning all the different systems and figuring out how to make your characters stronger can be incredibly addictive.

But as you become more familiar with the game, you start to realize something: the main objective of Wuthering Waves is to make you spend money. And unfortunately, this affects the game in several ways.

First, there's the constant sense of urgency. Events and character banners are only available for a limited time, which encourages you to prioritize them over the main story. This can really hurt the single-player experience because instead of exploring the world and enjoying the story at your own pace, you find yourself doing things in the wrong order just because you don't want to miss out on rewards.

Another thing you have to get used to is how the game treats its characters. You'll meet some fantastic characters throughout the story, and naturally, you'll grow attached to some of them. But once their particular version of the game is over, they often get very little screen time. The game moves on to introduce new characters for you to collect, while the ones you've grown to love are pushed into the background.

Then there's the progression system. In the beginning, you have so much content ahead of you that resources seem almost unlimited. You can spend hours exploring, completing quests, and making your characters stronger. But eventually, you reach a point where you've done most of what the game has to offer, and suddenly everything slows down.

You can't even farm as many resources as you want because the game puts a daily limit on how much you can collect, unless you're willing to pay. This feels particularly annoying in a game that is otherwise so much fun to play.

But by far the worst part is the randomness involved in making your characters stronger. I'm talking about Echoes, of course. You can spend days farming materials and upgrading Echoes without making any meaningful progress whatsoever, simply because you didn't get lucky with the stats. It's an incredibly frustrating system, especially when you've already spent so much time gathering the resources you need.

And of course, there's always the temptation to spend money. Getting a new character is incredibly satisfying, but it can also be ridiculously expensive. A single character can easily cost $200 if you have no in-game currency saved up. And if you want to fully upgrade that character by pulling multiple copies, we're talking about $1,000 or more. That's an insane amount of money for a character in a video game.

The good news is that none of this really matters when you're just starting out. As a new player, you probably have around 200 hours of fresh content ahead of you, and you can enjoy all of it without spending a single dollar.

So here's my advice to new players: Watch a YouTube video explaining the basics so you don't waste valuable resources. Save up around 60,000 Astrites before you start seriously pulling for characters. Until then, just use the free characters you get, learn to master the combat system, explore the world, and enjoy the story.

And most importantly, don't worry about the "meta." If you're unfamiliar with the term, it basically refers to which characters are considered the strongest. It's very easy to get caught up in this, and suddenly you stop caring about which characters you actually like and start caring only about how much damage they can do. In my opinion, that's a great way to ruin the game for yourself.

You can easily complete the main story with free characters. It's only certain endgame modes that really push you towards having stronger teams, and there's no reason to worry about those when you're new.

Also, don't feel pressured to pull for a character just because their banner is about to disappear. Characters return eventually, and there's nothing wrong with waiting.

My advice is to treat Wuthering Waves like a Zelda game. Take your time, explore everything, enjoy the characters and the story, and don't worry too much about the gacha system until you're swimming in Astrites.

Because the first time you experience this world is something you only get once, and it would be a shame to spend that time worrying about which character you should pull next.

[h1]I am a DAILY PLAYER since release: May 23rd, 2024. About to be 888 consecutive days, easily more than 1000 hours combined.[/h1]
[hr][/hr]
I'll talk gacha at the end. Forget "Genshin Impact" or "Arknights Endfield" for a second. If you're seriously considering "Wuwa" (in short), forget any other gacha game and focus on the gameplay experience. First things first: [u][b]What is it like to PLAY Wuthering Waves and why is it right (or not) for you?[/b][/u]

[h3]STORY[/h3]
Kuro Games used to be a smaller studio still when Wuwa version 1.0 got released. I've got an amazing first impression, but story-wise 1.0 is considered a bit of a lore-dump. That said, I urge you to stick with it, the time investment is worth it.
Without spoiling it, because you absolutely need to experience it by yourself, the story gets progressively better. The real jump in quality happened on 2.0 onward (around 20h in the main campaign, excluding exploration and side-quests). Generally speaking, players kept on being flabbergasted patch, after patch, after patch (...), and to this day, two years later, the sentiment persists. Cinematic cut-scenes + a fantastic soundtrack, most times superior to a lot of western AAA titles out there. [u]Story filled with adventure, comedy, heart and EPIC worthy of "CINEMA" reactions.[/u] Yes, more than one. Several!

[h3]COMBAT[/h3]
Combat is easy to understand and open to skill-expression, contrary to most adventure games inside its genre. [u]You're able to play as casually as you want and clear most challenges in your path, or go deeper and optimize your team's damage much further than otherwise.[/u] Team building is key in Wuthering Waves, not always around the characters' own attributes like "Fusion" or "Havoc", but their "OUTRO" skills, buffing each-other accordingly + much more.
How to equip characters? The open world provides! You can easily fetch for character equipment in the open-world itself thanks to the "echo" system. A bit like Pokémon, you fight and catch echoes. Each echo comes bundled with a specific set and stats. Creative way to equip characters while promoting open-world exploration. 

[h3]EXPLORATION & PROGRESSION[/h3]
[u]You are free to roam the open-world as you please, while obtaining gadgets along the way helping you further, completely free-to-play.[/u] Any other gimmicks you may own in the future through specific characters are inferior to the f2p way (the ability to FLY being the top tier one). And yes, you can run up walls and not deplete any stamina outside of combat.
Like any other gacha game tho, there's a specific stamina system to limit your daily character progression, it's called a "waveplate". That said, you're able to progress any character you wish at any given time according to specific domains. As a new player tho, I advise you to experience the story first while not worrying too much about your characters' maximum level.

[h3]ENDGAME[/h3]
If you care about endgame, this section is for you. "Powercreep" is healthy, it takes more than a year for a character to really fall off, sometimes two years. "Tower of Adversity" is the first endgame mode and one every player can comfortably clear. "Whimpering Wastes" is specific to crowd-control. Lastly, "Endstate Matrix" is the true DPS-check. Most may struggle with it. As a day-one player and "goldfish" (someone who spends very little real cash in the game), it took me a while to leave the struggle phase... Like everything in Wuwa tho, it is HIGHLY SKILL-BASED. Practice = improve!

[h3]GACHA[/h3]
[u]It's the best adventure gacha game out there.[/u] Competition is fierce & welcomed, every game needs it to thrive. As a new player you are able to receive A LOT of pulls for your premium characters or weapons. Choose your timing wisely, and you can get yourself a premium top-tier team in your very first weeks.
Loosing 50/50 to premium 5* characters will suck always, although the pity system is far better than most gacha games and the weapon banners are GARANTEED. At the same time, you can always choose which weapon to go for on the standard weapon banner. Most of those are useful, so the free-to-play experience appreciates it.
Every other patch you can always garantee a premium 5*, if not two. It's a fair system in my honest opinion. Plus, if you're comfortable with this, you can buy the "Lunite Subscription" and it will help your account much further while spending very little cash.

[h3]PERFORMANCE & ON-GOING UPDATES[/h3]
Currently it performs reasonably well, taking into account it's Unreal Engine 4. Quality of life improvements arrive every patch and they're not stopping with them. My current rig has zero issues with Wuthering Waves, although my previous one experienced stutters on a very specific in-game city due to the in-game's engine specific CPU limitations, it's reported.

While Wuthering Waves sets itself apart with distinct graphics and faster combat, it is hard to deny that a significant portion of the game’s core gives off Genshin Impact vibes.
Several features are directly shared between the two titles:
• Time-of-day mechanics: Players manipulate the clock in the exact same way to trigger specific world events or quests.
• Team rotation flow: The strategy still centers on swapping characters sequentially to maximize party synergy.
• Vertical traversal: Using the 'T' key to grapple higher into the air functions as a direct evolution of Genshin’s regional mobility mechanics, like Sumeru's Four-Leaf Sigils.
• Open-world progression: The exploration loop  relies on completing localized combat or puzzle challenges to unlock sealed treasure chests (etc. if more exists).

To be fair, Kuro Games definitely looked at Genshin and said "let's upgrade the annoying parts." Being able to smash the ESC key or the skip button to get away from endless blocks of text and unskippable videos is an absolute godsend.

Ultimately, whether these similarities are a positive or a negative comes down to personal preference. For players who love the established Genshin formula but want a more streamlined, action-heavy experience, Wuthering Waves offers a highly polished alternative. For others, the structural similarities might feel a bit too familiar. It doesn't necessarily replace what came before, but it successfully carves out its own niche by refining a very successful blueprint

NEGATIVE POINTS
- Story is definitely their Achilles' heel. It's horrendous.

- No male healer. It bewilders me that after 2 years, they still refuse to release a male healer in this game. 
- Team composition is boring. You don't have the freedom to try other team variations. Some characters just work if you pull a specific resonator.
- Optimization is also an issue for lots of players. I confess I didn't have many problems with that, but since they released Lahai-roi, my game stuttered or crashed a few times.
- Reruns are a mess. It is not acceptable to wait more than 1 year to pull for a character released in 2024 or 2025. I’m not even asking for an updated kit for old units, just the possibility of pulling for resonators you like. The devs punish you for not playing the game since day 1, and I don't understand why they think this is a great business model.

STORY
Now, I need to mention this aspect of the game because that was the reason why I quit the game recently. 
I know that not everyone who plays gacha games care much about the plot, but that's not my case. 
On the contrary, one of the reasons why I've played wuwa for so long was because I believed they could improve the story and focus more on post-apocalyptic topics, not fake romance.
However, after Mengzhou, it was crystal clear to me that devs unfortunately no longer care about the main story or character development at all.
The story is basically all resonators in solaris praising and worshipping Rover for being perfect (especially female resonators). Rover is always going to save the day. Anyone who dares to question the sentinels is considered a villain. Who wants to spend their time reading that every single patch?
Also, when it comes to female resonators, there is a formulaic story for all of them at this point. This game was never advertised as a dating sim, so I don't understand why pretend that Rover is in love with any of them. It's all about selling generic new resonators at this point.
I knew the writing would be severely affected the moment they removed companion stories. I don't agree that we all should feel obligated to engage with all resonators if it's not part of the main story. That's precisely why companion stories were great. You had the option to not interact more with a character you didn't like or wait a little longer to read their story when it was convenient for you.
Male resonators in this game have interesting stories, but the devs refuse to give them proper development. Jingran's situation just sums up how they just don't care about their plot or whatsoever. What kind of dystopian world is this that you can only interact with female resonators? Let's not forget that the first resonator they released was Jiyan. That's ridiculous. No wonder people praise Rinascita for everything else, but the plot.
Obviously, this game is very popular, and it's not gonna EOS anytime soon. They will keep profiting a lot from new resonators, but I no longer see the point of playing and spend money on wuwa if the devs themselves don't care about their own IP.

Small additin: So, they added a launcher with ads to the game now, so that you have to stare at them while updating, instead of letting Steam do it for you... Kuro, launch options and optionally downloadable content were always a thing on Steam; there is no need for it, and it's just a slap in the face for your players, not to mention: this doesn't do anything to benefit you, it only pisses off your users. Now, to continuing with my original review of why you should not ever get started with this game, terrible and anti-customer launcher aside:

Honestly, no. The game is mediocre at everything, even the things it tries to do well, or in some cases not, in the order of how well it does them: 

- Characterization 
Surprisingly this game has some pretty well written characters. It's a shame these characters are never actually executed on in any way that provides a good narrative outside of the lore tabs on the character page.

- Graphics 
Honestly, these days Endfield does the realistic thing better, and Genshin was always better at style, but now even at fidelity. The best cohesive and purposeful art direction to be found here is probably in the starting area, which is fine to actually quite good, depending on where you're looking.

- Actually running 
No. The game is so poorly optimized that I get half a second of stutters regularly when traversing even by walking, on a gen5 PCIE SSD, 32gb of ram, an i7 13700k, and an rtx 4070 with the lowest lod setting.

- Narrative 
No. The game has a lot of very good seedlings so to say in it's worldbuilding that it could cultivate into something that actually makes one cohesive whole without that being thrown out of the window for the rule of cool the next second, but it doesn't. It also has a lot of interesting story lines and characters it just forgot about. If they are brought back, it's just for fan service apparently, but that's a new thing that they experimented, at least with taking it to these extremes, in the last version.

- Animations 
No. Cutscenes are passable, but often tasteless. Dialogue animations range from good to offensive to look at, but that's mostly due to being slapped in the face with senseless sexualization to the extent that I can't take the game seriously anymore the moment it does it.

- Combat feel 
This is probably what it's marketed the most for, but this has the least actual depth to it's combat in any game I played for even remotely this long, or anywhere near as much. It's basically auto attack, and sometimes do a glorified qte with UI that imersonates actual combat ui as you'd see it in other games.

- Music 
No. The music doesn't fit half the time, and the other half is boring, or actively offensively mediocre. Besides for a few tracks I'll admit I'd miss if I followed my own advice, do yourself a favor and turn it off if you decide to play. The best music it has is found in the starting area and broader region, you can keep it on there and only turn it off once it gets bad.

- "Listening to the Community" 
No. It lost all it's identity to this.

As a bonus, the character designs range from the bare minimum to actually good. It's difficult to actually rank them against the rest of these points, as I feel like I'd do the actually good ones, as well as the many atrocities besides them no justice.

Unfortunately, after the massive success in 2024-2025, the game has been on the decline for about a year now.

The story is nowhere near as good, as it used to be. Old characters get forgotten as soon as a new region begins. Too much focus on random NPCs, and too little on the actual playable units.

The combat has been steadily getting worse. The game has been getting less units who allow for skill expression and freedom, and more of the ones, that only play one or two rigid rotations, requiring you to press like three buttons, and fit a couple of teams at best. Most DPS units need a premium support, forcing you to get two units just to be able to play one, otherwise they barely even function. Some new enemies introduce mechanics which only a few certain characters can comfortably deal with. HP inflation has been getting out of hand. A boss received 44% HP increase in two patches. Enemies in some modes have double HP compared to what they had a year ago. Meanwhile, old units do not get any buffs, which leaves them useless, forever stuck benched and collecting dust, because they can't clear anything anymore. If you look at the tier lists, you will see all the new units at the top, and all the old units at the bottom, with only a couple exceptions. Genshin Impact, HSR, Arknights 1 & 2, NTE, ZZZ all have tamer powercreep than this game. The first 1.5-2 years of this game were good, even great in terms of the meta. Older units could still clear, even if they required some effort. But now it's just doomed.

Optimisation issues that have been plaguing the game ever since 1.0, are still present, and now are arguably even worse. The optimisation fix that the devs promised and released a patch ago was a lie (unless you consider a literal 1-2% fps increase a fix). It barely made the framerate better (again, 1-2% increase), and even worse in some places, and did not fix the atrocious stutters, which have been getting worse almost every new patch. My pc runs CP2077, Silent Hill 2 remake and Battlefield 6 better than this game.

And don't even get me started on the mickey mouse events, man... A cheap vampire survivors knock-off twice? No, thank you. "combat" events, where all you do is take pictures of characters while they pose? No, thank you. Exploration events, where the whole event is just you clearing the map? That's not even an event, that's just normal exploration. 99% of this game's events feel like a chore, which nobody would even play if there were no rewards.

There are many more issues that unfortunately don't fit in the steam review's word limit, but simply put, WuWa used to be something great. A year ago I would recommend this game to anyone and everyone. But in its current state, I would say that it is barely playable anymore. Maybe worth for a new player for story, but that's about it. It's still a decent action RPG, F2P on top of that, so maybe it could be good for a new player to get in and play through the earlier story, but as a 1.0 player, I see no reason to bother with this game in its current state.

Okay I'm going to try to right the most objective review I can (I have way more hours than what steam shows since I previously played on the launcher until around 3.0). 

First of all, this game is quite frankly amazing to play, it's fun and full of plenty of good moments in the story and also is just overall near AAA-quality almost every time these days. I've been around since the absolute bug-riddled days of the game and I've never regretted sticking to it. Whatever money I spent I think they take and use quite well (usually I only get the battlepass and the daily login bonus thing). The devs are also clearly taking player feedback even if it takes some time to implement some things, at least they do it. I continue to play on a daily basis and Wuthering Waves has been one of the games in my rotation consistently for a good amount of time now. I especially like the things they've done more recently. They're also definitely trying their best to keep powercreep to a minimum though it is showing a bit still, I do appreciate the effort they are clearly putting in.

Now, there are also things that I don't really like about this game sometimes. Some of the spending events and other things are blatantly trying to get you to spend more money, and for those who want to go ahead I won't judge you. For those who want those things in the events that can't spend that kind of money however, it's frustrating at times to not be able to get them. Also, doing more reruns of older characters instead of putting them in a spending event is definitely also a red-flag for me. On top of that a character that is still as relevant Shorekeeper especially is somewhat concerning and also irritating. Also I don't really appreciate the fact that they're forcing the game launcher onto us even for the steam version just to get the SD, HD, and UHD toggles, I've already gotten it working just by using a simple script and getting the files for the UHD setting so clearly they could figure out a way to get it to work without that. I just don't see why they can't make a native alternative for steam instead of just making steam users use the launcher. It's the same issue ZZZ has as well. Events are also starting to get a little repetitive which isn't too bad but it's also somewhat frustrating at the same time. Also, exploration to grind for gacha material and whatnot is also definitely a hassle and a limitation for people who don't have as much time to play video games, but that's a different issue that I won't address too directly since I'm just listing my own cons right now and this adds way too many layers I don't want to bother getting into in a game review.

Overall, it's still a much better experience than most gacha games and I'll continue to play the game, but a lot of things can be improved. I don't really care about what others say as much since these are just my personal opinions so take what I say with the grain of salt required for reading someone's opinions if you see this review.

Echo farming/Gearing in this game is genuinely one of the most frustrating RNG systems I've dealt with. It's not just one layer of RNG, but several layers stacked on top of each other. First, you need the right Echo to drop. Then you need the correct main stat and substats. After that, you have to level it up and pray for the right substats, only to discover that your upgrades rolled into flat stats or some other useless sht instead of the stats you actually need. And don't forget the cost of tuning and upgrading all those Echoes just to find out they're garbage.

You can spend hours farming and end up with absolutely nothing worth using. Even when you finally get an Echo with the right main stat and decent substats, there's no guarantee the upgrades will roll in your favor. It's RNG on top of RNG on top of RNG. At some point, it stops feeling like progression and starts feeling like a fking slot machine. The worst part is that this grind isn't even a one-time investment. Every time a new character comes out, you're expected to go through the same exhausting process all over again.

This creates a really stupid cycle: pull a new character, spend weeks farming Echoes and materials to make them usable, invest a ridiculous amount of resources into their build, and then watch them get powercrept by the next character several patches later. Suddenly, the character you spent all that time building feels mediocre, and you're back to square one.

The endgame feels less like a test of skill or team-building and more like a DPS check designed around the latest limited character. The buffs and bonuses in endgame modes always tailored to the newest characters, while older characters and teams get left behind.

I have a plethora of great things to say for this game but then this review will turn into a reading nightmare so i'll keep it short:

- Super smooth and easy to learn combat while extra challenges lay for any souls veterans in the form of Tactical Holograms or any of the endgame modes (although some of them require highly invested teams rather than pure skill).

- Graphics are simply amazing some of the best in any gacha out there, the visual fidelity is up there for those who have capable hardware with support for raytracing as well.

- Story and plot take the cake for me in the best possible way and for a game that is completely free to download it's actually impressive how anyone can jump right in without paying a single cent and dive into this universe to explore some genuinely amazing narratives along with the associated characters they come with.

- The music in this game is well there is one word for it: PEAK, its really good and you will be adding some tracks on your Spotify list for sure.

- The gacha systems are a subjective matter and since the devs are generous you will easily secure one or even two time limited characters almost every patch unless if your luck is thinner than air. Weapon banners are guaranteed free of the 50/50 mechanic.

- Character designs are simply phenomenal, they really have talented artists in their care with some of the most unique outfits that i have ever seen. Their anatomy is very detailed and pristine especially in the later segments of the game (The Shorekeeper is bound to blow you away with her first appearance).

- Even if you are new to gacha this game is not that intimidating and goes easy in terms of UI, materials, currency management, levelling up characters etc.

Highly recommended for anyone who is interested, yes you can completely ignore the gacha aspect (although good luck with that since you will likely be tempted) and just have a solid time with the story and music.

It’s rare for a gacha game to make you care this much about its cast, but Wuthering Waves pulls it off.

Visually, the game is stunning. Clean UI design, atmospheric environments, and a soundtrack that perfectly matches the tone of each moment elevate the experience. Even small details—like the way characters interact with the world—show the developers’ attention to polish.

I've played wuwa since day 1 (I was playing through their main launcher) and have played it everyday till I quit. There were multiple reasons that made me decide to leave, despite having spent a lot of time in the game.

For me, the story was the most interesting it could be in Rinascita/Septimont, mainly because of the atmosphere and environment in these regions yet even there they had the repetitive formula of characters having a sad background story (something which eventually became so common in Lahai-Roi that it made the story very uninteresting to me). Eventually around patch 3.5, I had stopped caring about the story overall. Interestingly, despite trying to skip the stories, there were a multitude of places where the skip button was not added but should've been there. Also the devs seem to be very adamant to kill any of the important characters (ones you can pull for) yet they keep using the concept of death in very uninteresting ways where a character is "dead" or about to die and the main character comes and saves them, unless the character is affiliated (voluntarily or involuntarily) to the bad guys. Then the main character does not act but the affected character still exists somehow. Also there a multiple instances where a very dramatic story quest ends abruptly with a cliffhanger of sorts and then when the new quest arrives, the atmosphere is completely different and that ruins the immersion.

When it comes to the characters, there is a massive pool of female characters and there are very few male characters. Despite the obvious fan service that the developers are pushing with their female characters' designs, this is becoming tiresome, considering that almost every new female character's banner release comes with a quest showing their sad background story in the hopes that players would pull for the character or maybe even pay to pull for them. However, after that initial boost, most characters become irrelevant or even non-existent in future stories. As for male characters, I wish they'd made more male characters with cold, rough, aggressive features like a lone warrior  of sorts in terms of both character and appearance without being psychotic or silly. For now, the closest characters in this game with those features are Calcharo and Qiuyuan. Also them trying to re-make 4-star characters as 5-star and sell back to us is something I absolutely dislike. For now it's only Yangyang but the fact that they've even asked for my opinion about this in one of their surveys tells me that they are planning to continue this practice. I much prefer the original Yangyang and just have older characters receive an upgrade to their existing kits that makes them usable in the current state of the game. And the story that they used to make the change to Yangyang's 5-star form was just so uninteresting and repetative.

About the gacha mechanics, one of the reasons I started playing was because the gacha seemed to be more merciful with weapon banners being guaranteed, character event banners being 50/50 and if you lose, next is guaranteed plus all banners being up to 80 pulls to get a golden pull. Since the start I have lost 22 50/50s on the character event banner and have only won 10. This has made me reconsider my stance on any gacha mechanics because that experience was pretty bad despite being more merciful on paper compared to other gacha games.

Another thing that I really soured my experience was the fact that the game had many restrictions. For example, in Lahai-Roi they introduced the motorbike as a tool that you can use to move around. The problem that I had was that there was already a movement tool, called "flight" which was very convenient for me but flight as a tool could not be used in the newest zone and conversely the motorbike could not be used in the older zones. For some reason, instead of making those tools usable in zone so people can choose what to use, the developers decided that the bike is the only tool that can work in the newer zones from then on and even added an upgrade to the bike that gives it wings but you cannot fly in an upward trajectory with it like you can with flight which is very irritating. Why can't they just make both tools accessible everywhere? They made flight accessible in Rinascita and later made it work in Huanglong as well. Why not do the same for all other zones and for the bike? It's just stupid not being able to use whichever you want.

In terms of performance and stability, the game has had some problems on my device but they were minor at first. I've always had some random crashes or freezes but nothing significant. Also, initially the game had support for 120 FPS and it was running smoothly for me but that option was removed for my GPU for more than a year which i found unreasonable and complained in multiple surveys because my device was able to maintain 120 FPS even on high graphic settings. Then at some point (if I remember correctly, it was around the start of chapter 4), the 120 FPS option was back on but the game overall became buggy in a way I did not expect. Every time I start the game and it works for about a minute or two, there is a massive freeze for a few seconds, then the game recovers and then for some reason, one of my monitors shuts down and turns itself back on. There is no other game that does this to me. I also tried the steam version of the game and the exact same issue happened. And this bug has been happening to me for a few patches now. Plus I had also noticed a lot of random lag spikes that have been happening lately so I feel like the overall performance of the game has degraded quite a bit.

Lastly, the two things that eventually became the final straw for me were actually the combat mechanics and the combat events. When I started playing, I was enjoying the combat quite a bit. It felt fresh and there were more options to do fun stuff without being too complex. The bosses were interesting, the holograms were challenging though slightly annoying at the hardest levels but still fine. Also Depths of Illusive realm was probably the most fun combat event that wuwa had. My vision back then was to have more combat events where you fight hordes of monsters and they did add Whimpering but that still was somewhat limited since the monsters spawn in waves and the waves do not spawn all the monsters at once plus you have to do it for a set amount of time. For the last level of whimpering which spawns endless waves, it would be understandable to have a time limit but why have it on the other levels. Same with holograms - I don't want to be forced to do a boss within a window of time. Also as more characters, bosses and mechanics were introduced, I noticed that in order to do the most amount of damage for harder content like holograms, ToA, events with bosses and debuffs, etc. I was forced to do perfect rotations almost every time in order to succeed which started making the combat experience more strict and not as fun. Now that the game has almost 60 characters and has introduced an endgame (Endstate Matrix) where you can and are encouraged to use as many character as you can/have to get rewards having to master every character's rotation and do it without errors while also being ready to dodge and counterattack when necessary is quite demanding. And to top it all off, most hard-to-get rewards in these combat events are ones that would benefit the weaker players the most(ones that are mostly or entirely F2P) yet most people that can get those rewards, especially in Endstate Matrix are going to be people that pay and would not really need those rewards anyway. Also there is just so much focus around having combat be about boss fighting - Endstate is just endless boss grind, holograms are tougher and more annoying to kill, you get combat events where you debuff yourself, fighting bosses to get more points. (1/2)

Wuthering is what you would expect from a gacha: on the positive side, there is cool combat, beautiful characters, an open world full of collectibles, and some events. The gameplay is really what makes the game good. It has a fast-action combat based on rotations, meaning that every character needs to enter the battlefield, deal damage to charge a bar, and then switch to another character; in this switch, whoever is fleeing the field buffs the character that's entering it. This mixed with parries and dodges creates an intense and very fun combat.

However, on the negative side, the lore, for me, is not worth it. It's very complicated, has a lot of holes, and most of the time is just an excuse to make you like the new character so they can get your money. Some character histories are cool and you may enjoy them, but I think they can't reach their full potential because of how bad the world-building is.

Even so, Wuthering Waves is still a free game that you can have a lot of fun with for long hours, and when you reach a dead end or just get bored, you can just uninstall and wait for the next update to play it again.

I've actually been playing heavy since March 2025, and this game genuinely has a special place in my heart above all other gachas. Obviously, the game has it's fanservice side, as most gachas tend to, and like any other gacha, its got its cons (squints at the spending event). But there is still a very clear amount of love and care put into the game -- the story and the characters in it have so much heart to them, and it very quickly became one of my favorite games, which I didn't anticipate when I initially started it (I had just really wanted Brant at the time and didn't think I'd get attached to the story at all but I got hooked lol). I haven't been able to convince many people to start unfortunately, but the very few people I've managed to convince have fallen in love with the game, and have told me that they didn't think they would get so hooked in the beginning. If you like open-world games like Genshin but like the vibe of a more apocalyptic universe, this game is such a gem. And as a plus: the developers really seem to actually listen to their players a fair bit compared to other companies. 

My biggest complaint would be game size and lag if I had to name anything. I've heard a lot of complaints of bugs, especially around regions such as Lahai-Roi. I have a bit of a bulkier PC so I didn't notice it too much, but on the rare occasions I play on my Playstation instead, I definitely notice it a bit more (and have even had the game crash a couple times). So fair warning that the game is definitely significantly more enjoyable with a tankier computer. It can be done on less (my friend can run it on his laptop!), but you def might have to knock your graphics quite a bit to be able to handle it in those situations.

Overall, the game is incredibly fun and endearing, and the overall themes of humanity coming together are just so so beautiful. Plus, Rover is a very charming MC (I'm biased since they're my favorite character but-)

However, it is hard to praise the story when I felt not only slightly lost, but also bored, and didn't like that Rover was just traveling and continuing for the sake of duty, lacking much personal motivation. Overall a fairly alright region but way too long, a bit hard to follow, didn't give much motivation for Rover/the player other than just the duty to protect and help people, and I personally didn't get attached to many characters that were introduced this region. Perhaps Brant, Carlotta, Qiuyuan, and Zani but that's me being lenient. I guess if I had to describe the feeling I felt for most of Rinascita's story, I would say emptiness.

Lahai Roi's story (Chapter 3) is what sold me to this game. Genuinely surprised me because after Rinascita, my expectations were not super high. This region's story Arc is around half the length of Rinascita's story, which I think was near perfect for the story that was presented. To keep it simple without spoilers, I felt like most of the major characters had wonderful backstory: which includes us learning more about Rover from being tied in with another character, so that's a major plus. My favorite characters from this region were Mornye, Sigrika, Luuk Herssen, Denia, and Aemeath. Lucilla and Lynae are not my personal favorite characters but I still appreciate them far more than almost every Rinascita character. Music and overall quality remained as good as Rinascita. There were some story parts in Lahai Roi that actually touched my heart emotionally which is what surprised me. Sigrika had really nice and funny expressions too, which I hope gets passed onto more characters. Speaking of which, there were a lot of moments in this region where I just couldn't stop laughing because they made it so incredibly funny in a good way. This region's story felt far, far more cohesive than the previous regions. My favorite parts were Act 3, post Act 3 segue, Act V, Denia's segue and the final 'we choose the sky' segue. One caveat that I found was that I felt that the "Dark Side" lore was a bit out of place, but I could understand the imagery and what it represents so I'll give it a pass. The main verdict from me is that this is the best region that Wuwa has so far in terms of its story.

Since Mengzhou's story (Chapter 4) is still not fully out, I can't really judge it to its fulliest extent. I so far have enjoyed it better than Rinascita, although it is a step back from Lahai Roi. I think Qingxiao and Suisui are great characters, and I like the moments with Yangyang especially if she's with Suisui. I will say, the transition from Lahai Roi to Mengzhou was terrible. To me, Rover came to Mengzhou on a whim because of an issue they weren't fully aware of. Sure its understandable to be concerned but it did feel like an abrupt decision without much thought especially with how much Rover has made themselves home in Lahai Roi. Its a small-ish annoyance I have that some people may not care, but I do think Wuwa occasionally struggles with establishing transitions that doesn't make it feel like Rover is being dragged into another issue that they shouldn't need to involve themselves in but do so anyway because its Rover and the MC has to be the saviour of course. 

Not related to the story but I found that Mengzhou was unreasonable laggy. It looks beautiful with so much detail, but I think its a bit overkill, especially since places like Rinascita look great and don't have much lag at least in comparison. I could easily hit 120 FPS consistently in Rinascita even while flying but in Mengzhou, it can drop to as low as 50 while on the bike which is kind of a crazy difference. The developers can make things look beautiful while also not sacrificing on the optimization so I'm not sure why its like this.

Overall, I would recommend this game. Even if some aspects are up and down, I like good time killers and this is a good one. Experiencing Lahai Roi was worth it too. I do wish I could wipe my memory of Lahai Roi and replay it again lol. Mengzhou is pretty decent too and has good potential once Act IV comes out (which is tomorrow as of typing this). Some characters in the story I've already gotten really attached too as well making me want to grind this game just to pull them (Mornye whom I already have, Sigrika, and Shorekeeper). As a side note, a good device is definitely needed to handle Mengzhou and probably even Lahai Roi at decent frames.

The combat and character designs are great, but the progression systems make the game increasingly frustrating to play.

The biggest problem for me is the amount of RNG involved in building characters. Echo farming already takes a lot of time, but getting the right Echo, main stat, and useful substats is only the beginning. You can spend hours farming and still end up with nothing worth keeping. Then you have to deal with more RNG when upgrading those substats.

The gacha system adds another layer of frustration. Losing a 50/50 after saving for a character feels terrible, especially when getting another character can require a large number of pulls. If you also want their signature weapon, the amount of resources needed increases even more. It makes saving for characters feel less rewarding when luck doesn't go your way.

There's also the issue of power creep and increasingly large enemy HP pools. Some endgame content can feel more like a DPS check than a test of how well you actually play. Newer characters and stronger builds can start feeling necessary just to keep up with the increasing difficulty.

The combat itself is genuinely fun, and that's what keeps me playing. But the combination of gacha RNG, Echo RNG, and DPS-focused endgame progression** makes the overall progression feel more like a grind than something rewarding.

I enjoy the game, but I can't recommend it without mentioning how frustrating these systems can become.
