Before diving in, I've been playing both the OG Arknights and Endfield since day one. This review is written as of patch 1.6.

I've been with this IP for over half a decade, seen its highs and lows. Yet through thick and thin I still find myself drawn right back in. Both have a unique charm to them that other gacha games struggle to capture.
Arknights stumbled a lot in its beginnings before turning into something beautiful, so it stands to reason that Endfield being a different genre and style will inevitably follow suit.


The story has been a mixed bag in its opening act with Valley IV. While I've seen it as mostly an introductory chapter with setting up world lore basics, the pacing could've used a bit more work. All in all it was just "ok". The Landbreakers are portrayed as a bunch of savages, and Nefarith herself doesn't make for a particularly compelling antagonist, at least early on. The story certainly nails the visual spectacle and environmental design though.
The meat is in the Wuling region where the majority of the plot takes hold for 1.x. Much of the region features lush forests and a blend of traditional Chinese and modern architecture. So far it's my favorite depiction of China among gacha games. Those who played the original game might recognize the architecture style from the nomadic city of Dahuang (featured in "Here A People Sows"), with its predominantly agricultural setting. Beyond that, we have the desolate region of the Exclusion Zone, and a snowy region tied to Typhoeus's story. The pacing has improved, the presentation is top notch, and the narrative is slowly but surely finding its footing.
I'd say that if you're a fan of the original you should approach the narrative from a different perspective. There are things that only Arknights can do thanks to its visual novel format, and things only Endfield can do thanks to being a 3D Action RPG. The original's sidestories often jump between 3+ subplots across multiple scenes, featuring a large cast. Scenes like these are few and far between in Endfield.

Endfield by contrast presents most of the story through the lens of the Endministrator. Love em or hate em, they're here to stay. Doctor himself wasn't much of a character until the Vigilo sidestory either, 2 years into the game, so I'm more than willing to give Endmin a chance too. I don't necessarily disagree that there is too much Endmin "glazing", but the story has already moved past the most egregious moments present in Valley IV. Because they're our "blank-slate" MC, Endmin's characterization, or lack thereof, initially leaned heavily on one liners and a wealth of dialogue choices, However, the game also gives them proper voiceover and moments of agency. In spite of that, Endmin has been shown through the story to harbor self doubt and struggle with the burden they carry, culminating in the journey of self reflection and healing after the events of the NWEZ.

Some character stories are a mixed bag, most likely as a result of beta rewrites, such as Gilberta. Characters like Laevatain, Camille, and Typhoeus are what I would consider the standard to strive for in terms of presentation, plot, and character development. Some of these also serve as worldbuilding, giving us more information about other factions and their history such as Ses'qa, the TGCC, and the Samivegr. Others are weaved into the main narrative, such as Tangtang, Fangyi, Arcane, and tackle themes of struggle, loss, and a hope for a better tomorrow.

Character writing is phenomenal, with the majority of the cast making re-appearances throughout the story. It makes the world feel lived-in and it's a genuine joy to see the characters in more casual moments. Regional accents are another aspect I appreciate. I'm the type of player who sticks to CN/JP acting in gacha because I find that most of EN dub performance falls flat. Arknights is the exception: the casting feels authentic to its universe, where Terra parallels 18th-20th century countries, society, and politics.
The music is in a class of its own in my opinion. After all, Hypergryph is a music company which happened to fund games to promote their music.

Gameplay stands out from the rest in the gacha sphere by combining factory-building mechanics with action RPG combat in the style of Xenoblade, with your entire party present on the field. Instead of a solo journey, your party travels with you, they comment on things you discover, point out treasure, pick stuff up for you, and even help you plant/water crops. In combat, you have access to a shared resource called "SP" for casting skills. You can also trigger various combo effects upon meeting certain conditions, building towards each character's ultimate. The game features 5 different elements that interact in the form of Arts reactions, 6 character classes, and 5 weapon types.
On the surface, nothing that I said is particularly groundbreaking, but there's surprisingly a lot of depth to team building. Character kits are flexible enough to fit into multiple team compositions. Combined with fixed stats on gear, it leaves room for experimentation without wasting weeks or months of your life chasing that perfect artifact/relic/echo/disc. There are items that let you improve gear stats, and they are weekly gated. However, given how lenient the endgame is (outside of Contingency Contract of course), there is no need to worry about emptying the shop each time. 
Exploration is grounded, with no climbing or gliding mechanics. Despite the restrictions, it allows for clever level design: points of interest and vistas are discovered naturally, rather than just flying over the terrain. 
 
And now for the elephant in the room: the factory. 
Interacting with the factory is essential for account progression, story, exploration, and certain events. Outside of the core factory area, you'll use zipline towers to make exploration easier, place pumps to drain bodies of water or fill holes, craft bombs to blow up random walls and Aether cores, and fill bottles with different liquids to clear various environmental hazards. 
In the main factory area, you'll build production chains from the most basic ingredients into increasingly advanced recipes with some spanning more than 10 items. You craft powders, parts, bottles, batteries, healing items, etc. Components are crucial for crafting gear that your operators use. In the aforementioned shop you can trade using "Stock Bills", which you acquire by selling factory items to outposts or selling elastic goods through a fluctuating market to other players. In my opinion, it is easy to get into, and you can easily lose hours trying to perfect your design. It's one of my favorite aspects of the game, and I encourage people to give it a try even if it looks daunting. Be proud of your spaghetti production lines!
If it's too much to figure out on your own, there are plenty of resources online, and you can always use blueprints other players share.

The game is not perfect, and it definitely has its flaws, but past them you'll find a genuinely fun experience. I'd highly recommend watching the developer interview from Gamescom where they discuss the challenges they've faced making this game. You can tell they put a lot of effort into it, and they seem genuinely commited to responding to player feedback.
In regards its connection to the original game, I think it's pretty natural for a spin-off to carry over certain themes, story elements, or plot points from its predecessor. After all, it's still part of the same universe, so I see it more as building on what's already been established than simply relying on nostalgia. That being said, do consider giving the original a try if you like tower defense and deep worldbuilding.

To wrap it up, Endfield is definitely worth a shot for its combat, factory gameplay, and evolving narrative, and I have faith in the game's future.

[h1]A gacha that actually feels different[/h1]
[i]Written as of patch 1.6.[/i]

Day one player here. I've quit every other gacha except the original Arknights, and Endfield is the one that stuck. It's a sci-fi world with a realistic anime style, futuristic tech and spacecraft, populated by humans with animal traits. The only "pure human" you can play is the MC (for now?).

[h2]Story & Lore[/h2]
Set over a century after Arknights, in the same universe but a different region. Same races, different factions. You don't need to have played the original; it just makes the references hit harder.
The pacing is slow, but never boring, and since 1.4 every story patch has been a real treat, each with its own atmosphere. The pattern so far: a main chapter every two patches, with side stories in between that aren't filler but explore other branches of the lore.

[h2]Combat[/h2]
Simple but effective: auto attacks, skills, combos and ultimates, built around elemental interactions. You actually have to manage your rotation; it's not just auto attack and spamming E.
Bonus: your whole team is on the field with you, so you never feel like you're fighting alone.

[h2]Exploration & Factory[/h2]
Exploration feels great. You can place ziplines wherever you want and build relay towers to carry electricity across the map, which you need to power your ore, water and gas extractors. Expanding the network every patch is genuinely satisfying.
Yes, the factory is core gameplay. If you hate it, sorry. But you only need a few hours per patch, not daily upkeep.
The factory feeds the [b]best gear system I've ever played[/b]:
[list]
[*]No RNG, fixed stats
[*]No stamina: everything runs on factory and outpost resources
[*]Upgrades are completely free
[*]Gear presets to swap setups in one click (recent QoL)
[/list]

[h2]Character Progression[/h2]
[list]
[*]No weekly-locked resources, only daily growth materials, which you can also farm on the Dijiang
[*]You can max a character in 1 to 3 days, even on release day
[*]No need to farm every day unless you want an absurd stockpile
[*]Upcoming characters get a preview with their materials a few days before release, so you can pre-farm (great QoL)
[*]Dailies take 5 to 10 minutes: one quest gives the full 100 points, or you can just play other activities
[/list]

[h2]Dijiang[/h2]
Your ship and home base. All your operators live on board (if you have more than there's room for, the game rotates them for you), and you can assign them to different facilities:
[list]
[*]Craft XP materials for characters and weapons
[*]Produce rare growth materials for characters and weapons
[*]Run the Clue system, which earns currency for a shop with extra resources (nice bonus, not mandatory)
[/list]

[h2]Weapon Progression[/h2]
Weapons level up like characters, plus Essences: the "equivalent" of relics/artifacts in other gachas, at least for the RNG part. It's the only RNG farm in the game: stats are fixed, but getting the right Essence is random. Tickets help a lot, giving you around a 4% chance at your perfect Essence.
Essences upgrade up to +6 (and +3 for their skill), with a pity system on upgrades, so even with RNG you'll max them eventually. Honestly, it's not hard to farm, and once it's done, it's done.

[h2]Music[/h2]
Every genre you can think of, and half my daily playlist is Endfield OST. Honestly, at this point Hypergryph is a music company that happens to make games, so I expected nothing less :D

[h2]Graphics[/h2]
Gorgeous lighting and textures, and it somehow looks better with every patch. Water, wind and now leaf physics make the world feel alive. The snow region is my favorite; I could wander there for hours.
Character art and models are stunning, incredibly detailed, male and female alike, in every style imaginable.

[h2]Monetization[/h2]
Let's be honest, gacha isn't great by nature. But Endfield is one of the fairest I've played.

[b]Battle Pass[/b]
[list]
[*]Tier 1 costs 29 Origeometry (earnable in-game) and gives back 32. Just never drop below 29 at the start of a patch.
[*]Even F2P, you get a 6★ weapon for the featured operator each patch, or a choice of older weapons for free.
[*]The paid tier (€9.99) adds an extra weapon, weapon potentials, more resources and cosmetics (unnecessary, so obviously mandatory).
[*]No weekly XP cap: new missions unlock each week and old ones stay, so you can even speedrun the whole pass in the last week. Missed a limited event? The last week adds extra catch-up missions.
[/list]

[b]Character banner[/b]
[list]
[*]Hard pity at 120, 50/50 with no guarantee after a loss (only hard pity guarantees)
[*]Free 10-pull after your first 30 pulls (doesn't count toward pity)
[*]At 60 pulls, a dossier worth 10 free pulls on the next banner
[*]Losing the 50/50 can give you a limited operator from up to 3 previous banners: a 28% chance of a limited instead of a standard
[*]Each limited operator stays obtainable for 3 banners
[/list]

[b]Weapon banner[/b]
[list]
[*]Guarantee at 80 pulls, 25/75 system, 4% rate for 6★
[*]Each weapon stays available for 3 banners
[*]Separate currency (Arsenal Tickets), which you earn by pulling on character banners. Oroberyl can't be used here; only Origeometry works on both.
[/list]

[h2]Verdict[/h2]
The game feels generous and engaging. I don't mind logging in every day, and I genuinely look forward to every patch.
As a low spender (double top-up bundles in 1.1, then only pull-ticket bundles), I own [b]every character and weapon in the game[/b], more than in any other gacha I've played.

Just give it a try. What you've heard about Endfield may not be the experience you'll have playing it yourself.

[b]Recommended.[/b]

According to statistics, if you have participated in every event from launch through the previous version and purchased the Monthly Pass every month, you could have accumulated around 1,300 pulls' worth of gacha resources.
As long as you plan your pulls wisely (only pulling for characters when you have at least 120 pulls saved up), most players should be able to obtain the majority of the characters.

A lot of people complain that the gacha system is terrible.
However, compared to other major gacha games on the market, it's only slightly behind NTE in my opinion.
The reason people have such different experiences with the game largely comes down to its gacha system.
The game punishes every reckless gambler equally. If you don't plan your pulls, you'll eventually pay the price.
But if you manage your resources wisely, then at least up to the current version, even F2P players can obtain over 80% of the limited characters without spending any money.



There is no need to pull for duplicate characters to make them stronger. The game's balance is excellent. You only need to obtain a character at their base copy to make them work well. If you don't get their signature weapon right away, you still have two more versions to save up and pull for it.
The game's power creep is among the lowest in the entire gacha mobile game genre, and it is handled extremely well.
Unlike other games, such as Wuthering Waves and Honkai: Star Rail, which force you to pull for additional characters to meet team composition requirements, this game allows you to comfortably clear all content and claim every reward without spending any money.

The level design is more like solving puzzles than simply checking your team's combat power.
Even the game's hardest content, Contingency Contract, doesn't impose strict DPS or character requirements. Instead, it challenges you to think creatively and figure out how to use different characters together to find a way to clear the stage.
Of course, it's genuinely difficult, since it's designed to be challenging. But the sense of accomplishment you get from clearing it with 4-star or 5-star characters is incredible.
In the previous Contingency Contract, quite a few players even came up with strategies that allowed beginners to clear the stages using only free 4-star and 5-star characters.

There is no need to grind for equipment, either. Based on expected drop rates, most players should be able to obtain the required weapon modules within a week.

[h1] Arknights: Endfield - a "new" beginning at the expense of the old. [/h1]

As someone who had started their journey with Arknights in 2022, somewhere before the Stultifera Navis event on Global, it was difficult to properly form my opinion on Arknights: Endfield as I played, however, having sat around with my conflicting thoughts and actually witnessing how the developers handle the new updates, I think I can offer my opinion on why Endfield fails to deliver the legacy of Arknights.

When I first started discussing the current state of Endfield with other players, one thing that kept coming up was the idea that Endfield was never supposed to be a direct sequel to the original Arknights (I think this was confirmed by Lowlight, but a quick Google search alongside everything else I'll be listing down below suggests otherwise). Depending on who you asked, it was either a spin-off or an alternate timeline, something that would allow Hypergryph to explore their setting in new ways, without being restricted by the source material built within the original game since 2019. And honestly, were that the case, I would never have a problem with the game.

Don't get me wrong, Arknights: Endfield is an amazing game when you look at it purely from the gameplay, visuals and the content that it so far offers. The game respects your time, especially when it comes down to the material farming, gear artificing and essense farming. The AIC isn't nearly as mandatory, and there are various amounts of blueprints online if you feel like you don't want to tinker around with that aspect of the game. It was an amazing idea to explore an already established universe in a new way - new characters, new environment, new circumstances. Shifting from the source material and standing on your own would be the greatest strength that this game has.

However, having said that, for everything that Endfield seemingly does right, there's a whole bag of things that it does wrong. And after playing the game since release up until the patch 1.5, I'm struggling to understand what Hypergryph is actually trying to accomplish with Endfield. The game suffers a lot from an identity crisis. 

Arknights: Endfield constantly reminds you of its predecessor. The Land of Terra, symbolisms of Theresa's garden, the statue of Patriot, Rhodes Island's landship crashing into the Tower of Babel in the prologue - the game is full of references to the past events that shaped it. Even the main character of Endministrator seems to be more or less inspired by the ambiguous role of The Doctor in the grand scheme of things. We know that people of Terra fled to Talos-II through the Cosmic Gate, and we're explicitly told that Rhodes Island still operates on Talos-II. There are familiar faces, factions and concepts that carry a great deal of history from the original. All of that makes Endfield feel less of a clean break from Arknights and more of a reboot of the original ideas, without the devs understanding what made the original work in the first place. 

And that's where the confusion begins for me. If this is supposed to be a new beginning, why does it feel so reluctant to let go of the original? Conversely, if it's meant to be a continuation of Arknights, why does it seem so willing to change the very things that made the story and the world of Terra so compelling in the first place? 

Again, were it a completely separate universe - that would be completely fine. However, the game relies heavily on the already established identity of Arknights, and as such, this actively contributes to dragging it down. If I were to compare the two, we would have;

The writing that is dumbed down. The characters that are dumbed down. The worldbuilding that pulls from the source material, but is also dumbed down. Lore? Retconned. Strategic elements of combat? Nowhere to be seen. Contingency Contracts? A complete joke. Racial identity? Gone. Multiple interesting game modes to break away from the main story with tangible rewards? Also nowhere to be seen. The list goes on.

If you were to compare the writing of the recent chapters of Arknights, Endfield doesn't come nearly as close in terms of what topics it's trying to handle, even more so the overall theme and atmosphere of the game. Gone are the days of phylosophical debates and questions regarding the existence and survival in an oppressed world plagued by the Oripathy, or one's existance in a vast emptiness of the universe, forever locked in an endless cycles of rebirth as civilizations develop, prosper and die down. Now everything is sunshine and rainbows, whimsy and "Don't worry about it, Endmin." Oh, Originium? The massive double-edged sword that brought both prosperity and the suffering to the nations of Terra? Yeah, we cultivate that now. Despite the fact that we still don't have a proper cure to treat Oripathy outright. But don't worry. You're not here to think. There are no morally-grey characters, no questions that the game is willing to ask you, no stakes. Honestly, there isn't even a story that Endfield wants to tell you. Even if I were to compare the writing to the first chapters, Endfield still fails at presenting a compelling antagonist and their rival faction, like in the case with Talulah and the Reunion movement as a whole. Reunion was, and pretty much still is in the recent chapters of the story, almost a complete carbon copy of Rhodes Island. They had similar worldviews and ideals, with differing means to achieve said ideals. They had their own motivations, struggles and stories to tell, with some members either willingly joining or deserting to the opposing faction. Endfield? We have two antagonists that appear every once in a while to drop some vague exposition, before vanishing and doing it again and again. Not to mention that a large part of the game is just fighting the faceless Aggeloids that are more animal in nature. There is no narrative depth that could be tied to these. Even Seaterrors had more character in Arknights.

Of course, to see the root of the problem one would need to look at the Technical Test of the game, since these problems become more apparent if you do. Endfield arguably still had at the very least a shred of it's original identity during that test, both reflected in it's narrative and the combat loop that it offered, things that defined Arknights and made it unique. However, people didn't like the uniqueness that Arknights had brought to the table, and as such, the game had shifted it's priorities at the expense of what they've been building for 7 years. And for what?

As a result, the identity of Endfield feels too dull and sterile, with the writing feeling like something akin to the storytelling of Genshin Impact. I'm honestly baffled how the same company that wrote Chapter 15 "Dissociative Recombination" alongside the characters like Kal'tsit, Amiya, Doctor, Priestess, Theresis, FrostNova and the Patriot had managed to come up with this level of sanitized writing and uninspired characters in Endfield. 

So, if I were to sum up everything about Arknights: Endfield, it is a hollow shell of it's former self, catering towards the newer audience by re-hashing their old ideas into an amalgamated mess, all for the sake of attracting people that couldn't care less about the passion project of Hypergryph, expecting yet another Genshin Impact, Zenless Zone Zero and the like. It still has just enough references to the source material that pander towards the nostalgia of the old playerbase to keep them happy. I'm sorry, but including the Expeditioner's Jǫklumarkar OST in a Sami-inspired region of the game, along with inferior and arbitrary redesigns of the rehashed legacy Operators isn't going to magically fix Endfield's problems. 

It's honestly a shame, knowing what this game could have been if Hypergryph stayed true to their vision of the universe. If you liked Arknights for what it was - you will hate Endfield.

Let me start off by saying that I hate gachas. For three main reasons.

1. Oversexualization: gacha characters are frequently objectified, reduced, and sexualized to make them more appealing to audiences, and for players to form stronger connections so they can be milked for money. These aren’t characters, they’re products.

2. Shallowness: gacha stories and worlds are frequently constructed around characters, rather than having them be part of a world. This extends into combat being very shallow, and heavily stat based. And while grinding helps, only payment and luck can ensure players keep up.

3. Predation: random chance is inherently extremely predatory. Costs are high, time is heavily used up, and all of this is for small chances of acquisition. This is further amplified by the previous two points. So gachas will manipulate and push you into spending, often large amounts.

With all that said, Arknights wasn’t any of these. The story was mature, the world was deep, the characters felt like real people, the monetization honestly wasn’t that bad, and the gameplay while rewarding investment was heavily dependent on player skill. This is what made me love Arknights. And what I expected hypergryph to bring to endfield. But they didn’t.

If you liked Arknights because it was unique for a gacha, you will not like Endfield. Everything I loved about Arknights, from the mature story, deep worldbuilding, complex characters, and skill reliant gameplay is gone in Endfield. What's left is a pathetic husk of a video game being hard carried by the Arknights name, yet sharing none of the substance.

I hate Endfield with every fiber of my being. And there will never be another game I hate more than this, not one game that has been released, nor anything else that will ever come out. And I mean that seriously. What makes this worse is that the 2024 technical test displayed everything l've come to expect from Hypergryph. Everything that made Arknights tolerable to me. Everything that I came to respect about Arknights and Hypergryph. Unique gameplay for a gacha, mature story, deep worldbuilding, and characters that acted like people instead of trying to get you to buy them. And they deliberately moved away from this. It's a betrayal I'll never forgive. They had something unique, something that stood out, something that only needed polishing. And instead of polishing, they threw it all away.

The only good part is the factory, and even that’s been simplified to a ridiculous degree, robbed of what made it unique. If you want a factory game, look elsewhere. The combat as well has been downgraded. It’s definitely fun for the right people, but there isn’t anything about it that’s sufficiently unique. Again, unlike the technical test. You want good combat? Go play wuwa. The exploration as well just isn’t that great. The game enphasizes construction over simple exploration, such as ziplines (stolen from death stranding). But there’s so many built by so many other players so often that you rarely need to construct much yourself. So if you want good exploration, go play genshin. As for story. Oh where to start. It fluctuates between mid and bad and very bad and downright abysmal. It rarely ever treats characters like characters or lets them develop, at least not without the endministrator so they can forcefully insert romantic subtexts and elevate the self insert experience. The story is okay at its best moments, and torturous at its worst. If you want a good story, play limbus company, or reverse: 1999, or the original Arknights. Not this soulless, archetypal, haremslop,  ego stroking shell.

It isn’t unique. It’s following the leader, chasing trends rather than setting them. And that’s the biggest betrayal of the Arknights name.

Note: Although the steam version has just released, I have quite a bit more than just 7 hours in the game and have been playing since release.
[h1] For existing players: [/h1]
The new steam version is great. It runs just like the old versions, but you get to skip the launcher, and use all of steam's great features.

[h1] For new players: [/h1]
Arknights Endfield is an absolutely amazing game, and I highly recommend to anyone looking for a good gacha game, or a good factory builder/action RPG.

[h2] Graphics/Optimization [/h2]
The graphics are extremely high quality, with insane attention to detail and a beautiful world to go with it, but the optimization is so good that you'd barely be able to tell looking just at FPS numbers. With this PC (see attached specs) I can run 120fps@1080p on max settings with DLSS set to balanced with just some light stuttering, which goes away with DLSS on performance, all on Linux. On my laptop (7640U/integrated graphics) I can get 60fps@1440p on minimum settings with minimal problems. The graphics settings screen even has two bars at the top showing estimated system load, which makes picking out ideal settings for your system very easy.

[h2] Story [/h2]
The main story in this game has an incredibly engaging plot line, with plenty of great cutscenes, well written and well voice acted dialogue, and lots of engaging gameplay segments throughout to keep it from just becoming a movie. I'm always super excited to check out the latest main quest every time a new update releases. The side stories and character stories are amazing too. While they aren't all fully voice acted and have less/no cutscenes depending on the questline, the story itself is always still super well written just like the main story. I frequently fall completely in love with a character over the course of their story thanks to the depth of character shown for each one.

[h2] Characters [/h2]
The characters in this game are incredible too. The attention to detail and general quality of every aspect of design for every character is next level, with extremely beautiful outfits, detailed eyes, unique weapons, and more. The voice acting is next level too, with specifically chosen accents for different characters of different backgrounds making it feel that much more real. I find myself really loving a far higher percentage of characters in this game than I do in just about any other game I have played, even beating out Umamusume.

[h2] Gameplay (Combat/Character Building) [/h2]
Combat in this game is quite well tuned, and rarely feels like it's ever going on for too long or ends too quickly. It's also extremely fluid, and rarely feels like you're out of control, outside of a few specific very unlucky scenarios that can occur if you get knocked back and forth between two powerful enemies. Although you can't always build a team with just your favorite characters, you can definitely build a team for each one and have it be viable, and it is quite easy to switch between teams if you decide one is better suited for a specific situation or if you just feel like playing a different team. Building your own teams is not very difficult, though it typically requires a fair amount of reading, as the effects of each character's skills are thoroughly described and interactions are quite simple to understand. Each character also has a category that they get put into, along with some additional tags (ex. Damage Dealer, Cryo Infliction, HP Treatment) that makes narrowing down available candidates for different team slots quite easy. 

[h2] Gameplay (Factory Building) [/h2]
The factory gameplay is quite well done as well. If you want just a factory building game, Endfield is probably not the game for you, as the factory building is not the primary focus of the gameplay, and there are some design choices that make building super optimized factories a fair bit harder. However, if you treat it as one of the mechanics of the game instead of the main focus, it is quite good. It integrates well with other parts of the gameplay and the story, and the actual factory building, while missing some features that dedicated factory building games have, still is quite enjoyable as a secondary focus, and can be enjoyed by factory building game players like myself and also people who aren't typically drawn straight to factory building games when the time inevitably comes where you need better gear/tacticals.

[h2] Conclusion [/h2]
All in all, Arknights Endfield is an absolutely amazing game with beautiful graphics, extremely good optimization, well made characters, very fun gameplay, and a passionate dev team that listens to community feedback. 10/10, would play again.

[h1][b]Arknights: Endfield — Should You Play It?[/b][/h1]
 [b] After 150 hours on PC, I highly recommend this game! [/b]If you enjoy action RPGs, factory automation, crafting, and games with a million interconnected systems to get lost in, Arknights: Endfield might be exactly what you're looking for.

At first glance, Endfield looks like another anime gacha game. Underneath, it's a surprisingly addictive combination of action combat, factory management, tower defense, exploration, and resource gathering.


[h1][b]What Makes It Special?[/b][/h1]
[list]
[*][b]Combat:[/b] Your entire team fights together, with most attacks happening automatically while you manage abilities, team synergies, and ultimates. It's a satisfying hybrid between an action RPG and an auto-battler that actually makes me want to research builds and experiment with team compositions.
[*][b]Factory Automation:[/b] This is where Endfield really shines. You establish production lines, mine resources, manufacture materials, and build infrastructure to unlock new areas and advance your progress. If you enjoy optimizing systems and watching your production chains come together, there's plenty to sink your teeth into.
[*][b]Exploration & World Development:[/b]   Rather than climbing over everything like in Genshin Impact, Endfield makes you navigate deliberately using paths, ziplines, and progression-gated routes. You also develop outposts, support refugee camps, manage regional resources, and build automated defenses to protect your infrastructure.
[*][b]Gear Without the Endless Grind:[/b]   Equipment is crafted with fixed stats rather than randomly generated attributes. You can plan your builds and work toward specific gear instead of farming endlessly for the perfect stat rolls. There's still some RNG in equipment enhancement, but the overall system feels much more intentional.
[*][b]EtchSpace Salvage:[/b]   This extraction-style PvE mode challenges you to explore dangerous areas, collect valuable loot, manage limited inventory space, and escape before time runs out. It's a fun change of pace from the main gameplay loop.
[/list]


[h1][b]Surprisingly ADHD-Friendly[/b][/h1]

This is probably my favorite thing about Endfield. When I get bored of one activity, I can switch to another without switching games.

Tired of combat? Build a factory. Bored of production? Explore. Need a change of pace? Try tower defense or an extraction run.

All these systems feed into one another, creating a satisfying cycle of small accomplishments and long-term goals. There's always another project to work on, but I rarely feel forced to do the same thing for hours.


[h1][b]What Could Be Better?[/b][/h1]
[list]
[*]Enemies can feel like damage sponges, and enemy variety is limited.
[*]I'd love more side quests and opportunities to explore the world and its characters.
[*]The social systems have potential, but player interaction currently feels limited.
[*]Exploration can feel restrictive if you prefer unrestricted climbing and gliding.
[*]The gacha mechanics won't appeal to everyone.
[/list]

[h1][b]So, Should You Play It?[/b][/h1]

If you enjoy action RPGs, automation games like Factorio or Satisfactory, crafting, and strategic management absolutely give Endfield a try.  

Just don't go in expecting a traditional MMO or a straightforward action game. Its real strength is how it combines several different gameplay systems into one cohesive experience.

For me, it's the perfect game to settle into for an evening, follow a few rabbit holes, and gradually take over a planet with factories.

[b]Recommended![/b] Especially if you like your action RPGs with a healthy dose of industrialization.

Arknights: Endfield is a game that genuinely surprised me.

Its biggest strength isn't the action combat or the open world, but the industrial and automation system. Planning production lines, transporting resources, and watching an entire factory actually work gives a very satisfying sense of accomplishment. This is also what makes Endfield stand out from other anime-style open-world games.

The combat is solid, with some strategy involved in character skills and team composition, although it isn't the deepest action system in the genre. Exploration is enjoyable as well, especially because the industrial mechanics make the world feel like something you can actually use and develop, rather than just a map full of collectibles.

The art direction is another major strength. The combination of anime characters and industrial, post-apocalyptic environments works surprisingly well. The story and worldbuilding inherit many of Arknights' strengths, although newcomers may need some patience with the lore.

Of course, the gacha and progression systems remain potential concerns, and the PC anti-cheat system may also bother some players.

Overall, Endfield doesn't perfect every individual system, but it combines combat, exploration, characters, and industrial construction into something that feels genuinely unique.

Day 1 player and monthly spender here. You have questions. We will answer them.

[b]If I start now, how hard is it to catch up?[/b]
Very easy, a single limited DPS is enough to clear all endgame content because standard supports are all strong in this game. Eg. even the protagonist is an often-overlooked but surprisingly powerful universal sub-DPS/support hybrid who can be easily splashed onto any team in the game. They're genuinely worth building as a new player and will make your progression much easier. They can even be played as a viable main DPS. Limited supports are nice to have, but not mandatory, and only one of them so far truly feels meta-defining (Arcane). Everyone else is replaceable. You'll have a lot of story/exploration content to get through but the content cadence in Endfield is leisurely and relaxed with plenty of time to complete ongoing events so it won't take long to get caught up.

[b]I heard the factory gameplay is controversial, is it optional?[/b]
It's necessary for progression, but you can skip the vast majority of the work by copying blueprints made by other players. If you enjoy factory gameplay, you can build it yourself, otherwise just go watch some smart person on YouTube, copy all their blueprints, plug in all the things they tell you to plug in, and then you never have to touch your factory again until the next patch. Devs are aware a lot of players feel burdened by factory gameplay so they're careful not to overdo it.

[b]How is the monetization and pull economy?[/b]
Balanced around long-term play and designed to reward patient players. Monthly spenders who've been playing since launch can generally afford to collect most if not all characters, along with most if not all of their signature weapons. F2P players also typically report being able to collect a decent number of characters and weapons. However, even old DPS from 1.0 are still extremely competitive and you only need a single team to clear all content even in endgame, so you aren't pressured to pull every character and you aren't constantly fighting against powercreep and HP inflation. 

The gacha in this game heavily incentivizes saving up, this is not a game where you build pity. You either come in with enough to guarantee, or you risk losing everything. As long as you understand this rule and never gamble you will be able to reliably pull plenty of new characters and essentially get their signature weapons for free thanks to the weapon currency refunds you get from doing character pulls. Weapon banners last longer than character banners so you have much more time to collect them, and battle pass weapons offer second-best alternatives in case you'd rather save weapon pulls for someone else.

[b]What's the combat like, is this another Genshin clone?[/b]
On the surface it seems that way, but it's better to think of Endfield combat as an MMO-lite real-time strategy action game with a surprising amount of depth under the surface and a [i]massive[/i] skill ceiling. The difference in clear speed between a good Endfield player and a bad one is night and day. Think resource management, cooldowns, buff windows, smart teambuilding and careful timing; it is far more important to take the time to line up your team's skills and buffs properly as opposed to just pressing buttons as soon as possible. Basically, if you're constantly spending your SP as soon as you can, and pressing every combo skill immediately, I can almost guarantee you won't be doing your rotation properly, as many characters/teams in this game have resource gates and execution traps that will tank your damage if you just mindlessly press buttons. Rather than just memorizing your rotation, it's vital that you properly understand it so you can adjust around stage mechanics, enemy layouts etc.

[b]What about gearing? How many layers of RNG hell can I expect?[/b]
Almost none. Not even kidding, gear comes down to a weapon essence you slot into your weapon, and armor/accessories with set bonuses. Weapon essences have three random substat lines, but finding the perfect 3-liner for a new build is very easy and usually only takes me 1-3 days (if I didn't have one lying around already). You then spend junk essences for a chance to level up these substats, but there is no RNG here beyond how many attempts it'll take to level. Each level has a pity system in place too, so you will inevitably max out your weapon essence to a 100% perfect BiS state in no time. Gear is the same, except you craft it using factory-made materials instead. Gear has fixed substats, which can also be levelled, again with its own pity system. Endgame players can typically 100% max build a new character in about 5-10 minutes, this is not a game where you get trapped in the gear farming mines for weeks or months on end chasing lottery odds. 

[b]How much time investment does the game require? Can I take a break and come back later?[/b]
Dailies can be as quick or as long as you want, anywhere from 2-10 minutes, and you don't even have to do them every day unless you actually need the extra resources (most players who only build one or two teams don't). This game doesn't punish lapsed players too hard either, you'd only miss out on a limited banner who'd get a rerun eventually anyway and if you're only focusing on your favourite team every other character who doesn't improve your team becomes an easy skip anyway.

[b]Is the story any good? Do I need to know anything about the original Arknights?[/b]
It's a lot better than anyone expected, the early chapters can be rough but once the storytelling hits its stride, Endfield consistently delivers decent to excellent chapters and the character side stories are particularly noteworthy as almost all of them are good. You don't need any context from Arknights to enjoy Endfield, the writers make sure to explain any relevant legacy info for new players.

[b]Should I hyper-invest or build wide?[/b]
Wide, there's no question. Character dupes in this game are much weaker than in other games and characters feel complete with just one copy. Signature weapons are worth pulling (with currency you earn from doing character pulls), but the battle pass lets you choose a second-best option custom-built for every character. Endgame isn't so much about raw DPS checks, but rather solving various mechanical combat puzzles, so the wider your roster is, the more readily you'll be able to counterpick any given stage. Even so, every limited DPS can beat every stage anyway, just with varying difficulty due to stronger or weaker matchups.

[b]TL;DR[/b]: Having played since launch, it has improved a lot. There are still areas it needs to grow but for still being in its first year its come a long way.

[b]Pros:[/b]
* While the art direction is a departure from the original Arknights it still carries a lot of the visual identity from environments to Operator design. 
* English dub voice acting brought back multilingual voice actors, so operators have accents and can speak in their native tongues. I just wish they brought back the option to have individual language settings.
* The combat isn’t the flashiest but the combo trigger system opens a lot of avenues with how you can approach team building. 
* Factory management gets interesting when you get the hang of it. It’s not as deep as dedicated games but for a gacha it's pretty complex. Alternatively, you can completely handwave it by copying blueprints.
* Endgame grind is nearly non-existent; all armor components are produced through the Factory, weapon essences are easy to farm and are upgradeable so no rerolling, and weapon and character materials are quite literally farmed in the main player base.
* Weapon banners have a separate currency from character banners. It kind of goes both ways to be fair since weapon banner currency isn’t as frequently given out, and the amount you get from scouting doesn’t build up fast enough to allow you to pull both to hard pity consistently. 

[b]Neutral:[/b]
* Monetization is weird for me because on one hand I dislike that banner packs offer only offer tickets that expire while on the other hand Origeometry doesn’t really have a function beyond converting it to Oroberyl since there are no skins, so there’s not really a push to whale unless you want to scout every banner.
* The storytelling could be better. 1.4 was a big step up but I wish they brought back character/faction-focused storylines. The game hasn’t been out for a year so its honestly too early to call to be fair.
* I have no strong opinions on the gacha. I save for hard pity/hoard gems in every game I play so all the tiered dohickeys don’t really matter to me.
* There isn’t an Annihilation mode-adjacent yet. I’d have thought Etchspace Salvage was gonna fill that role but so far that’s been abandoned since 1.2 from last I checked. 

[b]Cons:[/b]
* Valley IV and its factions were very underutilized, especially with how long the Wuling story has been going on. Speaking of Wuling, please let us leave fantasy China already.
* The events are a little weak. Contingency Contract is always fun and Echoes of War is fine, but the other ones that were like obstacle courses or even the bow shooting gallery weren’t really it. 
* The whole account login thing is kind of a big oversight. I don't know why they had to have a strict grace period before you can add a different account especially since its just handwaved on other launchers if you log into the wrong account/make a new one by accident.
* Lappland and Texas have yet to be confirmed

Praise to Hypergryph, Glory to Hypergryph

Arknights: Endfield is an ambitious science-fiction action RPG that successfully combines tactical combat, exploration, industrial automation, and character progression into a distinctive adventure. Developed by Hypergryph and published by GRYPHLINE, the game transforms the established Arknights universe into an expansive three-dimensional experience where rebuilding civilization is just as important as defeating enemies. Its greatest attraction lies in the unusual relationship between combat and infrastructure development, offering players a rewarding mixture of strategic planning and action-oriented gameplay.

The story unfolds on Talos-II, a dangerous alien planet where humanity has spent generations recovering from devastating conflicts and environmental disasters. Players assume the role of the Endministrator, a mysterious leader awakening from a prolonged slumber with incomplete memories and an enormous responsibility. As the head of Endfield Industries, the protagonist must explore unfamiliar territories, confront emerging threats, and establish the foundations of a prosperous civilization. The narrative effectively combines personal mystery with broader themes of survival, technological advancement, and cooperation, giving the adventure a meaningful purpose beyond conventional heroism.

Exploration plays an important role in maintaining the game's atmosphere. Talos-II features imposing mountains, winding rivers, industrial installations, and untamed wilderness filled with dangers and opportunities. Players encounter hostile Ankhor forces, investigate mysterious phenomena, and work to eliminate the destructive influence of the Blight. The environments establish a convincing contrast between humanity's technological achievements and the overwhelming scale of the natural world. Discovering new locations feels particularly meaningful because exploration contributes to resource acquisition, territorial expansion, and the continued development of industrial facilities.

Combat emphasizes teamwork rather than relying exclusively on individual character strength. Players command operators with different abilities, coordinating their movements and chaining specialized skills to overcome enemy defenses. Battles reward an understanding of timing, positioning, and character synergy, creating satisfying opportunities for tactical experimentation. The ability to coordinate multiple operators gives encounters additional depth, while the real-time presentation maintains an engaging sense of momentum. However, managing several abilities simultaneously can initially feel overwhelming, especially for players accustomed to simpler action RPG systems.

The Automated Industry Complex is arguably the game's most impressive feature. Rather than treating crafting as a minor supporting activity, Endfield makes industrial production a fundamental part of progression. Players construct manufacturing facilities, establish automated production lines, and organize resources to support exploration and combat operations. The freedom to experiment with factory layouts encourages creativity and optimization, providing a satisfying sense of accomplishment as increasingly sophisticated systems become operational. Watching a carefully planned industrial network function efficiently can be just as rewarding as overcoming a challenging encounter.

Nevertheless, the factory mechanics introduce a substantial learning curve. Players primarily interested in storytelling and combat may find production management unnecessarily complicated, particularly when multiple resources and facilities require attention. The game works best when its systems complement one another naturally, allowing improvements in infrastructure to translate into meaningful advantages elsewhere. Fortunately, the availability of existing production layouts provides a useful starting point for newcomers, while experienced players can pursue more elaborate arrangements.

Character development contributes significantly to the adventure's appeal. Operators possess distinctive appearances, personalities, and combat specialties, encouraging players to experiment with different team compositions. Their involvement in the reconstruction effort also reinforces the narrative's emphasis on collective survival. The anime-inspired character designs complement the futuristic environments, creating an attractive visual identity. Detailed machinery, atmospheric landscapes, and polished combat effects further strengthen the presentation, while the soundtrack and voice performances contribute to the game's immersive science-fiction atmosphere.

The free-to-play structure makes the experience accessible without an initial purchase, although optional in-game transactions remain an important consideration. Character acquisition and progression systems can influence long-term enjoyment, particularly when players become invested in assembling specific teams. Maintaining a reasonable balance between free progression and paid conveniences is essential. Additionally, the interconnected gameplay systems may occasionally feel repetitive when resource gathering, equipment improvements, and industrial maintenance compete with the desire to advance the story.

Technical requirements are another consideration. The game recommends 16 GB of RAM, an Intel Core i7-10700K processor, and an NVIDIA GeForce RTX 2060, with approximately 60 GB of storage listed on Steam. Its combination of detailed environments and interconnected gameplay systems makes capable hardware desirable. Players must also use a GRYPHLINE account, and the inclusion of kernel-level Anti-Cheat Expert software may concern those who prefer less intrusive security implementations.

Regarding Steam Deck compatibility, Arknights: Endfield is officially classified as Unsupported on Steam. Valve indicates that support for Steam Deck and SteamOS is still being worked on, meaning handheld users should not expect reliable compatibility through the standard SteamOS environment. The game's anti-cheat implementation presents an additional potential obstacle. Players primarily interested in portable gaming should consider this limitation before investing significant time in the Steam version.

Overall, Arknights: Endfield stands out through its creative combination of industrial simulation and tactical action RPG mechanics. Its atmospheric world, engaging team-based battles, distinctive factory construction, and ambitious narrative establish a compelling foundation for long-term enjoyment. Although its complicated progression systems, monetization considerations, technical demands, and lack of Steam Deck support prevent it from being universally accessible, the experience offers considerable depth for players willing to embrace its complexity. It is particularly appealing to those who enjoy strategic experimentation, character collection, and the satisfaction of building something substantial within an evolving fictional world.

This is a fun game that I think is worth playing hence my recommendation. It's not a particularly fun live-service game that I recommend heavily investing into. Updates are quite slow, events are mostly basic, and you're also still dealing with limited Hoyo-esque character banners which are the main FOMO-inducing aspects of the gacha presented. 

It's frustrating that even if you are lucky to get a character early, you are encouraged to pull more if you also want their signature weapon. If you're okay with the battle pass weapons being anywhere from 5 to 20ish% weaker give or take depending on the character (which is usually fine given that endgame is not particularly fun either), then you can ignore this. If you see yourself logging in every day and claiming your monthly card daily bonus and doing your BP, you will have enough currency to get a lot of the limited characters, but getting **everyone** as they come out will either cost you nothing if you're lucky, or a good chunk of your wallet but considerably less than other AAA-budget gacha games depending on if you're getting their gacha weapon too.

The gameplay is mostly fun. I enjoy that I don't have to switch characters constantly, if at all, but you can if you want to. It's possible to access all the character's skills without needing to swap constantly. You just can't control their regular attacks which some characters may either prefer, or force you to control them when using their ultimate. I like that your whole party is fighting with you in battle and running around with you in the open world. Dodging feels generally good, and you really want to make sure you pay attention to not just the red flashes but the animations of the enemies to anticipate what's coming. The fun team combos are quite dependent on what all characters you have, which may lead you to the gacha screen.

The base building will not hit for everyone. I find it fun, but tedious as each update makes it feel like you need to swap things around. They recently tried to make it easier to do this but you will still have to do it for certain updates esp if there's a new base to build at. Thankfully there are blueprints to help you heavily expedite this process, but it's not always 100% plug and play and you may sometimes come across just bad community blueprints. Again as a game this feature is fun but the live-service aspect can suck a bit of fun out of it. All this to say that if you're a factorio/satisfactory type of player, this is definitely not going to reach those levels, but it may scratch the itch a little bit.

The main story has a few high moments that I enjoyed (and the music is just astounding and elevates moments well, along with incredibly impressive visuals and optimization), but personally I feel it could have been much higher. I say this only because I get the vibe they want to be very careful about presenting your character as anything but perfect (just with amnesia) and characters just praising you constantly, and also devs just trying not to enrage people by not killing or inhibiting any characters that would become a selling point for you later. 

Not that I want characters to die because that can be equally as frustrating to randomly see beloved characters die for the sake of the plot, but if you ever get the vibe that everyone has plot armor *or* you feel like the devs doesn't care about any characters living, it's just hard to be as invested. It's one thing for the main cast to have plot armor because it's a live-service after all. Whether I'm just tired of seeing the same cliches from me seeing this so any times, or something else, that's just how I feel. Gacha games naturally make me a cynic compared to ones that are one and done, because gachas have a deep vested interest to do things with the story and gameplay that make me want to roll even if it's not strictly necessary to progress.

That being said, of most AAA-budget gacha games I've played, this weirdly feels the least FOMO-inducing even if still very present. It at times feels like it didn't want to be a gacha, though I can't describe this feeling very well. A good part of that feeling may be because I was able to progress through the entire main story without being level or time-gated. If you are somehow too low level, you just do some of the many side-quests and collections if you ever are too low of a level, then you can proceed. That's always nice in my book.

Character gear and upgrades have set values so there's no grinding for months trying to get 3% extra crit rate. The game favours strategy and team building over gear score.

Monetisation is fair. You don't have to spend anything but getting the battle pass and monthly pass is plenty for regular players if you want extra pulls.

The surface level main story has your typical glazed amnesiac god protagonist complete with power of friendship themes, but the surrounding world of mega corporations helping to secure safe living conditions for residents of the planet is solid enough. The lore goes deep on this one for those that wish to venture into it as it shares the same world with a 7-year-old game.

This review contains very subjective opinion, glazing, and some comparison based on my day-1 experience (Jan 22, 2026) while playing another six gacha games daily. I can’t cover every aspect with Steam limitation. It’s best to experience by yourself with mindset of gameplay first.

[h1]Poeple of Talos-II[/h1]
In short, Endfield (AKEF) story is all about expanding and rebuilding civilization of planet called Talos-II set roughly 150 years after the events of original Arknights (OG AK). Both games share the same universe, lore, and terminology. No need to play OG AK to understand AKEF, it just gives more context and reference.

Partial amnesia MC can be cliché and the early solid chapters suffer from pacing issue for the sake of mechanic tutorial. But the story has been progressively getting better as developers understand how to fully utilize 3D technique to improve storytelling in each update. Expect slow-burn story which is common in gacha games. But full of charming casts, memorable moments, and revelation to keep you engaging the concept of pushing forward with hope.

[h1]Distinct yet Fascinating Style[/h1]
From the automated AIC technology to methodology of channeling magic from mineral called Originium Arts, I found world building is AKEF’s strongest point. A post-apocalyptic world with dystopian elements disguised as utopian. Animal-like people caused by Originium mutation and other lineages that have evolutionary history are just piece of lore and mythology that shapes unique identity of the game.
[url]https://steamcommunity.com/sharedfiles/filedetails/?id=3820228609[/url]
AKEF aesthetic choice provides perfect combination of sci-fi element and traditional design based on different regions. Clear silhouette design, costume resembling IRL tech wear, UI/UX, and more can be case study. I personally love color palettes and lighting that fit between anime aesthetic and realistic environment. No out of place feelings and pleasing to the eye.

[h1]Explore, Expand, Experiment[/h1]
The core gameplay consists of exploration, AIC factory, and combat. Each of them constantly gets updated and tweaked to keep things fresh. Here’s brief of some gameplay loop you can expect:
- Players explore the area with party (up to 4 members) fight alongside with you, solve world puzzles, discover hidden loots, and platforming using gadget and movement like old adventure games.
- The AIC plays the major role of map/resource navigation and character progression using AIC productivity. Allow players to freely place things like zipline, extractor, turret. Map geometry also affects how you place, giving sense of sandbox play and map utilization. It resembles classic automation simulator like Factorio / Satisfactory.
[url]https://steamcommunity.com/sharedfiles/filedetails/?id=3820228609[/url]
- The full-party combat (inspired by ARPG like Xenoblade Chronicles, Final Fantasy) that emphasize team building, positioning, and reaction timing to maximize physical/art status on enemy. Moreover, the gear system (product of factory) adds extra layer of complexity how players approach team synergy and open up possibilities compared to most heavy-rotation ARPG.

The early game demands time and participation to get basic understanding of automation. Once everything is settled, the progression naturally flows and cover general content/event if you care for pull currency reward. I did test on lv.50 gears and got all rewards including contingency contract (seasonal endgame). Plus, base units are decently strong and versatile for most contents, making the new units totally optional if you really like them.

There’s no shame using online blueprint if you dislike factory aspect or time constraint. Although you still need to manually connect power / pipe to main hub, I don’t think that’s a big deal. Community interaction is part of idea Hypergryph focuses and expand on social platform like SKPORT.
[url]https://steamcommunity.com/sharedfiles/filedetails/?id=3820232223[/url]
Another thing worth mentioning is farming weapon essence which drop RNG stats to keep player grinding. Built-it pity system allows player to upgrade stats using unwanted essence. Failed upgrade yields gel used for guarantee upgrade. Nothing waste in process of maxing out essence. Meanwhile some games could take week/month for a perfect single relic that feels disrespecting my time.

Overall, the depth of team building and introduction of more hybrid units are designed to compensate amount of movesets. Even low-rarity units have their own role to counter stage mechanic. Fun to experiment and master, satisfying to pull off with crispy SFX sound effect and flashy yet readable SFX (except few units). The combat is just pure fun and engaging in its own way especially major boss fights.

[h1]Monetization[/h1]
Talking about limited banner. Yes, people freaked out because of no pity carry over limited banner like other big 3D titles. AKEF doesn’t need that to follow that formula. Mathematically, it has slightly better base rate of 0.8% 6 stars unit and guarantee at 120 pulls, lower ceiling in comparison. First 30 pulls give free 10 pulls and first 60 pulls give free 10-pulls for next banner. Every pull gives you Arsenal Ticket for weapon banner with rate of 4%. Moreover, you can get rate-up unit from previous two banners.

However, the system is best designed to favor for people who plan to guarantee in order to get enough arsenal ticket for 6-star weapon while punishing lucky players that get 6-star unit too early. My concern is lack of option to earn ticket aside from banner/credit. If you approach the game with compulsive gambling mindset for dopamine hit. This is not a game for you.

One the bright side, pulling new 6-star is optional. I don’t feel pressured to pull certain unit for certain stuffs unlike other games. The illusion of generosity in gacha often comes with endgame that rely on dupe-reliance to make that unit feels complete and less clunky to play. I’m glad it doesn’t follow mainstream formula. Base copy unit (potential 0) can clear everything. Even F2P can purchase free battlepass for alternative 5-star weapon which does decent job. A game with low incentive pull and least FOMO is pretty rare nowadays.

[h1]Voice / Soundtrack[/h1]
OG AK has reputation of wide range of music genres (music company!). AKEF is no exception, slowly branching into region-based theme and vocal tracks. There are moments that music does heavy lifting thanks to many artists who bring narrative to life by melody and lyrics.

The voice talents also did outstanding job of diverse regional accents and some native language, adding personality to character. Similar to what they did in OG AK. But again, it’s up to personal preference. Some prefer EN because of the joy of hearing native speakers and some just stick to expressive JP voice.

[h1]Performance[/h1]
AKEF runs on a heavily modified version of Unity engine. Giving dev team fully understand of their capability result in one of most optimized Unity game I experienced so far. Runs very smooth with beautiful effect and baked lighting. Lacking day/night cycle is a trade-off for stable performance and I’m totally fine with it.

My only issue I found is rare texture glitch which related to AMD user and cursor glitch (fixed by disable AMD Enhanced Sync).

[h1]Closing[/h1]
For me, AKEF feels like a good-old single player with live service second. It got overhated because gacha players allergic to something different and tribalism. Doomposting serve no value for me. I just enjoy playing and being immersed. AKEF has strong foundation and can be further improved or changed for company profit. But now I genuinely appreciate Hypergryph passion and communication in perspective of players. Survey do matter as they take action while still stand by their vision and gameplay philosophy over aggressive monetization.

I’m not here to convince anyone. But if you ask me, it feels good to play and comfort to stay.

Before we dive in into the review itself I want to mention that I had been looking forward to the game since the announcement of its development by Hypergryph. [hr][/hr]
[h2] Gameplay [/h2]
Gameplay of Arknights Endfield is quite complex, but more in the sense of offering a bunch of various things to do. The core systems are: combat, factory and exploration.
[b]Combat[/b] is not hard to grasp and offers a lot of room for experimentation. You lead a 4-person squad into battle while controlling one character yourself. Every operator has manually-triggered battle skill, combo skill that procs when certain conditions are met and powerful ult. Also you can dodge and switch the character you control during battles. I played the mobile game, avoided Endfield for a long time because I was already sick of and hated the 3D open-world gacha formula, and only picked it up a few months ago exclusively for the story and characters. Starting late might actually be the only reason I was able to enjoy the game and its story to the fullest, as I didn't have to suffer through the earlier versions or endure months of dry patches just to get to the good parts.

[h3]Story, Soundtrack & Graphics[/h3]
Some people find the story quite boring, but personally, I've found it to range from decent to excellent. I didn't have high expectations, given how the game's formula can limit its potential, but Hypergryph has been nothing short of creative in its approach to storytelling.

The story, presentation, and soundtrack are all a breath of fresh air compared to most 3D gacha games, which mostly consist of talking heads. That said, I admit that the earlier parts of the story are quite slow-paced. I'm also getting tired of the CCP-mandated Chinese region that seems to appear in every 3D gacha game, and I'm glad that it will be over soon.

I don't think I need to say much about the graphics. Honestly, they're among the most polished I've seen in any gacha game, despite Endfield being built in Unity.

[h3]Gameplay[/h3]
The gameplay is fine, again, I mainly play for the story and characters, but so far, I prefer it over the usual quick-swap systems. One detail I particularly like is seeing my other party members follow me around, which reminds me of Xenoblade.

The factory gameplay is fun, even if they're a bit basic. However, some people might dislike this aspect since it requires some brainpower and can take hours to set up.

Gear progression is refreshingly simple as well. There's hardly any RNG to speak of, so you don't have to spend weeks or months farming and praying for the perfect substats. There's also very little FOMO, and premium currency isn't locked behind high-difficulty content. It keeps things relaxed and fun.

That said, the lack of a tower defense mode or tower defense events is quite disappointing.

[h3]Gacha[/h3]
The gacha is whatever. I initially wasn't planning to spend any money on this game, but I ended up liking it enough to spend some of my disposable income each month to support Hypergryph's efforts. Honestly, the game seems far more generous than most. I've been able to get every character and their signature weapon while spending significantly less than I would in other gachas, where I'd usually have to pay at least five times as much. In Endfield, you can realistically get every character and signature weapon just by purchasing the monthly subscription and battle pass.

[hr][/hr]
Overall, Endfield is the most polished gacha game I've played, and it keeps improving with every update.

While the update and event frequency might disappoint people who play nothing but gacha games all day, I find Endfield very friendly toward players who have a life and other hobbies.

That being said, the game's core formula and the need to stay mobile-friendly inevitably limit its potential, particularly when it comes to the factory gameplay and certain other aspects. For that reason, I'll never fully stop hating the 3D open-world gacha formula.

I have played this game every day since its launch roughly 9 months before it came to Steam so add roughly 80-100 hours to my Steam time. This game is another example of why Hypergryph is so respected in the gacha space. Their ethic towards the player and monetization really shines. Do not feel forced to rush through this game as a newbie. Take your time and work through it slowly but surely at your own pace.

Daily Play: Great balance of fun stuff to do without turning into a daily chore. Game time goes up during each major update to complete new content and try out new stuff. Then a clear and easy flow sets in for daily players that keeps daily grind reasonable and satisfying. Having a game where partner AIs in your team actually feel helpful and relevant is great. 

Combat: They have got it to where you can play one character and half-control the other 3 while the AI picks up the other halves of their functions for you. I very rarely have any issues in combat with the partner AIs doing dumb stuff or not helping where I want them too. They are also good about not getting their butts kicked and dying on me. Unlike some games where the skills and mechanics get really complicated, Endfield has a good balance of keeping things understandable without being boringly simple. Take your time learning the combat over the long-term the deeper mechanics make sense after doing it for a bit.

The Factory: If you enjoy factory games you will love this system, even if it purposefully does not go as hardcore as dedicated factory management games. The reason for this though is those of you who do not want to put up with that type of gameplay can easily do it casually or simply import factory designs from online. Lot of great blueprint makers on the web. I find that over time the factory stuff grows on folks to where they start doing more and more of it themselves or do like I do and import a min-maxed factory and then learn what actually makes it min-maxed so I can tweak it and reverse engineer it as I see fit over subsequent patches.

The Gacha: As I mentioned at the start, Gryph is pretty well known for being better than other gacha companies in terms of respecting player's time and money. It is very easy to stay F2P if you so choose but if you are willing to pay a bit here and there you will get good value each patch for buying one or two of the packs and helping sustain the game. The gacha rates themselves are not the best, as it is very very hard to get more than one of a character, but thankfully getting duplicates of a unit or weapon is not really needed. I encourage you to stick to just a base copy of characters you want/need and only go "all in" for someone you personally like and want to 100%.

I would say it is pretty easy to learn, though if u want to make the most efficient and compact factories possible it can become quite a challenge. 
I've probably spent most my time building as efficient and compact factories as I could and really enjoyed it.
There is a blueprint function where u can place down pre-made factories, though they aren't very good. 
U can also make ur own blueprints to save a design or share with ur friends/other players. 
I would recommend the top-down view when building but that's just my personal preference. 
-
[h2] Combat: [/h2]
The combat feels good but is pretty different from other gacha games, so could take some time to get used to. 
The bosses and enemies are pretty diverse and have different attacks and ''elements''.
The boss fights all have cool animations and unique attacks. Most aren't too difficult but also not too easy. 
[spoiler] I struggled a LOT with the 3rd boss so make sure to be well prepared. [/spoiler]
-
[h2] Characters and Builds: [/h2]
All the character models are very detailed and high quality, though 4* and 5* characters are a bit less detailed than the 6* just like most gacha games.
The ''Gear'' system is pretty easy to understand the basics though hard to master. It doesn't have any RNG compared to some other gacha games like for example Genshin Impact's ''Artifacts''. 
Which weapons are good on different characters is easy to know as there is a ''Recommended Weapons'' button.
-
[h2] World Exploration: [/h2]
The different areas of the world are diverse and beautiful, but the game sadly is ''Semi-Open World'' and feels quite ''locked down'' compared to other open world gacha games. 
I don't really enjoy exploration as I prefer the freedom u get in other games but that's just my personal opinion.
-
[h2] Story and Lore: [/h2]
I've mostly skipped though the main story but it for sure has a bunch of lore to explore if u like that. 
-
[h2] Graphics and Optimization: [/h2]
The game is very beautiful and well optimized. I get 80-120FPS at 1440p (DLSS Quality) with everything at max settings.

-
[h2] Audio and Soundtrack: [/h2]

A nice touch is the different regional ''accents'' some characters have (maybe some NPCs too idk forgot)
