Do not let the hourse fool you. I have spent hundreds of hours in it, also on Steam as a third party game. I will keep my review as spoiler free as I can.

The game runs incredibly smooth and looks stunning. A lot better than WuWa with its UE4 WITHOUT turning my PC into a jet engine. The computer is usually very quiet during the game and rarily spins up.

UI is the cleanest I have seen in any gacha game and I immediately grasped how it was constructed. Same with the controls.

Gameplay is very unique as control you walk around and fight with your entire 4 people team instead of a singular character. You still control one character primarily, but you are free to switch between them and none of their abilities is automated except basic attacks. You are in full control. It is less about you doing flashy stuff than your team working together and supporting each other with abilities and combos. The AI is usually very decent at dodging and seems to be tied to how well you avoid abilties too.
The combat is overall not too hard outside of the endgame content like Contigency Contract and from the feeling is somewhere around Monster Hunter World with very clearly telegraphed attacks and very responsive characters.
Speaking of which is the uniqueness of the fights. Instead of HP inflation in other games, you get actual boss mechanics straight out of Heroic/Mythic MMO runs. Once you get to the second boss in the game in Valley IV, you will see what I mean. Once you get to the final boss in Wuling, you should be in love with how these fights and that they go beyond other games that are usually glazed a lot more. Hypergryph is a music studio after all that decided to make games.

Valley IV functions as a tutorial stage to explain the setting to you and is rather slow and could use some more love. Wuling, especially the finale is where the pace is picking up and you can see OGknights writing and design by Hypergryph showing through and it gets finally darker in the story. Hopefully more of the mature storytelling in the near future. Overall the storytelling is phenomenal, many characters I did not like intially grew onto me on how things were told and shown to me. Even NPCs you only briefly meet.

The voice acting is incredible. Just like OGknights, hiring native speakers to give them the perfect accent and way of speaking makes the come alive + music sung in a language that is basically dead? Yeah, of course Endfield has that.

The next big standout are the puzzles that are not merely petty distractions, but sometimes require some actual brain activity and are generally fun to engage with for the rewards.

What also requires brain activity is the factory system that Endfield uses for its ingame shop and lategame gear. People who played and love Satisfactory or Factorio, this is for you. For the rest of us it is reddit or KyoStinV. Seriously, what can this guy not do well?

For completitionist, you do need external tools to fully find every chest, the game has purchasable sensors for that.

Anyhow, lets talk about the biggest thing in this that stands positively out among all gacha competitors. The gacha system and monetisation. It highly rewards low spending of around 15€ a month by buying the monthly card + the battlepass.
 
The battlepass comes in three sections. The first row is free. The second row costs Origeometry, which is farmable and if you play through the pass, you get back more than what you invested. The third row is what you buy with real money and has the biggest rewards. Not that the other rows would be bad, as they are essentially free. What stands out are two things: 1. There is an overflow system actually giving you gacha currency if you stack the battlepass over its maximum level 2. The last week has a catch-up system making 1 even more profitable.

Similar goes for the Headhunting Gacha. While I am incredibly unlucky, I never had issues finally getting a character at the 120 hard pity. Hypergryph gives out enough tickets and ressources to acquire them. Furthermore, there is rarily a moment where you really need to stack mutliple copies of a character to acquire more limit break buffs going for S5, which I really appreciate as they do not give absurd damage or other boni.
In addition, the Gacha system helps you on low pulls and further pulls. After 30 pulls on a new banner, you get one FREE 10 Pull (Not counted towards pity), after 60 you get one FREE 10 Pull on the next banner. On a re-run banner, you get the FREE 10 roll at 30, 60,90 and so on. The free 10-pulls earned along the way do not count toward your progress for the 120-pull selector guarantee. Progress and free-pull bonuses can carry over across parts/reruns of the same banner series.
Yes Endfield has a weapon system too, but it is bound to the Headhunting Gacha. So while getting cool characters, you acquire the ressources needed for their weapons without extorting more money out of you.

Glory to Hypergryph!

So who is Endfield for? The OGknight players that want to play in 3D, oldschool MMO players that like cool and challenging bossfights, factory builders and people more interested in a mature storytelling compared to similar titles. We have not reached the head on a plate moment yet of "Hortus de Escapismo" in OGknights, but one can hope for the future.

DO NOT listen to online opinion pieces and especially not most gacha players' opinions when it comes to to this game (or any game for that matter). Arknights: Endfield. What a fascinating game this is.
I spend little to no money on free-to-play games, so gacha mechanics are very unappealing to me. However, I was drawn to the setting, open world exploration, and the AIC factory. So I gave it a try.



[h1] The Gacha [/h1]
I am pleased to report the gacha part of this game actually feels fair. Part of that is simply because I just got plain lucky, so I can't help but have some bias. I pulled my favourite operator [Pogranichnik] somewhat early into the game. But even if I didn't get lucky, all players were given an item to get whatever 6* character they wanted for free at the time. It has no expiry date, and I don't really want any other operators, nor a minor % bonus to Pogranichnik's power, so it sits in my inventory.

I must also mention that at no point did I feel it necessary to grind or gamble on gacha to progress through the main story. I could make my operators stronger, but it would only be necessary for completing dedicated challenging game modes like Echoes of War and getting their rewards.

That said, it [i] is [/i] a gacha game. With FOMO, daily and weekly challenges, gambling, and a lot of very bright and shiny things to buy in the store with real money. If you're someone who is vulnerable to that sort of thing, I cannot in good conscience recommend this game to you.



[h1] The Factory [/h1]
The early game AIC factory building gameplay could be better. It takes longer than I'd like just to unlock the thing, and even longer to unlock automation recipes that are remotely challenging to optimize. You see, factory progression is locked behind main story progression. And there are a lot of main story quests to do.

The early game in general has a lot of tutorial pop ups. Too many. And even more so in the early game AIC factory. Just try to bear with it.

The late game AIC factory building gameplay is very fun. There is enough mechanics to consider that I am rarely certain that what I have built is optimal, and that is exactly what I want to see in my automation games! It is complex, yet fair.

And the reward? You get some much appreciated progression material at first, but no more after you buy out their stock with factory tickets. What is consistent is that the factory will be your main source of gear and healing items throughout the game.

There's also AIC factory events! For about a month, a handful of new recipes are available for automation with some progression materials as incentive. These are the only events that I like. Apart from that one space event. That was nice too.

It is unfortunate that my factory in Valley IV has no real purpose right now. I have a setup which outputs a modest rate of factory tickets, but nothing good to exchange it for! Even the endgame gear requires recipes that you have to automate outside Valley IV.

You can also just use blueprints made my other players, if you really don't want to play with factories.



[h1] The Writing [/h1]
Oof. The writing in the early game is not good. The antagonists do not feel threatening, and I am not emotionally attached to anyone in the story. The player character is often praised for things that are impossible to fail, which feels really weird.

And that is such a shame because the writing in the main story does improve later on, and the writing for the operators' backstories is phenomenal! I'm talking about the text largely locked behind a trust stat of each operator's profile. Reading Pogranichnik's profile was my favourite part of this whole game.

But alas, I doubt we will ever get more written about Pogranichnik. It's just not as profitable to make new content about old characters. A fate which I hear is all too common in other gacha games.



[h1] The Music [/h1]
The combat music is adequate. Not particularly memorable. But the rest of the soundtrack is magnificent! It really brings the game to life. A fine addition to my collection of video game lofi!



[h1] The Exploration [/h1]
This game is open world with structures that you can build. These structures can even appear in other players' worlds! Kinda like Death Stranding. I love Death Stranding! So how does it compare? 

Well, it fails to capture the same vibe. Death Stranding's world is harsh, unforgiving, and dangerous. The very terrain is a literal obstacle, and therefore player built structures often make the game much easier in a way that encourages cooperation.

Arknights: Endfield has a lot more enemies, there's no doubt. But it's also a power fantasy. The enemies never feel scary, and walking is often easier than setting up a zipline. You can build automatic turrets to appear in other player's worlds, something that Death Stranding does not have. But I never thought to myself 'Yes, a turret here would really help out the next guy. I should build one.', it was more like 'This spot spawns a lot of enemies with loot I want. I could fight them, but I don’t want to. Deconstruct all of my previous turrets and rebuild them here.' and any turrets that happened to be already built there by other players did not feel like they made any difference.

I am aware there are also delivery missions in this game, but that too does not capture the same joy I had when playing Death Stranding. Also these missions pay in factory tickets, which I have already automated plenty of.



[h1] The Combat [/h1]
Right. This game has combat, so I should probably mention it. It's alright. By far most the most challenging part of this game's combat is reading and comprehending your operators' abilities and passives.

[i] Let me give you an example. Pogranichnik is a physical damage character who is great at SP generation. But he needs another operator to generate vulnerability stacks for Pogranichnik's kit to function. Chen is great at just that, stacking passive damage bonuses every time you push a button with her. But if you let Lifeng apply the first vulnerability debuff, you get even more damage bonuses. And Da Pan does more damage with his combo skill, but only if you generate exactly four stacks of vulnerability. So there's a certain rotation of buttons to press for optimal DPS, depending on who you have in your party. Executing the rotation is easy. Figuring out the rotation is hard. [/i]

If you understood none of what I wrote above, that's fine. You can get through the main story just by mashing buttons, even with a group of just the three free operators you start with plus anyone else.



[h1] Conclusion [/h1]
I enjoyed this game, and will continue to do so. But would I recommend to someone who loves Factorio or Death Stranding? Eh, no.

This is a game for those who enjoy open world questing, like in Final Fantasy XIV.

[h1]Preface[/h1]
Arknights: Endfield is a "Strategic" Action RPG with Factory Sim Gacha game, quoting the strategic because you will start questioning of how much strategic this game actually is, and ill let you decide yourself. Endfield was a Sequel and Spin-off set 150+ years after of the game "Arknights" a RTS Tower Defense Mobile Gacha game (there is a PC client tho), both developed by Hypergryph.

[h1]Gameplay (8/10)[/h1]
In Endfield you will play as The Endministrator, another gacha main character who lose their memory. You are leading Endfield Industries an independent company that pioneer the research, exploration and industrial development of Talos-II, hence the infamous and unique Factory Sim gameplay.

Not gonna talk much about the factory since i dont really have the knowledge and experience of the genre. The factory building feel pretty casual even for a newcomer like me in the genre. the factory building is one of the major gameplay that will play a big role in farming for materials, consumable and character gear (Artifact in Genshin, Echo in wuwa) and yes they fully run afk once you set them up even when you logout from the game. if you dont really like factory building there is a blueprint system that you can copy and paste from other player, but still you pretty much need to understand the basic through the tutorial, if not i dont see the point of playing the game.

And for the combat, yes its action but not that quick and flashy combat like Wuwa or ZZZ, its pretty slower and "strategic". Again while this strategic element of the game are pretty debatable but i will tell you what i feel is the intention of the dev in their vision for this game to be strategic. You will control 4 Operator in a team where they altogether present on the field which is pretty fresh and neat. There will be various Classes, Elements, and Weapon Type for the Operators to build a team. The team building in Endfield is super flexibel compared to others due to how the Operators are designed to have various synergy with other Operator. And complete it with various enemies match up it finally show what is the dev intention for the strategic aspect of this game. It maybe not feel like it at first and i understand because that is what i feel when i just start the game, but later on when you reach the early hard content "Umbral Monument" and "Echoes of War" and the real infamous end game hard content "Contingency Contract" it really shows the strategic aspect the dev intended.

[h1]Narrative (7/10)[/h1]
Sadly, as an Arknights avid reader. Endfield story is pretty dissapointing for me. The story revolve a lot on main character, The Endministrator, to the point of many stuff happened with Endmin in it, sometimes it does neccessary, and sometimes it does not. tho its pretty understandable due to its a 3D game where the strory telling are so different than Arknights with its Visual Novel story telling.

But actually its still pretty enjoyable, except all the relationship bait of Endmin with other character that most of the time feel cheap and unnecessary. and with all the story progress until now after 10 months since the release, it grows pretty good tho stagnant still. and with the recent special program that reveal the direction of Endfield in the future, it looks promising. The lore and worldbuilding are really good, especially with its connection with Arknights. there is a lot of reference here and there but please dont be discouraged and feel the need to cover the first game, you could start from Endfield just fine.

[h1]Visual (10/10)[/h1]
The strongest aspect of this game, its visual and aesthetics, and its amazing. They really put a tons of effort in their visuals, the stylized atmosphere with their fixed lighting, the art style and design of their character with high quality models and texture, the map, scenery and environmental design, and UI/UX design are phenomenal. im loving it.

[h1]Music and Sound Design (9/10)[/h1]
Hypergryph are well known as a music company in a facade of a game dev. i really love many of the OSTs especially the bgm of various map, and even soundtrack for the map introduction. The sound design are well made too, from the menu to the world its really good, even each Operator have their own unique step sound, pretty neat right.

[h1]Gacha[/h1]
The gacha are okay-ish, its pretty good with the Operator gacha, but the Weapon gacha are pretty problematic for me, you will get the Weapon gacha currency from pulling the Character banner and it will be the main source of income. the other source are exist but pretty unrealible. You will find yourself needing to pull and mess with your Character banner pity just to gain Weapon banner pulls.

Story and lore is extremely indepth with immersive world building, great English voice overs.

There are FPS stutter issues that result in massive FPS drops in some areas of the game. Performance issues arise mainly when around your AIC (Factory building part of the game) or when quickly navigating the UI/character menu. My framerate will drop from 120 FPS down to 25-35 and stay locked on it until I restart the game or reload an area. 

Character designs are detailed and varied. Progression system is very detailed but easy to understand along with a gear system so you can equip your characters with armor and weapons. Additionally your unlocked companions can be 'assigned' to areas of the game to provide stat boosts to production of items, moral and trust gain. You unlock more of these options as you progress through the main story.

Some of the music has a Dues Ex vibe and suits the science fiction setting of the game. There's a lot of different music tracks. 

Along with the resource gathering, factory building, combat you also get to upgrade your own space ship and outposts. 

This game is well worth jumping in to atleast see if you like it considering it is free to play. 

Downsides include the gacha system where you appear to need to hit hard pity all the time before getting the featured weapon via the ingame charter system. 

Another big negative is the factory building. It starts off simple and fun. But in Wulang each new area adds more complexity and new materials. Now it feels like you need a university degree with the amount of complexity just to produce some parts to craft gear. The early area of Wulang is fine. The later areas are a struggle and grind. You will waste hours and even whole days only on that. It's too much. 

This would explain why the game is struggling to retain playerbase.

[h1][b]Arknights: Endfield | A Game That Won Me Over Until the Very End[/b][/h1]

150+ hours played (including the standalone launcher) | Recommended

I want to look at Arknights: Endfield from two perspectives: as objectively as possible, and through the eyes of someone who genuinely loves this game.

[h1][b]The Fan Perspective: The Love Is in the Details[/b][/h1]

What makes Endfield so special to me isn't simply its attractive characters. Hypergryph manages to create characters who feel like more than just fan-service designs. Of course, some characters are clearly designed to appeal to certain tastes, but I get the impression that they have their own identities and exist beyond that purpose. The attention to detail in their clothing, expressions, movements, and animations is outstanding. Everything feels smooth, deliberate, and believable.

The world itself is a visual treat. I rarely stop so often in a game just to look around, admire the scenery, or inspect small details. Endfield makes exploration feel rewarding even when you're not actively completing a quest.

Compared with other games in the genre, such as NTE, I personally find Endfield's character presentation and animations particularly impressive. It's the kind of craftsmanship that makes me appreciate the work behind the game.

[h1][b]The Factory System: More Than Just a Side Activity[/b][/h1]

One of Endfield's most distinctive features is its factory gameplay. You build and expand your own production network, manufacture consumables and equipment materials, and gradually automate more of your resource production.

The available space and resources can feel restrictive early on, but as your network develops, you gain more room to optimize and expand. There is a surprising amount of complexity here, especially for players who enjoy logistics and production chains.

That said, don't expect something on the scale of Satisfactory. Endfield offers a more streamlined version of factory building, designed to complement the RPG rather than replace it. And importantly, you don't have to be a factory enthusiast to progress through the game. Blueprints shared by the community can also make the system much more approachable.

[h1][b]Story and Content[/b][/h1]

The story takes some time to get going. The beginning introduces the world, its characters, and its underlying conflicts, which can make the pacing feel slow at first. But once the narrative gets going, it delivers some genuinely exciting and memorable moments. Personally, I found parts of Endfield's story exceptionally engaging.

There is also plenty to do while progressing through the game, especially for newcomers. Events and regular updates continue to add new activities and content.

However, players who have reached the current endgame may find the experience more repetitive. Permanent challenge content exists, but much of it revolves around relatively linear combat encounters across different difficulty levels. Compared with the more developed endgame activities in games like Wuthering Waves or Honkai: Star Rail, Endfield still has room to grow.

That's not necessarily a deal-breaker for me. The game launched in January 2026, and I believe it deserves time to develop its long-term content. Still, I hope to see more varied endgame activities that give players a reason to keep improving their characters and teams.

[h1][b]The Objective Perspective: Combat, Progression and Gacha[/b][/h1]

Endfield is a free-to-play gacha RPG. You can enjoy the game without spending money, but collecting every character and maximizing their potential are two very different goals.

I've personally spent around €15 per month on the game and currently own almost every available character. That's my experience, not a guarantee that the same budget will work for everyone. Your results depend on your pull resources, luck, and how carefully you plan your spending.

The character banners deserve a closer look. The featured 6-star Operator generally has a 50% rate when a 6-star is obtained, but Endfield does not use the familiar system where losing that 50/50 guarantees the featured character on the next 6-star pull. Instead, the featured Operator can be guaranteed within 120 pulls through the banner's guarantee system. This makes planning important, particularly if you want a specific character.

Weapons are another part of character progression. Each Operator benefits from different weapon stats and effects, and signature weapons can make a build stronger. However, I don't consider signature weapons mandatory for enjoying the game or clearing its content. Alternative weapons are available, and the difference matters more to players who want to optimize their teams as much as possible.

For me, this is where the monetization can become frustrating. Getting every character is one thing; collecting every signature weapon and maximizing every character is another. Players who chase perfection should be prepared for significantly higher costs.

[h1][b]What Could Be Better?[/b][/h1]

Beyond the endgame, I see a few areas that could use improvement:

Story pacing: The opening takes time to establish its world and may not hook every player immediately.

Repetitive endgame: Permanent combat challenges offer something to do, but they could use more variety and more meaningful long-term goals.

Factory complexity: The production system is a major strength, but it can also feel overwhelming before you understand how everything connects.

Gacha uncertainty: The banner guarantee helps, but obtaining specific characters can still require substantial planning and resources.

None of these points ruin the experience for me. They are areas where I believe Endfield could become even better.

[h1][b]My Final Verdict[/b][/h1] 💙💙💙

Arknights: Endfield is a game that won me over through its world, its characters, its animations, and its attention to detail. The factory system gives it a distinctive identity, while the story provides some genuinely memorable moments.

Objectively, the game still needs a more varied endgame and could improve its pacing and progression systems. Its gacha mechanics also mean that collecting everything isn't realistic for every player without spending.

But despite those weaknesses, I keep coming back because I enjoy being in this world. That's what matters most to me.

It took a while, but thankfully customer support sorted out this bizarre login system and I won't have to wait until April 2027 to sign in with my account (lol). Now I can review the game properly.

Endfield has some of the most phenomenal character designs and visuals for any mobile port I've ever seen. The team's dedication to worldbuilding, visual designs, and quality of cutscenes (which is difficult to do when there are so many) is indeed admirable. Going with different accents instead of cookie-cutter voice actors is incredibly refreshing, and the gear system, compared to other games, is such a breath of fresh air.

And the factory? Well, the most notable downsides of the system fall in to two categories. The game is designed to allow players who don't wish to engage much with the factory to copy-paste blueprints and be done with it. This is stopped by 1.) Excessively long tutorial screens, even beyond the factory, and 2.) The way certain materials (gas) is extracted means many hours spent tediously coordinating supplying your factory.

There's also the annoyance of having to tear down and the factory every new update.

And the gacha system? People say, with how much harder it is to hit pity, it is worse than other systems. From my observations, it is indeed much harder to get characters, but much easier to get their weapons. To me, this means this game is less f2p friendly for casual players who only sometimes log in, but more normal for everyday players, who in the process of pulling a character will certainly get the currency required to get their weapon, instead of it being a separate banner that also uses oroberyls. This is also somewhat allieviated, however, by character dupes not being nearly as detrimental as they are in other games.

Apart from these certain grievances with the factory, and as well the gacha system (perhaps slightly lowering the oroberyl price from a stunning 5,000?) the game is a phenomenal, quality example of what happens when the art team is allowed to work their magic and the rest are dedicated to the game's quality.

Endfield is the only third person action gacha game I played continuously for longer than other gachas. Played from day 1, with 400 hours of playtime according to AMD Adrenaline, and have been enjoying it since. I like the factory building. I like the story and world building. I like it's overall aesthetic and style. I find the combat satisfying and the control feels nice. The character progression is good so far. For a gacha game, it respects my time a lot. It's relatively new, so it still lack late game contents.
Positive experiences overall, so I recommended it.

[b]Long version[/b]:
Factory building is my main interest in playing the game. I really like the factory building in Endfield. While of course it is not comparable to something dedicated like Factorio or Satisfactory, it served its purpose for the gameplay. If you expect deep factory mechanic like those two, this game is not for you.
The factory makes Endfield so much less grindy compared to other gacha games because it automatically grinds the necessary materials for me.
Though, the factory building itself can be frustrating and time consuming, especially when new contents for the factory dropped. Since I always built them myself, I can spend hours tweaking, improving, and even rebuilding the factory until it is stable and yields good output. Despite that, it's a build-and-forget feature. For me, it's only every 3-6 weeks when I have to do maintenance on those factories.
There is a blueprint mechanic that let you share your factory layout with other players. This way you don't even need to build them yourself. Though I like building it myself so I didn't really use it.
Also, not only you can place machines in a designated factory area, you can also place some machines and facilities outside, and some facilities placed outside is shared to other players, it's similar with DEATH STRANDING I think.
Then, there's the management side of the factory, with it's own currency called bills. It is one of the goals of the factory. Every region have different bills, and it's required for unlocking things in that region. You can trade factory products for lots of bills, then you can use it to buy items. Also, there's a mini stock market mechanics, courier minigame, and others sources to acquire more bills.

Now overall story and world building. For context, I played OG Arknights before. In AK, I always liked its overall vibe like the dark mood, and dystopian world setting. While AK narratives feels a bit realistic (idk how to say it, like there are things that can and does happen irl), Endfield so far feels more fantasy-ish and more futuristic, also the vibe is a lot brighter too.
Though it has been very enjoyable for me. From main storyline, character stories, and some side stories, they're awesome. It's one of the reasons I still playing the game. And also one of the reason I'm returning to AK again when the PC client is released.

For overall look and presentation, I like the semi-realistic graphics and less cartoony looks of Endfield. I also like the general tone that's less vibrant than other games.
The places looks gorgeous and stunning. I also like the setting that the planet we are in is orbiting a gas giant and we can look at it on the sky.
Facilities you built overworld blends with surrounding area and doesn't look out of place.
Character designs are awesome and cool. Always liked them since AK.
The musics is awesome. Exploration BGM blends nicely with the area and atmosphere and pleasant to listen to when exploring. Combat BGMs are bangers. And music released outside of the game is awesome too.
I also really like the stylistic graphic design shown on some screen and UI.

For my experience in combat mechanics, I don't have much experience on 3D action gacha combats outside Endfield. I do find the combat in Endfield quite satisfying and very nice to control.
I like the slow-mo dodge animation, a bit reminded me of NieR, feels satisfying whenever I perfectly dodge attacks.
Now, I have to talk about a mechanic that I always nitpick from these 3D gacha games. Usually, when you have a team, you have to switch between characters in order to do combos with them, I find it feels awkward, therefore I didn't really like it. In Endfield, all characters in your team are deployed and fight with you in combat, you just tap keys to do combos, it feels so good to control. One downside of this is when you need an enemy to lock to you, it can instead lock to the other characters and get in your way. Despite that, Endfield hit the nail of that nitpicky mechanics I didn't like from other games, it is another reason I kept playing this game. Though, you DO able to switch characters mid-combat, but there's currently no reason for it, at least for me. Also, when exploring, your teams interacts with their surroundings, like help picking drop items, and sometime calls you for things like hidden chests, it's very neat.

Character progression is good, quite easy, and not complicated in my experience.
Character and weapon EXP mats is mostly passive, they're produced automatically in the base, or as event rewards. If desperate, the stages drop rate is fine.
Some materials you get from around the world is usually enough if you pick them once a week, at least for me (they refill 2 items everyday). Having Zipline setups for these deposits helps tremendously.
The gear system is awesome right now. Gear stats is fixed, no RNG. Gear materials and enhancements are obtained through factory products and incomes, so the gears is very much automatic.
Weapon essence farming can be automatic as well. You get those from overworld arenas. You can just build turrets around it and watch them finish the fight for you, you only need to manually activate it and claim the reward.
A handful of high grade materials do needed to be farmed in stages manually.

For dailies, Endfield is very respectful to your time, some even think it's not good for the game itself. My dailies in Endfield is quick. Usually around 5-10 min when there's absolutely no additional thing to do. It's not grindy for a gacha game too, which I appreciate very much.
Endfield is relatively new compared to other gacha games, so the late game content is still lacking. It does have some late game contents released. The notable contents that I enjoyed currently is Echoes of War and Contingency Contract (CC). With those two, I finally have a reason to properly build my characters. Echoes of War is similar to those timed arenas from other gachas. And for CC, it's originated from AK, and it's always been my favorite game mode, the devs still nails it in Endfield. 
Headhunting (it's gacha system) is okay, it's not a problem for me. I only get who I really want, and skips who I don't want (even meta).
Although, I don't like signature weapon gacha. This applies to all gacha games with similar thing. Like, why do I have to pull for their weapons as well???

All that said, my overall experience is positive. I enjoyed my time playing Endfield. Will likely to play it more until I can't for whatever reason.

For those who are not cavemen, this review will be broken into 6 sections starting with:

[h3][Gacha][/h3]
The cash milking system in this game is… comparably one of the most F2P friendly gachas out there. You can obtain the featured character on the 120th pull, guaranteed 6* on the 80th pull, and weapon banner currency comes from pulling on the character banner. If you obtain a 6* before the 120th pull, there is a 50/50 chance to get the character, but losing the 50/50 can reward any featured character from the last two featured banners. To point out a negative of this system, getting characters early will yield in not getting any weapon banner currency and there is no significant way in the game to earn said currency. However, every character gets a free alternative weapon that can be obtained in the battle pass. I’ve personally have been lucky enough to earn all characters except 3 as of now, and out of those featured character’s only 2 of them do not have their featured weapon. So far, I have been completely F2P. This is my experience, yours might not be so lucky, just a warning.

[h3][Combat / Gear][/h3]
When the game first launched I thought the combat sucked, but now after fully understanding it, it has become one of the favorite. It’s not that flashy, and flashiness there never gets in your way. Critical thinking is needed for certain fights. Bosses have actually mechanics instead of being just being HP sponged meat bags (but not in the early game. Mechanics start to ramp up as the game progresses.) To accommodate this, the team building in the game is really good. So many characters can work with others because the game uses a few core system that most characters specialize in. So because of this you end up with the obvious meta teams, but also some wacky teams, and “this going way better than I expected” teams. But these teams need gear and this is where once again Endfield shines. Unlike every popular 3D gacha game, there isn’t any randomize sub-stat gear in this game. There are two forms of gear: Gear and Artifacts. Gear is crafted and will have predetermined stats. Artifacts come will random stats (wait, let me explain) but when farming them you can pick some stats that are guaranteed to roll. And the stats you are trying to roll are more like main stats. After you get the Gear / Artifacts you need, you just have to level them and leveling them is like playing a very generous Korean MMO.

[h3][Story][/h3]
Alright, the story is pretty mid in the beginning of the game but does become less mid by the middle. For me personally, the story does not start to get good until you start to reach the end of the Wuling arc (Yinglung Pass and beyond). Just as a warning, the story is filled with vague posting but I feel like it’s intentional and not because the writers have no idea for what’s next. Endfield’s story is simultaneously telling two plot lines at the same time: the current objective at hand and the history of the Endmin (vaguely, of course). And no, previous knowledge of the first Arknights game is not needed but it does help (I am currently reading it myself). Another thing is characters actively feel like they belong in the world as they exist well before or after their banner (depending on the region). Characters don’t meet you for the first time, trauma dump their entire life’s story on you will pretending your some romantic interest, then leave you after they get what they wanted. Sadly, every character will treat you with no hostility like 99% of the time. The story presentation in this game is top notch. The transitions from and to gameplay, cinematic shots when entering new areas or when a new boss is revealed, English voice work has accents for the characters, and the music is just…

[h3][Music and Sound Design][/h3]
Do yourself a favor and get some good headphones or have a nice audio setup. The music and sound design of this game is really good, but I do think that the music is class above the rest. In this game music is not just background filler, it used as a tool to emphasize moments in the story, the cinematics, and in combat scenarios. Just to give an example, the music for the boss fight Alleikhreos. [b][u]DO NOT GO AND LISTEN TO THE MUSIC UNTIL AFTER YOU’VE BEATEN THE BOSS.[/u][/b] The reason is because it contains story spoilers and the music fits in perfectly with the cutscenes. Listening to the 4 tracks (yes, four) of this boss fight before fighting the boss will absolutely ruin the first time experience. However, if you refuse to heed my warning, the safest track to listen to is ACHERON. Crywolf and YMIR made absolutely bangers to go along with the boss fight and I don’t think I’ll be forgetting this boss for a very long time. https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=5T9Yni0CfKQ

[h3][Events][/h3]
There are a healthy mixture of combat oriented and mini-game events. For those who want to play a gacha game that actually gives you events for the main reason you play the game, look no further. Currently, there are 3 reoccurring combat events: Umbral, Echos of War, and the infamous Contingency Contract. Umbral takes existing enemies then ramps them up to 11. Not by increasing their HP or damage but by modifying their abilities to fun and ridiculous extremes. Each stage is a combat puzzle that needs to be solved. Echoes of War is more like the typical endgame mode. Takes the same principle of Umbral but is more tone downed. Unlike other gacha games, the timer does not really matter. I have never felt time being the main pressure of these two events since the start of the game. Then there is Contingency Contract. If you love torturing yourself, or pushing yourself to the extreme, or want to prove you are that gamer, then this mode is for you. CC allows you to make your own difficulty by allowing you to select your own desired restrictions. And no, max difficulty is not required to achieve all the rewards, but clearing max difficulty does give you the bragging rights.

[h3][General][/h3]
The game is really optimized so performance should not be an issue if you have a decent rig and the graphics are absolutely stunning. My experience has been mostly bug free (can't really recall one). And no, I didn’t forget to mention the factory, the factory is important but in its current state, you update it once a patch and never have to touch it until they add new recipes. The devs do provide QoL updates and popular player request within a reasonable time frame (not months or years like some other games). Feedback seems to actually get listened to so if you have a genuine complaint or idea, during survey time, explain it in detail. Some stuff that I’ve requested (and probably a lot of others) were addressed after a patch or two.

I genuinely think this game will grow into something special over the years. With most gacha games I’ve played, I would’ve started to feel the burnout at this point but with this game I have none. I’ve been playing this game since it launched almost a year ago I can confidently say this game is currently one of my favorites.

Launch player here. Endfield is not for everyone, but it's a very unique, stylish, beautiful and interesting mix of genres that will really satisfy the right person. It's also one of the only games in the gacha space that I think truly qualifies as "game first, gacha second."

It is a party ARPG, an automation/factory sim, and a semi-open world exploration game dotted with collectibles and puzzles. It is not groundbreaking at any one of these specific things, but the way they interconnect is pretty unique and I don't think any game other than Death Stranding has quite tried to do what it's doing. 
If you're not a factory guy, you can mostly bypass it with community builds, though I would recommend against doing this because building your own factory is a big part of the fun. If you are a factory guy, this is not as deep as Factorio or Satisfactory, but there's enough going on - especially when you get to Wuling - that it's definitely worth your time.
If you're here for the combat, I will be the first to say that it is serviceable at best and slightly clunky at the worst of times. This is basically Xenoblade autoattack combat, with stagger, ultimates and reactions to keep things interesting. The combat shines during boss encounters where you must balance dodging mechanics with managing your party, and the game seems to know this and so few sections of the game make you deal with time limits, as is common in gachas. One of the main endgame modes, Umbral Monument, is all about gimmicky encounters in which a you must succeed in a specific way and it's pretty fun.

The story is very mixed. The initial arc, Valley IV, is very slow, with a lot of plodding dialogue and exposition. Think ARR in FFXIV. When you finally get to the second arc, Wuling, things improve... mostly. There is still a lot of plodding dialogue and exposition, but the story begins to have a much more interesting cast, as well as actual stakes and forward momentum. The recent story chapter, featuring the North Wuling Exclusion Zone, was excellent and one of the best story chapters I have played in the entire gacha subgenre hands down.

Endfield has a fairly controversial gacha system. Unlike other recent popular titles, where when you lose a 50/50 your next rare character is guaranteed to be the rate-up, which rolls over to future character banners, is not present here. Instead, there is a fixed number of rolls you must hit before you are guaranteed the rate-up, and it resets with each banner.
The result is a system where impulse pulling is punished, which an inverse of most other gachas today which all encourage impulse pulling.  The rates are not significantly different in Endfield from other gachas, so what actually matters is the pull economy. And Endfield gives slightly more pulls than other popular games when you factor in limited pulls such as those attained from logins and the exchange shop, but they expire.
In short, save your pulls for who you want and make sure you have enough to get them, and the system works fine. The same can't be said for the limited weapon gacha, but I won't get into that here. Suffice to say it's a bad system and everyone wants it changed.

So far, just about every patch has made the game better, and it is a much better game now than it was back in January, and recent previews of future content are pretty exciting.  The game's future at the moment looks pretty bright.

I had already experienced the beautiful worldbuilding, storytelling, and gameplay of so many games from a plethora of genres, and the comparisons I was drawing to these hundreds of games felt almost unfair to a certain extent, but playing OG Arknights reinforced the issues I already had with AK:EF because I saw the potential, the talent, and capability of the developers and writers.

[h3] What The Game Does Well: [/h3]

	AK:EF has great attention to detail in the design of its characters, from the different animations after every attack sequence, to the idle animations, sprinting, attire, etc. However, AK:EF characters fall short compared to some of the competition and how notable (and relevant) characters can be in other games for me personally. The voice acting from NPCs and characters features great, diverse accents as well as notable figures in the voice acting community. The music and OSTs in-game are also some of the best in the genre, something Hypergryph has always done well since OG Arknights, and they manage to bring out a few notable tracks here. However, I’d like to see what they manage in future settings, as well as more purely orchestral OSTs and more of the same diversity we see in OG Arknights music. The EPs also haven’t been memorable compared to the OG. The art present within the game is amazing, and it's nice to see talented artists being credited for their amazing work. It would be nice to see Hypergryph transition to using their art skills in the composition and creation of 3d environments. Graphics are well ahead of the competition, with great views and some well-thought-out visual composition. The almost experimental and abstract composition of some of the cutscenes is definitely worth going further into, and there are some notably unconventional cutscenes that are striking/pleasing to the eye, while others are fluid with great combat segments. Lastly, and most importantly, the game runs on a heavily modified version of Unity, and what HG has managed to build is something else. The optimizations and stability in AK:EF are absolutely AMAZING. To pair the high-poly, complex factory system, detailed characters, and beautiful settings with such amazing performance and minor/no bugs is impressive and talented work by the dev team.

[h3] The Negatives From Gameplay To Story And Everything In-Between: [/h3]

		Formulaic gameplay ruins a player’s immersion and engagement, and it's important that a story is capable of flowing naturally without relying on repetitive gameplay elements to push it forward, especially when it comes to map design (for example, gathering 5 items or activating 3 bells). In gacha games, where pure gameplay is provided through events and endgame/replayable content, a narrative is allowed to flow separately; you are able to really focus on and design your narrative gameplay around the story itself rather than designing your story around the gameplay. With the philosophy of Endfield’s exploration and combat gameplay, enemy design and mechanics are weighed and valued more. Small gimmicks, variations in enemies, and nostalgic designs aren’t going to be sufficient in improving gameplay. Initial basic enemy designs have been a letdown. The ‘landbreakers’ of the game take on a more Borderlands style, and they lack any sort of motive and are mindless and mentally deficient from a narrative perspective (which I personally despise). From a gameplay perspective, they feel static, unorganized, and non-threatening. Boss fights are something to look forward to, as they have seen a noticeable improvement leading up to 1.4, but it would be nice to have more meaning and motivation behind the fights (give me a sense of urgency or emotion behind why I’m fighting something). Additionally, they don’t feel interactive at all, with basically every boss just running preset attacks into open spaces without any targeting to pressure the player or create a back-and-forth (and if you’re lucky, one basic gimmicky mechanic as an attempt to provide substance to the fight).
	Everything could be forgiven if they solved the most important underlying reason for this review. OG Arknights has an amazing main story that is even outshone by some of its more impressive side stories, filled with mature and complex themes and conflicts that touch upon political complexities, discrimination, censorship/propaganda, hope, etc with heavy inspirations and references from notable, classical, and historical works. The worldbuilding, lore, and the environment/mood it creates for the player are amazing, but AK:EF lacks all of this. Dialogue lacks any substance, any meaningful/powerful quotes, or even just a realistic, grounded conversation between characters (+MC is not fully voiced with one-choice dialogue options). After release and 9 months of updates, it still lacks any sort of notable characters, any sort of interesting conflict, or mature themes that are placed front and center for the player to engage with. In many ways, AK:EF takes what was so meaningful throughout the OG story and renders it completely meaningless. The developers have attempted to appeal to the widest range of audiences and alienated a core audience due to a lack of direction. The most blatant proof of this was a quote they presented during Gamescom 2026, where the developers described Endfield as "A happy and positive story about hanging out with cool animal friends, defeating the bad guys, and building a new world together". The worst part is that it's accurate; the game can be dumbed down to that mindless statement that sounds like it was written by an 8-year-old. It has continuously been a letdown at every point in the story, and without a complete tonal shift, it seems irredeemable in my eyes. The damage is done.

[h3] Concluding Statements [/h3]

	Please note that this review is made up of both personal opinions as well as some of the community sentiment I have seen throughout my playtime. Having already invested hundreds of hours, supporting it financially at launch, and seeing the potential it has, I want the game to be something I can proudly recommend to others. And to be perfectly clear, it is most definitely a gacha game I would be comfortable recommending to most 3d gacha players, but that’s partially because it fits the standard of low-quality mindless slop that’s present in the industry. Perhaps some of these critiques are harsh, but this is coming from someone who has played dozens of the most notable titles from other genres, and I think it’s important to compare gachas to ‘normal’ games, considering their high revenues, which should show they have the capability to invest in creating a better experience for players. There is no excuse as to why these games shouldn’t be held to a higher standard in order to deliver an actual experience.

[h2]Review[/h2]
Arknights: Endfield is a gacha game like no other. Its unique twist is of course the factory gameplay, but it's often praised for its lack of FOMO: most rewards are permanent and can be claimed at your own pace through usual progression. Another praised aspect is the magnificent Unity-powered graphics that are so well optimized you can play on any last-generation PC (like mine) or even older mobile devices. A friend of mine, for instance, plays on an almost 10-year-old Samsung tablet with no issue.

[h3]Factory[/h3]
The factory gameplay offers a challenge to those seeking it, but there is a blueprint sharing system that allows the uninterested to skip it entirely. It shifts slightly with each version and generally encourages continuous improvement. For the moment, it's not as deep as dedicated factory simulation games, so you might not enjoy it if you have thousands of hours of Factorio under your belt.

[h3]Combat[/h3]
The combat is a genuinely unique 4-character system with a slight learning curve to truly optimize it. It might infodump you at the beginning, but it's not that hard to understand, even though a big portion of the playerbase spams skills willy-nilly. Still, that casual approach is plenty viable because...

...most pulling currency rewards are very easy to get, even in endgame content, and the game doesn't require high-level skill to acquire them. This is why I consider the game easy overall, despite featuring optional hard content that rewards you with nothing more than prestige on your profile.

[h3]Grind and Resources[/h3]
There is legitimately not much to grind. You really only need one maxed-out main DPS and modest investment (~level 60) across the rest of your team to clear all content for the foreseeable future. To put the resource generosity into perspective: despite starting two months after release, I’ve managed to level almost my entire roster to level 80 just by doing daily tasks. I’ve even spent stamina (time-gating resource) on ridiculous side projects like finding perfect essences for every weapon in the game, even those I don't own.

In [i]essence[/i], resource grinding takes about two quick fights every other day, costing around 15 minutes total of dailies. Actually, the game might almost be too generous.

The game is also remarkably F2P-friendly. 5-star characters like Avywenna are exceptionally capable and more than enough to clear all content. Pulling currency is abundant throughout world exploration and permanent game modes. I’ve managed to secure almost every limited character so far just by picking up the monthly welkin (daily bonus).

[h3]Story[/h3]
The story is a bit of a controversial topic because it isn't anything mind-blowing at the moment. While it improves with every major update, you shouldn't expect the intricate and deep world of the original Arknights for now: Endfield is still firmly in its world-building phase. Plenty of other reviews do in-depth reviews into the story details, so I won't rehash what's already been said.

[h3]Conclusion[/h3]
Ultimately, Arknights: Endfield finds a niche in the gacha landscape with its factory gameplay, but more surprisingly also with its gentle monetization practices. It respects your time, avoids predatory FOMO mechanics, and lets you engage with its systems as deeply, or as casually, as you want. The studio listens to the community and feedback very attentively. If you're looking for a visually impressive, low-stress game with great gameplay hooks, it is well worth giving a try.

Arknights: Endfield looks great, plays well, has excellent character design, and feels very polished. Combat has real depth if you learn the skill-trigger rotations, but you can also just mash and still clear content.

I started playing ever since it came out on January 22nd, 2026, and I’ve had a lot of fun so far. I think it’s the best looking 3D gacha game and it performs really well with my outdated setup (I got a better CPU recently, but it performs just as well as it did with my i5 9600-KF).

I couldn’t ever really get into OG Arknights as tower defense is not my thing, but the character design always caught my attention. When this game was announced years ago I was excited.

Combat is fun, and having all of your characters on the field is nice. I think the difference between people who enjoy it and people who don’t is whether they actually learn the system or just mash. Since this depends on combat skills that are triggered with specific actions, it’s very different from the 1-2-3 rotations we’re used to with Genshin and/or Wuthering Waves. And that’s the good part. If you want to bother learning them, you can. All you get is the satisfaction of doing a lot of damage, and maybe a trimmed badge. Otherwise, you can just mash and get your rewards. And this is because Hypergryph has been going for a no FOMO approach.

You can obtain any premium currency given through the “endgame” modes by just simply participating in them or completing the easy stages. There’s no cringe timer slop forcing you to sweat and clear a stage within 2 minutes.

Another thing that I love about this game is the lack of RNG when raising characters. You have the usual mats, credits and uncap materials to level them up, but when it comes to gear, it’s crafted, and all of it has fixed stats. You don’t have to login daily to farm 3-5 times the same stage and hope you get 1-2 good pieces, just for them to go to shit because they roll shit stats or min rolls. There are essences, which you equip to your weapons. These are farmed, sure, and there’s RNG, but it doesn’t take more than a couple of attempts to get one that matches the weapon you’re farming for. That’s because there are tickets you purchase with regional bills that let you pick a few stats, so your drops have a combination of them. It narrows this down significantly, so there’s no pain really.

Some people may be impatient, because your gear and essences need you to dump lots of duplicates or fodder to level it up. This is a non-issue. You don’t need to have all your gear artificed or your essences maxed out for anything to do since you can clear everything with base characters. And it doesn’t take forever either. I have dozens of essence fodder at this point, and the components/bills you need to craft gear fodder you get over time.

Other complaint I often see is the factory. You don’t have to engage with it if you don’t want. Just search for blueprints online to get a fully optimized factory in a few clicks, and you’re done. Simply go to KyostinV’s youtube channel for this.

There was a lot of dooming about the gacha system too. If you cannot control yourself and you always “build pity” because you need a rush of dopamine of getting something you didn’t want, sure, it’s bad. So far, I have 29 operators and have been able to pull everyone I wanted plus someone I didn’t really plan for. It’s as good as any other system. I’ve had really bad streaks in GFL2 and WuWa, as well as good streaks (currently 5 50/50s won in a row in WuWa) so I don’t feel there’s that much of a difference. I’ve skipped three banners so far (Yvonne, Gilberta and Tangtang), then pulled on everyone else, and got everyone, so pull income is decent. Can’t say it’s great because I don’t keep track of the exact numbers. I only purchase the battle pass, not even the monthly. The only thing I don’t like is that they give banner specific pulls, which sucks but I’m used to it and it has turned to be kind of irrelevant.

The overworld is a series of closed areas, it’s not as vast as Genshin or Wuthering Waves. I personally find this refreshing, and I feel there’s more attention to detail to the environment because of this. Personally, I often stop to look around and appreciate the landscape. They genuinely have made some incredibly beautiful scenery. Exploration is not that much of a chore either, and there are in-game items that show the location of chests, aurylene, etc. as well as an official map tool online you can use to find everything (Kuro please do this bruh...)

Boss design is cool. They are fun, but you only fight them once or a couple of times. Same happens with Umbral Monument. This is good. You don’t have to come back every 2 weeks to do it all over again for 3 pulls and hope the current stages even cater to your teams (elemental restrictions or needing the newest meta unit). Some people want to be inside a game all day everyday and always have something to do, even if it’s the same things. I appreciate that Hypergryph has not given up to loud people demanding 100 events that take 10 hours to complete each every patch. This is finally a high quality 3D gacha that doesn’t pressure you at all. Do not give up HG, the cadence of content is fine.

This is a high quality 3D gacha that doesn’t pressure you. Hypergryph has kept the content cadence sane instead of flooding the game with endless 10-hour events. For people coming from original Arknights: it *is* different, but still good.

This game builds up on everything Hypergryph did wonderfully with Arknights and either keeps delivering just the same, or tries fresh new ways to show us something different.

I'll try to break down into categories to make it clearer:

- Music
There's this long fandom joke that Hyperphyph is a music company first and a gamedev studio second, and Endfield keeps the trend. The soundtrack is incredible and enhances the mood of every single moment, from the calmest to the most intense.

- World design
Talos-II is gorgeous, and being able to experience "Arknights" in a walkable world can be a breathtaking experience. And they keep improving on every new area, not just in the nice vistas and overall beauty, but on how it communicates the game's lore and how it integrates with game mechanics.

- Characters
Instead of the old approach of having multiple character designers, Liduke assumes the lead role here, and she keeps delivering. The vibes of "practical tacticool with cultural inspirations" are still there, but now they're coupled with an incredible animation team and the voice acting we came to expect from recent Arknights. There's personalities, looks and gameplay styles for a lot of different tastes.

- Gameplay
The fighting is more complex than what you get from a ZZZ or Genshin because how your entire squad is in the field at the same time, and their synergies now combine in real-time for all four, opening a lot of possibilities. The control scheme is simple, but the skill ceiling is pretty satisfying.

- Factory
....I had to put this separately from the "gameplay" part. Because *oh how the factory grows*. Every new chapter expansion keeps adding new layers of complexity to the factory. And while you don't need to be a full-blown Factorio/Satisfactory nerd to enjoy it, you *will* have plenty to play around, specially as the story unfolds.

- Story and Lore
If you don't know Arknights, it's a dark, post-apocalyptic "science-fantasy". The same carries over to Endfield, however the twist is that this is a new world, where its recolonization was heavily influenced by all the peoples and factions that the heroes of Arknights helped reform in their days. The result is a civilization that took vast steps towards healing old scars and developing their cultures in new directions. ...However, Talos-II is not the most hospitable world, and some of the eldritch interplanetary threats still being revealed and explored in original Arknights carried their influence here as well. This all means there'll be a mix of familiar and new, new allies, returning friends, surprising twist on previous lore, and certainly lots of new threats and mysteries.

- Graphics
...It's amazing what Hypergryph managed to pull off from this heavily customized version of Unity. It keeps a very likeable anime-esque aesthetic, but the detailed materials rendering gives them this interesting sense of "physicality" without making it overdetailed or uncanny. Lighting, shading, texturing, everything is phenomenal, but the greatest aspect here is the animation and effects departments. Every movement, every impact frame, every dynamic camera, it all comes together to deliver the emotional state of whatever you're watching.

Summary:
It's a very good game. It had a lot of growing pains early on, as it was finding its footing on a game that has a *much* bigger development scope than original Arknights, and some aspects suffered from it at first (particularly story pacing). But with every new update and expansion, things improve vastly, the story gets more interesting, the pacing improves and we get the Arknights experience we wished for since the very beginning.

Overall, I can't recommend this enough, specially for the price of free. You only pay with your time, and if our tastes align, you're probably gonna have a good one anyway.

[h1]If you're looking for one of the most polished and unique 3D gacha games out there, Arknights: Endfield is definitely worth a look.[/h1]
The gameplay, graphics, music, and optimization are all extremely well done. The gacha system received criticism, but it has been shown many times that this system is more generous than most other 3D gacha games, with NTE perhaps being one of the only exceptions. 

[h2]Combat[/h2]
The combat is fun and unique, with surprisingly deep mechanics that give the developers plenty of room to design interesting characters and, especially, team compositions. The variety of team compositions really makes every unit you pull feel viable for a longer time. I love the fact that every unit in your team is fighting alongside you without any swaps. That truly sets this game apart from other gachas. If you've always wanted to see what more grounded and interactive combat could look like in a 3D gacha game, I can definitely recommend Endfield.

[h2]Exploration[/h2]
The exploration is a breath of fresh air in this genre. If you're tired of vast open-world gachas with Zelda-style climbing, but still would prefer the world to be big rather than having multiple loading screens between small areas, you'll probably enjoy Endfield's approach. You can shape how you traverse the world by building ziplines wherever you need them, giving exploration a genuinely sandbox-like feel. Each patch adds one or two new sub-areas. Individually those locations are not that big and can easily be explored in 1-3 days, but combined they form a huge open world area with different stories, characters and probably environments from now on. Given how much love and attention the developers have given the Wuling region, I can only imagine the potential of future regions.

[h2]Story[/h2]
The story can feel slow, especially at the beginning. That's understandable for a live-service 3D gacha game that's only 9 months old. Endfield is built on a universe with a very strong history of world-building, so there's a lot of room for the story to develop over time. I would especially recommend not judging the entire narrative based on Valley IV arc. It clearly reflects an earlier stage of development, and some of its rough edges stand out compared to the newer content. Patch 1.4 made it clear that the developers have huge plans for expanding the game's lore, and after playing it, I can't wait to see what the future holds for us.

[h2]Factory[/h2]
If you're worried about the Satisfactory-style gameplay, don't be. It looks more complicated than it actually is. If you end up disliking it, you can always use other players' blueprints which are super convenient to use. Personally, I'd recommend giving it a chance because, at the end of the day, you don't need to optimize your factory to its fullest potential. Even relatively simple factory setups can produce more than enough resources for trading, giving players with little or no experience in this genre plenty of room to experiment and build a decent factory at their own pace.

[h2]My biggest complaints so far are:[/h2]

I've played 2 other gachas, Genshin Impact and the OG Arknights. The latter I also still play. So those 2 will be my comparison points.

Overall I would say OG Arknights actually beats Endfield by virtue of being almost 8 years old, with major QoL updates, tons of permanent content and a story that had time and resources to develop. But, among 3D gachas, I find myself hard pressed to find one that is preferable to Endfield.

My main pain points with Genshin Impact and most of other 3D gachas are predatory weapon banners, RNG gear and overly grindy progression system. Endfield sidesteps all of those:
1) Weapon banners are served by a separate currency that you gain by pulling on character banners. While this means that you sometimes get fewer weapon pulls if you're lucky on the character banner, their signature weapon banner stays for 2 more character banners so you have time to catch up. Plus, free version of battle pass gives a second best weapon selector for all currently and previously released characters, which is usually 80-90% as strong as the signature weapon. Currently I have around 2/3 of characters in the game, with all 6 stars having either signature or second best weapon, on a completely F2P account. In Genshin Impact, I had 0 signature weapons despite paying for pulls on several banners.
2) Gear is completely RNG free, available to craft with predetermined stats from materials earned through factory.
3) Progression is somewhat grindy but massively streamlined compared to Genshin, since gear isn't RNG (as mentioned above), materials aren't gated behind certain days of week and gatherable materials can be optimized both by passive production in the base and by constructing zipline routes to make manual gathering extremely fast. You also don't need to farm for overworld enemy dropped materials, as those are only used for consumables that grant temporary buffs and generally aren't worth it.

I should also add 2 cents about the factory system. It's nowhere near as complex as dedicated factory management games and is almost completely skippable by virtue of shareable blueprint system that let you follow someone else's guide and copy-paste their entire setup. I myself had never used shared blueprints and set up all my factories myself, which makes for an interesting one-and-done puzzle vastly preferable to the daily material grind normalized by other 3D gachas.

I don't have much to say about the story, as I'm not a big story enjoyer in games in general. The start is rather mediocre, but the latest 3 patches had seen a sharp rise in quality.

The art, environments, and especially music had been stunning, as expected from a studio that made OG Arknights. More than one track from the OST has made it into my daily playlist.

One major praise point I have to give is the optimization. I have not expected this game to be able to run at all on my rather outdated PC, but it gives a smooth 60 FPS on low settings. And on Linux it runs with no real issues provided you have the up-to-date DW-Proton version.

Arknights Endfield is a game that I've had a lot of conflicting opinions on. I'm a day one player for both Arknights and Arknights Endfield as well as a beta tester (including for this very Steam version!), I've been invested in this franchise from the beginning and a big fan at that; Endfield is a strong, unique game that struggles with it's own identity sometimes. I don't think I've played many other games that have gone from "it's so over" to "we're so back" from patch to patch this consistently, but the core gameplay and systems are enough to keep me engaged through ups and downs; and with the latest version previews, things are certainly looking up.

Combat in Arknights Endfield isn't ultimately that different from it's contemporaries in the action gacha RPG space, but does a few things different that will make or break your experience here. If you hate how you can only use one character at a time in a game like Genshin Impact or Zenless Zone Zero, you'll be happy to see the party of four featured in Endfield. Instead of ability skill cooldowns, Endfield operates on an SP system where performing basic attacks builds up your SP which allows you to use one of the skills from your party members. There's classes and an element system at play here but it gets a little deeper than just "use guys of the same element to win." Of course you can do that but there's also several cross element interactions which adds more team building potential; there's also a combo system where each character has a second skill activated under a unique condition and you can build around these as well. It's really nothing too crazy, it's action gacha combat with a little Xenoblade sprinkled on top but when it works and you have a synergistic team destroying a boss with combos it's fun.

There's more to the gameplay here than just the combat though, and it's no small part; if you're expecting the factory and resource mechanics to be a minor element that you can ignore, you're going to be disappointed because these elements are core to the game. For those really averse to them, there's a blueprint system that makes it very easy for even the most smooth-brained gambling addict to assemble a strong base, but it's pretty rewarding to learn the systems on your own. I've never really been interested in factory sim type games but having it as a major mechanic of an action game oddly works for me. It's very rewarding to learn and construct production lines that produce tangible items for you to use; medicine, gear, sewage to dump directly into the local rivers... there's also a whole trade economy with stocks you can buy and trade as well as selling some of the stuff your factory produces, it's a seriously unique factory system unlike anything I've tried before and I think it's a great boon to the game overall. Personally, I enjoy the slightly slower pace of it all compared to similar games; there's no gliding or climbing, it's all comparatively very grounded using real constructs like ziplines if you want to move around quicker. Another common element in other contemporaries is ridiculous grinding for drops with randomly generated stats, not something you need to worry about here. You will have to grind for the drop with the right stats for your weapon, but you can select two of those stats using tickets so there's very little RNG, and no random stats once you do get the right one.

Now, story in Arknights Endfield has been... a mixed bag so far... mostly leaning towards bad. So many people quit during the opening story arc in Valley IV because it's so talky, long, uneventful and slow, that I'm pretty sure they've already introduced the ability to skip to the end and get right to the second main story arc in Wuling, which itself is at least more engaging if anything. The story has struggled with consistency with one patch being really good and exciting and interesting and the next being a boring uneventful slog; operator episodes have had the same issues. Some are deep, important and impactful stories that are important to the operator and others are basically just having a little date with them where you'll hold their hand, stare into their eyes, and they'll tell you how important you are to them... I really don't like these. One of the main draws to the original Arknights game for me was the way your character wasn't the center of the universe with every woman trying to get a piece but Endfield so far seems interested in exactly that, with any one on one time spent with an operator, almost always a woman, feeling like a psuedo-date with a lot of touching and longing stares for a boss and his employee. 

Character writing however is great, there's so many fun and appealing characters who rarely feel like they're just there to advertise something for you to gamble for. Regional accents are also something I'm a huge fan of, it adds a lot of authenticity to the characters when they have accents that reflect their real-world regional equivalent. Endmin, the player character, has certainly been something of a problem so far, though. Despite being an amnesiac who doesn't even do all that much you will be showered in praise for every little thing. You are Jesus and everyone else is here to endlessly affirm, praise, or vaguepost in your direction. Endmin and his past are intimately tied into the story but the way he's portrayed is groan worthy more often than not, especially when characters are subtly (or not so subtly) flirting with him. He's also trapped in this bizarre limbo state where sometimes you choose answers for him, sometimes you don't. Sometimes he speaks, sometimes he gestures and the other party just acts like he said something. Endmin is in an in-between place of being a blank self insert but also a pivotal character and his portrayal has varied, never quite settling in a place where I actually like him. 

Music is great, voice acting and translation are solid, performance is excellent, the giant scale epic boss fights are hype and the environments and characters are extremely detailed and just pleasant to look at, I'm a big fan of the general aesthetic and style. For me Arknights Endfield has been a rocky road of ups and downs but nothing has shaken me off the rails and I'm still on board to see what the future of this game will be. It's hard to say anything definitive about a live service game as everything I've written here is subject to change and could be entirely wrong or obsolete by the time you're reading this, and there's so much to this game I'd love to discuss but Steam reviews apparently have an 8000 character cap so I already had to cut two paragraphs covering the gacha and side content; but I believe in the team behind Endfield and have a lot of fun with it despite it's issues and believe this is a game with enormous potential. If a unique action RPG with deep factory mechanics and animal people sounds appealing to you, give this a try. Also go check out Arknights if you like strategic tower defense, deep worldbuilding, war crimes, or just want more of the LORE of the greater Arknights universe.
