This might be a long one so strap in.
I really enjoy this game, the community, and even appreciate the dev's most of the time for the hard work they put in. However, all good things, feelings and emotions must eventually come to an end. "Anything that can go wrong will go wrong" - an apt quote I would like to use for the recent changes made in the game. I'm not going to dance around the matter, the sobek nerfs were beyond what I expected to come from DE. I shill and defend the devs as much as I can; stick with them, on their side through questionable changes, and make excuses for them when the changes maybe don't hit the mark they intended because I believed that their ends justified the means. 
This sobek change however, the timing, reasoning, and severity of it is the proverbial "straw that broke the camel's back". I do not understand why *now* is when they choose to nerf a beloved weapon in this way when it has been strong for years. Believe it or not, I could have defended a nerf to the sobek within a range, for example, nerfing the range of the AOE splash during the recursion and/or the percentage damage a bit, but to nerf the recursion, the range, AND the procs from external sources (e.g. cyte and saryn's added status effects) is just wild to put it lightly. I think using the veil of it being too strong for an event that's "once in the game's lifetime" is such a cop-out they should've owned with their full chest.
On the other side of things, I got my friend into this game specifically because I KNEW Saryn and acid shell's power fantasy combo was something he'd greatly enjoy. Imagine how it felt helping him get to the stage  where his power fantasy is about to come to fruition, he's invested hours, days, and weeks, just to get slapped in the face with this. How do you think that reflects on me as the one who incessantly recommended this game to him?

I cannot in good conscience recommend this game anymore because I'm now terrified that "strong" things in the game that are seen as "meta" now can randomly get nerfed at the behest of DE's mercy. 

I do love warframe. It would be disingenuous to say otherwise, but I am truly disappointed in DE, I'm disappointed in the nerfs, and I'm disheartened that my friend has permanently dropped this game as he's lost faith in living out the power fantasy this game eludes to having. After all, warframes are sometimes seen as Gods, but even Olympus had its Titans.

I hope DE avoids having more dramatic nerfs like this in the future before we are all left wondering "What will they take away from us next"?

Performance: I spent over a 9000 Hours playing Warframe on Xbox which ran quite well, over time they upgraded the performance of consoles but levels got more demanding, in two of the play spaces (1999 & Entrati Labs) the Xbox would rarely reach 50FPS, mostly running at 35-40, which took away from the experience, however on PC I've been able to consistently run the game on High settings at 180FPS (Yes I know how specs work) I am praising the way the game has been optimised correctly, I've played hundreds of games, and Warframe is genuienly the best optimised game out of all of them, which rarely has technical issues (Last I can remember is when Railjack was new)

Story: Once you get to The Second Dream (Main Quest) Warframe can have some of the most interesting and emotional storytelling I have ever had the pleasure of witnessing, which will likely become the main interest for new players, if you like stories and want to try Warframe, play it for the story, though some grinding is needed, it can take about 150 hours to get through the grind AND the Story, though there is a lot.

Gameplay: Warframe has fluid and fun gameplay, it can be boring on your own, but most multiplayer games are, the game has A LOT to grind for, you'd have to spend thousands of hours getting everything, though that is not required for the full experience, you don't need everything, if complicated builds are not your thing and if you hate repetition, I don't recommend playing Warframe outside of the story, but if it IS your thing, or your introduction to it, you'll likely love it, as it's not overly complex or confusing, of course it will take some time, the game also has a lot of different things you might need to learn, so try to keep it easy and do things at your own pace.

Crafting & Platinum: The game has a Crafting mechanic, where you will not only have to get the resources or parts for Weapons and Warframes, you then have to wait 12-24 hours for most Weapons (time does pass when the game is not open) or 24-72hrs for Warframes, there are some Weapons that can be bought in their Built state from the Market or some of the best weapons can obtained from special enemies later in the game in their Built state, you can rush crafting for Platinum (Premium Currency) which you can trade with other players, so the game has it's own ecosystem of trading just for Platinum

There are two major issues with the game right now: its current director and their questionable decisions, and an increasingly passive, repetitive, and undemanding community.

Unfortunately, this is no longer the same game with the same kind of community it once had — a community that was demanding, active, and constantly looking for ways to improve the game.

These days, a large part of the community seems to consist of people who simply repeat the explanations provided by the developers without questioning the flaws in their reasoning or even considering whether better solutions exist.

On the other side, we have developers who seem to approach every issue by choosing the easiest and first solution that comes to mind, without properly thinking it through or considering the consequences of their so-called "balancing" decisions on gameplay and on the time players have invested in building their characters.

A perfect example is how they effectively nerfed several characters, such as Saryn, whose gameplay had a perfectly reasonable synergy with Sobek and its Acid Shells augment, simply to address Cyte-9's overpowered mechanics. And why didn't they just nerf Cyte-9 directly? God knows why.

There are plenty of other examples across different aspects of the game, and I'm sure experienced players know exactly what I'm talking about.

The result of this vicious cycle of developer laziness and poor decision-making, combined with a passive and undemanding community that blindly trusts developers (who are, after all, just human beings capable of making mistakes, which is completely understandable) as if they were some divine authority, is a situation where constructive criticism, genuine demands, and better ideas rarely get enough attention to reach the people making the decisions.

And this is the game we are left with:

Countless wasted builds, hours of investment, and characters being power-crept, only to have other characters nerfed in an attempt to stop that very same power creep.

Countless good mechanics being removed, nerfed, or even "equalized," resulting in players abandoning them and moving on to something else. In other words, instead of actually balancing things, they simply move the problem from one place to another, often making previously viable builds completely useless in the process.

Poorly optimized maps and areas where even a system locked at 60 FPS can suddenly drop to 45 or even 30 FPS.

And these are just a few examples.

Warframe is an absolute masterpiece and one of the best free-to-play games ever created. The amount of content, depth, customization, and sheer variety this game offers is unbelievable. There are hundreds of hours of gameplay to enjoy, an incredible universe to explore, countless weapons and Warframes to collect, and an amazing progression system that constantly gives you something new to work toward. The combat is incredibly satisfying, the movement system is second to none, and the developers continue to prove that they genuinely care about their community and their game.

One of the things I appreciate most about Warframe is its monetization model. Digital Extremes deserves serious credit for showing how free-to-play games should be handled. The ability to earn premium currency through trading, obtain an incredible amount of content through gameplay, and enjoy the vast majority of the experience without feeling pressured to spend money is genuinely refreshing. Purchases feel optional rather than mandatory, and supporting the developers actually feels rewarding because of how much they give back to the players. It's a fantastic example of how a free-to-play business model can respect its community while still being successful.

What makes Warframe even more impressive is the continued dedication to updates, expansions, story content, and new features. The developers consistently give players reasons to return, and the game just keeps getting bigger and better. The community is another huge highlight, with so many helpful and welcoming players willing to guide newcomers.

Warframe isn't just a game; it's a living, constantly evolving universe that respects your time, rewards your dedication, and gives you an incredible amount of freedom. Digital Extremes has built something truly special, and I hope they continue supporting it for many years to come. Thank you for setting such a high standard for free-to-play gaming. [h1]Warframe: The Endless Treadmill of Manufactured Boredom[/h1]

[h2]Introduction: The Illusion of Space Ninja Supremacy[/h2]
Developed by Digital Extremes, [b]Warframe[/b] is frequently praised in the free-to-play market as a shining beacon of consumer-friendly game design. On paper, it promises a hyper-stylised, high-speed power fantasy featuring cybernetic space ninjas, fluid parkour, and hundreds of unique weapons. 

However, beneath its flashy, high-fidelity exterior lies a deeply bloated, profoundly disjointed, and structurally broken experience. It is a game that values breadth over depth, masquerading artificial time-gates and an endless, multi-layered grind as meaningful content. It is less of an interactive game and more of a beautifully rendered digital spreadsheet designed to waste thousands of hours of your life. Honestly, after dealing with the constant roadblocks and forced waits, the core structure of this game feels like a total [b]piece os shit][/b].

[hr][/hr]

[h1]The Critical Breakdown[/h1]

[h2]1. The Core Loop: A Mile Wide, But an Inch Deep[/h2]
Warframe’s biggest structural flaw is its complete inability to meaningfully iterate on its core gameplay. The game has expanded rapidly over the years, but instead of refining what works, the developers continuously introduce entirely separate, half-baked islands of content that are abandoned immediately after launch.
[list]
[*] [b]The Content Island Syndrome:[/b] Mechanics like Archwing (space flight), Railjack (ship combat), and the various Open Worlds operate in completely isolated silos. The resources you spend hundreds of hours grinding in one zone are completely useless in the next, destroying any sense of cohesive progression.
[*] [b]Total Absence of Endgame:[/b] Once you have optimized your mods and weapons to deal millions of damage, you realize there is absolutely nowhere to use them. The "endgame" consists entirely of running the exact same low-level missions you did in your first hour, just with exponentially higher enemy health pools.
[/list]

[hr][/hr]

[h2]2. The Progression Nightmare: Pay or Wait[/h2]
While Warframe technically allows players to earn everything without spending real money, the mechanics utilized to incentivize premium currency (Platinum) are aggressively anti-consumer and disrespectful of player time.
[list]
[*] [b]Mobile-Game Style Time Gates:[/b] When you finally spend days grinding the rare components to craft a new Warframe, you are forced to wait a literal [b]72 real-world hours[/b] for the foundry to build it. Weapons take 12 to 24 hours. This artificial stalling serves zero gameplay purpose other than to bully the player into spending premium currency to skip the wait. The mechanics in this loop are absolute [b][shit][/b].
[*] [b]The Inventory Slot Tax:[/b] You have severely limited slots for frames and weapons. If you do not pay Platinum to unlock more slots, you are forced to permanently delete weapons and characters you spent dozens of hours leveling up just to make room for new ones. 
[/list]

[hr][/hr]

[h2]3. Horrendous New Player Onboarding and Systems Bloat[/h2]
Attempting to play Warframe in the modern era without having three distinct wiki tabs open on a second monitor is an exercise in pure futility.
[list]
[*] [b]In-Game Obfuscation:[/b] The game refuses to explain its most critical systems. Modding mechanics, damage types, status procs, and Lich systems are buried behind opaque menus and horrific user interfaces. 
[*] [b]Unchecked Feature Creep:[/b] Rather than cleaning up the baseline experience, the game features a staggering amount of abandoned, bloated systems thrown at the player simultaneously with zero cohesion. It is an overwhelming mess of acronyms and currencies designed to induce burnout.
[/list]

[hr][/hr]

[h2]4. Power Creep and the Death of Engagement[/h2]
Any semblance of tactical gameplay or challenge died years ago. Modern Warframe is an automated clicker game dressed up as an action title.
[list]
[*] [b]Mindless Power Creep:[/b] Due to years of unmanaged balancing, players can easily build characters that wipe out entire maps of enemies instantly through walls without ever looking at them. 
[*] [b]The Co-Op Disconnect:[/b] Playing with a squad doesn't foster cooperation; it turns the game into a visual-effects-heavy race. You will routinely load into a mission only to chase a high-level player who clears the entire map instantly, leaving you to sprint through empty hallways picking up dropped loot. It is profoundly unengaging.
[/list]

[hr][/hr]

[h2]Definitive Conclusion[/h2]
[b]Warframe[/b] is a masterclass in psychological manipulation and artificial longevity. It hooks players with exceptional movement mechanics and a flashy art style, only to trap them in a predatory cycle of grinding for the sake of grinding. You aren't playing to overcome challenges; you are playing to watch a progress bar tick up so you can unlock a weapon that lets you watch the next progress bar tick up slightly faster.

If you value your time and crave games with tightly designed loops, meaningful narratives, and true mechanical depth, stay far away. Warframe is a glittering, endless treadmill that will leave you completely hollow after hundreds of hours.

[b]Critical Assessment Matrix[/b]
[list]
[*] Narrative Cohesion: 4.0/10
[*] Progression Design: 2.0/10
[*] New Player Onboarding: 1.0/10
[*] Respect for Player Time: 0/10
[*] [b]Overall Definitive Rating: 3.0/10 — A Beautifully Painted Waste of Time.[/b]
[/list]

tl;dr: great game, but with a dev team so capricious it made me miss WoW.

Warframe is a really fun game, with incredible gunplay, movement, and an in-depth building system that proves addicting. In fact, I'll likely return and update this review if it improves! With that being said, Warframe, as it stands, is fundamentally held back by how its devs choose to handle multiple aspects of it. This includes things like:

Adding Actual Organized Group Content for the first time in years, BUT still actively refusing to add a group finder system, forcing you to use an archaic recruit chat system. Compounding this, Icebind, while incredibly fun and one of the highlights of the game right now, is partially reliant on having teammates that know basic mechanics. The baseline difficulty of the game does not prepare the average player to know what a "mechanic" is, leading to a lot of friction when combined with the group-making system that became obsolete in the late 2000s. Many things in the game reward organized and efficient group play (See: Radshares, Arbitrations, Arena nodes), but not having a large dedicated friend group means you're going to have a really bad time actually doing any of it with how fast the recruitment chat moves.

Really bad time-gating, with most forms of gearing up being locked behind weeklies (Archon Hunts, Icebind, Netracells, ETA, EDA, just to name a few). I can't blame them for this- as weeklies are the best way of getting player retention. However, the current Incarnon Genesis system is obnoxious, taking [b] NINE WEEKS [/b] to fully cycle, getting longer with each new update to the system. Combine this with how Digital Extremes often uses Incarnons as a band-aid fix for underperforming/old weapons, and each new week makes getting the Incarnon you're chasing more and more annoying? Miss a week? Too bad, have fun waiting another several months for it to come back! In addition, there's a lot of grinds in content islands that end up taking tens of hours of time-gating and grinding for... Not much apart from the very specific thing you want for your build. Warframe really doesn't respect your time, and it knows this.

Warframe as a whole has terrible QoL, especially before the "endgame." Crafting times take upwards of 3 1/2 days for a new frame, not including the grind itself. A particular gripe of mine is how cumbersome the HUD can be sometimes, with no way to tell what the tens of buff and debuffs that pop up mid-fight are apart from the very short, missable text that appears when it first triggers- and even then, you don't know what it does without looking it up afterwards. The trading system, while made palatable by a third party website, shows a troubling side of Digital Extremes that seemingly expects its playerbase to do the heavy lifting in making its incredibly archaic systems work through use of third-party websites, Discord servers, and Wikis.

Worst of all and the primary reason I've left, is Digital Extremes' utterly baffling kneejerk-heavy balancing philosophy. They have an incredibly bad history of nerfing anything that's not what they [i] want [/i] to be meta into the ground, leading to an incredibly stale buildcrafting experience that's been solved since 2019. This leads to a hostile relationship with the game's own playerbase when combined with the game's premium currency, where people who spend money on builds feel as if they've been rugpulled when they get nerfed out of nowhere. A telling example of this was quite recently, with how Icebind and its primary reward, Riven Splicing, was rolled out. A few weeks after Riven Splicing was released, one of the traits only attainable by Riven Splicing was target nerfed, with a comedically low compensation given out. This pattern of whack-a-mole style nerfs effectively deleting anything that outperforms their precious Incarnon weapons, combined with making a proper build in a manner that doesn't involve weeks of grinding often requiring real money, has slowly turned the playerbase against each other. Especially with the recent Acid Shells nerf, I've seen people turn on each other and threaten to try and get each other's playstyles nerfed to keep their own safe for a little longer. This has slowly made the community more aggressive and gatekeeping over the past few years, sometimes even harassing content creators who make videos on their builds. While harassment is obviously never justified, can you really blame players for becoming more guarded about their builds? After all, the build you spent real money on can't be nerfed if you spend [i] more [/i] money to hide your weapon names and further conceal its true identity behind a skin, right?

Warframe is one of those games I always find myself returning to. Thanks to regular updates, patches, and new content, there's always something new to explore. Even after reaching the endgame, you can easily take a long break and jump back in whenever you feel like it. Once you've understood the core mechanics, getting back into the game is surprisingly easy.

One of the most interesting features is the variety of mission maps. Since most maps are procedurally generated, their layouts change with every run, making even familiar missions feel slightly different each time. While the core mission types can become repetitive, Digital Extremes regularly introduces new game modes and mechanics to keep things fresh.

Another major highlight is the incredible variety of Warframes, weapons, and modifications. There are countless opportunities to experiment with different builds and develop your own playstyle. Once you reach the endgame, you'll eventually realize that almost any build can become viable with the right combination of mods and equipment. This freedom is a huge part of what makes Warframe so enjoyable to me.

Overall, Warframe is an outstanding free-to-play game with an incredible amount of content and excellent replayability.

Ratings:

⭐ Graphics: 5/5
For a game released in 2013, Warframe still looks absolutely impressive. The detailed environments, visual effects, and overall design can easily compete with many modern games, in my opinion.

⭐ Complexity: 4/5
Warframe can be quite overwhelming for newcomers. Many mechanics are barely explained, and the game doesn't provide much guidance early on. Fortunately, there are now countless guides and community resources that make learning the game much easier.

⭐ Resource Usage: 5/5
Warframe is one of the best-optimized games I've ever played. Despite its impressive visuals, resource consumption is relatively low, allowing even many lower-end systems to run the game at high graphics settings.

⭐ Endgame: 3/5
Warframe doesn't really have a traditional endgame like Destiny 2 or other RPGs. Instead, it mainly revolves around farming resources, optimizing equipment, and preparing for future updates. Experimenting with different builds remains enjoyable, but the gameplay loop can eventually become somewhat repetitive. That's why my rating is a little lower here.

Warframe is a fantastic game for those who look for power fantasy and grinding, and don't mind long waits and repetitive content, which is also some of it's biggest weaknesses. 

As a TLDR:
Good things:
-Interesting and unique setting, story and worldbuilding with pretty engaging characters and story beats 

-Great designs and mechanics which engage the player and encourage creativity and learning to master in higher level combat. 

-Meaningful rewards and events from every location which encourages revisiting and working with team members to collect.

-Fun alternative modes like railjack and archwing which are fully fleshed out with their own reward trees. Want to be a swashbuckling space pirate? Now you can!

-Cool weapons with massive customisation for all playstyles which allows for any playstyle from mass death to sly spy

-Great music (personal opinion)

Weaknesses:
-Extremely poor explanations of...everything. If you don't look up guides for the story, gameplay and mechanics you are screwed completely and won't have a clue what's going on. As such going into this with a friend is a must I would say.

-Main game is Repetitive. It's tough to design missions for a game of this type, but you have the options of: Kill everything, kill everything in a specific spot (with dlc of several spots), kill everything on the way to an objective, or kill everything but avoid the laser grids. If you want more out of this game, you won't find it.

-Long. Warframe is a game that feels like it pushes for constant expansion and improvement but locks the crafting for that improvement behind 1-4 days of waiting irl. You need to constantly be crafting in order to feel like you're not being inefficient, which might be a good thing for some but I personally have a gripe with it.

Game is great. Easy recommendation if you don't need a challenge – just don't go in blind.

[h2]The good[/h2]

[b]Visuals and vibe[/b] – very good. I would probably have bought it even if it was only about visuals.

[b]Movement[/b] – the best. Never seen anything close in any other game. Feels like driving a racing car.

[b]Teamplay[/b] – pretty good. I play almost everything with a friend, and that's significant value in my book.

[b]Economy[/b] – very good. You can spend real money, but it's also easy to farm. You can buy a lot of things and significantly reduce the grind if you don't want to be bleeding edge. The game is also pretty generous, you get freebies etc. You can easily get the thing you want, but it's very hard to get everything, because there's just too much stuff.

[b]Optimization[/b] – very good. Playable everywhere, no lag (especially in recent years).

[b]Customization[/b] – pretty good. You can make your frame match your mood and general visual style, and you can't mess it up too hard.

[b]Music / writing[/b] – very good. The art side in general is a big standout.

[b]Mastering mechanics[/b] – my most memorable experience was cheesing the Index with spawn rates. Building the team and my loadout for a particular challenge is sublime.

[hr][/hr]

[h2]The not so good[/h2]

[b]Ideas over polish[/b] – a lot of the game is more "ideas" than polished experience. There's also a lot of extremely outdated stuff that still gates your progression, and the game doesn't do a good job telling you which is which.

[b]Lots of useless content[/b] – I'd say around 90% of it. There are some godly challenges, but they're pretty hard to find.

[b]Bugs[/b] – not too many in recent content, much more in older parts. You can lose mission progress because of a glitch (e.g. getting stuck in immortal Operator form). A lot of bugs stay for years.

[b]Not challenging / low skill expression[/b] – sure, you can take a weapon that does no damage and try to play a mission. But it won't be fun at all: you'll be nervous the whole run and will probably lose. A 1000h veteran and a newbie would both be instantly shredded on Steel Path if the build isn't right. I tried to play the game "my own way" and it failed hard – it's very slow, you die a lot and make almost no progress, because the game is balanced around pretty fast players.

This is also where the fun of mastering mechanics runs out. Not being challenging is ok for me – I mostly enjoy exploring different mechanics and mastering them, and I leave as soon as the interesting new mechanics are depleted. But once you know the basics of a mechanic, you may find you can't meaningfully improve. There are some improvements here, but it's still mostly artificial and it's very easy to hit the limit.

[b]Build diversity is weird[/b] – there are ok builds, and there's Hildryn. The difference is night and day, like a gun vs an artillery battery. It's very hard for me to reason why I'd run another build if it's guaranteed to be significantly less effective and there's absolutely no way to bring it even close. E.g. I put 4 Forma into Valkyr and she tickles enemies, while with Hildryn I just delete them off-screen.

[b]Weapons[/b] – not sure. I had some fun with weapons, but there isn't enough difference in experience. It's just easier to take something consistent that doesn't need much dexterity, since dexterity doesn't scale into Steel Path.

[hr][/hr]

[h2]Verdict[/h2]

Easy recommendation if you don't need a challenge. I wouldn't recommend playing it blindly though – some guide/plan would improve things a lot.

[h1][b]TL;DR: fun for casuals, terrible for min-maxers. Developers have a history of making "knee-jerk-reaction" patches.
[/b][/h1]
This is a game in which you're a space """ninja""" with almost godlike abilities and weapons that could definitely be classified as "war crime incarnate". It's fun if you're a casual; it's engaging enough to retain even the most hardcore of grinders. However, don't be too efficient at playing the game or risk having sweeping nerfs to the game's fundamental mechanisms.

Some terms before we start:
[b][i]Warframe[/i][/b]- a kind of characters you can play as in the game
[b][i]KPM[/i][/b]- amount of KILLS you can achieve PER MINUTE
[b][i]AE[/i][/b]- AMMO EFFICIENCY which is a chance at which you do not consume your ammo (100% or more means you have infinite ammo)

This game has had a history of patches that could be considered knee-jerk reactions. As of writing this (late October, 2026), there is an event called "Epoch Operation: Taubound" where players need to grind for a specific material that is randomly dropped from killing an enemy type in order to unlock and exchange for some very nice cosmetic items; and the more enemies you manage to kill, the more of that material you get. The players decided to utilise (some would argue "abuse" but I prefer somewhere between the two) a niche, high KPM build of a very overpowered Warframe together with a mediocre weapon augment. Keep in mind, this combination had existed in the game for a long time and were utilised only for grinding another specific material. The developers, seeing this uptick in the usage of this loadout, had decided to nerf the weapon augment, which can create an explosion upon the death of an enemy and it can chain to other enemies as well. Funny thing is, they did not touch the very broken Warframe who can: refill a weapon's magazine for as long as he has the energy to do so (which is very easy to do), imbue his ammo with elemental attributes with guaranteed effects on hit, see through all terrain, and shoot through all geometry in the game for an infinite distance. The nerf also touches on other niche death-chaining weapon augments. The issue is that, without a Warframe to give the weapons buffs, the augments were next to useless by themselves. However, the developers saw otherwise, and decided to target the wrong thing. The result is that while this same combination is now still quite effective with its KPM capability only going down by around a quarter or a third of its original potential, other loadouts with different Warframes see a far drastic hit in performance and other similar augments become even more obsolete than before.

Another popular example of this type of reaction is the "Operation: Scarlet Spear" event, where another Warframe was able to use his intended ability to crowd-control enemies and made grinding for this event more tolerable (it was not an enjoyable event). The developers, seeing how the players were able to (in my opinion) play the game as it was designed, decided to permanently change how the mechanics of the main enemy type present in the event, whom was never touched on for years, and gave them the ability to slowly mitigate ALL Warframe abilities to the point where they become completely immune. So essentially, if an ability is used on that enemy repeatedly or if they are affected by an ability for an extended amount of time, those abilities will soon not work on them anymore. This is a good design for an enemy type which canonically can adapt themselves to fight against Warframes. However, this change had very bad timing and was considered to be a reaction to how the players were able to efficiently approach the event.

One more example would be the change to a new addition to the Riven system which, in my opinion, was not thoroughly tested before implementation. A "Riven" is a modification that you spend a specific resource called "Kuva" to gamble for rare combinations of stats that can drastically improve your weapons. During the same time as the Taubound event, they received a new system where you can combine existing stats into newly added stats by using a "Riven Splicer". One of those is "Ammo Efficiency" (AE), which removes the need to reload forever if it reaches 100% or more. After the release of this new system, players hyper-focused on that stat and some spent up to millions of Kuva, thousands of Platinum (the game's premium currency) on trading with players, and a lot of Riven Splicers (which you can only obtain 3 every week and every Riven can only have it applied once) to obtain a Riven with that stat. Mind you, before the addition of this new Riven system, you could already reach 100% AE through numerous methods. With this change, every build that utilises AE had been, essentially, shot in the knee (very apt to this "knee-jerk reaction"). This in no way changes how the game is perceived to the casual player where one would hop into a mission and watch things explode with a click of a button. WARFRAME: THE ELEVEN-YEAR ACADEMIC DEGREE IN LOOTING & LOCOMOTION
Genre: Sci-Fi Space Ninja Simulator / Spreadsheets in Space / Digital Hoarding Engine

Verdict: 10/10 Combat Fluidity | 0/10 New Player Onboarding

The Hook
You wake up from a thousand-year nap as a biomechanical space ninja clad in sleek, alien armor. You do a bullet-jump that launches you 50 meters through the air at Mach 2, slide beneath an enemy laser grid, spin 360 degrees, and slice five clone troopers into neatly organized butcher shop cuts using a neon sword.

You look at the screen and whisper to yourself: "This is the greatest free-to-play game ever conceived."

The Reality
You finish the introductory quest. You open your ship's navigation console, look at the Star Chart, open the Modding Bench, check the Foundry, look at the 50 different syndicate factions, examine the 12 distinct open-world standing ranks, and realize the game expects you to earn a master's degree in nuclear physics just to understand how elemental damage works.

You open Google and type: "Warframe beginner guide 2026 update 44 edition condensed." You are met with a 45-minute YouTube video, three subreddits, and an entire community of veteran players chanting: "Just complete the Star Chart, bro, the game gets good after 200 hours!"

The Breakdown
The Movement System: Absolutely unmatched. Going back to any other shooter after mastering bullet-jumping, double-jumping, wall-latching, and void-slinging feels like moving through a tub of cold molasses. Gravity is purely decorative.

The "Free-To-Play" Economy: It’s actually legendary. You can earn the premium currency (Platinum) entirely by selling rare digital rocks and weapon parts to other players in trade chat. You don't buy your power—you farm parts, trade with a guy named xX_LootGod_Xx, and build a multi-million-dollar inventory out of thin air and pure grind.

The Wiki Dependency: If the official Warframe Wiki servers ever go down for more than 15 minutes, 80% of the active player base will immediately forget how to craft a weapon or farm a specific relic tier.

The Lore Evolution: You start off fighting cloned Grineer soldiers in rusty hallways, and before you know it, you’re flying actual spaceships, controlling time-traveling 1999Boyband-era Protoframes, running around alternative dimensions, and managing emotional trauma on a cosmic scale.

Final Assessment
It’s an absolute powerhouse of a live-service titan. It's a game where you log on "just to farm one Argon Crystal," get distracted redesigning your Dojo, refit your favorite frame's fashion, optimize a red-crit build, and suddenly notice the sun coming up outside.

You can farm rare items, trade them with other players for the premium currency (Platinum), and buy whatever you want without ever spending a single dollar of real money. The game respects your time and effort, making it one of the fairest Free-to-Play models in gaming history.

If you are willing to put in the time to learn its systems, Warframe is an incredible journey with virtually endless customization, top-tier gameplay, and a remarkably welcoming community.

Years ago I would have recommended this game. But recently I've not enjoyed the gameplay as much, and the story is completely off the rails. The immersion of a grim, post-apocalyptic, sci-fi setting is utterly gone. Space ninjas was always the brand, but nowadays it rings hollow. We're no longer space ninjas. We're 'children' (so-to-speak) of an eldritch entity, possessing whatever Warframes are supposed to be these days (the lore is cooked), in order to fight off solar-system level threats. 

Warframe used to be grounded in some overarching lore:
-The solar system was colonised by Orokin.
-The Orokin empire is gone, various factions are fighting over the scraps.
-You are a relic of the Orokin empire, you skirmish against said factions.
Simple.

Now with addition of alternate timelines, I don't know what's canon and what's been retconned (it seems like a lot though). And I honestly find it hard to care anymore. Why should I? Everything and nothing is simultaneously canon and not canon. Wow, how novel and fun, and respectful of the lore!

And let's not forget Goonerframe. Increasingly, gooners are marketed to over everyone else. Yes, Goonerframe was always a thing, but it was never this egregious. I personally am against that sort of thing, but it sells very well so DE doesn't care. Don't believe the Goonerframe allegations? Just check what sells on the in-game marketplace, and look at what people post about the game. And don't forget the in-game, NPC dating app.

I've been playing for nearly a decade, so the sunk-cost fallacy is strong with me, and I'll probably even come back. But the reality is that the quality of the game has gone downhill. Its identity nearly a decade ago stands in stark contrast to its identity today. I miss the grit and scale of the old Warframe. 
-"Muh cosmic being"/"Muh alternate timelines"/"Muh evil faction is actually misunderstood," are all lame, lazy, played-out tropes. 
-Old Warframe's lore died for this? Sad. 

Don't waste your time on this game. The lore is completely bungled. The gameplay is repetitive. Warframe still has some amazing aspects that I adore (modding, customisation, trading, etc.), they just don't make up for everything else anymore.

A Masterpiece That Keeps Me Coming Back – 600+ Hours and Counting

With over 600 hours in Warframe, I can confidently say that this game has given me an experience unlike any other. The fast-paced combat, incredible movement system, extensive weapon and Warframe customization, and satisfying progression make it easy to lose track of time. There is always something to farm, a new build to experiment with, a weapon to master, or another challenge to overcome.

What I appreciate most is the sheer freedom the game offers. Whether I want to become a melee powerhouse, experiment with different abilities, or push my limits in endgame content, there are countless ways to play. The community is also one of the game's strongest points, with many experienced players willing to help newcomers. And the fact that the game is free-to-play without requiring you to spend money to enjoy its core content makes it even more impressive.

Of course, Warframe isn't perfect. The learning curve can be overwhelming for new players, and some of the grind can feel repetitive, especially when farming specific resources or equipment. Certain mechanics and systems aren't explained clearly enough, so beginners may need to rely on the wiki, guides, or other players to understand what to do next. The sheer amount of content can also feel intimidating at first.

Despite these drawbacks, I highly recommend Warframe to anyone who enjoys action games, looter-shooters, deep customization, and long-term progression. It rewards patience, experimentation, and dedication. Even after 600+ hours, there's still something that keeps me coming back.

Warframe is more than just a game you play for a few hours. It's a journey that continues to evolve as you do. If you're willing to learn its systems and embrace the grind, you'll discover a game with an incredible amount of depth, freedom, and replayability.

[h2]Random advice for new players:[/h2]

After mastering early weapons (reaching level 30 with it), if you check the wiki and find they are NOT used in any other crafts, feel free to delete them as long as they are not rare, hard to get, or something you like. Generally, if you can cheaply buy the blueprint, you can discard it, but always check. I recommend checking the wiki to both see how it's acquired, and if it's used in construction of another weapon before you consider deletion.

Later on you will gain the ability to 'subsume' (think of it as 'recycling') a Warframe, freeing it's slot and basically 'deleting' it, and gaining the permanent ability to put one of it's abilities on any other Warframe you choose, this is useful for freeing slots up for new Warframes and safely 'discarding' Warframes you don't care for, seek to get the prime version of, or can easy reacquire later, without 'wasting' your effort. Started playing this back in 2015, while it has had its ups and downs, the core gameplay was still enjoyable. However every update this year (2026) has been a let down. The Old Peace which was at the tail end of last year had a bad story, but at least the new modes they added to play were fun.


Follie's Hunt - Black inky enemies on a dark tileset with a 'threat' that would make your screen hazy with darkness, making it a visually unpleasant mission. On top of that, being forced to play as operator. I play WARFRAME to play as WARFRAMES, not the stupid void child.


Jade Constellations - Hyped up as being a big story quest. Ended up being complete garbage. The primary two characters Sirius & Orion get next to no screen time and basically no dialogue. The secondary two characters serving as mentors for S&O never had their motives explained or even hinted at. Just a "We must fight for our reality". Incredibly lazy story writing.

The missions it added were also bad, full of bugs, forcing you to use a railjack that is not your own. Hell, could barely even be called "railjack" content, which it was advertised as. One version of the mission dispels your abilities and buffs every 10 damn seconds which makes it incredibly annoying.

Then there was the new frame(s). The devstream specifically stated "Orion's black hole ability would grow in size and strength with every enemy it kills" Yet it ended up as a terrible pure crowd control ability. Congrats DE, on managing to make the ability of summoning A LITERAL BLACK HOLE lame. Truly impressive.


Iceblade of Narin - No story or quest. Not even a new mission type. Just a new enemy to farm in an unfun tileset. That would have been fine but DE decided they would fix what ain't broken. They changed the lighting of the game and committed the cardinal sin of changing fashion frame colors. Now ALL of my warframes' fashion look off. Ranging from being not exactly how they should look to being completely ruined in terms of fashion. Pretty much all voidshell skins were ruined by this change.

Though not as serious an offense as the above, they also decided to "prank" the community by adding an ARG into the update without announcing it. To complete it was to pull the sword out of the ice of whatever. Funny thing is though, this was impossible to do for any free-to-play players. It required the new warframe itself to accomplish, which takes at minimum 3.5 days to build, assuming you get all the parts on the first day.

But the winner got it a couple hours after the update came out. Making it a pay-to-win event no one knew was going on. On top of that, the winner got his in-game name revealed to the entire playerbase in an in-game email. Bet he had to deal with some private hate messages due to that. Despite people praising this game's community, not everyone in a community of around 50 million are kind.


I remember seeing a post on twitter by Reb (Warframe's creative director) defending Marathon on its release (or maybe before, timeline is fuzzy for me) saying "All it takes is one bad update, we've been lucky" or something to that effect. Even back then I thought it was funny, because warframe has had many bad updates even before this year. But players stuck around for the core gameplay. So long as new content didn't change the core gameplay, it would be fine.

But changing the lighting throughout the entire game, changing the way colors look on fashion? That might as well be changing the core gameplay. Every looks worse now. Somehow managing to be too bright and too dark, sometimes at the same time. Visual clarity has been going down hill for a while now but this update was a steep drop. I find myself no longer wanting to play and I highly doubt tau will even be good judging by literally every other update this year, let alone good enough to justify continuing to play a game that has disrespected all the time and money spent on creating the perfect fashion for my warframes.

Even if I continue playing, I do not recommend it. Your time would be better spent elsewhere.

Truly an amazing free-to-play game. I've clocked in ~180 hours of playtime at the time of this review and can say for certain that this game truly lives up to expectations. With F2P games, I'm always skeptical about the microtransactions, however, Warframe handles them in a way that I would consider perfect when balancing between player experience and generating income. There are microtransactions present in the form of the premium currency platinum, but unlike many other F2P games, players are able to consistently earn reasonable amounts of platinum through grinding resources to trade with other players. Furthermore, progression is not locked behind spending money. You can very easily progress through the entire game and all the main quests without spending a single dime. However, there are some annoyances specifically around long wait times to craft items(which can be sped up by using platinum). 

Beyond the games player-friendly monetization strategy, Warframe excels most notably in it's gameplay. The movement is most definitely a standout feature for me. Moving around levels feels very smooth and dynamic, and you can do so at very fast speeds which makes it all the more enjoyable. Combat is also something that I enjoy a lot. There are many weapons, warframes, and loadouts to choose from. Each warframe has a unique playstyle and set of abilities that allow for a deep level of customization and build optimization. That expands to the weapons as well, allowing high levels of customization for players.

Overall, this game is pretty damn good.

I came back after 10 years away and ground through everything I’d missed. I’m considering another hiatus, with the TAU update as a good stopping point until DE gets a handle on balance.

2026 has felt like one giant playtest for concepts DE didn’t bother testing themselves, which would explain the constant bugs. Does DE even play their own game? It doesn’t seem like it, probably because Soulframe is promoted nonstop, even at Warframe events like TennoCon.

The 6-man mode feels like an open beta. There’s no matchmaking, and it forces a 6-player layout that exists nowhere else in the game. The rewards are uninteresting for veterans, and the one good one, the riven splicer, is reportedly getting nerfed already. Replayability is capped at 3 keys a week, with a maximum of 6 stored. Out of keys? You can’t play with friends, even when no rewards are at stake. Oops! The mode also promotes meta-only play, the opposite of what a game about build diversity should do. Don’t bring the right frame or build? Bye.

Elite Archimedea (EDA/ETA) isn’t challenging content. The only challenge is finding loopholes around the awful RNG modifiers the game throws at you in the name of “difficulty.”

Balance feels pick-and-choose. Fun options get nerfed in the name of fighting AFK, while far stronger ones that clear rooms effortlessly are left alone (Cyte-09 + Sobek) or newly introduced (Gun Grendel + Sobek, Banshee + gas augment). These lock down entire maps with gas clouds and make spawn-camping and AFK trivial. Cyte-09 got even better if you splice a gas riven onto the Sobek. Awesome! So which is it, DE: is AFK acceptable or not?

Arcane Persistence is the same story. It arrived with Update 41 as a genuine alternative to shield-gating, and a day later DE hotfixed it so Nullifiers and magnetic procs switch it off. Their reasoning was that it made players immortal. Fair enough, but now the arcane fails exactly where survivability matters most, while the gas-lock builds that trivialize whole maps stay untouched. Variety loses again.

The Ammo Efficiency nerf on the new riven splicer is apparently the right move, since it keeps the same old guns on top and leaves all the mastery fodder unusable. The top guns are on top because their riven disposition is so high, and coincidentally they’re also Incarnon weapons. Most need only a few shots to charge Incarnon mode, which makes their ammo practically infinite, and the gun is fully reloaded when the mode ends. They also have much better stats than regular guns, so nothing short of max-disposition riven + Incarnon can compete. Maybe DE just wants the weekly money from selling Incarnon Adapters to impatient players.

Now imagine building a weird gun around 100% Ammo Efficiency for infinite ammo, at the cost of stats, arcanes, Incarnon mode, and disposition, just to have fun with something niche. DE’s answer: nerf it and keep the meta, because boring equals fun.

The game has 600+ weapons, yet only a handful get used, because the rest are nerfed, restricted, or unusable. You end up using the strongest options anyway, fun or not, because some tasks are chores and the path of least resistance wins. DE keeps restricting players on multiple levels, to the point where Warframe, a game about Warframes, has become Gunframe.

Modern live-service baggage has crept in too. None of this existed in its current form when I left in 2014. There are daily login rewards, Nightwave (a free season-pass-style grind where your leftover creds expire when the season ends and everyone restarts at rank 0), and now limited-window login rewards for frame reworks: Banshee was free only if you logged in between September 23 and October 7. Add Baro’s 48-hour visits every two weeks, daily and weekly resets, and 3 keys a week in the 6-man mode, and the game keeps telling you when you’re allowed to play. It’s all built to boost login numbers and engagement, and eventually to get you to spend money. That’s fair, since every studio needs revenue, but it doesn’t change the fact that this is here to stay.

DE seems willing to burn its veteran base to chase Destiny 2 refugees. It courted those players during that game’s shutdown, and now they’re leaving again after its revival, while veterans get let down again and again. It feels like DE is chasing new players for quick money because the old playerbase is slowly receding.

It’s still an okay game, but expect meta slop from here on. Bye, build creativity.

[h1]Delta Force – 4/10. The Wrong Kind of Clone Wars.[/h1]
[h2]Introduction – So Much Potential, So Little Immersion[/h2]
I genuinely wanted to enjoy Delta Force.

Large-scale modern warfare, impressive environments, military vehicles, extensive weapon customization, and different combat roles? On paper, this sounded like exactly the kind of shooter I would love.
And to be fair, some parts of the game are genuinely enjoyable.

Unfortunately, the longer I played, the more I realized that Delta Force was heading in a direction that simply didn't appeal to me.

What could have been an excellent modern military shooter became another overly arcade-like experience with questionable design decisions.

[h2]Warfare – Easily the Best Part[/h2]
Warfare was undoubtedly my favourite mode.
The large maps, combined-arms battles, vehicles, and impressive environments created some genuinely exciting moments.
I enjoyed exploring the maps, experimenting with different equipment, and participating in massive firefights.
When everything worked, the scale of the battles could be fantastic.

The problem was that these moments were frequently undermined by the game's overall presentation and mechanics.
A great battlefield means very little when the actual fighting constantly reminds you that you're playing an arcade shooter.

[h2]Support – My Class From Beginning to End[/h2]
I played Support from the very beginning, and I never felt the need to abandon it.

I enjoy helping my teammates, providing covering fire, keeping the squad operational, and contributing to objectives rather than simply chasing kills.
And yes, I absolutely loved machine guns.
There's something incredibly satisfying about supporting an infantry advance with sustained fire.

I also appreciated the extensive weapon customization. I preferred realistic-looking configurations that made sense to me rather than blindly copying whatever happened to be strongest.

Unfortunately, the weapon meta gradually became another source of frustration.
When everyone starts chasing the same overpowered setups, personal preference and experimentation become less rewarding.

[h2]The Operators – A Battlefield Full of Clones[/h2]
This was easily one of my biggest problems with Delta Force.
I absolutely hated seeing identical operators everywhere.
The same faces, the same characters, and sometimes even the exact same operator fighting on both sides.

Seriously, what kind of clone war is this supposed to be?

For a modern military shooter, this completely destroyed my immersion.
I would have much preferred traditional military factions with distinct uniforms, equipment, and recognizable soldiers.

Games like Red Orchestra 2 and Heroes & Generals understood how important faction identity could be.
Delta Force had impressive environments, but the character system made its battles feel artificial.

Instead of participating in a believable military conflict, I often felt like I was watching the same handful of characters fight copies of themselves.

[h2]Gameplay, Teammates & Monetization[/h2]
The gameplay was simply too arcade-like for my taste.
I don't expect every military shooter to be a hardcore simulator, but I do appreciate a certain level of authenticity, tactical depth, and believable combat.

Delta Force never quite delivered that feeling.
And then there were the teammates.
Sometimes the greatest threat wasn't the enemy team, but the people supposedly fighting alongside me.
Poor coordination, questionable decisions, and players ignoring objectives could make an otherwise enjoyable match unnecessarily frustrating.

On the positive side, I didn't find the in-game store particularly aggressive.
I never felt that I absolutely needed to purchase something to enjoy the game. The available skins simply weren't very appealing to me.
Monetization wasn't what drove me away.

The gameplay direction was.

[h2]Final Verdict – 4/10[/h2]
Delta Force isn't without merit.
Warfare is a genuinely enjoyable mode, the environments look impressive, weapon customization offers plenty of possibilities, and playing Support with a machine gun could be great fun.

But its excessive arcade elements, repetitive hero operators, frustrating teammates, and meta-driven weapon choices gradually ruined the experience for me.

The biggest disappointment is knowing how much potential was there.

With more believable military factions, a stronger focus on authenticity, and less emphasis on hero-style gameplay, this could have been something special.

Instead, I eventually lost interest.

[b]Rating: 4/10 – Great ideas, enjoyable Warfare, but ultimately wasted potential.[/b]
I wanted a modern military shooter where teamwork, equipment, and faction identity mattered.
What I got was an impressive battlefield populated by an army of identical operators.

[b]I've fought enough clone wars in Star Wars. I didn't need another one here.[/b]

This review is only about the Warfare mode and Black Hawk Down. 

Warfare, well, it's a straight Battlefield 2042 clone. A good clone though, the best free to play Battlefield clone available now. It's worth to just download and play couple of hours, it's fun and all, but it has many issues and needs polishing to keep you playing more. Each time a round ends you return to the lobby, faulty spawn system, matchmaking has issues and there's not many players on Warfare mode apparently. Because, I was playing with the same players for a whole day, and the game was not even full. Some issues I've seen mentioned by others are bots, which I think they do exist, but I can't verify that since it's not stated by the game like in BF2042. Another issue mentioned is the Anti Cheat system causing problems, I haven't met any problems with it, with a quick research it seems that ACE does the same with every major Anti Cheat system.

Black Hawk Down, I'm a huge fan of the movie and love the fact that it got made into a campaign with good graphics and based on the movie. BUT, I've tried playing it Solo since launch, it was impossible because it was made as a co-op experience and the difficulty was really hard. Since then, they finally released Solo mode which supposedly is easier, but the design of the game is keeping it from being playable. I played until mission 3, where I gave up, I like the fact that it is difficult, but I can't enjoy it when I'm insta-killed by the bots from 1mm of clearance through a door /wall/window. Every time you launch you need to act like you speed running the game, remember each enemy position, so as not to get instantly killed or consume your med kits in silly encounters. Also, bullets seem to not register all the time, enemies don't appear even when you aim at them etc. It wasn't the difficulty that was hard, it was hard fighting the game system apparently!

Another major issue since launch was controller support, at some point if you played through Steam, there was a communtiy map for controllers but it wasn't the best since the game was not native to it. Finally the devs released controller support, but it's faulty, buggy and incomplete. i.e. In game match of Warfare, spawn screen, you press to change character/weapon/whatever,  selection appears and map spawn fades. You should be able to change your weapon right? NO. You can change which spawn point you want! But not the weapon. You have to press 2-3 times the button again to be able to select. Ok then let's select the spawn point on the map, let's toggle to where I want to spawn. Well, NO. You can spawn everywhere except where you want. Selection is stuck and doesn't let you spawn there and spawns you randomly. The same thing happens to BF2042 by the way.

Anyway, just play the game to have an opinion, have fun as long as you can, until the no players and bugs ruin the fun for you. 

P.S. New map launching today looks fun and cool, reminiscent of Siege of Shanghai-BF4, but I done with the game.

Lobbies on Zero Dam (the first map you play):
Game is very sweaty but once you get used to how people play and gear up with a team you become one of those sweaty people. I am not one of those sweaty people so I get bot lobbies constantly, it gets a bit boring only getting bot lobbies but I figured out if I play with a teammate I get real lobbies.
7/10

Guns, Mods, and Ammo:
The guns play very well in games, ammo can get expensive but if you play blue ammo minimum you should be fine. mods are fun, it adds a lot of diversity to how you can play, for example the AKM, you can make a gun for hip fire build for close up fights, a gun for less recoil and better stability for further fights, or just throw all your money out of the window and buy the most expensive stuff for fun. The TTK (time to kill) is very short in normal/hard mode taking about 0.15-0.45 seconds to kill somebody depending on what they have. Though in easy mode it pushes that TTK down to 0.45-1 seconds to kill somebody because the maximum ammo type you can bring in is blue, while normal/hard is gold/red. Marksman and snipers guns are OP if you're sneaky with it, most people in Delta Force know almost the entirety of ZD (Zero Dam) so if you're not in a uncommon spot you will die to people fast TTK. In my opinion if you're gonna use snipers in easy mode, don't, they don't do enough damage because of the blue ammo to one shot them in the head.
9/10

Maps:
I haven't played all of the maps yet but i have played Zero Dam, Layali Grove, and AZ3 and my favorite map out of those 3 is AZ3. Zero Dam is a small, easy map for beginners to get use to the game, but most just use it for fast PVP fights. Layali Grove is a huge map for the beginners to go to after Zero Dam, I don't know much of that map but I do know there's a lot of cool missions, lots of fishing, and lots of really long range fights, so maybe bring a long range rifle for Layali Grove. AZ3 is a huge, special map that opens up at specific times of the day for an hour each time. The map is also a really good fishing spot and has probably the best missions you can do in Delta Force (to my understanding).
8/10

Economy:
The economy is very balanced. You can easily spend the perfect amount of money you want on a kit no matter what. Getting golds and reds are pretty rare but definitely doable. Nothing much to say about the economy its just good.
7/10

Cosmetics:
Skins look great, they're just expensive. Most skins normal players are gonna get without spending money is recolors. But if you spend money you'll have some really good looking skins. The only skins I don't like of their price is the melees, every melee skin besides Blackhawk is gonna cost you $80-$150 to get, which is absurd but its a mobile game so what do you expect.
6/10

Graphics:
Decent, nothing special but nothing bad.
8/10

overall one of my favorite games I've played yet

I really love this game, but right now I spend more time in the queue than in raids.

Getting into a match, especially solo, is almost impossible. I have to manually pick server, map, squad fill and ranked, and with that many combinations there's no way to know which one will actually find a game. I've sat 45 minutes in queue and still not got in. Prison is basically impossible to get into. Even at peak time with ~100k players online and a full squad, Brakkesh queues were 20+ minutes. I'm on the last Fate mission and can't finish it because I can't get into a game.

What would fix it:
- Let us queue multiple servers and maps at the same time
- Show realistic wait times before queuing
- Let squad fill fall back to solo if no team is found

The second big problem is how hostile the game is to new and average players. "Easy" lobbies are full of God of War tier players in full gear. If I started this game today, I probably wouldn't play more than once. It's not fun to pick easy mode and get wiped every raid by players who shouldn't be there. Skill-based matchmaking, or at least keeping top ranks and full kits out of easy lobbies, is badly needed.

The core gameplay is great. Fix matchmaking and I'll gladly change this review.

Recommended — the best free shooter on PC, and it’s not close

I came to Delta Force expecting a Battlefield knockoff with a cash shop bolted on. Two years later it’s the game I recommend first to anyone who wants big-team warfare or an extraction shooter and doesn’t want to pay sixty bucks to find out if they like it.

Warfare is the headline mode and it delivers: 32v32 on big, well-built maps with armor, helos, and jets, and an objective flow that rewards squads who actually push and defend instead of farming kills. The maps have real variety — Cracked and Shafted are tight urban slugfests, Threshold and Knife Edge open things up for vehicles, and the seasonal additions have mostly been winners. Operators add just enough ability flavor to give classes an identity without turning it into a hero shooter. The healer that drags you out of a firefight and the engineer who can seal a doorway change how a point plays.

Operations is the mode I didn’t expect to love. It’s a proper extraction shooter with the hard edges filed down: a real gunsmith, meaningful ammo and armor choices, and a loot economy where losing a kit stings but doesn’t end your week. Zero Dam is a perfect teaching map, Layali Grove and Brakkesh are where the sweat lives, and the difficulty tiers let you choose your risk. Solo-queue matchmaking and a Normal difficulty on the harder maps were smart additions.

The support has been relentless. Every season brings a new operator, maps, weapons, and real balance passes, and the crossovers have been fun rather than obnoxious. The game runs clean on mid-range hardware, cross-play works, and the monetization stays cosmetic. Two years in, the player base is healthy and the devs are still listening.

If you’ve been curious about extraction shooters or miss the old 64-player Battlefield feeling, install it. It costs you nothing but the download, and odds are it stays on your drive.

[b]Delta Force – Warfare Review[/b]

For people who have only played the game for a few hours, there are actually two main modes, or three if you include the campaign, which I’ve never touched. Only a couple of hours of my playtime went into the extraction shooter. I mainly play [b]Warfare, the Battlefield-style mode[/b], so this is a review of that mode.

[b]TL;DR:[/b] It’s a fun, run-and-gun shooter with large-scale battles.

[b]THE GOODS[/b]

[b]Gunplay and Gunsmithing[/b]

The gunplay and gunsmithing are VERY GOOD. There’s a lot of weapon variety, and some guns being exclusive to or tied to specific classes adds more variety to the gameplay.

The game has a futuristic theme when it comes to character abilities, but nothing feels too game-breaking. The operator skills are cool yet relatively grounded for the most part. For example, only a few specific operators have movement-based abilities, so you don’t see everyone sliding around and sweating like crazy. Scanning abilities and wallhacks are also pretty brief, giving you more of a quick glimpse of enemy positions rather than letting you track everyone constantly.

At the end of the day, [b]it’s still mostly about gunfights rather than ability spam.[/b]

[b]Bots Aren’t That Bad[/b]

There are a LOT of bots, but honestly, I don’t mind. There are only around 3–4 teams of real players per side, with the rest being filler bots. And to be fair, killing bots can actually be pretty fun, especially when you’re getting spawn-killed by sweats.

[b]Generous Events and Rewards[/b]

The game is pretty generous with its events and rewards. They give out a lot of premium currency, to the point where you can actually do a full draw in the store without necessarily spending real money. It’s nice to see a free-to-play game being this generous.

[b]Low System Requirements[/b]

Despite how good it looks, the game has relatively low system requirements. Even my old PC can still run it at Ultra settings, which is pretty impressive.

[b]THE BADS[/b]

[b]200 GB. YES, 200 GB.[/b]

The game takes up around 200 GB of storage, which is ridiculous. And for some reason, every seasonal update seems to require you to redownload almost the entire game. Seriously, what is up with that?

[b]Cheaters or Just Really Good Players?[/b]

When I first started playing, I thought those players dropping 100+ kills per match were cheaters. Now that I’m dropping 100+ kills myself, I’m not so sure anymore. 💀

That said, there are definitely moments when your team gets completely steamrolled by some dude with an Asian-character username, and you genuinely can’t tell whether they’re just cracked at the game or actually cheating.

Some cheaters are more obvious, like those who shoot you through walls and do other suspicious stuff. Thankfully, in my experience, those encounters seem relatively rare.

[b]Vehicles Are Unbalanced[/b]

Vehicles, especially tanks, can be pretty unbalanced, and the available counters, like rocket launchers, feel underpowered.

On open-field maps, tanks can just snipe people from a distance and retreat to repair after taking a few hits. Rockets barely tickle them unless you have several players firing at the same tank simultaneously.

It can get frustrating when your team has very limited options to deal with a tank that’s practically farming kills from across the map.

[b]OVERALL[/b]

It’s free, and it’s fun. At least [b]Warfare mode[/b] is.

If you’re looking for a large-scale, Battlefield-style shooter with satisfying gunplay, plenty of weapons to customize, and a fun run-and-gun experience, Delta Force is worth trying.

*My Experience with Delta Force – Team Matchmaking Needs Serious Improvement*

I've been playing this game since its release, and after spending so much time playing it, I've noticed several problems. The biggest issue, in my opinion, is team matchmaking.

In 32v32 matches, around 10–15 players are bots. I don't consider this a problem by itself. The real issue is the unfair team balancing. Sometimes, the enemy team has fewer bots and more skilled players, while our team has more bots and fewer real players. This makes the match extremely difficult and unfair.

Another common problem is the skill gap between teams. Sometimes, our team has fewer experienced players and more beginners, while the enemy team has more skilled players and fewer beginners. This creates an unbalanced experience and makes matches frustrating rather than enjoyable.

There are also several other issues that need to be addressed. For example, when I use smoke, it sometimes disappears from view when I move a certain distance away from the area where it was deployed. This allows enemy players to see and shoot me even though I should be covered by smoke.

Shotgun damage also needs to be reduced, as it can feel too powerful in certain situations.

Vehicle damage is another concern. Sometimes, when the enemy team fires rockets at our vehicles, the damage seems much higher than when we fire rockets at enemy vehicles under similar circumstances. This feels inconsistent and needs to be investigated.

On top of these issues, the game has many other bugs that need fixing. I've also encountered players who appear to be using cheats. Unfortunately, reporting them doesn't seem to make any difference, which is very frustrating.

After playing for so long, I'm honestly becoming disappointed with the game. I wanted to enjoy Delta Force, but these ongoing problems are making that increasingly difficult.

*The developers really need to improve team matchmaking and balance, fix the bugs, address weapon and vehicle damage inconsistencies, and take stronger action against cheaters.*

At this point, I'm seriously considering switching to another game if these issues aren't addressed.

A Disappointing Reimagining of Black Hawk Down

I have roughly 40 hours in Delta Force. I played the original game when it first came out, and I genuinely enjoyed the large-scale multiplayer mode. It wasn't perfect, but it was fun and had potential. After hearing about the controversies surrounding the developers, I took a break from the game. I recently came back specifically to try the Black Hawk Down DLC, and honestly, it's incredibly disappointing.

This feels nothing like the original Black Hawk Down experience. The atmosphere, presentation, and overall execution miss the mark badly. The soundtrack and audio choices are particularly frustrating, coming across as stereotypical and borderline offensive rather than immersive or respectful of the subject matter. As an American playing a campaign about American soldiers, I found the way certain things were presented genuinely off-putting.

The gunplay feels terrible, the visuals are underwhelming, and the frame generation implementation leaves a lot to be desired. For a game that should be relying on immersion and intense combat, the technical issues and poor gameplay make the experience feel cheap.

My biggest issue is that this doesn't feel like a faithful or thoughtful portrayal of the events it's based on. The writing and presentation feel disconnected from the subject matter, and the whole experience leaves me questioning whether the developers understood what made the original memorable in the first place.

I came back with an open mind and a genuine interest in giving this DLC a fair shot. Unfortunately, I came away thoroughly disappointed. I cannot recommend buying or playing the Black Hawk Down DLC in its current state. If you're expecting a faithful, immersive return to the original experience, I'd save your money.

**Minha opinião sincera sobre Delta Force: decepcionante.**

Apesar de ter uma jogabilidade interessante e alguns modos de jogo bacanas, o Delta Force deixa muito a desejar quando o assunto é monetização. Senti falta de um modo Battle Royale, mas o que realmente me fez perder o interesse foi a ganância absurda por trás do sistema de compras.

Praticamente tudo parece feito para arrancar dinheiro do jogador: skins de armas, personagens, armamentos e diversos outros itens. E o pior é o sistema de roletas, que transforma até a compra de um pacote em uma aposta. Você não compra diretamente o que deseja: precisa gastar tentando a sorte até conseguir o item. Quer gastar pouco? O sistema faz de tudo para dificultar isso e incentivar você a gastar cada vez mais.

**Isso não é oferecer opções de compra, é explorar a vontade do jogador de conseguir determinado item.** Em vez de simplesmente comprar o pacote desejado por um preço justo, você fica preso a sorteios e gastos sucessivos, sem a garantia de conseguir aquilo pelo qual está pagando.

Na prática, o jogo passa a impressão de que tudo tem um preço, e quem não estiver disposto ou não tiver condições de gastar fica para trás. Quando a monetização começa a comprometer a experiência e cria vantagens para quem investe dinheiro, a competição deixa de ser tão justa.

Minha avaliação é simples: a jogabilidade até tem potencial, mas o sistema de monetização é péssimo, abusivo e desnecessariamente complicado. Não recomendo o Delta Force e, sinceramente, vou desincentivar outras pessoas a jogarem enquanto essa postura continuar.

**Jogo bom conquista o jogador pela qualidade, não pela insistência em esvaziar a carteira dele.**

Delta Force — Better Than I Expected, But Not As Good As I Hoped

Honestly, I didn't expect to like Delta Force this much. Going into the game, I was expecting something with a bit of a mobile-game feel, maybe some Valorant/Fortnite-style elements, but after actually playing it, my opinion changed quite a bit.

Especially the gameplay is really good. There were moments when I genuinely thought, “Battlefield 2042 would have been so much better if it was like this.” The large-scale battles, vehicles, gunplay, and overall combat feel reminded me a lot of Battlefield. And the fact that it's free makes it even more impressive.

The graphics definitely aren't bad either. Some people compare the game to a mobile game, but I didn't really feel that while playing it. Yes, it has a somewhat more stylized look, and you can feel a bit of a Valorant/Fortnite influence in some of the character designs, but this kind of art style is used in a lot of games nowadays. It's not a big problem for me.

So far, I haven't tried the other game modes. I've mostly played the Capture-type mode and Deathmatch. So I won't say too much about modes like Operations. The 5v5 mode also looks promising on paper, but honestly, I don't think it would change much about the game's overall problems.

Because my main problem is the progression system.

The weapon unlock system feels completely built around challenges and grinding. Instead of simply unlocking things naturally by playing, you constantly have to complete specific challenges. After a while, it turns the game from something fun into an unnecessary grind.

In fact, I think Battlefield 2042 did this better, even with all of its problems. At least 2042 had a more established progression system. In Delta Force, having to chase challenges just to unlock weapons feels unnecessary to me.

Another problem is cheaters. The gameplay is genuinely good, but when you run into people cheating, it ruins the whole experience. In a competitive game like this, cheating is a serious negative for me.

And then there's the 230 GB issue. 230 GB is a ridiculous amount of space. The graphics aren't bad, and the game isn't lacking in content, but that file size still feels unnecessarily huge to me.

Still, I have to give it credit: it is much better than Battlefield 2042. Especially when it comes to the overall combat and battlefield feeling, Delta Force does a good job. I was genuinely surprised at first because it turned out to be much better than I expected.

But despite all that, I wouldn't really recommend this game.

The gameplay might be good, but the grind system, challenge-based weapon unlocking, cheating problem, and 230 GB file size are too much for me. I also haven't tried the other modes yet, so I'm not going to make any definitive claims about them, but I don't think the 5v5 mode would fix these fundamental problems either.

If you're looking for this kind of Battlefield experience, just go play Call of Duty, or go back to the older Battlefield games. Especially Battlefield 1 is still a much better option. Delta Force does some things really well, but overall, it's not a game I'd tell people to go out and play.
