I had looked at this game a couple of times, but the mixed reviews put me off (along with the large file size). Anyway, 58hrs in, its been fun, although I absolutely get the people that have been dissapointed by it. I've been manly playing warfare, i.e. the 32v32 Capture mode and not extractions. Sometimes matchmaking is a bit weird.

The game is an ARCADE game. Like if you try to shoot someone from across the map with a pistol, you could hit, but also it'll take 10 bullets to get a kill or more. Weapons have damage and fall-off over a range and that's that. I know some will be ok with it, others will not like it at all. You have operators with abilities of varying "Realism". Think if Apex Legends tried to LARP as a Battlefield/Mil-Sim hybrid, you would get something like this. Its extraction mode is no Tarkov(smaller map, fast paced, but still PvPvE, 3man teams), you can set up guns to get CS-like crosshairs, and I could go on and on. 

The gun attachments are a lot, and coupled with the calibration you can tweak a gun to your liking and that makes the gun play in matches quite rewarding. The maps are large, you can get various angles or try different things. Operator abilities add a nice layer to the game and so far I like the interaction and balance between gun play and abilities. I also like the fact that while not all weapons are available across all classes (Assault, Medic, Engineer, Scout), you get multiple classes of weapons per, so e.g. Medic's get all SMG's plus a selection of Assault Rifles, Marksman, Shotguns too. The skins, given multiple different attachments (stock, barrel, hand covers, muzzle attachments, etc.) are very detailed and OK (never been a big skins guy, but I always wanted to have a couple - SO FAR in the month+ I've been playing, I've gotten a few for free. For a free game and my experience, its quite chill about giving out free stuff, although I haven't played e.g. Apex, Overwatch or CoD in 2-3 yrs at least, so this is neither here nor there). 

Its ranked mode is just counting the points you get in matches. Its not different queue or anything. Its effectively a tracker for your games in a given season. I would have liked a pure ranked mode BUT I assume it'd be hell to balance maps, operators and loadouts; I bet there are a million cheese strats to be found if it had pure SBMM and a Win/Loss based MMR ladder. This makes certain angles in certain maps actually unknown to a few players in lobbies, so there's randomness in games, which I appreciate rather than the opposite (e.g. R6 siege where you're expected to hold/attack certain angles in certain games, because there's a clear meta or best approach - I have like 30-50hrs in R6 all time, don't shoot me if this is wrong, but I hope you get the point I'm trying to make. This is subjective of course, but I'm 31, I work full-time and I don't have the capacity to sweat games right now.).

Go in expecting an arcade, fps, shooter LARPING AS A MILSIM, and you'll have fun imo. The bugs people complain about are real, although for me, not consistent. A Casual Player’s Perspective on Warfare and Operations
I’m mainly a solo player and I’m almost 60, so I would consider myself, at best, an average player. I also have a busy life and only a few hours available for gaming. Because of that, I don’t play every game mode, so this review is mainly based on my experience with Warfare and Operations.

Warfare
Overall, I really enjoy Warfare. When you get a good team, it can be a lot of fun and make for some great games. Of course, there are also matches where you end up facing very experienced players while having bots or less experienced players on your own team, and those games can become quite frustrating and feel like a long uphill battle.

That said, I can definitely recommend Warfare. The gunplay is excellent, the gameplay feels good, and I find myself enjoying it most of the time.

Operations
My main reason for writing this review, however, is Operations.

Operations is an extraction mode, which means that when you die, you lose what you brought into the match as well as what you collected along the way. I actually like this concept, because it adds tension and makes every decision more meaningful.

The problem for me is the difficulty progression between Easy, Normal and Hard.

As a casual player, I find the jump from Easy to Normal extremely large. In practice, it can sometimes feel like there is very little middle ground between the two difficulties.

On Easy, you can currently take in fairly high-level equipment, while Normal allows even stronger gear, including Gold Armour. That equipment can be very expensive to obtain, and losing it after only a few rounds can wipe out a significant amount of the money and resources you have built up.

Hard then takes things even further with equipment such as Red Armour, which seems more appropriate for highly experienced players who have the resources and skill to handle that level of competition.

For me, the biggest issue is what happens on Easy. Occasionally, highly experienced players — including streamers and very competitive players — enter Easy with equipment and weapons that are far beyond what a new or casual player is realistically able to compete against.

When that happens, they can quickly eliminate less experienced players, take their loot, and move on. From the perspective of a casual player who is still learning the game and trying to build up resources, that can be a discouraging experience.

I think this is something worth looking at because Easy should really feel like an accessible place for new and casual players to learn Operations and gradually improve.

A Possible Solution
Personally, I would like to see clearer separation between the three difficulty levels.

For example:

Easy: Lower-tier armour and weapons, with a reasonable cap on the value of guns and equipment that can be brought in - No Purple armour, blue and below.

Normal: Allow stronger equipment, perhaps only Purple Armour, giving players a clear step up from Easy.

Hard: Keep the highest-tier equipment, such as Gold / Red Armour, for experienced players who are comfortable taking on the additional risk.

The exact equipment limits are obviously something the developers would need to balance, but I think the important thing is to create a clear progression between Easy, Normal and Hard.

A new or casual player should be able to start on Easy, learn the mechanics, build up some resources, become more confident, and eventually feel ready to move into Normal. At the moment, that progression can feel quite punishing and I just can not move to normal, my skill is too low for the players currently playing in normal.

Overall
I want to make it clear that this is not a negative review of the game. I enjoy playing it, particularly Warfare, and I think the gunplay and overall gameplay are very good.

My comments about Operations are simply from the perspective of a fairly casual, mostly solo player who doesn't have unlimited time to play or the skills of a highly experienced player.

I think Operations has a lot of potential, but the progression between the difficulty levels could use some attention. Making Easy genuinely accessible to new and casual players, while still giving them a clear path toward Normal and eventually Hard, could make the mode more enjoyable and less intimidating.

The game is good enough that I want to keep playing it. I just think Operations could use some balancing and progression changes to make it easier for new and casual players to get into the mode, stick with it, and gradually improve.

If you enjoy tactical shooters where logic goes to die, this game is for you. Otherwise, it is an exercise in pure frustration.
The vehicle combat is laughably broken. There is nothing more humiliating than hitting an enemy tank four consecutive times with an anti-tank rocket, only for the tank to shrug it off like a mosquito bite, turn around, delete you from existence, and casually drive away. To complement this, the infantry gunplay feels like you are shooting marshmallows. Having to dump an entire magazine into an enemy just to eliminate them completely destroys any sense of tactical realism. The weapon balancing is utterly chaotic, with attachments and stats that make absolutely no structural sense, all while the community battles a glaring, unchecked influx of cheaters.
To make matters worse, the map design features some of the most absurd checkpoint layouts ever conceived. The spawn dynamics are so poorly implemented that you are frequently eliminated the exact millisecond you spawn, trapped in a loop of cheap, unavoidable deaths due to fundamentally broken mechanics.
For this game to survive and not flush its immense potential down the drain, the developers urgently need to implement the following fixes:
• Vehicle Balancing: Completely overhaul vehicle health pools and significantly buff anti-tank damage so that heavy armor actually fears specialized infantry.
• Caliber-Based Ballistics: Recalibrate weapon damage profiles based on actual bullet calibers, ensuring logical and consistent damage per shot.
• Map & Spawn Overhaul: Redesign checkpoint layouts and introduce strict spawn protection or smarter spawn positioning to eliminate instant deaths.
• Anti-Cheat Enforcement: Show a genuine commitment to fair play by investing heavily in proactive anti-cheat measures to clean up the lobbies.
• Core Systems Polish: Introduce sweeping optimizations to the fundamental, nonsensical gameplay dynamics before adding more broken content.
Until these critical structural flaws are addressed, I cannot comprehend how anyone with a shred of self-respect can waste their time playing this game. It has incredible potential, but in its current state, it is simply disrespecting the players' time.

The game suffers from severe balance issues, including indestructible vehicles that dodge rockets, overpowered operators with zero counterplay, and randomized weapon bloom that turns gunfights into luck-based RNG rather than skill-based combat. The publisher, Level Infinite (a subsidiary of Tencent), is accused of gaslighting the community while pushing a predatory loot box model involving "Mendelbricks" and cosmetic bundles. The Black Hawk Down campaign is a boring, unbalanced port with terrible controls and no co-op, while the main Warfare mode lacks identity, serving as a watered-down Battlefield 2042 clone with stiff movement, poor sound design, and maps designed for mobile rather than PC.

Ultimately, Delta Force is a cash grab that ignores its player base, offering a frustrating, unfair, and unpolished experience that fails to justify its existence in a competitive market.

After all the hype around this game, I finally gave it a shot. I played the original Delta Force back when some of today's gamers weren't even a bad idea yet. So I thought to myself: "Well grandpa, you're 20 years older now, surely the game is 20 years better too." Full of optimism, I waited for my wife to leave for a weekend tea party with her friends, grabbed a coffee, sat down at the PC, and prepared for greatness. What I got instead was a lesson in disappointment.

I still remember the old campaign. Those were the days. Simple, fun, and hard to stop playing. This new one seems obsessed with realism, except not the fun kind. It's the kind where somebody shoots you from a bush, a rooftop, a window, or perhaps another dimension, and you never even see who did it. If you want realism, go all in. If you want fun, go all in. This game somehow misses both targets with remarkable accuracy.

The multiplayer didn't save it either. The whole thing feels like it desperately wanted to knock Battlefield 2042 off its chair but forgot to bring a chair of its own. One minute it's pretending to be a serious tactical shooter, the next it's trying to be a fast-paced arcade fragfest. The result is an awkward identity crisis where nobody seems quite sure what game they are actually playing.

Maybe younger players will see something I don't. After 40 years of gaming I've learned that graphics get better, sound gets better, and marketing gets much louder, but gameplay is still king. Unfortunately, this king seems to have wandered off and left the throne empty.

Honestly, even if this game were free, I wouldn't install it again. I'd rather give the money to the kids and let them buy some candy. At least with candy you know exactly what you're getting.

Third: Maybe this game can be more enjoyable when you have already party of 3 people total to play with. I did not have that opportunity and wasted 200h of solo playing with eventually squad filling that puts you with people that speak their own languages or for most of the time they do not know what the mic is and what is its purpose.
Fourth: Maps are divided into three modes; easy, normal, hard. Easy is filled up with bots from time to time but after protection period this mode is more like normal, where everyone gears up with 1-2M value and probably comes to have enjoyable time against new players when they get their asses kicked on other modes. Normal and Hard are with unlimited gear meaning that Normal became Hard, because there  are playing mostly sweats of this game with maxed gears, or some incredibly talented players can run this with medium gear. Waiting times for Normal modes are also incredible as those modes in my assumption are never filled with bots (Personally never even once I played against bots on Space City) Maybe on the basic map (Zero Dam) its more common.

Generally, if you as a team of sweating bros would like a challange and fun battle royale hero shooter then its for you.
Otherwise if you are lone wolf that looks for a game  I advise that you will not make my mistake enjoying this game on protection period and Easy Mode to later get hit hard with 0.5s TTK while fully geared from some guy that is jumping like monkey in pursuit of running banana.

You prepare for normal game with gear and would like to challange yourself -> You wait for raid around 10min -> Unlesss you are ratting, you end raid after 2min of spawn from some skilled player with no way to improve (Yeah sometimes you get lucky and you fight someone with similar game experience but that is hella rare, because they are also mainly cleared out by different sweats or premades). The game itself is okay, but the gameplay and overall experience are honestly very disappointing.

I have played this game for around 4,500 hours, and despite putting that much time into it, I still haven’t found some of the rare red items. Meanwhile, I regularly see players with brand-new accounts getting these items almost immediately. At some point, you have to question how the loot system actually works.

The ranked system is another major problem. The matchmaking feels completely unfair. You can end up playing against players with significantly higher ranks and much better gear, with very little sense of balanced matchmaking. It makes ranked games feel less about skill and more about who has the better gear or progression.

Cheaters are also a serious issue. They seem to be present constantly, and in this game it feels like they are on another level. You report them, and you're supposed to get your gear back if action is taken, but in my experience, that rarely seems to happen. Losing gear because of a cheater and then not getting it back is incredibly frustrating.

Then there is the in-game economy. Buying items and currency seems completely out of control. When you can spend £20 and get around 100 million in-game currency, it raises serious questions about the balance of the game and why this is allowed to have such an impact on gameplay.

After spending 4,500 hours on this game, my honest opinion is that it simply isn't worth the time investment if you're trying to progress seriously. Maybe you can play the easier mode and just have some fun, but even there, you can end up facing highly ranked and heavily geared players, which makes it difficult to actually enjoy the game.

I don't regret playing the game, but I do regret how much time I've invested into a system that often feels unfair.

The game has potential, but the matchmaking, loot system, cheating, gear recovery, and in-game economy need serious attention.

Zenless Zone Zero is the best gacha game on the market right now and here is why:

GACHA SYSTEM-
The gacha system in this game is similar to other Hoyo games where you are guaranteed the banner character if you lose the 50/50. ZZZ however, also makes sure to never forget this pity so you can save for months and months and still be guaranteed your next character if you ever fail to get someone. 
The premium currency (Polychrome) you can earn is also significantly more generous than most other gacha games I've ever played and is by far the best in the Hoyoverse games. 
Theres also many patches where otherwise limited banner characters are given for free, or special banners that dont have a 50/50 so you are guaranteed to get the character you pull for. 

In summary, the gacha / premium currency in this game is at a level of generosity typically reserved for the type of gacha games that dont have good gameplay to rely on instead. Speaking of which...

GAMEPLAY-
This is one of the most fast paced BeatEmUps youll ever play. The story missions are extremely easy, but the endgame content is extremely challenging, relying on great reaction time, managing the kits and meters of your characters, and insanely fast paced character combos and rotations during breaks in enemy defenses. Depending on your team comp, this game can get so complicated that high level gameplay can disorient even seasoned players. 
Mind you, if youre looking for mindless fun, you should probably stay away from endgame challenges unless youre willing to spend big. Speaking of which....

FREE TO PLAY FRIENDLY-
Im not going to pretend im a FTP player but i do have a FTP second account that can typically score in the midrange for the endgame content. You are given so many banner pulls for free you can reliably pull at least once a day, oftentimes more. The old characters have been powercrept quite a bit by the newer agents, but they are still very usable (especially the supports) most of these older agents youll end up getting for free just by playing daily. No one gets into a gacha game for the playstyles anyways, we all enjoy these games because of the characters, and these old characters are some of the prettiest designs ive seen from the genre... speaking of which....

ART DESIGN-
The art in this game is beautiful. You dont have to be an artist to tell that they put a lot of work into the designs and drawings of their characters. What I like even more than the art however, is the absolute spectacle in each characters moveset and gameplay. These characters just look so cool flying around the screen swinging their weapons. The special effects and animations pair nicely with the smooth 3d animations of the characters performing these actions, strong attacks feel strong, parries feel clean, ultimates feel ultimate.

STORY-
Ill be honest this is probably the weakest part of the game, but its still gripping enough to be enjoyed (pause). The game is on season 3 of its story right now, and it is by far the best of the three seasons. Season 1 was grounded and interesting, great for players who care more about the individual characters and their personal stories. Season 2 was the real introduction of the main bad guy, and is probably the weakest point in the story. It still has strong points, and isnt bad at all, just quite bland compared to the other two seasons. Season 3 introduces new characters while focusing on the best parts of the old seasons, creating an actual great storyline that anyone who played the first two seasons would easily get sucked into and invested in. 

In summary, Zenless Zone Zero has the gacha system of a game that would have bad gameplay, and the Gameplay of a game that would have a bad gacha.

Yes, this is a gacha game. No, I don't like that. Yes, it compromises the artistry that the game has to offer. 

But the artistry is still there. The combat systems are fun and dynamic, the animation is like nothing else out there, the music almost never misses, and the story (while somewhat shallow at times) works overtime to endear you to basically every character in the roster, even if they give a "bad" or "cliche" first impression. Even outside of the combat, most of the gameplay events and activities offer some fun character moments and snippets of gameplay riffing on other genres, from tower defense, to Fall Guys, to auto chess, to...whatever genre the hotpot scooping game is (it's secretly one of the best ones). The in-game arcade even has a surprisingly fleshed out Survivors-like. 

Even the gacha mechanics are better here than I've seen or heard of elsewhere (although I've mostly only played Genshin myself). The system itself is gambly (some might say predatory, and I wouldn't really object), but the game gives out more free currency than almost any other gacha I've heard of, along with free character unlocks and stuff at anniversary events. New characters are objectively stronger than most older ones, but old characters also get "potential" unlocks that buff them up from "useless" to "shockingly good". Endgame modes encourage chasing the newest characters with buffs and enemy types targeting their strengths, but because the game is fairly skill-based, many of them can be completed with subpar teams (e.g. of the same element or damage type) if played efficiently. I haven't spent a penny on this game, and I've occasionally managed to clear the highest reward threshold on the endgame modes--seeing how hard I can push that has been a lot of fun.

Honestly, it kinda sucks seing Zenless Zone Zero get written off as nothing more than a “gooner game” when there's so much about it that I genuinely love. I've seen so much more to this game than what people make fun of online, and it feels like all the effort and creativity that went into making it gets completely overlooked. I can understand why people make the jokes, but when that's all anyone seems to talk about, I feel like they're missing out on what actually makes ZZZ such a good game. It's more than just the character designs, and I wish more people would give it a fair chance before judging it

Once you look past all the jokes surrounding it, ZZZ is genuinely a great game. The story is interesting, the character writing is surprisingly good, and the cutscenes have some genuinely hilarious moments. The cast has so much personality and the interactions are fun to watch, and the game does a great job balancing serious moments with its more goofy side

The combat is another thing I think people underestimate. Sure, you can get away with button mashing when you're starting out, but there's actually a decent amount of depth once you understand how your characters work together. Learning their kits, figuring out rotations with timing assists and building a team with good synergy makes a noticeable difference. You can absolutely mash your way through some fights but only some cause mid-end game most enemys will one shot you, and understanding the combat makes it a lot more fun

And for gacha game, ZZZ is pretty generous with your time. You obviously don't get away from all the usual gacha mechanics unfortnatly, but I've never felt like spending money was necessary to enjoy the game or make progress. Character building is also relatively painless compared to some other games in the genre. You can get a new character to a solid, usable state without spending weeks grinding, which makes experimenting with different teams a lot more enjoyable

So if you've been thinking about giving ZZZ a try, don't let its reputation or the endless memes online put you off before you've even experienced it yourself. Give the story a chance, spend some time getting to know the characters, and don't just skip everything to get straight to the combat. There's genuinely a lot to appreciate here, and it's a shame that so much of the discussion around the game gets reduced to a handful of clips and jokes. ZZZ deserves a lot more credit than it gets

At the time of this review, this is my first (and only) gacha game.

I started playing ZZZ with the release of 2.0 (when it got added to xbox) and I have played hundreds of hours in the game since.

Tldr; Combat stands out, The story is good (2.0 - 2.5 may be a slog for most however), and honestly only play this game for new story content if you just want a fun time with no stress. If you like the game enough to play it more outside the story, you will have some annoyance from how the game will force you to progress slower (gacha system problem) and trying to get new characters (why are engine banners 75/25). However, it’s pretty forgiving compared to other gachas and (imo) there’s more fun to be had once you can build teams and clear endgame. (Also more challenging content).


Most if not all of its problems come from the fact it’s a gacha game- which is mainly a problem for non gacha gamers. However, that doesn't mean you shouldn’t try the game at all if you’ve never played a gacha game before. If you like anime, you’ll probably like the story in this game, and you can play through the entire story with little interaction with the predatory gacha systems of the game, as story content will have "default" agents for each mission which are leveled and built enough to clear them. The combat is simple on the surface, and you can play through and enjoy the game without having to learn the more complicated aspects of it. 

The story/characters are always the main appeal of gacha games, and as mentioned above, this game’s story is indirectly hurt as it’s a gacha game. This is mostly noticeable in the main 2.0 storyline, which may turn people away from the game completely. The game did bounce back very well after 2.5. As of 3.3, the story is much, much better than before. However, another problem caused by the “gacha of it all” is that some of your favorite characters may never/rarely show up again as HOYO will always move on to the next shiny new toy.

Now, the gacha part. Don’t spend money to get new characters. It’s HUNDREDS OF DOLLARS to guarantee a character, and THOUSANDS to max out mindscapes and engine. (I will say though- we must always thank those whales that let us F2P this game whenever we pull). If you play through the events and log in a few times a week, you can typically get one character every patch (unless you’re very unlucky…. Gacha systems…). 

New characters will always get shilled in endgame for a period of time, so meta is always in flux. So pull for who you like, and build a good team around them. Even without a hard shill, a well built team can usually clear the endgame (to full clear endgame you’ll need at least 3 teams). The one exception is if you build a full A-Rank team. That probs wont clear nowadays you need some limited S-Ranks to help out your A-Ranks now.

[list]

[h2]Cons:[/h2]

Here are the points in no particular order of importance.

Character design: despite the infamy of this game, I can’t see how someone could consider most of them goonworthy. Their costumes are so tame that I can only guess that people that think it’s too revealing or the physics are too provocative come from some place where burqas are mandatory for women.

User Interface: simply obnoxious to navigate. Way too many systems and submenus to navigate, oftentimes confusing to a point of fatigue.

Level-up Mechanics: unnecessarily convoluted, there are so many currencies and resources to administrate that it’s just a chore to go through.

Setting: while the hub locations are beautifully made and there are some activities that you can unlock, the actual missions are set in repetitive places you’re gonna see time and time again.

Quests: the mission structure is straightforward fetch quest back and forth with combat and the occasional light connect-the-dots tier minigame.

Story: there’s so much long-winded, inconsequential dialogue that during the first chapter I deliberately started skipping all of it, even the resumes. I recommend only reading them if there’s an agent that you’re interested in for characterisation purposes.

Cutscenes: due to the limitations of a mobile release, most of it is conveyed in an unengaging visual novel style. With the characters looking at you, talking to each other in still poses with no voice-overs or the occasional artbook/comic book scene (these are nicely done at least). What is aggravating is that the cinematics for contrast are unnatural, overly animated, unskippable and can’t be paused. So if you wanna take a leak in the meantime be careful brcause the game can throw you straight into combat.

Combat: pushing the obvious keychain-jangling, perhaps it’s the only redeemable thing of this game, the animations are cool and it can get pretty frenetic. It’s only screwed up in challenges and training, since so many consist of damage-sponge bosses that guarantee early tendinitis.

Part of this is admittedly because of my own personal dislikes about the game, but I find it hard to want to keep playing.

To the game's credit, it has more of a cohesive story than I was expecting, it's respectable and if you just like a serialized kind of game with fun characters that this may be up your alley. The character designs are fun, much of the dialog is voice-acted which is nice, and visually I think it looks nice. Environments are details, complete with graffiti and posters and all kinds of other things.

But all that being said, this is kind of pitched as an action game and after all the re-updating through the launcher after updating through Steam, creating an account, logging in after creating an account because for some reason I had to keep restarting, and then watching the very long opening cinematic, I think it took me something like 2 hours to actually get to any part of the game where I could control a character and do anything.

When there is the ability to perform combat, it is fast, fun, and responsive. I do actually enjoy playing it, but combat is usually book-ended with 30 minutes or so of either boring tutorial tasks that just keep on coming and coming, or lengthy dialog to set up the next mission, or cinematics, or other things that are just continuing to take up time. This is [i]not[/i] the kind of game you can boot up after a long day of work and just have some stupid fun beating up monsters and getting some new loot.

The game's loot system is poorly explained and over-complicated in my opinion, but that's kind of the whole UI to me. Which is the major issue with the game that I dislike the most. Every single menu in the game is a chore. I think that the this must have been a mobile game first so that most of these menus would have been navigated by touch, because every awful, labyrinthine menu in this game is a horror to use. Even from the main screen in the game, you can press start, but also hold various other keys to access either a menu wheel or single-key shortcuts to menus. There are tons of menus for promotions, and the shop, and the new player upgrade path, and the character screens, and equipment screens, and there are just so many I feel like every time I log in I end up finding a new menu that I didn't even know existed. Sometimes claiming your rewards is pressing in left stick, sometimes it's 'Y,' sometimes it's 'A,' or 'X,' or whatever. Even from menu to menu the confirm option changes, and this leads to a weird second-guessing of all the dialogs because you're never sure what the correct thing is to press. Sometimes 'B' will close the current menu and back out, but sometimes it does nothing... Sometimes 'Start' confirms, but sometimes it doesn't do anything or does something completely different.

I could see myself becoming invested in the game's story, it's still more time-consuming than I was initially expected but at least makes sense and has definitive arcs (at least from what I played) but the game's unforgivable UI experience really makes me want to smash my controller sometimes, especially when you spent 20 minutes after logging in to look for all of the stupid '!' notices for free things to check off or earn that never seem to be fully able to locate no matter how much you check and where you look. Please fix this.

That aside, I am also on the fence though about a game like this with such a fast pace of action combat that seems determined to keep you from that combat for as long as possible.

⭐ Zenless Zone Zero — A Stylish, Energetic, and Irresistibly Charming Ride

🎨 Visuals & Character Design
Zenless Zone Zero is a masterclass in modern character styling. Every Agent looks like they walked straight out of a high-end fashion spread and into a battlefield. Their designs are bold, expressive, and full of personality — the kind that makes you stop for a moment just to admire the details.

The animations are smooth and lively, giving each character a confident presence. Movements feel energetic, polished, and full of attitude, making the cast feel even more charismatic and memorable.

⚔️ Combat & Gameplay
The combat system is where ZZZ truly flexes. Fast-paced, rhythmic, and incredibly satisfying, every encounter feels like a choreographed action sequence. Swapping characters mid-fight feels seamless, and the impact of each hit is backed by stylish effects and crisp feedback.

The game rewards timing, awareness, and creativity, making battles feel fresh even after hours of play.

📚 Story & Worldbuilding
New Eridu is a city bursting with life, neon lights, and dimensional chaos. The story blends humor, mystery, and emotional beats in a way that keeps you hooked. The characters don’t just look good — they have depth, charm, and interactions that make the world feel genuinely alive.

The Hollow missions add a unique twist, mixing exploration with dynamic encounters that keep the pacing sharp.

🎶 Music & Atmosphere
The soundtrack is a full vibe. Bass-heavy tracks, stylish transitions, and energetic beats elevate every moment. Even navigating menus feels cool thanks to the game’s slick audiovisual design.

💫 Character Highlights & Complimenting Statements
🐺 Void Hunters — “We don’t chase trouble. Trouble chases us.”
The Void Hunters bring raw attitude and swagger to every scene. Their confidence, teamwork, and chaotic charm make them impossible to ignore. They fight like they’re showing off — and honestly, they are.

🐼 Shifu — “Stay close. I’ll handle the heavy lifting.”
Shifu’s calm strength and protective presence give the game a grounded warmth. He’s the kind of character who feels reliable, composed, and quietly charismatic — the gentle giant who always has your back.

🔥 Dialyn — “Watch closely. I don’t repeat my performances.”
Dialyn is pure flair wrapped in precision. Her movements are sharp, stylish, and full of personality. She fights like she’s dancing, and every animation feels like she’s teasing the battlefield itself.

⚡ Lucia — “Try to keep up. I won’t slow down for you.”

I'll start with what hurts the most: the foundation here is genuinely good. Combat is fast and rewarding, and team building has real depth once you understand how kits interact: passives that only switch on with the right teammates, rotations where swap order matters, elemental reactions you can plan around. Boss fights are often a showcase of art direction. The twin ballerina boss tells its whole story through the arena before a single line of dialogue, and it gave me chills. I pulled Claret purely because her gameplay looked fun. That's how strong the core is. Edit: I LOVE the english VA of the game. This and the combat are too good to be here. 

Then everything built around that core works against you.

[h2]Monetization and progression[/h2]
[list]
[*]Endgame demands specific characters, and those characters are locked behind the same currency the endgame is supposed to pay you. If you don't already have the roster, you can't earn what you need to build it.
[*]Weekly rewards are crumbs. Grinding a mode for 160 Polychromes a week feels like being paid in snacks.
[*]Progression is drip-fed by energy. I've had to wait a whole day just to run two missions and level up a new character once.
[*]New and returning players get it worst. I watched three banner rotations go by without being able to pull for the characters I actually wanted.
[*]Most outfits are paid, and nearly all of them go to swimsuits or the idol trio.
[/list]

[h2]Tutorials[/h2]
Tutorials on the level of the Wolverine game, maybe worse. The systems themselves are simple, and I could easily have learned them by exploring on my own. Instead, every tutorial dims the whole screen, locks you out of everything except the one button it wants you to press, and buries you in pop-ups that feel like three full pages of text, just to say "click here". It's the laziest possible way to teach a game. My biggest tip for new players: get an autoclicker, or use a turbo button on your controller, and spam through the tutorial dialogue. You won't miss anything you can't figure out yourself.

[h2]Character design[/h2]
The roster is overwhelmingly female. New male S-ranks are so rare that the only one across a long stretch of updates was literally a robot. And since Season 2, female designs have become steadily more compromised. Season 1 had "fanservice" that still told you who the character was: Yanagi is a deputy chief in a shirt and tie. Now we get a law enforcement officer (Cissia) patrolling the streets in barely any fabric, and Claret, the director of the workshop that forges the setting's legendary weapons, in an outfit so skimpy it stops being sexy and just becomes vulgar. Nobody in-world even reacts, which breaks the setting completely. Pants seem to have been discontinued. Childlike designs come with the classic "she's actually a thousand-year-old dragon" excuse. Meanwhile, the original cast got pushed aside the moment the new factions arrived.

The marketing makes it worse by selling splash art instead of what actually makes the game good. Every single person I tried to get into this game dismissed it as "a bunch of hentai dolls". A good boss fight was the only thing that ever impressed them, but even that couldn't break the hentai barrier.

[h2]Community[/h2]
Just look at the Steam reviews: the people here are Hentai Vs Furries-level gooners, and unfortunately, that's the audience the devs are aiming for.

[h2]PC performance[/h2]
The game runs on DirectX 11 by default, and that works fine. DLSS only comes with the DirectX 12 mode, which you have to enable yourself through the checkbox in the launcher, and that mode runs badly. So on PC you get to choose between a game that runs well and the upscaler. The lag spikes still happen on DX11, but they're less noticeable.

[h2]Verdict[/h2]
A brilliant foundation, a predatory casino, tutorials that don't teach, and designs aimed at the worst type of fanbase. Personally, I'll keep playing for what's left of the gameplay, because that part is still really good. But I wouldn't recommend anyone start playing it now.

Calling Zenless Zone Zero a “gooner game” because of some jiggle physics is honestly just disrespectful to the amount of work, creativity and passion that has clearly gone into this game.

Behind all the memes and allegations is genuinely a great game with an awesome story, really strong character writing and cutscenes that are actually funny. The characters have personality, their interactions feel natural and the game knows when to take itself seriously and when to just have fun.

One thing I especially love is how the story is presented. Instead of just throwing cutscene after cutscene at you, ZZZ constantly switches between traditional cutscenes, interactive comicbook sections and actual gameplay. It gives the game its own identity and keeps the storytelling from feeling repetitive.

The combat deserves more credit too. At first it can look like a game where you just mash buttons until everything dies but once you actually learn your characters, their kits, rotations, assists and how they interact with each other, there is a lot more to it. Button mashing works until it doesnt. Actually understanding your team makes the combat way more satisfying.

Its also surprisingly F2P friendly. Obviously its still a gacha game but Ive never felt like I need to spend money to enjoy it or progress. Another huge positive is that ZZZ actually respects your time. Building a new character doesnt feel like signing up for several weeks of grinding before youre finally allowed to use them properly. You can get characters into a good and usable state relatively quickly and then improve them further if you want to.

If youre thinking about trying ZZZ, dont let its reputation online decide what the game is for you before you’ve even played it. Give it a genuine chance, dont immediately skip through everything and actually let yourself get invested in the story and characters. There is a lot more to this game than the few clips that constantly get passed around online and I think it deserves to be judged for what it actually is.

F2P Review of ZZZ 

Story 8/10:

Enjoyed the main story and how it plays out like a JRPG. The bulk of play time would be the main story events, and it often feels like watching anime. The story is somewhat coherent across seasons, with S1 having a strong dynamic with both siblings and characters, while S2 felt more emotionally heavy with its S2 characters and story. I really wish they had co-develop the siblings more, it kinda fell off as the seasons progresses (and I miss Eous).

Combat: 9/10

Satisfying combat system with the combination of dodge parrys and agent swaps. The combat can have a wide range of styles and can be as simplistic as button mashing to planning combos between agents - this all depends on the agents you have rolled for. There is an intricate system of agent building, team building, factoring attack types to bosses and the final payoff is very satisfying, when your fully built team is able to shine. Also somewhat fun to research on these teams. Disappointingly, the end-game content is not kind to F2P accounts (or skill issue?)

World-Building: 9/10

There are moments when I would just idle around in Lumina Square, Port Elpis, Failume Heights and Booastrum. The music tailored to each of these places is amazing and I am just impressed at how much love the developers have placed into these places. During trust events with agents, some of the little shops have a renewed purpose and its always fun to see how different characters interact with these assets (especially Tin Master's Coffee). A huge amount of effort can go into making these places come to life, like the Suibian Temple construction and adopting Inky!  

F2P Friendly? 7/10

The game gives you about ~240 polychromes per F2P account. This means you can likely roll up to 3 favourite agents, if you happen to win all 50-50s. You can either choose to roll for meta and go all-in for the combat optimisation to clear end-game content OR roll for your favourite agents. The latter will then feel like your own personified ZZZ world, as your favourite agents will appear in-game more often, as you level up in Trust Events. Last note, the game can get rather 'grindy' for its dailies, but the HIA OST feels therapeutic.

Final Score: 9/10

Back then, I only saw Nicole Damara, and I was already blown away! When it finally came out on Steam, I was able to try it out for myself and explore it on my own.

All in all, ZZZ is my absolute favorite donghua/anime-style game! 
The entire world design, how it works, the gameplay, and above all, the Women are just fantastic and perfectly match my tastes!

Gameplay: In a way, it's kept fairly simple and accessible to everyone, but it can be quite challenging if you want it to be. It plays very well with a controller and mainly features a “hack-and-slash” style of gameplay.

Mini-games: The developers have kept things very varied and included a ton of different mini-games. There’s something for everyone. You can tell here and there that it was designed for mobile devices, but they’ve optimized everything perfectly for keyboards and controllers so they play well too. They’ve really gone all out to offer as much as possible. It’s really great!

Graphics: In this regard, I've often been impressed by how good it looks and how detailed it is in all the right places. The entire design has been rendered beautifully.

Animation & Physics: They really put a lot of attention to detail into this! They know their craft and have done an absolutely amazing job! The videos and sequences are so great! Some of it is among the best work I've ever seen.
The physics—well, it's perfectly balanced and really brings out the perfection of women just as it should!
Just walking around, exploring, or fighting. It's just beautiful to look at!

Waifus & Crushes: Another thing ZZZ nailed in every way is the Women in the game. It’s literally a waifu paradise! So many truly amazing Women. They really poured their heart and soul into this aspect. Nicole had me hooked right away, but as I played, I got to know so many other amazing Ladies that I was constantly blown away. Most of them are among my absolute favorites in the entire gaming industry. Above all, I love how perfectly they’ve captured our divinity.

Even among the guys, there are a few who are cool and whose types I really like.

Gacha: For a gacha game, they don't really force you to spend money, and the game relies almost exclusively on this one principle. There are other things you can buy, but they aren’t absolutely necessary. They’ve also set a monthly limit on some items—presumably to prevent you from spending too much and possibly to protect people who might otherwise get into debt. So, generally speaking, the pressure to spend isn’t very high, and you can easily play through the game without spending anything.
Whenever I feel like it, I invest more for fun. My approach is this: It’s a fantastic game that’s available to me for free. So I’m happy to support and fund the development studio and everyone involved for their great work.

Story & content: As I said, the whole thing was crafted with a lot of love, and it offers an unbelievable number of possibilities. I've already put in over 120 hours, and it seems like there's just as much still waiting for me. It's just crazy how much you can do.

Menus & Management: If there’s one aspect that isn’t quite ideal, it’s this one. There are a lot of menus—some are a bit hidden, others are buried deep—and you have to think about where this or that was. It’s overwhelming at first. At the beginning, I tended to ignore it and didn’t really deal with it until much later. Once you’ve learned it, you understand how it works, but it takes time.

Overall: Not only is it one of my absolute favorite games, but it's also my favorite universes. I just love everything about it!

You do have to parry attacks and dodge, on top of that your damage is dictated by how well you build that character like how most hoyo games are built. and the community is also super friendly than the other hoyo communities in my opinion. This game does have that 50/50 system where you get a character that isn't the limited character on the banner/patch you are pulling, you get a standard character that you can pull for in the regular banner! To get a limited S star, you need to have at minimum 90 pulls if you aren't on a 50/50. To guarantee a character you need at least 180. ^_^ it's just a downside of zenless zone zero, and don't worry if you lose! Characters will usually get a rerun in a future patch, so if you still want them you can always save up again to get them!

I do definitely still recommend that you save your money though, since sometimes this game releases events where you have to spend at least 200 USD to get a certain cosmetic for your profile!! And for f2p players, save up the free rewards for the characters you really really want! Don't waste all of your pulls in one go since the character may get a rerun in the future and you also have to consider the state of your account before you pull that character, since the game also is based on character synergy! There are tons of guides on how to build characters and what their best teammates are.

for those who may hear the terms "soft pity" and "hard pity" in the community when you first join, those are mechanics to ensure you get a character. for characters, soft pity is kind of a hidden luck boost starting at around 75 pity, hard pity is at exactly 90 pulls, since thats when your game forces an S star. for w-engines/weapons, soft pity is 65, hard pity is 80.

Actually fun combat for a gatcha. Action arena fighter split somewhere down the line between Musou and Kingdom Hearts. Focuses on parries and quick reactions while dumping ults during damage windows or building up elemental thresholds. Game has a pretty wide player skill expression with team flexibility and the character builds. Soldier 0 Anby plays like your 10 year old self spamming Sora's Sonic Blade in Kh2 while Banyue is a cyborg monk rekka with custom combos. In a game genre that is expected to powercreep characters to sell more the devs take the time to go back and give new tools to existing characters people got attached with. Characters are the gatcha focus, but the game is  pretty f2p friendly overall; enough pulls per patch to get one pitty S rank / 5 star character. Respects your time; it is a game that you log in to do dailies for but you can have them done under 2 minutes. Material farming has an energy charge system attached but has a backup storage of 10x your daily limit, so you can do them all on your time.

The world is pretty interesting. A post-post apocalypse where there are ever growing dungeons call Hollows grow around the periphery, having to be battled back. A backdrop of you and your sibling running their own blockbuster to rent vhs out; getting wrapped up in the shenanigans of a pretty fun cast of characters. Characters are fun to get invested in, music is a lot better than it has any right to be, and there are many small things to see and do in-between patches. Seriously go listen to the music on -App of your choice-. DAMIDAMI, Still Vacation, Dance of Death; a large range of different genres with high class talent.

Game has had a pretty large shift in direction due to community feedback and the devs are constantly trying new things. The main loop originally had a top down dungeon crawler (think Mystery Dungeon or Etrian Odyssey) that led into single instance combats, but was changed to a hallway limited 3d world (Final Fantasy X/XIII or Kingdom Hearts BBS) that has interspersed combat. There is a lot of debate about the major shift in the community but the game isn't shy about trying new things. We've had bullet hell mini-games, pinball, rhythm games, a couple rouge-like modes, a bangboo-themed auto battle chess, tower defense, cooking mama minigames, and a multiplayer raid that showed up for two weeks and still was probably the best thing added. 

For downsides, it is a gatcha. Meaning you gamble in game & paid currency for your chance at the waifu/husbando of the month. As much as I have fun with this game, it comes with the big red flag of if being detrimental to people with poor financial habits. Only play this game if you can restrain yourself. Otherwise it's just normal gatcha player gripes: Buff the rest of the older characters, re-run older characters, better pity system, you've heard this before. 

Not sure how it runs on PC, game absolutely fried my last phone. Runs pretty well on the steam deck but you need wifi to play it.

If what I said sounds interesting check it out. Interested to see where this game goes in the future.

As of writing this review Zenless Zone Zero is quite literally the best gacha game currently on the market. 

The characters and story are well written, the voice acting (even in english) is incredible and the sheer range of designs this game offers make sure that anyone will like at the very least one character.

The combat is fun, rewarding to learn and surprisingly deep and the game offers a wide range of different experiences even in the weekly grind, not counting events or story missions, that are quite unique on its own.

The developers have also been incredibly generous with the amount of free currency and items you can obtain by just playing the game and doing dailies and weeklies. Not to mention entire characters and their signature equipment in certain events like anniversaries.

The game does have its cons though.
The main one, in my opnion, is the obvious one for Hoyoverse games- The 'artifact' system. Or how this game calls it, the Drive Disks. Sure you can farm many of them quite quickly, but there is no guarantee that any will be usable, no less good. But this is something you'll only have to worry about for the endgame.

Speaking of the endgame, that is another flaw. The endgame modes of this game require 3 fully built teams, which means a total of 9 characters. You can clear endgame content without having the 'best' characters, but it will be quite taxing on execution. You will eventually be able to have this and more, but, it will take a long time. (I play since the game's original release and have a total of 4 fully built teams, as a very light spender, not f2p.)

The last con i can list, is that, for some characters, id say around 60% of the S rank cast, you are required to not only pull the character, but also their signature equipment (W-Engine) as not doing so, may cause them to have severely limited utility or damage output. But there are many characters that also work without their signature, so it is something you will have to look up and evaluate on a case by case basis.

Overall, i'd say that if you play gacha games, ZZZ is an absolutely excellent game. If you don't play gacha games but are wanting to try one out, this is THE gacha game to start with at the moment.

I followed this game ever since a teaser for it came out, and since they were accepting beta testers. I've been called a gooner over it, and I'll be fair - it is indeed a gooner game. On a separate review for another gooner game, I stated that everyone likes their own gacha games, and that a majority of people like Zenless Zone Zero because everything jiggles in all the right places. That is true. If you want to compare it to Genshin Impact, you definitely can. If you want to whale on it, you definitely can as well. Aiming to get 6 copies of Z-Engines, optimal Disc Drives, and 6 copies of characters are a grind - I can't stress this enough. If you came for a challenge, similar to Wuthering Waves, I would say ZZZ is easier. Very realistically, these things are what would make someone turn their back away from it.

But, is it a good game to introduce to people wanting to get into gacha/roguelike games? Yes. Is ZZZ based on skill? Partly, you'll have to time things. Your damage is dictated by your build and character. Are you playing them right? Regardless, what I will comment is that ZZZ has been one of the more stylish gachas I have played ever. Zenless Zone Zero has a great story, a friendly community, and a modern art style that couldn't be anymore appealing. As an internal, personal request when the beta was finished, I felt that they needed to focus more on the music, and after doing so, I couldn't be happier. The developers know their audience, and from watching so many character demos, they are great at marketing the characters themselves. Astra Yao, Ellen Joe, and Lycaon's have been my absolute favorites - not because they are a stereotype, but because the artists themselves go ALL out with the theme the character's themselves are supposed to represent. They also design their characters in a way that encourages you to look for details; looking under the eye or clavicle for moles, or wearing certain clothing to emphasize a physical part of the character. They want you to ask questions. Why is he wearing an eyepatch? Why do they have pointy teeth like a shark? 

Behind what makes an art style so lovely, and a cast of unique characters all the more better - their cutscenes, their gameplay, and the single press of a button expresses impact. When they swing, the motion feels like there is force to it. It is so clear that their movements have the intention to kill, and not hold back against their enemies. The deeper you get into the game, you'll find that the enemies will also start doing the same. Now, while the swaying and jiggling is so exaggerated, I think it is fun for it to be as such. I've been a day one supporter, and even after dropping it for a bit as it gradually grew, just for me to come back to it later - the game still has the same feelings I had when I first played it. With every perfect dodge and perfect counter, there is flow. It can be mindless if you'd like it to be. The only improvement I can see being implemented or recommended would be to include that same display of impact in character abilities and movements, within dialogue. Each character already has their unique playstyles. Why not make them say something wild before/during a fight or as they are about to hit someone to the moon?

Zenless Zone Zero has always been worth trying. Especially now that it is on Steam, and since they've made it clear they'd like to pave their own path in F2P games. It rivals NIKKE in story and character designs too, but it's unfair to compare them. NIKKE is more unhinged anyways.

Having played since 1.0, I can confidently say ZZZ is definitely the best gacha game I've ever played. It isn't gorgeous like WuWa, not big or open  like Genshin, but it sure wear its own charm. Besides the usual gacha game design elements it really does have a lot of unique and charming things going on. 

The main pull of the game is its high paced combat and at that to me it sure is enjoyable and fun, especially compared to other games within the genre like Genshin and WuWa where it just feels a bit too repetitive, (also HSR, though it is a lot different). Frankly, I love the combat in this game especially when there are so much room for optimisation despite having quite a low skill floor, making it suitable for both casuals and tryhards such as myself.

Like any other gacha games, the characters within ZZZ are amazingly designed and the offer the most unique models out of any gacha I've played. Though not a big concern for me, sometimes I do find that the game tends to unneccessarily sexualise its characters which can be gross and straight up concerning at times. 

A small shoutout for the game's graphics, it's simple and nothing too crazy like Arknights Endfields but beautiful and pleasant to the eyes regardless. There can be performance issues at times however, despite me running on what I'd consider a pretty decent rig.

Finally, the gameplay loop. I log in and do my dailies for 5 minutes and that's it. To some it is a con, but for me it's a pro that a gacha game actually respects my time. Even the weekly grinds and endgame modes only take me about 30 minutes to complete them all. When there's new events and stories they barely take any time to complete, I usually just wait until the end to do it all in one sitting.

TLDR: If you enjoy WuWa esque visuals but more quirky and urban, fast paced combat, low maintainance daily grind, this game is perfect for you.

My updated review about Zenless Zone Zero;

-- NOTE --
To begin I have a favor to ask, please read these cohesive reviews from us players, we want to simply say one thing: Try ZZZ first before believing common rumors or what you see online through short form content, ZZZ in most of this media is portrayed in a bad light, and wrongfully so to steer people away for no real reason, at least that is what I believe personally. I hope my points below can bring to light what I and many others believe makes ZZZ unique.

-- GAMEPLAY --
- It's hard to put ZZZ's gameplay into one little section, because it has so much diversity to it, whether it be side-quest gamemodes, event gamemodes, the combat itself, there is a LOT of content for you to enjoy, and I fully mean that. But to keep it short let me break it up:
- The direct combat, which is inspired (officially stated) by street fighter and has the action style of devil may cry (I find) works just so so well, everything flows into each other so seamlessly it just feels awesome to fight and use characters, from the chain attacks (combos) between characters to special mechanics like blocking boss enemy control skills (basically a very high damage attack) it doesn't just feel cool, it also SOUNDS cool, the sound design carries a lot of this extra detail.
- A few gamemodes I found notable, the extraction gamemode, the battle tower, the roguelite gamemode, the retro arcade, the pinball machine, the watchdogs like investigator gamemode. They are all just so unique and I really loved doing them, there is still so many many more than those.
- Some people might be concerned about the gacha aspect of ZZZ, and of course since it's a "gacha" game there is luck based banner pulling and a lot of stuff in terms of leveling characters is revolved around luck, which shouldn't come to anyones surprise. However, what I can say is; ZZZ rewards you, and it rewards you VERY, VERY generously with premium currency, you will be fine for hundreds of hours before permanent rewards completely dry up and your reliant on rewards that come from every patch, however even THOSE give so much you'll be okay. 
- Performance is obviously also important for people, not much I can say though, with all raytracing features enabled ZZZ runs with mediocre FPS as can be expected and works completely fine with 140+ FPS with upscaling and or frame gen enabled, turning off ray tracing, ZZZ probably runs on any PC thats from the last few years.

-- MUSIC --
- ZZZ is within my top 3 spots for the best OST of any game, simply because of how much diversity and creativity has been put into each and every soundtrack, Sān-Z / HOYO-Mix have absolutely set the bar up higher for any future music I will hear in other games simply because of that, sound design and music matters so much for any game and here, especially in ZZZ I find, they have proven they are capable of producing and delivering, each and every time.

- STORY --
- ZZZ by far delivered (and still is, the story is NOT over) the best story out of any story game I've played, simply because of how much emotion, creativity and love for it's own world and design it has shown. EVERY time it needed to deliver it did, Every impactful moment has such beauty and thought put into it, the music that fits right in, the beautiful still shots that are hand drawn to convey the current scene and absolutely magnificent fully animated 3D cutscenes during the peak of the current plot, it didn't disappoint in any of these. Coming back to emotion, even if this sounds a little corny, a lot of moments of the story have brought up tears, they've done everything right in those moments to warrant it.
-
I would also like to point how well voice acting is done in ZZZ's english version, every character portrays their personality and traits so good I feel bad for skipping voicelines.
-
Additionally, outside of ZZZ itself, the character demo's and episodes posted on their social media were all so worth it to watch, even for anyone that doesn't play the game directly something like Ramielle's Character Demo "Just like old times" is so wonderfully put together and only adds to the game, even indirectly, I recommend anyone to watch it, it's only 6 minutes.

ZZZ is a great game. There's lots to love. HOWEVER, there are some downsides.

Pros:
-The combat is great. 
-The music is absolutely incredible. 
-The animations are crazy, both gooner and non-gooner. 
-The characters are super unique and are well written. Their kits are typically very fun too.
-The dialogue is great and does an incredible job being both serious and downright ridiculous. One character will have a Berserk-level tragic upbringing, and another will just be some dude that models his whole life and character off a cool TV character.

Cons:
-Much of the community is best avoided. Its not as bad as blue archive, as the ratio of adult-proportioned characters to characters that any sane person would go "Oh yea, thats someone's kid" is significantly higher. Age old excuse of "Naw, thats a 100 year old lady" is often provided, but like I could understand just a petite character. The game has those too, but there are some that are just so obviously child coded that I worry. Simply, just avoid any part of the community that mains the characters in question. They are NOT safe spaces.
-It's a gacha game. You will never get every character you want AND be able to min-max them fully without spending a LOT of money. Free to play IS viable, but you should fully expect that you will *never* get everything you want or need for your builds. The whole experience is built to make you want to drain your wallet.

Things that could either be a massive pro or a massive con:
-Its a gooner game. Most of the female characters effectively walk around in either lingerie or swimsuits but with extra steps or capes or whatever. It's not to say the outfits dont have genuine effort put into their art, but the amount of lace, slightly-too-tight belts, sheer fabric, and garters in the outfits in this game is absurd. The jiggle physics are absurd. The characters will often whip their asses in the air. The animations are so smooth and fluid and fully serve the game's goal of making every female character as hot as possible so you want to buy them. There are continuous and never ending camera shots of every possible body part that could be attractive to somebody. Butt? Check. Belly? Check. Legs? Check. Thighs? Check. Hips? Check. Feet? Check. Arm-pits? Yup, its here. Dawg, there is a character with DETAILED armpit folds. Characters will end certain combat moves in poses that are comparable to the Jack-O pose, contorted to positions that most living humans cannot achieve, but ultimately serve to accentuate the aforementioned body parts as much as possible. I genuinely cannot say this any simpler way: ZZZ is tailer-made to be gooner-bait.
-ZZZ is a lot more mobile game coded in its play than something like Genshin or WuWa. When not in combat missions, t's a series of walkable spaces with shops, random NPCs, and occasional interactables. In combat missions, its basically just a series of rooms with big open spaces in the middle where you fight things, then move on to the next. Don't expect some crazy immersive world.

All-in-all, great game. Just remember to avoid the community, keep your wallet safe, and don't even bother if you are anti-gooner.

I have given this game more than 2 good, honest hours of my life. It is the most disappointing hack-and-slash game I think I have ever played. So many of the game's concepts and systems have the potential to make for a fun and addicting combat system, but the extremely shallow depth of the characters you only have access to once you start the game (who also happen to be the only Company of Agents that have such an enjoyably electric dynamic which spurred me on to slog through this game) along with the frankly disappointing enemy design from a company as big as MiHoyo leads to a game experience that reveals itself as extremely monotonous and boring once you look past the flashy lights and admittedly fantastic animation work. There is very little depth to the combat system; characters have little to no resources or options to let the player truly explore their approach to the enemies. The active tagging system, and the 3 Agents per mission structure could have led to a very exciting and deep combat system. Instead, the combat system requires you to do very little in the way of difficulty (I played through the entire first chapter on the hardest difficulty, with any real challenge being taken away due to the incredibly easy parrying system). It is an incredibly disappointing, and frustrating experience which left me dissatisfied at nearly every single turn. If you are fine with a simpler hack-and-slash combat system with beautiful animation, and you truly don't mind a story that can and will disappoint you at many turns, and character designs that are very "gooner"-centered (nearly all of the adult-looking women have very exaggerated jiggle physics), then I would recommend this game to you. If you are like me, and you truly enjoy Character Action/Hack-and-Slash Games which allow you to get lost in their combat system and really get invested in the character's kits that you play as, then I absolutely would not recommend this game to you. Zenless Zone Zero looks like a slam dunk of a game on the surface, but when actually digging into the game's content it ends up being very shallow and disappointing.

I was asked by friends for a few months to try this game out before it came to PC, only picking it up after finishing some other projects and other games.
A lot of them hyped up a ton of characters, the setting & Worldbuilding, multiple parts of the story that could be their own books in terms of length, and especially the gameplay being a solid Action packed game packed to the brim with content. Described as a a different take to Devil May Cry 5 style game with multiple characters to swap between. Something that someone as picky as me would enjoy, for someone who does not enjoy 95% of mobile based games.

While the Worldbuilding is pretty good, and a fair number of the characters are interesting in backstory and design. (Even the male characters for many of them. Shocking for a mobile game).
The main thing that I can't recommend this game on is the gameplay. I really wasn't a fan of how little depth it had, and even amount of it there was in actual gameplay focused sections.

Lots of cutscenes & dialogue sections that are a mix of skippable, and un-skippable segments that are surrounding the sections where I can play the game and go into combat, but the combat felt rather lackluster, and rather boring.
ZZZ's Combat is very one button, or just button mash until specials/ultimate attacks are available, which even then don't feel as strong as they should be for an attack that requires such a big charge up. The ability to dodge into a counter/parry, or swap out into a parry is an OK option that causes some stuns/staggers but that's all it really feels like I'm doing. It's not challenging, it's not rewarding, and getting the characters to be stronger (and just getting more/new characters in general) is really bad. Straight up gambling to get a character and thus a new way to play the game... Yay.... I hate gacha... It isn't fun or rewarding, but it's unfortunately extremely required in order to keep playing the game as you go through the story. You don't always get trial run characters to play as either.

As for leveling up the few characters I have like Trigger... I'm not a fan of having to farm a bunch of materials via challenges or multi-menu deep options to make the sniper character Trigger more effective in combat. I just prefer to play through them in a level, defeat enemies, and get stronger that way. But I guess that's not how majority of Mobile based action or RPG games work anymore.

In the end, after playing the game for about 7 - 8 hours ( Closer to 10 if I include load times and idle times when looking up information/guides for the game.) It's not for me, and I just don't entirely see what others are getting out of it even as they cross the 40 - 50+ hour mark into the triple digit playtimes. Or maybe I just think mobile games are

Here's hoping that those new Hoyoverse games shown off recently are more my speed. Hopefully a full fledge game you own 100%, singleplayer, with plenty of mechanics in the game. That sounds good.

Where do I even begin?. There are so many things wrong with this game that I could go on forever. Honestly, seeing how popular it still is despite all these ongoing issues is ridiculous.

Let's start with the wishing system. Getting enough wishes in this game is practically impossible unless you're willing to spend hours completing the entire storyline, keeping up with daily commissions, and grinding through endless content. Otherwise, you're pretty much pushed toward spending money.

Speaking of spending money, let's talk about the paywall and customer service. There have been multiple complaints from players about fraudulent charges, poor customer support, and situations where players have reportedly had their wishes deducted after requesting refunds for purchases they didn't authorize. How is that acceptable? Punishing customers for disputing unauthorized purchases is an absolutely terrible way to handle customer service.

Now, moving on to the storyline. How has this game been around for so many years without adding a proper dialogue-skipping option? Other games offer this feature, so why can't Genshin? Not everyone wants to spend hours sitting through endless dialogue and unnecessarily long story quests. Some players are here for the combat, exploration, and character-building, not to spend eight hours listening to dialogue. At the very least, give players the OPTION to skip quests and dialogue they aren't interested in.

And before anyone says anything, yes, player feedback is another major issue. It genuinely feels like the developers rarely listen to what their community has been asking for. There are so many quality-of-life improvements that players have requested for years, yet many of these problems continue to go unaddressed.

Next is character-building and material farming. Why are certain character materials locked behind specific days of the week? I understand having a rotation for certain activities, but restricting essential materials on multiple days is unnecessarily frustrating. Not everyone has the time to log in on a specific day just to farm materials. Some people have school, work, and other responsibilities. If you miss the day, congratulations, now you have to wait even longer. It makes an already tedious grinding system even worse.

Another major disappointment is the lack of diversity in the character roster. I would genuinely love to see more representation of different cultures, backgrounds, and people throughout the game. While Genshin incorporates different cultural inspirations into its regions, I still feel there is room for much more diversity in its character designs and representation. It would be nice to see the developers put more effort into expanding that aspect of the game.

Honestly, I could list plenty of other problems, but I don't want this review turning into an entire essay. Genshin Impact has so much potential, but the constant frustrations surrounding its reward system, customer service, dialogue, farming restrictions, and lack of meaningful community feedback make the experience exhausting.

If you're looking for a gacha game, I would honestly recommend checking out **Punishing: Gray Raven** or **Wuthering Waves** instead. In my experience, they offer a more enjoyable approach to rewards, combat, and player feedback.

At this point, Genshin has given me more migraines than enjoyment. There is so much that could be improved, but until the developers start taking these issues seriously, I personally wouldn't recommend this game.

**Save yourself the frustration and look elsewhere.**

A masterpiece for fulfilling wanderlust, but endgame is incredibly disappointing. Updated review given in v7.1: The world building in recent patches has been so satisfying that I felt compelled to raise my rating from two stars to three stars. The endgame and most of the recent kit designs since my last review (given in v6.6; see below) are still a complete travesty of this game’s amazing elemental combat system. Over the course of the v6.X versions, rather than game knowledge checks or team building puzzles, the endgame modes have all become time-based dps checks or, worse, quasi-character checks where the win condition is almost always just bringing some collections of characters who are or have recently been on sale. No thank you; I’m going back to the breathtaking and element-rich open world to play with the whacky teams I have personally assembled among the 100+ characters in the game, because I feel like playing a cryo burgeon team and putting Lauma on prototype amber and everyone else on favonious weapons, instead of worrying about a 475% enemy HP multiplier in a timed, uninteresting fight in a barren endgame dungeon that cannot be finished without a select few characters (who are or have been recently on sale).

Edited review given in v6.6 (Luna V) on the very unfortunate and total decline in recent combat design quality:
If you care about interactive gameplay, stay away from Genshin Impact. Recent enemies such as the Knuckle Duckle in the endgames as well as recent character kit designs in the Nod-Krai region show that the dev team no longer cares about the very thing that makes Genshin combat unique and fun: Elemental interactions that care about elemental gauge and application quantity, rate, and order. As a prime example, the minions that the Knuckle Duckle spawns (in Luna V’s Stygian Onslaught) do not even show their elemental auras. On the character kit design’s side, all the moon-wheel characters have their respective kinds of so-called “lunar reaction damage” built in their kits, which do not care about enemy elemental aura, thereby essentially nullifying the intricate dance of elemental applications that is the entire point of the gameplay.
	This recent abandonment of fun for the sake of (elementally) braindead kits like those of Varesa, Skirk, Ineffa, Flins, Nefer, Illuga, and Zibai is deliberate. The devs know how to make (elementally) engaging kits, but now they are actively punishing the players for having fun with their unique elemental system, a trend exemplified by Varka’s kit, which punishes nontrivial elemental reactions, that was released just last week.
	The rating is one star higher than the lowest possible score because of the story, world building, and music, all of which remain excellent and arguably have even improved over time, as well as for the engaging character kits, which exist but have become increasingly rare, as well as having been deliberately phased out of relevance in the endgame modes by the unprecedentedly aggressive HP inflation in the last few months.
