My Problem With Sumeru. This game is pretty good, overall, for the kind of game it is. I’m not overly interested in the story, but I love exploration and doing quests. As a Tighnari main from my first day, one of the areas I had most awaited was Sumeru. I was a newer player; so it had been out for a while before; but I was careful not to look too far into it. One of my favorite things in a game is a deep, lush, beautiful forest, which I was looking forward to, from what I knew and also what Tighnari mentioned about the Avidia forest. Sadly, what I hoped would be a sprawling forest was more like about two dozen or so large trees spaced somewhat closer together than in the rest of the regions, along with some clever angling of the cliffs to produce what could be called forest lighting. I get trees are hard to make that detailed, but I wish the area known for its forests had actual… y’know, forests. I flew all over looking for a real, thick, lush forest, and found areas that could more accurately be called “glade” or “wood.” But no forest. :(

My other problem lies mainly in character design, in specific, the “jiggle physics.” I understand that it’s pretty typical for games like this, even if I personally find it a little distasteful, especially when pushed to the extreme. But it drives me nuts that the female characters wearing armor or thick layers of clothing still have so much “jiggle.” 

Also, can we optimize the storage system please?

So yes, mostly little things like that, and small matters of taste. It is, at very least, worth a try, given it’s free. My best advice: get yourself a Tighnari.

Decline of Genshin Impact. I have been playing Genshin Impact since launch, and while the game was once genuinely enjoyable and rewarding, it has increasingly become a frustrating experience, especially for f2p players.

One of the biggest issues is how aggressively the game now seems designed around monetization. Primogem rewards feel increasingly stingy compared to the growing number of characters and banners being released. Many newer 5-star characters are also heavily dependent on other premium 5-star units to unlock their full potential, creating a system that feels less about strategic team-building and more about encouraging players to spend money.

The rewards from events have also declined in value. In the past, major events often rewarded players with unique weapons that could be used by a wide range of characters. Now, players are frequently given cosmetic weapon skins instead. While cosmetics may appeal to some, they offer no gameplay value, making event rewards feel significantly less meaningful.

Another major problem is the ever-increasing length of quests. Story content that once felt engaging and well-paced has become bloated with excessive dialogue and unnecessary filler. Some quests can easily take four hours or more to complete. Most players have jobs, families, studies, and other responsibilities. Many of us play games to relax after a busy day, not to sit through hours of mandatory dialogue before reaching the actual gameplay.

This leads to perhaps the most frustrating issue of all: the lack of a proper skip button. Not every player is interested in every piece of lore, and forcing players to sit through endless conversations is simply poor user experience. If the story is compelling, players will choose to engage with it. Giving players the option to skip dialogue does not diminish the quality of the narrative—it simply respects their time.

The developers recently announced that future updates will allow players to advance dialogue more quickly without waiting for voice lines to finish. While this is a welcome improvement, it still misses the point. Faster dialogue is not the same as a skip button. Players will still be forced to repeatedly click through conversations line by line. After years of player feedback, it is difficult to understand why a simple and widely requested feature remains absent.

Genshin Impact still has a beautiful world, excellent music, and enjoyable combat. However, the game increasingly feels designed to maximize player spending and engagement metrics rather than respect players’ time. As a launch-day player, it is disappointing to see a game that once felt generous and exciting become so exhausting and frustrating to play.

Love this game, but here is some feedback!. Overall, this game was absolutely addictive and amazing, from the theme songs to the nostalgia of the quests… this game just feels like pure art. From the lore, to the art, everything just feels right. 
I’ve started playing in 1.0, but lost my account due to my old iPad storage just being enough to hold like 2 games 😭 However, I’ve just recently made a new account to start fresh! As much as I love Genshin, there are a few things that tick me off, such as;

Lack of diversity in the game: Natlan showed little to no diversity when it’s supposed to represent Africa and South America, but I found that all of the characters that were supposed to have darker skin, just had a light brown or a greyish skin tone. As someone who is South American myself, I found myself to be very disappointed in the lack of diversity, especially when it comes to giving the characters melanin. (Somehow all the characters are still whiter than a sheet of a4 paper)

The constant feel of misogyny: I am fully aware that there are indeed female characters that are very powerful, though there are only a few of characters that have clothing that do not show any skin. I’ve also noticed that the female characters are all made for the male gaze and for pure fan service, yes, there can be SOME female characters that do show skin, but it gets to a point where the character designs feel repetitive with the detached sleeves and short dresses, which causes a lot of fans to not look forward to newer female characters. 

The chibi characters: As much as I hate to admit it, there are only female child like characters, and none are boys. Honestly, it gives the impression that they are “loli” based/themed, which is honestly disgusting. I would honestly love a new character that has the same child/chibi-like look, but for the character to be male. 


In conclusion, these issues are very easily fixable, but I do believe myself that the feedback I gave was very valuable feedback. Hoyoverse, please, please, please make a change and take my feedback in consideration, since a lot of people do share the same opinions and thoughts as me. The sole reason why choose to give this advice is because I love this game, and I’ll love to see diversity and modest characters, without everything feeling repetitive and boring when it comes to character design. 

Thank you for taking the time to read this!

Longtime issues. For as long as I’ve played, the game has had a lot of issues for a long time, especially regarding the pull counts in a given version and the general quality of life, but the quality of the game has gotten noticeably worse in recent time. 

Since the addition of Miliastra Wonderland attention towards the development of the main part of the game has diminished. For one, there has been little to no map expansions through the course of Nod-Krai, only haven gotten three tiny regions and being in version 6.6.

The powercreep has shifted pretty significantly since Natlan as well, it hasn’t been a major issue until it really started rearing its head in Nod-Krai as well. In Natlan, you still had access to the region-exclusive mechanic of Nightsoul and could benefit from weapons and artifacts that interacted with it through the four star characters. But in Nod-Krai, four star characters have no access to the new Lunar Reactions that were introduced with the region, which is pretty unfair, there should be ways to interact with new mechanics without having to pull for the shiny new five star character. 

This issue is made worse by the over saturation of these mechanics being shilled in end game content, which makes it even more difficult to get Primogems. While not impossible to do without Lunar reactions, not being able to utilize them makes the battles far more tedious and usually requires much more investment into your characters to do enough damage to offset the inconvenience and time wasted. 

I love this game, but I want to see it improve. I hope that Hoyoverse will eventually take some of the criticisms of the community to heart.

Critical Reviews are all Nitpicky and Genshin is Excellent. Time and care have clearly gone into the design and storytelling of each region to fit them in with their real-world counterparts. The game runs smoothly on lower settings even on older phones with occasional buffering, though only during teleport sequences or the more resource-heavy cutscenes. Character designs are beautiful and characters are rebalanced even years after their release. I have loved this game since around 2022 and am very happy with the direction it is going in. Monetization is limited, with no ads and entirely being supported by its gacha system. Every character is obtainable without purchase, I have many sought-after characters despite never having spent a penny. Surveys are released regularly to review how users interact with the world of teyvat and what could improve the game. Overall I have never been happier with a free mobile game, and I even enjoy this title more than many paid titles.

a honest and realistic review. Here is my realistic review-
Pros:
Honestly, I absolutely love the graphics in Genshin Impact. The art style is gorgeous, the animations are perfectly smooth, and every region feels real and alive. There are so many tiny environmental details that make exploring fun, and it genuinely reminds me of games like Zelda in a good way.

One of my favorite things is how each Nation has its own culture, architecture, music, food inspirations, and traditions based on real-world locations. It makes the world feel diverse and immersive instead of repetitive. The soundtrack is also amazing.

I also appreciate the amount of effort put into the voice acting. Most of the voice actors do an amazing job bringing the characters to life, and some performances are genuinely memorable. Even if certain voice lines can feel repetitive or unnecessary sometimes, the talent behind them is still obvious.

Cons:
One issue I have with the game is the lack of darker-skinned playable characters. Considering how many Nations are inspired by different cultures around the world, it feels disappointing that there still isn’t much visible skin-tone diversity in the cast. Even with regions inspired by warmer climates and diverse cultures, the representation still feels limited.

Another huge problem is how increasingly pay-to-win the game feels. Grinding for Primogems as a free-to-play player has become exhausting, and the rewards often feel tiny compared to how expensive the gacha system is. Saving for characters can take forever unless you spend money regularly, which makes the game feel less rewarding.

I also really dislike the direction many of the newer character designs have taken in 2025–2026. Older designs were iconic, and balanced, but now a lot of characters seem overly revealing or heavily focused on fan service. I understand some players enjoy that style, but personally it’s become excessive and makes many newer designs feel less unique or meaningful.

At this point, it feels like HoYoverse cares more about selling characters than improving player experience. The world and lore are still beautiful, but the lack of meaningful rewards, the stronger push toward spending money, and the repetitive fan-service-heavy designs have made the game much less enjoyable for me overall.

As a Long-Time Genshin Player, I've Never Seen the Community This Frustrated. I've been playing Genshin Impact for years, and honestly, I've never seen the community this angry, exhausted, and divided.
Genshin has always had drama. We've argued about character kits, anniversary rewards, resin, endgame content, and a hundred other things over the years. But what we're seeing right now feels different. This isn't one controversy that everyone will forget in a week. It's years of frustration finally boiling over all at once.
The biggest issue for me isn't even a single feature or update. It's the growing feeling that HoYoverse has stopped listening to the people who actually play the game.
The 64 Pull Situation Was a Slap in the Face
The recent patch economy was honestly embarrassing.
When players realized the patch only gave around 60 to 64 pulls, people were shocked. In a game where getting a single five-star can require far more than that, it felt ridiculously stingy. Some of the banners featured highly anticipated characters, yet free-to-play players couldn't even guarantee reaching soft pity.
Every time this topic comes up, the same argument appears: "You don't need every character."
That's not the point.
The point is that Genshin is one of the highest-grossing gacha games in the world, yet it still feels determined to give players the bare minimum. After years of success, many of us expected the game to become more generous, not less.
Powercreep Is Real, Even If People Don't Want to Admit It
For years, Genshin players proudly said the game didn't have powercreep.
Technically, older characters can still clear content.
But that's not what players mean when they talk about powercreep anymore.
The newer characters keep getting mechanics that feel increasingly important for high-end content. New reaction systems, new team archetypes, new gimmicks, new ways to bypass challenges. Meanwhile, older characters that people spent months saving for are slowly becoming less attractive compared to the latest releases.
Can you still clear Spiral Abyss with old units?
Sure.
Does it feel like the game increasingly wants you to pull newer characters?
Absolutely.
The pressure isn't coming from raw numbers. It's coming from design.
Why Are We Getting Miliastra Instead of What Players Actually Want?
This is probably the most divisive topic right now.
Some people genuinely enjoy Miliastra, and that's fine.
But a lot of players look at it and wonder why so much effort is being spent on side content when the core game still has so many unresolved issues.
People want better event rewards.
People want meaningful endgame improvements.
People want old event weapons to return.
People want more permanent gameplay systems.
People want quality-of-life updates that other games figured out years ago.
Instead, we're getting content that many players describe as feeling disconnected from what made Genshin popular in the first place.
Genshin became successful because of exploration, worldbuilding, and adventure. When development resources seem focused elsewhere, frustration is inevitable.
Even the Story Isn't Safe Anymore
This one hurts the most.
For years, the story was the thing that kept many players invested.
People spent countless hours reading lore, watching theory videos, and discussing mysteries that had been built up since launch. Expectations were high because HoYoverse spent years creating those expectations.
Unfortunately, a lot of recent story developments have left players disappointed.
Some major reveals didn't hit as hard as people expected. Some plotlines felt rushed. Some character arcs felt unsatisfying.
Not everyone agrees, of course, but the fact that story criticism is becoming this common says a lot.
When even the lore community starts losing enthusiasm, that's usually a warning sign.
The Moderation Problem Is Making Everything Worse
The thing that frustrates me most is the feeling that criticism isn't being addressed.
Every time players complain, there are accusations of deleted comments, locked discussions, banned users, or criticism disappearing from official spaces.
Whether every accusation is true or not almost doesn't matter anymore.
The damage comes from the perception.
When players feel ignored for years, they stop giving developers the benefit of the doubt. Every moderation action starts looking suspicious. Every deleted post becomes evidence of censorship.
Instead of calming things down, it makes people even angrier.
The Competition Problem
A few years ago, Genshin had a luxury no longer available to it.
It had no real competition.
Now players can compare Genshin directly with other games that offer better quality-of-life features, better rewards, better communication, and more responsiveness to player feedback.
The uncomfortable truth is that many Genshin players are starting to realize they don't have to settle anymore.
That's why the frustration feels so intense.
Players aren't just angry about rewards or balance changes. They're looking at what other games are doing and asking a simple question:
"Why can't Genshin do this too?"
Final Thoughts
I don't think Genshin Impact is a bad game.
If it were, people wouldn't be this upset.
The reason the community is so angry is because people still care. They still love the world, the characters, the music, and the story. They want the game to succeed.
But passion eventually turns into frustration when players feel ignored long enough.
Right now, Genshin Impact feels like a game that's relying on its reputation instead of earning goodwill from its community.
The game is still successful.
The game is still popular.
But for the first time since I started playing, it genuinely feels like a large portion of the playerbase is losing patience.
And if HoYoverse doesn't start listening, that patience may run out completely.

Not as friendly and giving compared to other hoyoverse games. I’m writing as a long-time player who genuinely enjoys Genshin Impact and wants to see the game improve. There is a lot that Genshin does exceptionally well. The art direction is beautiful, the world design is immersive, the graphics are polished, and the story has many memorable moments. It’s clear that a huge amount of care and talent has gone into building the game.
That said, one of the most frustrating parts of the player experience is the lack of a proper skip button for dialogue and cutscenes. While story content is appreciated, not every player has the time or desire to sit through every conversation, especially during repeat content, commissions, or slower event dialogue. Other HoYoverse titles have shown that skip features can exist without harming the overall experience. Giving players the choice would simply respect their time and make the game more accessible.
Another major issue is the scarcity of free Primogems. Compared with other HoYoverse games, Genshin often feels far less generous with premium currency, rewards, and pull opportunities. This becomes especially noticeable for free-to-play and low-spending players who want to stay engaged but feel constantly limited. Other HoYoverse games tend to provide more rewards, more frequent incentives, and a stronger sense of progression.
Genshin Impact has the foundation of an amazing game, and that’s exactly why these issues stand out so much. The visuals, music, combat, and world are excellent. Choose the one that best suits your playstyle—each character has their own distinct approach: some excel at crowd control, others focus on dealing damage, and there are even support characters capable of reviving teammates. This adds great variety to every match. The setting, inspired by Eastern fantasy, is stylish, and the combat animations are truly spectacular.

[h1] NARAKA: BLADEPOINT — I Came for the Combat, Stayed for the Fashion, and Forgot How Clocks Work[/h1]

[b]784 hours played. 32 days and 16 hours of my life. Zero regrets. Mostly.[/b]
I've spent 784 hours playing NARAKA: BLADEPOINT, so I think I've earned the right to talk about it.

Is it enough time to master the game? Probably not. Is it enough time to develop an unhealthy attachment to virtual cosmetics? Absolutely.

NARAKA combines fast-paced melee combat, incredible mobility, beautiful character designs, tons of events, and enough content to keep you busy for an alarming amount of time.

You launch the game thinking, "I'll play for 30 minutes."

Three hours later, your dinner is cold, your sleep schedule has filed a missing person report, and you're saying, "Just one more match."

Welcome to NARAKA.

[h1] Character Customization: The REAL Endgame [/h1]

The character customization system offers plenty of options for facial features, hairstyles, colors, and other details. Add the gorgeous skins, outfits, and accessories, and you've got a recipe for disaster.

A very beautiful disaster.

Seriously, the art team deserves a raise.

You can spend hours creating the perfect character, adjusting every little detail until everything looks just right. Then you finish and realize you haven't actually played the game.

Your enemies are practicing combos. You're studying color theory.

They're preparing for battle. You're preparing a fashion show.

And somehow, you're having the time of your life.

After 784 hours, there's always another character to customize or another tiny detail that MUST be changed.

At this point, NARAKA is two games in a trench coat: a combat game and a character customization simulator.

And I'm not sure which one I'm better at.

[h1] Events Everywhere! (Goodbye, Free Time) [/h1]

NARAKA does a great job with events and seasonal content. There's always something to do, from completing missions to unlocking cosmetics.

You log in to complete your daily missions. Easy, right?

Wrong.

You notice an event, check the rewards, discover another mission, and spot a skin you absolutely need.

Suddenly, your original plan is gone, your bedtime is in danger, and you're doing missions you didn't even know existed five minutes ago.

Daily missions aren't missions anymore. They're a legally binding contract.

You don't log in to play. You report for duty.

Congratulations, NARAKA. You've reinvented unpaid overtime.

[h1] The Battle Pass: Your Wallet Is Safe. Your Free Time Isn't. [/h1]

You can purchase the Battle Pass with Gold and earn all that Gold back by completing all [b]115 levels[/b].

Finish the pass, recover your Gold, and put it toward the next one. Save it, and you can keep the cycle going without spending real money on every new pass.

Your wallet: "Finally, some peace and quiet."

Your free time: "I've been sacrificed for the greater good."

There's just one small detail: you have to complete all 115 levels.

[b]The Gold comes back. The hours don't.[/b]

Considering I've already played for 784 hours, I'm probably not the right person to ask for time-management advice.

[h1] Playing With Friends: Friendship Is Temporary, Chaos Is Eternal [/h1]

Playing with friends makes NARAKA even more fun. You can coordinate attacks, develop strategies, and save each other from terrible situations.

Of course, that assumes anyone remembers the plan once the first enemy appears.

One person is fighting, another is running in the opposite direction, and someone is asking what just happened.

Teamwork makes the dream work.

Unfortunately, nobody told the team what the dream was.

Winning together feels great, but sometimes the funniest matches are the ones where absolutely everything goes wrong.

[h1] RNG: Random Number Generator or Personal Enemy?[/h1]

Trying to get a specific cosmetic can be painful. You know exactly what you want, open your rewards full of hope, and the game gives you literally anything else.

You try again.

More disappointment.

Again.

Nothing.

At this point, you're conducting a scientific experiment on the relationship between hope and suffering.

You start wondering whether the game knows exactly what you want and deliberately avoids giving it to you.

When you finally get something amazing, it feels fantastic. Until then, you're questioning your luck and possibly the entire mathematical foundation of the universe.

You close the menu and reconsider your life choices.

Then you open it again.

Because apparently, we never learn.

After 784 hours, I've concluded that RNG and I have a complicated relationship.

I want the cosmetics. RNG wants me to suffer.

It's not healthy, but I'm too invested to leave.

[h1] So, Is NARAKA: BLADEPOINT Worth Playing? [/h1]

Absolutely.

The combat is exciting, the customization is extensive, the skins are gorgeous, the events keep things fresh, and playing with friends makes everything better.

Sure, RNG can be frustrating, but it doesn't take away from how enjoyable the game is overall.

If you enjoy action games, collecting cosmetics, customizing characters, and playing with friends, NARAKA is absolutely worth checking out.

Just be warned.

You start playing for the combat.

You stay for the cosmetics.

You spend an hour customizing a character, get distracted by an event, complete your daily missions, play with friends, and get wrecked by RNG.

Then you look at the clock and say:

"Okay, just one more match."

Congratulations. You've officially become part of the problem.

[h3]784 hours played. 32 days and 16 hours gone. Still playing.[/h3]

I could have learned a new language or become a responsible adult. Instead, I learned that the perfect shade of blue matters, daily missions are legally binding, and RNG is my natural enemy.

Would I do it all again? Absolutely.

[b]10/10 — Would lose track of time again.[/b]

Your wallet is safe. Your free time, however, is another story.

[h3]Send help. Or Gold. Preferably Gold.[/h3]

9/10 I was not entirely convinced at first but upon learning the game, this has got to be the best battle royale ever made. Picture Sekiro-like combat on a set of different battle royale maps with a lot of characters, each having their own (gimmickey) set of abilities and playstyles that you can choose.
 It's melee favored, because ranged weapons are mainly used to poke the enemy before engaging or to catch them from escaping. Tare limited to durability and that takes time to replenish amidst the fight and to collect beforehand, upon other things that you will loot during the match. But that's of course not everything in the game.

The combat is really high quality and despite what noobs might want you to believe; button mashing will quite literally get you owned. There is an increidbly in depth attack system full of combos, for every single weapon that can dictate your entire playstyle or approach to combat and a set of souljades that go from neat stacking buffs to literal alterations that enhance your current weapon attacks.

There are some annoying and spammy ultimate abilities, however they can only  be used once per fight and most of them leave you unable to chase, which makes securing kills pretty hard, as the movement in this game is probably the most important part.

Whatever can't catch you, can't fight you. And whatever can't fight you, can't kill you. With that being said, when starting out freshly, there certainly should be a lot of players that will be able to defeat you, since that is how niche competetive games work. With not enough casuals the sweats start cannibalizing eachother and thats not even neccessarily a bad thing, but as a new player with an unrecognized MMR you will mostly fight against bots in the beginning until the game starts dropping in real opponents, Even if I know that the guy that chased me down through the whole match will probably end me, I can at least start learning his attack pattern, like with some Sekiro boss. Or maybe I could just sneak away and let him take out his wrath on some other unfortunate souls. That kind of experience is entirely unique to Naraka.

The game is completely Free to Play and everything I describe in the following segment are purely optional cosmetics that do not alter the mechanical gameplay. The in-game store is detailed and if you don't find luck with mostly free lootcrates that have an unmissable chance system, should you get unlucky enough, You could also purchase some cosmetics directly from the store for mostly real money. However, the game to me seems quite generous and whilst I spent some real currency, I also got multiple legendary outfits, weapon skins and cosmetic accessories and extremes (even rarer) just by playing. Since the community on asian servers (f.e. china) is so large, there are tons of events where they hand out free stuff and I managed to get quite lucky with some legacy lootboxes.

Sadly the only negatives I have to give is the games incredible size on my harddrive. Whilst that can be explained by tons of modes. Next to the usual battle royale casual, and ranked with solos, duos and trios, with some vanilla - like event modes or a team deathmatch. We also have f.e. the whole single player/ coop stuff the extraction mode, some event mode,.. Whilst everything is semi-regularly maintained, you can occasionally hit the 10-20+ GB seasonal patch, but that's probably just an internet (skill) issue on my end. It runs surprisingly stable and you will quickly have patched access to the newest settings (upscaling algorythms, etc)
The only real bad thing that to me isn't objective is, that the game keeps getting shoved into a direction that to me looks more like a mobile game. Flashy new characters that basically force a disengage when ultiling since they will statcheck you. That#s not really bothering me though. What's awkward to me is the powercreep that leaves older and more beloved (and balanced and more fun to fight) characters in the dust.  Then again, with enough gamesense on these aforementioned characters you can definitely still perform. Just maybe not as easily. It's a difficult debate and calling something "no skill" in an enviroment where "hold checking" has become the basic means of traveling the map on foot.

Overall the best free game that I haver ever played. And I definitely haven't played enough, If you can give this game a shot and learn just the basics of the simple movement tech or combat 1&1, you will find yourself become anime. And that's also a feeling that no other game can provide.

Naraka: Bladepoint is one of those games that feels strange at first, but once the combat finally clicks, it becomes incredibly hard to put down.

The biggest strength is definitely the combat. Fights are not just about having better gear — timing, positioning, counters and knowing when to attack actually matter. Every weapon feels different, and there is always something new to learn. The movement system makes it even better, especially the grappling hook and climbing. Chasing someone across the map or escaping a fight by flying over rooftops never gets old.

I also really like how much room there is for improvement. At the beginning, you will probably get destroyed by more experienced players, but after some practice you start understanding combos, spacing, counters and different hero abilities. Winning a difficult duel after that feels much more satisfying than winning a typical BR gunfight.

The game also has a great visual style. The characters, weapons, animations and environments give Naraka its own identity, and the combat often feels more like a martial arts movie than a traditional battle royale.

There are definitely some frustrating parts. The learning curve can be rough, matchmaking is not always fair, and ping/netcode issues can make certain fights feel completely out of your control. These problems can be especially annoying when you are trying to improve.

Still, the core gameplay is so unique that I think Naraka is worth trying even if you normally don't like battle royale games. If you enjoy competitive combat and games where getting better actually changes how you play, this one can be seriously addictive.

In terms of pure gameplay, Naraka is a great and unique battle royale. The combat feels great, the characters and their abilities are well designed and fun to use. It essentially is fighting game style combat with a mix of moba / hero shooter esque character abilties and ultimates. It also offers an insane level of character customization where you can really go off on the details if you enjoy that.

However, the reality of the gameplay experience has a few glaring issues, mostly related to the game's lack of popularity in the west. Essentially 95% + of the playerbase is Chinese, playing on the CN server. The other servers have an extremely small population. It is extremely easy to become a top 500 player or a top 100 on the leaderboard of a certain character because the amount of people playing on the NA / EU servers is so small. ( That's why its funny that some of the people in these reviews are saying proudly that they're top 500, lol sweetie we all are.)

This lack of playerbase leads to the biggest issue of playing on NA servers: the queue times. In the earlier ranks, queues will be manageable because the lobbies are completely full of bots, but when you get to higher ranks they become ridiculous. Outside of peak gameplay times, I struggle to get games at all and regularly wait 15-30 min and straight up have my queue time out. 

During more popular times its still a dice roll whether the queue will pop within 10-15 min. When I do get into a game, its with the same 10 people who I see over and over, the top ranked people on the server because those are the only people who play the game in NA. This obviously gets tiring quickly. It's a shame because if the game had a healthy population in the west it would be a blast.

Its possible to play on the Chinese server with some workaround but if you are in the US the ping will be very high. However, the queue times are only 1-2 min at all times and the lobby is full of actual players. It creates a sad dilemma for NA/EU players, would you rather maybe get 1 game an hour on low ping or play regularly but with very high ping?

Cons:
- Matchmaking is an horrendous mess. Below Solar you will be matched primarily against bots (which isn't too bad up to Silver since you are learning the basics of combat) but past the Solar point, you'll match against top 100s of the server. Understanding mistakes and improving on your own at that point is pretty rough
- Netcode: completely client based. If a player has high ping, they get the advantage because you can rubberband people into hitboxes and miss hits.
- Rig based: Higher FPS means higher animation speed, which means higher dps.

NARAKA: BLADEPOINT. What a game...I was first introduced to Battle Royales with Apex back during it's release in 2019. I quickly grew to love the genre and went on to try others such as Fortnite, PUBG, and even Warzone (who hasn't played 1 of those anyway?). I remembered seeing Shroud try out Naraka a year after its release though it was still going through heavy testing and bug fixes at the time. I finally decided to give the game a try in December 2023 and was instantly hooked. The fast paced, high skill ceiling combat is truly what makes this game unique. I love how you can even customize some of the playable characters with a pretty detailed character creator. I tried a decent bit of the character roster, but the one whom held my heart was Matari <3. I was eager to play ranked to get better but I believe you have to level to 30 first before queueing. Pretty much all of my matches were Solo Queue. I was truly blessed to pick the game up as it was ascending it's peak. Based on current data the peak concurrent player count  on PC was 385,000 back in 2024 which is when I last played. Even during then queue times for Solos ranged anywhere from instant to upwards of 10 or so minutes depending on the time of day. Unfortunately now the player count is at an all time low. There's still a dedicated fanbase, but the numbers have been declining ever since season 14. If they experimented with various game modes I'm sure that might boost it to a certain extent, I'm not aware of much of the changes outside of balancing since I last played. The biggest question you're probably wondering is why I'm not currently playing now, well to put it simply I feel as though I have beaten the game. I leveled up to be able to play ranked Solos and got to just under Platinum. My very last game was my best ending in 24 kills (out of 48 and maybe 1 or 2 of those were rebirths) and also getting first blood. I don't think I'll ever be able to replicate that and I'm glad it turned out that way. I've managed to cover content on it by making 3 montages on my Youtube channel as well. For those who haven't tried the game please do, this is not only one of the best games I've ever played but one of the last few games with a dedicated team of developers passionate about keeping the game genuine through anti-cheat and monitoring malicious player activity. For those of you that still play, keep grinding the Herald's Trial for Glory...

While I do understand that filling in matches with bots is in an intentional thing to presumably "teach" people how to play and reduce queue times, however, it is arguably more painful to just simply put up with bots than I anticipated. This is becoming more and more common and if I'm honest, it drives me absolutely insane.

I’ve played a lot of battle royale games over the years, but honestly, Naraka: Bladepoint feels like something completely different in the best possible way. Most BR games focus only on guns and positioning, but Naraka mixes fast-paced movement, intense melee combat, grappling hooks, mind games, and mechanical skill in a way that feels incredibly satisfying once you get into it.

At first, the game can feel overwhelming. There are so many mechanics to learn — combos, counters, focus attacks, movement tech, hero abilities, weapon matchups, and timing. But that’s exactly why the game feels rewarding. Every fight feels like an actual duel instead of just “who saw who first.” When you win a fight in Naraka, it genuinely feels earned.

One of my favorite things about the game is the movement system. The grappling hook alone makes traversal insanely fun. Flying through trees, chasing enemies across rooftops, escaping impossible situations, or suddenly turning a fight around with mobility never gets old. The game feels fast, fluid, and stylish almost all the time.

The combat is probably the strongest part of the game. It’s easy to understand the basics, but there’s a very high skill ceiling. Good players can outplay opponents through timing, reads, positioning, and smart decision-making instead of pure luck. Every weapon also has its own personality. Some weapons feel aggressive and explosive, while others reward patience and precision. Learning different weapons keeps the gameplay fresh even after many hours.

Visually, the game is beautiful. The environments, character designs, outfits, animations, and overall atmosphere are genuinely impressive. The art direction gives the game a unique identity compared to other battle royale titles. Some moments honestly feel like scenes from a martial arts movie.

Another thing I appreciate is that Naraka creates memorable moments constantly. Whether it’s surviving a chaotic 1v3, winning a duel with 1 HP left, landing a perfect counter, or swinging into a final fight out of nowhere, the game creates stories naturally. Few multiplayer games give me that adrenaline rush anymore, but Naraka still manages to do it.

Of course, the game isn’t perfect. The learning curve is brutal for new players, and sometimes matchmaking can feel rough when you run into extremely experienced players. There are also moments where server issues or ping differences can be frustrating. But despite those problems, the core gameplay is so strong that I keep coming back.

What really makes Naraka special for me is that it rewards improvement. The more time you invest, the more the game opens up. You start understanding mind games, spacing, combo routes, movement tricks, and team coordination on a deeper level. It feels satisfying to notice your own progress over time.

Overall, I genuinely think Naraka: Bladepoint is one of the most unique multiplayer games released in recent years. It combines skill-based combat, mobility, strategy, and cinematic action better than almost any other battle royale game out there. Naraka is a Chinese game that had the potential to be a fairly decent FG-based multiplayer product but made the incredibly unfortunate decision to use Unity and is built by a team whose only experience with Unity is transactional netcode in cellphone games. Given that Unity is a poorly-performing disaster of a cash grab at the best of times one can only expect good things when the greed of both worlds unite in a singular hyper-sticky smile-inducing idol-glazing handshake.

Naraka is plagued by technical issues of the most absurd nature. Just like Fallout 76 it uses no Delta Timers, so animation speeds and thus their notifies (damage events, for example) are completely dictated by FPS. This means everything from combos to float times to locomotion are entirely dictated by your processor and being on the receiving end of a hardware diff is a lot like being abducted by ET and having your genitals sucked clean off by little green men. CN tournaments have an FPS cap, but everywhere else in the game world is a wild west where the game's extremely CPU cache hungry performance problems render it virtually unplayable for anyone not using an X3d processor. If you're sub 300 FPS many core mechanics of the game will become so inconsistent you'll be convinced many of the double-digit players that still actively play this product in NA are hacking, when in reality they're just paying over a thousand dollarydoos for the exclusive opportunity of having an advantage in a dead game. That isn't to say the game isn't filled with hackers, though - only CN has an active moderation team, and Doujin is still filled with endless videos of people blatantly changing memory values willy nilly to fly around, machinegun slap people to death in Penglai, grab and teleport people into the skybox and other goofy nonsense. But all it takes to de-facto cheat in this game is run the right CPU - GPU virtually has no impact on the game performance at all and putting the game on an M2 doesn't change the fact you can bake a loaf of bread in the time it takes to reload, something that may be an often occurance for you if, like me, seeing the disconnect window always results in the game irrecoverably freezing. This has killed me more times than I can count, and not just because I'm canadian and our education system is the laughing stock of the third world.

To make matters worse the netcode is similar to that of Halo PC. Naraka is an extremely tight game when it comes to frame timings, but you wouldn't know that because it was exclusively built to be run in China's server ecosystem where all players have LAN speeds. Even ping as low as 30 can experience a ton of inconsistencies in global, though the specifics of why are often debated, with everything from the netcode itself to server tick rate being brought up. The reality is I can play third-person shooters with Australian hosts at 250ms and it will be a far more enjoyable and reliable experience than the 80ms I get in NA. Throw in the FPS issues and it becomes clear why the people who say this games issues lay in marketing are exclusively those running 40ms or lower and 300fps or higher. Oh, to be young and willfully malicious. By the way, most people who play this game do so to look for internet girlfriends. If you play a female character you might be fortunate enough to receive PM's and friend requests from colorful characters just like in the good old days of Battle.net or World of Warcraft. Yes, I do offer eDaddy services. You can pay me in cat hair.

While not everyone will be able to figure out why the game feels like such ass to play, they'll still feel it. Player retention is extremely low in Naraka because it takes hundreds to thousands of hours to grasp the basics of its fairly deep combat system and the extremely unnecessarily jank "mechanics" like 211, repair dodging, and crouch cancelling, none of which are healthy for the game but have yet to be fixed, yet this system is commonly sidestepped by an ever-increasing obsession with transformers and heroes with absurd paragraphs-long abilities that grant them the ability to either ignore half the game through gold focus and iframes, including many other hero skills, and deal insane damage often for free. Anyone telling you transformers aren't busted is generally an Inor or Yoto player trying to fly under the radar. Throw in the developer's absurd obsession with touch of death on a game that confuses the hell out of players who've religiously competed since it first launched, increasingly obnoxious weapon designs, an anti-cheat that contributes nothing but stalls, constant crashes and bugs, and you've got a damn mess. Watch NBPL and see people still pull off ToD's with grapples alone on fps cap and you are vomit.

It's a shame, since Naraka is one of the few products released in quite a few years that doesn't feature a prominence of QTE's and other nonsense that detract from third-person combat, and the battle royale aspect, while a source of much disdain for many, is nonetheless quite interesting in this kind of a design. Unfortunately, the technical issues far oustrip anything that can be summarized in a mere text review. Rubberbanding is just an accepted norm, disconnecting or crashing in Maelstrom is part and parcel, and the ingame ping indicator is tied to the game thread leading to extremely bizarre and mysterious interactions. The situation with Naraka is so bad that players have conducted years-long witch hunts against each other, convinced any given person is a cheater, when in reality they merely won the geographical lottery and have an x3d processor. 

The developer, of course, doesn't give the slightest shred of a shit what anyone outside of CN thinks, though it's debatable if they care about what anyone inside of CN thinks, either. We're just refuse fed the rare bread crumb, and plenty of collabs and features remain CN only, like chatting. It's so bad that the Mr. Black collaboration didn't even bother to air the cartoon at localized times, so in NA we could only view it at 3am. It's like they just forgot that different parts of the world have different time zones. Lol, no, they didn't forget, they just don't care. Now when it comes to things in their product that would actually take an hour or two to fix, like all of the countless holes in the geoemtry, floating objects, busted mantling behavior, busted collision meshes, the disaster that is Maelstrom... well, it's no shock nothing actually improves. Instead, they made DX11 completely unplayably laggy for me somehow. Fantastic.

It wouldn't take much effort to fix the vast majority of Naraka's egregious issues which is precisely why they have never been fixed and likely never will be fixed. So long as you don't take the game too seriously you can probably make it work. But by the time you leave bot hell and start encountering actual players you'll be instantly thrust into facing off with Hypernova, Numza and a slew of server hoppers running at 150ms hoping to find a queue because their own server also only has a few hours of activity. Watching numerous high-level streamers of this game will tell you that pretty much only Hypernova, whose games amount to effortlessly farming the unfortunate fools that think they'll actually be able to get good at this game, finds the experience enjoyable in any manner. Yet still the few still married to the masochism of enduring the lash of the spanking will continue to march on, unable to find anything else that gives them the satisfaction of self-flagellation quite like this game does. Only when you find yourself begging daddy for more as you lay in a blood-soaked pool underneath the staircase while various eRumis spam cat emoticons at you to the sound of two hideously deformed Tarkas slapping each other while doling out $2000 USD for a hue shift on a bane or $500 USD on a poorly weight painted hair mesh do you truly begin to understand the essence of the Chinese gaming experience.

This free to play visual novel with adventure and roleplaying game (RPG) elements by NLB project features two short stories in Am I a Monster and Return of Red Riding Hood, New Adventures. In Am I a Monster, it features an unnamed male protagonist who has suddenly turned into a wolf and is hunted by fearful townspeople and police officers. The protagonist (the player) must decide what to kill and to eat as he gradually becomes more attuned as a wolf or retains his human form.

In Return of Red Riding Hood, New Adventures, it continues with a parody of the classic children's fairy tale where the mother of the same unnamed girl in NLB project's earlier game Return of Red Riding Hood Enhanced Edition tries to tell a bedtime story of Little Red Riding Hood to her daughter to get her to sleep at night.

As a young teenage girl Little Red Riding Hood, she lives with her mother and receives a task by her mother to gather ingredients to make a basket of sorrel, ham or cottage cheese pastries to deliver to her grandmother who is a forester and lives alone in a cottage inside a forest. After making the pastries, the game will transition to the visual novel part of the game where Red Riding Hood or her mother will deliver the pastries to their grandmother and encounter Wolf and/or woodcutters along the way.

Having played this game for over an hour to get all endings and achievements, the RPG elements in Am I a Monster is a highlight of this short story where the ending and a few encounters will turn out differently depending on whether the protagonist becomes more attuned as a wolf or not.

In Return of Red Riding Hood, New Adventures, the funny and imaginative scriptwriting in this short story is the main highlight of this entire free to play game by itself. It retains the same amount of comedic humour from Return of Red Riding Hood Enhanced Edition that can be ridiculous and funny. Having played the earlier game Return of Red Riding Hood Enhanced Edition, there are less tragic endings this time, possibly because the mother knows better how to get the girl to sleep without making her cry, unlike the girl's brother. As such, I have also decided to shorten the Big Bad Wolf to just Wolf as there are fewer bad endings involving Wolf actually devouring Little Red Riding Hood or any member of her family.

All the endings and achievements are easy to obtain where a published community guide is available at the time of this review. Hope this game will have a higher confidence metric in future.

Among the cons, in Am I a Monster, it feels too short and doesn't give enough variety in the form of having more differences between being more attuned as a wolf or as a human being. This leads to a bit of wasted potential as an RPG which could possibly keep readers interested in the game longer. When comparing the number of endings in Am I a Monster with Return of Red Riding Hood, New Adventures, the former has much fewer plot branches and endings. The plot and storyline is still interesting enough to read through in any case. In Return of Red Riding Hood, New Adventures, due to the large number of plot branches and endings, the short story only has 5 save slots available, it would be nice to have more save slots for this game or short story.

Recommended as a free to play game with nice artwork, classical background music and for those who like a short visual novel featuring wolves in two short stories, one of which contains many comedic twists to the classic fairy tale.

Naraka: Bladepoint is:

50% skill
30% panic
20% “what just happened”

⭐ Recommended if: you enjoy competitive, skill-heavy combat and don’t mind losing while learning
⚠️ Not recommended if: you want a chill battle royale or dislike getting outplayed repeatedly

NARAKA: BLADEPOINT, developed by 24 Entertainment and published by NetEase Games, is a bold reinterpretation of the battle royale formula that replaces traditional firearm-dominated encounters with fluid, high-intensity melee combat. Set in a world inspired by East Asian mythology and martial arts traditions, the game drops up to 60 players onto a sprawling map where survival hinges on mechanical mastery, mobility, and tactical awareness. Since transitioning to a free-to-play model, it has attracted a broad and competitive player base, positioning itself as one of the more distinctive entries in the crowded battle royale genre.

What immediately separates NARAKA: BLADEPOINT from its contemporaries is its combat system. Rather than relying primarily on guns, the game emphasizes swords, spears, greatswords, daggers, and other melee weapons, each with unique move sets, combo strings, and counter mechanics. Combat operates on a rock-paper-scissors philosophy built around light attacks, charged attacks, and parries, creating layered duels that reward timing and mind games rather than reflexive trigger pulling. Victory often depends on reading your opponent’s intentions and executing precise counters at the right moment. While ranged weapons such as bows and muskets exist, they function more as complementary tools rather than the dominant strategy.

Mobility is equally central to the experience. Every player is equipped with a grappling hook that dramatically reshapes traversal and combat flow. You can zip across rooftops, scale cliffs, chase fleeing enemies, or instantly engage in aerial assaults. Wall-running, parkour mechanics, dodges, and fluid animations make movement feel dynamic and expressive. The verticality of the map design encourages creative positioning and constant repositioning, ensuring that fights rarely remain static. Encounters often unfold across multiple elevations, turning battles into fast-moving spectacles that blend martial arts choreography with strategic maneuvering.

The roster of heroes adds another dimension of depth. Each character possesses unique active and ultimate abilities that shape playstyle, from crowd control skills and defensive barriers to mobility boosts and burst damage techniques. These hero abilities inject variety into matches and encourage experimentation. Some heroes excel in solo duels, while others shine in team-based modes, particularly in the trio format where coordinated ability usage can swing entire engagements. The interplay between hero powers and weapon mechanics gives the game a light hero-shooter flavor without overshadowing the importance of mechanical skill.

Progression and customization further enhance long-term engagement. Cosmetic skins, weapon designs, and character outfits allow players to personalize their experience, with monetization focused largely on aesthetics rather than gameplay advantages. Seasonal updates frequently introduce new heroes, balance changes, and limited-time modes, keeping the meta evolving. While some players have criticized the cost of certain cosmetic items, the core gameplay remains accessible without mandatory purchases, maintaining competitive integrity.

Despite its strengths, NARAKA: BLADEPOINT presents a steep learning curve. New players can find themselves overwhelmed by the complexity of the combat system and the speed at which experienced opponents execute combos and counters. The skill ceiling is high, and early matches may feel punishing until the core mechanics become second nature. Technical concerns such as occasional matchmaking imbalances, server latency issues in certain regions, and optimization hiccups have also been points of contention within the community. However, ongoing updates have aimed to address these concerns and refine overall performance.

Visually, the game is striking. Environments draw heavily from mythological landscapes, featuring ancient temples, bamboo forests, mountainous fortresses, and dramatic skyboxes. Character designs reflect a fusion of historical martial arts aesthetics and fantastical elements, contributing to a world that feels both grounded and stylized. The sound design complements the action with impactful weapon clashes and atmospheric musical cues that heighten tension during late-game circles.

Ultimately, NARAKA: BLADEPOINT succeeds because it dares to diverge from genre conventions. It transforms the battle royale structure into a test of martial skill and spatial awareness rather than pure marksmanship. For players seeking something different from traditional shooters—especially those drawn to competitive melee systems and high-mobility combat—it offers an exhilarating and deeply skill-based experience. While its difficulty and competitive environment may not appeal to everyone, those willing to invest time into mastering its mechanics will discover a layered, adrenaline-fueled battleground that stands confidently apart from its peers.

Alright, let's actually provide a constructive review. Why are people "review bombing" naraka?

We paid for NArAKAA : Bladepoint, we supported it throughout its lifespan, it was popular and liked by its community, and turning a happy profit each year.

When Blizzard announced Overwatch 2, the big new feature they announced, the entire premise that made it "worth the sequel treatment" was the PvE campaign mode. Hero talent trees, customizable abilities, an expansive co-op campaign that would add to the story and lore. We were told it was going to be so much work that they wouldn't be putting out updates for Overwatch any more, they were re-allocating the staff to work on this new project.

With no updates, and no content, naraka;bIadepussybussy poitn fights mugen 10/10 movie started to get stale... people grew tired and bored, spending less time in the game, or moving on. Many of us stuck with the product, playing a little each week just to keep fresh... waiting for the new campaign mode. For a lot of us, playing became a chore, something we were doing out of habit, so we'd be ready for the new campaign...

But the new campaign wasn't the premise that established OW2, it was the pretext. It was a lie. Blizzard abandoned the PvE campaign a full YEAR before OW2 launched - but continued to push it in marketing as the big new feature. It's even in the announcement trailer for OW2, and on the roadmaps. They knew they'd canned it 12 months earlier, but they knew that's what people wanted, so kept putting it front and centre to get people's money, to get people to buy into the project. ----

What does OW2 ACTUALLY offer then? What did they work on for those two years that was so important that they couldn't make content for OW1, the product people paid for and were supporting?

1) They overhauled the graphical engine:

Before, Overwatch would play on a relatively low spec computer, and it'd be smooth. Now, it stutters and stammers in the menus. They've added this weird shiny plastic finish to everything in the world, heroes and environment alike - so where before, heros would "pop" against the background and be easy to follow, now everything has the same texture to it, and it all merges together into visual noise - especially at longer ranges. They've compensated for how bad this looks by adding lots of additional flashy effects and explosions, that makes it much harder to see anything amidst the chaos. A PvP game at this pace relies heavily on quick disambiguation of what you're looking at, so you can react and compete, and the new engine makes this impossible without turning all the effects back off... meaning that the two years of development is for a feature best disabled.

The new engine also has a weird slippery "feel" to it. Reviewers who'd played Overwatch for 50 hours came into Overwatch 2 and reported "look! it's the same Overwatch you love, but it's F2P now! Just ignore the monetization and you can play this great game for free!" Established long term players with thousands of hours were on reddit complaining that their hitboxes were all over the place and shots that would previously "feel" like a dead certain hit were just completely whiffing, and they didn't understand why. All the timings are messed up.

2) They reworked most of the heroes:

TLDR: they screwed up the game balance. Previously, one of the biggest appeals of Overwatch was that you could find a hero that suited your play style, and main them, getting good at whatever suited you best. Some people like sniping, or hitscan run and gun, some people aren't good at reactionary aim and instead liked to focus on positioning, tactics and strategy. You could make a big positive different to your team by playing lucio or mercy, and paying attention to your surroundings, and positioning yourself in the right place at the right time to make the difference.

With Overwatch 2, the damage and healing behaviour has been reworked heavily. Now, the one tank on the team is insanely chunky, and it's near impossible to kill them quickly - with healer support, they can just stand in the line of fire and laugh. Everyone else dies almost immediately, regardless of who their aggressor is.

Team-fighting now is very one-note, you have one tank who's immortal if they have support, and you have four hitscan DPS characters following them - there's not a lot of difference between supports and DPS characters. The teams try to pick off the other team's DPS/Support characters, and when they pick a few off, they can finish the tank and take the objective. Repeat. There's no room for variation in play style at all, you either play a DPS and try to kill the other team DPS, or you play a tank, and try to position correctly - maybe picking off an enemy hero that gets too close to you.

I understand a lot of this came from feedback at the professional levels, where support players were complaining that they wanted to have more direct impact in teamfights, they wanted the game to feel more like other FPS games - but for a large portion of Overwatch's playerbase specifically, the appeal of the game was that you could do something else and still matter.

3. They got INCREDIBLY greedy with the monetization...

It's a longstanding argument that lootboxes are terrible in modern gaming... but Overwatch was one of the few examples of Lootboxes done right. Most of the long-term players of the game actually liked the system, that just rewarded you for playing the game and let you unlock whatever content you wanted relatively quickly. I started playing OW1 with the first anniversary, cleared the weekly boxes from arcade every week, and at the launch of OW2, I owned every single item in the game. Those who didn't have the time to invest in doing everything could still quickly unlock specific items they wanted (and let's be honest, when you have your favourite skin, how much do you care about unlocking other skins?) - and those who didn't want to spend hours unlocking stuff could spend a little cash to get it - if they wanted to.

The new system puts almost everything behind a paywall. The minute number of cosmetics on the "free" track are often insultingly lazy, simple recolours or minor alterations, while they put serious effort into skins that you can only buy for $20. Naraka: Bladepoint is a thrilling and inventive twist on the battle royale genre, swapping out guns for gravity-defying melee combat. It combines the strategic depth of a fighting game with the high-stakes, last-player-standing format, creating an experience that feels both fresh and intensely rewarding.

Gameplay revolves around 60 players battling on a sprawling island, scavenging for melee weapons, armor, and magical buffs called Souljades. Where it truly shines is its combat system—a precise dance of parries, dodges, and combos where button-mashing guarantees a quick defeat. Learning the rhythm between light, heavy, and charged attacks, while reading an opponent’s movements, is essential. The high skill ceiling is intimidating at first, but immensely satisfying once mastered.

Movement is equally exceptional. The map is almost entirely scalable using parkour and grappling hooks, making traversal fluid, strategic, and often outright joyful. This verticality extends combat into the treetops and across cliffsides, encouraging creative engagements and dramatic escapes.

Hero abilities add another layer, especially in trios. Coordinating skills like Matari’s stealth teleports or Tianhai’s giant Vajra transformation leads to tactical, synergistic team fights reminiscent of a MOBA. That said, the characters themselves lack compelling personality or lore, feeling more like combat vessels than narrative-driven heroes.

The game does have notable drawbacks. New players face an overlong stint against lifeless bots that teach little and drain excitement. Server instability can also disrupt the precision-based combat, though connectivity has improved since launch. Additionally, while the buy-to-play model avoids pay-to-win, its cosmetic economy is unnecessarily convoluted, with multiple currencies and loot boxes that feel designed to push players toward premium purchases.

Despite these flaws, Naraka: Bladepoint succeeds brilliantly in reinvigorating the battle royale formula. It exchanges gunplay for exhilarating sword-clashing duels and replaces bland landscapes with a playground of vertical freedom. If you’re seeking a challenging, kinetic, and deeply strategic take on the genre, this is a cut above the rest.

Verdict: A superb and refreshing melee-focused battle royale, hindered only by tedious bots and a messy cosmetic system, but elevated by phenomenal combat and movement.

Performance & Optimisation Issues
First of all, here are my PC specifications:
RTX 3060 Ti / 16GB DDR4 RAM

I genuinely do not understand why a game positioned as a “near-AAA” title requires a level of RAM usage and caching comparable to a quadruple‑A title like GTA V—and this is with all graphics settings turned to the lowest possible level.

What is even more ridiculous is that during actual matches, under the same graphical settings (again, compared to GTA V), Naraka: Bladepoint causes noticeable stuttering and performance drops.
Does the development or operations team simply not optimise the game at all?

The map itself is not particularly large, yet the resource consumption is disproportionately high.
Is the assumption here that because the map is small, optimisation is unnecessary?

The problem is not limited to matches either. Even in the main lobby and character interface, the game frequently stutters.
I will not even compare this to GTA V here—let me put it another way:
When you play Genshin Impact or Wuthering Waves on PC, do you experience this level of lag in the lobby or character screen?

According to the system requirements listed on the Steam store page—both minimum and recommended—I will not even question whether those specifications can reliably run the game.
However, the store page states “55 GB of available storage space”, while the actual installation size is now close to 80 GB.

Is the game genuinely being maintained and operated properly?

Matchmaking & Team‑Mate Issues
Next, the matchmaking system.

Firstly, I cannot understand why ranked matchmaking takes around 10 minutes, only for the match to begin with barely 5 seconds left to select a character.

Whether I can even pick the character I want is already uncertain
Then I am expected to choose a spawn location within the remaining few seconds
I do not consider this a reasonable design choice—even in non‑ranked modes, this would be unacceptable.

Then there is the team‑mate issue.
I do not understand why, despite having a maximum reputation score, I am frequently matched with players who have very low reputation scores.

That alone is not the biggest problem. The real issue is this:

One team‑mate is AFK
The other behaves like an AI bot
Meanwhile, the enemy team consists of three players ranked near the top of the global character leaderboards.

What makes this even more absurd is that if I die first, I am forced to spectate:

one AFK team‑mate
and another team‑mate running into walls and moving in a grid‑like, bot‑like manner
Otherwise, I am penalised.

Truly fascinating design.

After reporting this to customer support, the response was equally astonishing.
The only answer I received was: “You can report them.”

That response is about as helpful as going into a fast‑food restaurant, asking for a burger, and being told:
“You can buy a burger.”

Loot Drop & Equipment Distribution
Finally, and most confusing of all, is the loot drop system.

I genuinely do not understand how the drop ranges are calculated.
Why is it that at the start of a match, nearly all the equipment I obtain is white‑tier, while my opponents appear fully geared in gold?

In a ranked match just now, I opened five or six loot piles at the start, two of which were gold‑tier piles, yet everything I obtained was still white‑tier gear.

That alone would already be frustrating, but it gets worse:
almost everything that dropped was ranged weapons.

Shortly afterwards, I was chased down by a squad consisting of:

two enemies wearing gold armour
and one wearing purple armour
Aside from this specific match, in nearly every single game, I am forced to rely on Leyline Altars to upgrade my equipment.
Otherwise, from the beginning of the match until the very end, I am left using mostly blue‑tier gear.

This happens regularly.
Sometimes, even Leyline Altars fail to provide purple equipment.

I am genuinely curious as to why, when we are all players in the same game,
other teams consistently appear fully equipped with gold gear,
while for me, even purple gear feels like a luxury.

NetEase's Latest Free-to-Play Brawler: A Solid Contender with Some Strings Attached

NetEase has a knack for delivering polished free games, and this one is no exception—think Fortnite's fast-paced chaos stripped of the toxic lobbies, flashy cosmetics, and griefers. The core gameplay is a blast: snappy, melee-focused action with grapple hooks enabling deadly combo attacks that feel borderline overpowered. Ranged options exist but wisely take a backseat, keeping the emphasis on close-quarters frenzy. Matches are simple yet addictive, perfect for quick sessions.

Visually, it's stunning—vibrant arenas that run buttery smooth once you tweak the settings. I shaved off a noticeable input lag (a few milliseconds on defaults) via the options menu, transforming it from "good" to "better."

That said, inventory management is a pain, especially in full servers. Picking up loot or swapping gear mid-fight? Good luck—it's clunky and chaotic, possibly by design to amp up the tension. NetEase's signature menu overload is here too, burying you in layers of options and purchases(either real or game loot).

A quick note on game hiccups: HCVI (anti-cheat) was disabled initially, sparking some community panic, but the November 2025 update fixed it. Data privacy concerns linger—NetEase loves collecting user info—but I found no reports of intentional hacking or intrusion into a user's PC.  However tons of accounts getting hacked via phishing not on NetEase's fault list though.

Broader gripes: NetEase's aggressive acquisitions of indie studios and franchises, followed by shutdowns or content locks, sour the experience. It's predatory and kills promising projects players were hyped for.

FINAL Verdict: 8.9/10
Deducting a full point for the menu maze (classic NetEase) and 0.1 for the publisher drama. If you can overlook the corporate baggage, this is a must-try freebie.

[h1]Naraka: Bladepoint[/h1]
Naraka: Bladepoint stands out in the overcrowded battle royale genre. It's not just another shooter with long-range firefights, but a hardcore action game focused on melee combat, parkour, and Eastern aesthetics. The game offers a unique experience but demands high engagement and patience from the player.

[h3]A Ruthless Entry Barrier[/h3]
This is perhaps the most painful issue. Naraka does not forgive mistakes for newcomers. The controls are overloaded: you need to hold buttons to change dodge, combine mouse and keyboard in non-obvious ways, and the parry system requires perfect timing. If you start playing now, you'll face dozens of hours of farming bots in ranked or quick play before you can put up a fight against real players.

[h3]Network Infrastructure and Regions[/h3]
The server infrastructure is not always stable. Moreover, even on European servers, there is a high chance of encountering players from Asia with low latency (ping), which is critical in a game with such timing-demanding gameplay. Asynchrony often leads to phantom hits, where the parry animation has played but you still took damage.

Still the most unique BR available. It has its flaws which will be addressed below but lets start with clearing up some misconceptions/outdated information regarding the game. The most obvious deterrent for potential new players to even install the game is that it requires HVCI to be turned off. While this was true when Windows 11 was new, this requirement was removed via an update several months later. HVCI is no longer required to be turned off as of this review and all other reviews that mentioned this issue are either outdated or just trolling. Next, there are claims that the game is infested with hackers (some reviews claim up to 90% of players are hacking). This is completely false. I have spent over 3k hours in the game and the number of people that were hacking/using some exploit can be counted on one hand. There definitely are players who still use hacks/find exploits but they are a small fraction of the playerbase (the same can be said with any other BR). The devs also publish weekly banned players lists to remove hackers and keep such behaviour in check.

With the misconceptions out of the way, lets move on to the negatives. First of all, the playerbase in the West (NA/EU servers) is tiny compared to Asia (SEA/AS servers). If you play on SEA/AS servers, kindly skip to the next paragraph as matchmaking is not an issue. For NA/EU servers, most new players will only be playing against bots (and winning most matches) in ranked mode until Solar. Assuming that they have the patience to reach Solar, newbies will then be placed in lobbies with top server players and proceed to be obliterated by them. Such matchmaking is understandably frustrating for new players as the learning curve can seem too steep. This is the point where newbies quit because they are demolished by veterans almost every match past Solar rank. Personally, I have also experienced this when I was new to the game so all I can say to new players is: Stay patient & "Get Good". Participate in custom lobbies to learn Neutral/combos/movement tech and you will be able to put up a fight against good players eventually. 

Another negative is the abysmal server disconnects during games, especially in crowded areas/endgame fights. These can vary in severity from being mildly annoying to causing the match to be lost. These glitches can happen quite often too, sometimes a few times during every match on bad days. You will experience screen stutters in mild cases, to seeing the screen buffer icon while the screen freezes and tries to reconnect to servers in worse cases. There is also the less common but potentially game breaking bug where you are sent back to the login screen during a match if you use certain hero skills, such as Tianhai's combo breaker F skill. As of writing this, the hero skill bug seems to be fixed but I will update this review if it happens again.

Finally, I shall address positives after all that doom and gloom. From all the previous points mentioned, you may think that all the drawbacks outweigh the positives, but I beg to differ. This is hands down the most unique BR available. Its depth of combat and movement mechanics is unmatched by any other modern game of its genre. Fights against real players are satisfying regardless of outcome once you have learnt the basics of Neutral/True Combos/Scalerushing. In a world where most if not all new games try to make you feel like a champion, this game constantly reminds you of your shortcomings in skill. You will lose way more than you win until you "get good". You will need to earn your wins which in turn feel much more fulfilling. I would also like to mention that there is a PvE mode called Showdown which is similar to Souls-like games and an extraction mode called Rift Traversal for those looking for something other than the BR. I highly recommend trying Showdown if the BR/PvP is not your cup of tea as boss fights there are just as challenging and fulfilling at the highest difficulty.

In conclusion, Naraka stands out as a unique melee-based BR experience in a sea of shooter BRs. 
Is it perfect? No.
Does it have technical issues? Yes. Sometimes.
Is it challenging but fulfilling to learn and improve? Absolutely.
Is it fun? Hell yea.
More importantly, is it worth your time? Find out for yourself.
