[h1]==================================================
STOP SELLING PROGRESSION
A GREAT GAME BURIED UNDER P2W SYSTEMS
==================================================[/h1]

Lost Ark has one of the biggest problems a game can have:

[b]The actual gameplay is really good.[/b]

The combat feels fantastic.

The classes are fun.

The raids can be genuinely challenging.

The boss fights are some of the best parts of the game.

And then you look at the progression system.

[h1]>>> AND THERE IS THE PROBLEM <<<[/h1]

You can spend real money on Royal Crystals.

Royal Crystals can be used through the official currency exchange to obtain Gold.

Gold is one of the most important currencies for progression.

There are paid Powerpasses.

There are premium progression rewards.

There are paid systems designed to accelerate character progression.

Call it "pay for convenience".

Call it "pay to progress".

Call it whatever makes it sound nicer.

[b]If real money can buy character progression and power, I call it P2W.[/b]

==================================================
[h1]>>> "BUT YOU STILL NEED SKILL TO RAID" <<<[/h1]
===================================================

Yes.

Of course you do.

Paying money does not magically teach you raid mechanics.

But that completely misses the point.

P2W does NOT have to mean:

[b]"Credit card -> automatically kill final boss."[/b]

The problem is that two players can spend completely different amounts of time reaching the same level of character progression simply because one of them opened their wallet.

One player farms.

One player waits for weekly progression.

One player collects materials and Gold.

Another player can spend money and accelerate a significant part of that process.

[b]That is the problem.[/b]

==================================================
[h1]>>> "BUT YOU CAN GET EVERYTHING FOR FREE" <<<[/h1]
======================================================

Yes.

Technically.

And technically I can also walk across Europe instead of taking a train.

That does not mean both options are equal.

If something requires an enormous amount of grinding for one player while another player can significantly accelerate that progression with money, then saying:

[quote]"But you don't HAVE to pay!"[/quote]

does not magically make the monetization fair.

[b]POSSIBLE FOR FREE != NOT P2W[/b]

==================================================
[h1]>>> THE GAME HAS IMPROVED <<<[/h1]
======================================

I will give the developers credit where it is deserved.

Catch-up systems have improved a lot.

New and returning players receive large amounts of progression support.

Old progression has been streamlined.

Solo raids exist.

Events can push characters much closer to current content.

That is genuinely good.

But...

[b]Making the grind less painful does not magically remove the P2W monetization sitting on top of it.[/b]

==================================================
[h1]>>> THIS GAME DOES NOT NEED THIS <<<[/h1]
=============================================

This is what annoys me the most about Lost Ark.

The game itself is already good.

The combat is good.

The raids are good.

The classes are good.

The bosses are good.

So why does progression need to be monetized like this?

Sell me:

* Skins
* Mounts
* Pets
* Cosmetics
* Emotes
* Character customization
* A cosmetic Battle Pass

If I enjoy your game, I WANT to support it.

[b]But stop selling progression.[/b]

A player's character power should make me think:

[b]"Damn, this person played a lot."[/b]

Not:

[b]"Damn, this person played a lot...

or has a really healthy credit limit."[/b]

==================================================
[h1]>>> STOP NORMALIZING THIS <<<[/h1]
======================================

The gaming industry keeps getting away with systems like this because players keep defending them.

[quote]"You can earn everything without paying."[/quote]

[quote]"It is only pay to progress."[/quote]

[quote]"You still need skill."[/quote]

None of those statements change the basic fact:

[b]MONEY CAN ACCELERATE CHARACTER POWER AND PROGRESSION.[/b]

If you enjoy that system, fine.

But I am tired of pretending that selling progression suddenly stops being P2W because the free alternative technically exists.

==================================================
[h1]>>> WHAT MAKES IT WORSE <<<[/h1]
====================================

There is actually a fantastic game underneath all of this.

That is why it is frustrating.

Lost Ark could have been a game where I happily spent money because I loved playing it.

Instead, the game constantly reminds you that money can make progression easier and faster.

There is a huge difference between:

[b]"I want to spend money because this game is good."[/b]

and:

[b]"I want to spend money because I am tired of the progression."[/b]

Developers should WANT the first one.

==================================================
[h1]>>> FINAL VERDICT <<<[/h1]
==============================

Lost Ark has excellent combat.

Great raids.

Fun classes.

Satisfying bosses.

And a progression system I absolutely do not want to support.

[b]I would love to recommend Lost Ark purely based on its gameplay.[/b]

But I cannot recommend monetization where real money can directly accelerate character progression.

[h1]STOP SELLING POWER.
STOP SELLING PROGRESSION.
LET PLAYING THE GAME BE THE PROGRESSION.[/h1]

==================================================
[h1]>>> AND REMEMBER <<<[/h1]
=============================

The hardest Lost Ark raid mechanic isn't dodging AoEs.

[b]It's dodging the cash shop.[/b]

And if your honing RNG is bad enough, don't worry.

There is always the secret legendary class:

[h1]VISA / MASTERCARD[/h1]

* Instant progression buff
* No honing required
* Works with every build
* Available directly from the cash shop

[b]100% success rate.

No RNG required.[/b]

From someone who bought all the Founders Pack I'll say, the gap is just too big, there is no way to catch up to the whales. 

Let me break down for whoever reads this: 

If you want to play exclusively solo, you are going to have fun. It still have one of the best gameplay of any Action MMO out there, hands down, and solo raids are caught up to the latest available raid for us in the west (1 raid behind KR).

If you want to play anything other the solo or normal mode for the raids, forget it. You are not going to catch up the whales. And if you do in gear level, accessories and engravings and the other thousand power mechanics this game have? Still, you don't have roster level, you don't have titles, you ARE going to be gatekept. 

If you have all that, you have to maintain it. How? The same way from the past. 1 main, 5 alts (btw, you have to invest resources on each alt so they keep up with higher level content). You simply can't generate enough gold solo to keep 1 high level character afloat and caught up with the latest content. You HAVE to raid on 6 characters oooooooooor.... swipe hard.

Lost Ark is a free-to-play action MMORPG that combines fast-paced combat with dungeon crawling, character progression and a huge amount of endgame content. I can choose from a variety of classes, explore the world of Arkesia and gradually build a stronger character through quests, raids, islands and other activities. Its combination of MMO progression and flashy action combat gives it a distinct identity.

The combat is easily the strongest part for me. Skills feel powerful and responsive, and each class has its own mechanics and abilities to learn. Chaining attacks together and positioning myself correctly can make even ordinary encounters satisfying, while harder fights require me to understand enemy patterns rather than simply relying on stronger equipment.

The class variety is another major attraction. Different classes can play completely differently, from close-range melee fighters to ranged damage dealers and support-focused characters. I enjoy experimenting with classes because learning a new one can make familiar content feel fresh again.

The world is also packed with things to do. Quests, islands, collectibles, sailing, dungeons and raids give me plenty of activities outside the basic combat loop. The amount of content can be impressive, especially when I start exploring the game's many optional systems.

The endgame is where Lost Ark becomes particularly demanding. Raids require teamwork, precise mechanics and knowledge of the encounters, and successfully clearing a difficult raid can be extremely rewarding. Learning a complicated boss fight with a group and eventually executing everything correctly is one of the game's best experiences.

The biggest weakness is the enormous amount of progression and daily management. There are many currencies, upgrade materials, tasks and systems to keep track of, and keeping multiple characters progressing can start to feel like a routine rather than an adventure. The game can demand a significant amount of time if I want to keep up with the endgame.

The free-to-play structure is another limitation. I can play without spending money, but progression systems and optional purchases can make the overall experience feel heavily focused on long-term engagement. Players who dislike grinding or monetisation systems may find the later stages particularly demanding.

The story and questing are also less consistent than the combat. There are some enjoyable moments and impressive set pieces, but a lot of the early questing can feel like something I am completing simply to unlock the more interesting content later. The world is visually impressive, but the narrative does not always match the quality of the combat.

Overall, Lost Ark is an impressive action MMORPG with excellent combat, a huge amount of content and some genuinely challenging endgame encounters. I love experimenting with classes and mastering the fast combat system, while the heavy progression, daily routines and free-to-play structure can make the game feel like a second job if I take it too seriously. For players willing to invest the time, however, there is a tremendous amount to explore.

Rating: 7.5/10

I've unlocked about 24 monster hunter style bosses (guardian raids) and legion raids are phenomenal (Dark Souls bosses meets World of Warcraft/Destiny 2 wipe mechanics)

The Legion raids will come online after the 13th continent you visit (South Vern) so if playing from the beginning you're looking at 60-80 hours to get to that part of the game unless you skip forward (which you can do immediately).

Valtan wipes: ~15
Vykas 1/2 wipes: ~30

I was shocked to see how big the game is but the original release in South Korea in 2018 only released with 8 areas which had expanded to 13 for the NA release, and we're up to 20 now.

Can't speak for the true endgame today as that's in lands I've yet to explore but suffice to say: it's worth it alone for the solo legion bosses because I like both WoW and Dark Souls - these bosses are cinematic & tough.

Bosses have a rock, paper, scissors mechanic: counter for blue, stagger for yellow bar, and weak spot damage for tail bosses. Legion bosses demand these skillsets on your bar for some wipe mechanics.

Every continent drops a brand new set of gear upon completion so you'll need to save the old sets if you want to beat bosses again "at level" or just run one of the 30 new classes (2 specs each). Make sure to try each class and I'd recommend gunslinger if you get bored of Diablo's 6 button setup; how about 20 buttons to press?

No doubt the headache of the grind and greed will seep in once I've make it to the end game but at this point, you're getting 2011-2024 development to the tune of 200 million for free. It's high value set to entice players back in and no doubt all roads lead to Rome but for now, I can't see why anyone wouldn't go in for some decent story content, amazing moments, and excellent solo boss encounters.

A word of note: I've seen about 30 people in my travels. Servers will be merged soon but strictly as an mmo it's dead unless you're doing the current raid. Kiss any PvP or world bosses or legacy content like Argos or 4/4 dungeons goodbye (remix of dungeons you will solo) - not really a dealbreaker for me as I value new content and very little content is missed here. Hell, Destiny 2 deleted half their game, I'd say only about 5% of Lost Ark doesn't currently work well without a group.

-Sailing is boring and pointless, I auto-sail and get up to grab a cup of coffee
-Character development is rare and I didn't recognize NPC characters that showed up ten hours later
-Playing this as an arpg can be a slog - the enemies simply don't do much outside of major boss moments; set everything on hard
-Collecting gear, skills, and upgrades falls off after level 50
-The main fun of the campaign is playing a new character, 8 button rotations get old after 20 hours
-Every land comes with a new system, prepare for major homework
-A dodge every 8 seconds on solo bosses is too long
-Non-emergent gameplay, you'll simply have to know what any boss does before committing to any longer animation attack - this is by far the worst part because it means you burn the dodge then get hit by the following attack
-A returning player base is highly unlikely, the same gambling systems have just been tacked onto the back of the game

Lost Ark is an incredibly popular and successful ARPG from Korea, but the Korean servers are not legitimately accessible if you live outside of Korea.
This steam version is the highly anticipated Global Release that finally allowed North America/ROW to get a taste of the game.

On the global release, the [u]game was approximately 16-18 months behind of Korean[/u] servers in terms of the available content, patches, balance changes, bug fixes, new classes, raids, etc. We received a very barebones version of the game in 2022 without any quality of life (QOL), which was divisive at the time. They intended to catch the game up to the Korean servers over time, which they've done for the most part. I believe the contention regarding this to be solely from the lack of QOL on release, as it made sense to spread out the new classes/raids over time instead of giving us Korea's version on day 1.
It is currently only 2-6 months behind in content now. (Feel free to correct me.)
This resulted in accelerate release schedules which might've pressured a lot of the community to feel like they couldn't keep up with the "power curve" that the general population was at. My further points compound onto this.

[u]The game suffered from severe botting issues and aggressive monetization problems even as far back as 2022.[/u]
I've been around since TF2, and I have never seen a botting problem as bad as the one Lost Ark had in it's prime.
I can recall personally reporting hundreds of these bots over the course of my playtime. You would still see them every single time you log in, without fail.
With botting problems comes in-game economy problems. While not completely dead, the economy became incredibly stunted and it make it very difficult for legit players to progress at a normal pace. 

[u]This led to many people feeling like they needed to RMT to keep up with the pace that they desired.[/u] The game featured a RNG system for "honing" or improving your gear that was quite literally gambling. It was incredibly disliked and very few quality of life changes were ever made to remedy this. And the changes that were made took a long time to be implemented.

You would farm materials for a few days or a week, sit down to "hone", or upgrade, your gear as it was an anxiety ridden process with how expensive it was, you would end up failing a 1% chance, then you would feel pressured to purchase more materials with real money to finish off that honing chance that you just barely missed. 
I recall watching friends screenshare on discord whenever they went to hone their gear as we all watched. [b]It was literally like watching someone play slots.[/b]

And trust me, [b]the RMT was NOT cheap...[/b] Even if whaling is your thing, you needed some SERIOUS money to be able to do it in this game. I remember $100 equating to a negligible amount of currency back in 2022. It wasn't nothing, but it definitely didn't feel like you just spent $100. The Korean version of the game is infamous for this, as an absolute top-tier whale weapon, (an Esther weapon), could cost anywhere from $30,000-$100,000 to max out depending on your luck with honing.

Then there's the community.. I'm not sure what to say that the other 10 reviews around me aren't already saying. It was really bad. The community was incredibly toxic and had an extreme gatekeeping problem as early as the very first raid release. You basically NEEDED to study up and clear the new content right when it came out to get your foot in the door for future clears of the same raid. If you wanted to learn a raid boss a week after it released and you didn't have friends/connections, then it was an absolutely miserable experience. You basically didn't exist without your certificates saying you've killed the boss before.. You would simply never get invited to groups - and the ones you do get invited to are essentially bottom of the barrel. 

I'm not talking about 8 new-players that are willing to learn the raid.. I'm talking about 2 bots, 1 afk, 1 toxic carry, and 3 people that just won't communicate whatsoever in a mechanical and strategical fight that requires coordination. After experiencing this firsthand, I made an effort to always clear the new content immediately. (After clearing content, you would get a badge to denote yourself to others. Groups would see this when deciding whether or not to invite you to a raid. This was mostly in the form of player titles.)
That being said.. The boss mechanics in Lost Ark's raids were better than what I saw coming even from Mythic Raids in World of Warcraft as I was also playing that alongside Lost Ark. [b]I had more fun progressing and learning on Kakul-Saydon than any other boss in any MMO, including Cutting Edge raiding in WoW.[/b]

All of this negative.. But there is 1 thing that keeps this game in my mind to this day, wishing I could do it all over.
Of course, I'm talking about the combat. [u]Lost Ark had the best combat in any ARPG to date.[/u] I'm a PoE1 alpha veteran, Diablo 2/3 veteran, and WoW 15-year veteran. None of those games even came close to how addicting and fun the combat in Lost Ark was. The build crafting, while solved for the most part, was still incredibly in-depth and allowed for a lot of customization. It was fast, you had optimal rotations, and you could not really button mash your way to victory in this game. 

[b]Everything was so snappy, fluid, and satisfying.[/b] While most of my time was almost exclusively spent between 5 separate bard characters and 1 paladin, I can only imagine how some of the fast-paced DPS classes must have felt to play in the end-game. 

The lows were low, and no one will ever deny that. But despite that, a lot of people felt some magic with this game at one point or another. Nothing scratches the itch for me like this game used to.

I hope another game can recreate this experience again one day. The mechanical raids, the incredibly intricate and complex combat system, and the exploration/sailing. The highs were so high.

Lost Ark is essentially two different games packaged into one, and that dichotomy is exactly why it sits at a mixed rating on Steam.

 It offers some of the most exhilarating, high-stakes combat in the entire MMORPG genre, but it is deeply buried under a progression system that feels increasingly like a second job.

Here is an honest breakdown of the current consensus:

The core gameplay—the raids, the boss designs, and the actual feel of combat—is top-tier. If you enjoy games that reward mechanical skill, pattern recognition, and precise execution, the endgame raids are genuinely spectacular. 

The character classes are distinct, the animations are polished, and the boss fights feel like a genuine accomplishment when you finally clear them. For the first hundred hours or so, the journey through the world and the progression into the mid-game feel incredibly rewarding.

The problem, and the reason for the mixed reviews, arises once you hit the endgame and realize what the game expects of you to keep up. The progression loop is heavily reliant on resource accumulation, and the community standard for gear levels has risen to a point where "gatekeeping" is the norm. If you don't have the "right" gear, stats, or experience, getting into parties for raids becomes a frustrating chore.

Many players feel that the game has devolved into a cycle of daily and weekly tasks across multiple characters. It effectively forces a grind that many find incompatible with a healthy lifestyle or a casual gaming schedule. The economy and the gear-honing system—which involves high-stakes RNG failures—are widely viewed as mechanisms designed to push players toward microtransactions. While you don't technically have to pay to win, you certainly feel the pressure to swipe your card if you want to skip the tedious, burnout-inducing grind required to stay relevant in the latest content.

The verdict is that Lost Ark is a gorgeous, combat-focused masterpiece that is unfortunately hampered by its own progression design. It is a game that respects your mechanical skill during a fight but often fails to respect your time outside of it. If you have the patience to grind, enjoy a highly competitive raid scene, and can ignore the aggressive monetization pressure, it remains a unique experience. However, if you are looking for an MMO that allows you to play at your own pace without feeling like you are falling behind in a digital rat race, you will likely find the current state of Lost Ark to be more frustrating than fun.

In a world where the MMO genre is pretty tired, Lost Ark's very explosive, determined, fast-paced combat system, their dynamic vertical progressions (which can be a negative at times, but it's never meant to be a sprint, it's always always been a marathon), a number of beautiful landscapes and biodiverse biomes with illustrious NPCs and monsters alike, paired with a number of contents outside of pure raiding, comes a fresh take on the idea of how an MMO should be.

It's bad; really bad. Amazon hasn't shut down Lost Ark specifically but they did effectively abandon their entire in-house gaming ambition, axed New World completely, laid off key members of the Lost Ark community team including people who had been there five plus years, and pivoted toward AI party games and a Snoop Dogg courtroom game which is a sentence that should tell you everything about where their priorities now sit. Lost Ark itself is technically still getting updates since Smilegate actually makes it and Amazon just publishes it, but the western support structure around it is increasingly threadbare and the future beyond the current publishing contract is genuinely unclear.

Anyway.

Lost Ark is gorgeous and completely hollow in equal measure and I say that having bounced off it harder than most.

Smilegate built something with real visual ambition, the isometric action combat looks incredible in motion and the production values are frankly staggering for a free to play MMO. The world is enormous, the class roster is deep, and for about forty five minutes it absolutely sells the premise.

Then the systems start arriving. Layer after layer of progression currency and enhancement materials and upgrade paths that exist primarily to obscure how much of the actual game is behind a time gate or a wallet. The genre has always done this but Lost Ark does it with a confidence that borders on aggressive.

The grind not clicking early is the game telling you something honest about what the next several hundred hours would look like. Sometimes the preview is the whole story.

[h3]Lost Ark: Two Games in a Trench Coat[/h3]
⭐ [i]Recommended (with caveats)[/i] | 150hrs | Solo PvE only
https://youtu.be/G7VFNgR2SM0?si=VwTHeId7EmE8kaj9
[b]The Paradox:[/b] This is simultaneously one of the best F2P PvE games I've played AND a predatory pay-to-win nightmare—depending on how you play it.

[h1]Why the PvE Version Slaps:[/h1]

[b]Combat & Controls:[/b]
[list]
[*]Diablo-style isometric gameplay that's fast, fluid, responsive
[*]Only 8 keys (QWERTY + ASDF)—no hotbar hell, no piano-playing your keyboard (okay there's a few more buttons than these so you're still playing piano but its chopsticks rather than flight of the bumblebees)
[*]Feels badass. Actually makes you feel like you're doing cool shit.
[*](Controller exists but plays like a drunk toddler in a Barbie cruiser—don't bother)
[/list]
[b]Constant Variety:[/b]
[list]
[*]Pilot a mech (yes, really)
[*]Explore the open sea on a rocket-powered orca
[*]Shrink down and help tiny villagers round up ladybugs
[*]Climb inside the mouth of a rock giant
[/list]
Every few hours the game shifts what you're doing, which keeps ADHD brain locked in

[b]Systems Stacked Like a Deranged Lasagna:[/b]
[*][b]1,250+ Mokoko seeds[/b] (like Korok seeds from Breath of the Wild)
[*][b]900+ cards[/b] with stat bonuses, resistances, set bonuses, and awakening mechanics (basically gacha-game gear sets)
[*][b]11 different collectible types [/b](each with milestone rewards)
[*][b]Stronghold system:[/b] house upgrades, decorating, pet upgrades, resource farming, ship dispatches with their own leveling
[*][b]Sailing:[/b] your own ship with levels, crew, skins, stats, plus hundreds of islands to explore (each a loot box gamble)
[*][b]Rapport systems:[/b] make friends by playing guitar and giving gifts
[*][b]Gear honing, engraving, cooking, gathering, world bosses, raid bosses[/b]
[/list]
It's dense. Like navigating American healthcare, but actually fun and understandable.

[b]The World & Story:[/b]
[list]
[*]Gorgeous, richly detailed Korean fantasy world
[*]Engaging story (surprisingly good for a F2P game)
[*]Hundreds of hours of solo content without mandatory endgame grind
[*]Doesn't feel like an MMO (global chat exists but nobody uses it—basically single-player, which I actually prefer)
[/list]

[h1]Why Endgame Sucks (And How It Traps You):[/h1]
Once you hit max level and finish the story, the game transforms into something completely different.

[b]The Monetization Trap:[/b]
[list]
[*][b]10+ different currencies[/b] (yes, really—it's intentionally confusing)
[*]You can literally [b]buy gold with real money[/b]—gold is the premium currency used for character upgrades
[*][b]Pay-to-win is baked in.[/b] You can straight-up buy power.
[*]Cosmetics are mostly earnable, but everything else? Cash shop.
[/list]
[b]The Grind Hellscape:[/b]
[list]
[*]To stay competitive, you need to grind [b]6+ characters [/b]simultaneously
[*]Each character needs gear honing (RNG-based upgrades that fail constantly)
[*]Honing requires materials that drop from raids and dungeons
[*]You run out of free materials fast and hit a paywall
[*]The only way to progress faster is to spend money on materials or gold
[/list]
[h1]The Subscription Trap (Crystalline Aura):[/h1]
[list]
[*]$14 CAD/month for a "premium membership"
[*]Gives: 10% XP boost, quality-of-life features (remote storage access, faster stronghold research, extra daily rapport actions)
[*]Sounds harmless. It's not.
[*]Once you buy it, you realize there are better things to buy (like Azena's Blessing for honing materials)
[*]Then you're chasing the next purchase, and the next, and suddenly you've spent hundreds
[*]I broke my no-spend resolve for this. My friend Ember (1000+ hours) immediately told me it was dumb. He was right.
[/list]
[b]The Competitive Pressure:[/b]
[list]
[*]"Competitive endgame" means: raid progression, PvP rankings, staying relevant in guild wars
[*]To do any of this, you need to be geared
[*]To be geared, you need materials
[*]To get materials fast, you need to either grind 6 characters or pay
[*]The game is designed so you can't do both without burning out or spending money
[/list]
[b]The Result:[/b]
[list]
[*]People spend thousands trying to stay competitive
[*]Burnout is real (see: Ember's Stockholm Syndrome after 1000 hours)
[*]The game becomes a second job, not entertainment
[/list]

[h1]Verdict:[/h1]
❌ [b]DON'T PLAY IF:[/b]
You feel the need to reach endgame, optimize your gear, or stay competitive. This game will:
[list]
[*]Financially destroy you ($50-200+/month to stay relevant)
[*]Emotionally drain you (endless grind, RNG failures, FOMO)
[*]Turn gaming into a second job
[/list]
Save yourself. Seriously.

✅[b] DO PLAY IF:[/b]
You just want a massive, gorgeous, content-rich solo PvE experience. You'll get:
[list]
[*]200-300+ hours of engaging content
[*]Zero mandatory spending (the game is fully playable F2P)
[*]A beautiful world to explore at your own pace
[*]One of the best F2P PvE games available right now
[/list]
[h1]The Spending Reality:[/h1]
[list]
[*]F2P: Completely viable, zero pressure
[*]Light spender ($5-15/month): Crystalline Aura for QoL, totally optional
[*]Endgame chaser: $100-500+/month to stay competitive (don't do this)
[/list]

Pros:

+Raids. The best in the business that’s all I can say.
+ Lot of story, side quest collectibles. Tons of hours of content
+ number of classes you can play and ways you can play them
+ Graphics
+ Overall gameplay/combat 
+Character Customization/Skins/Mounts/etc.
+Story and Lore. Don't read in-game, watch a video if you're interested.
+Monthly Updates.
+Horizontal Content.
+NOT P2W. In the sense that it would cost a million dollars to be the strongest legally. If paying any money at all for power is P2W in your eyes, then yes Lost Ark is P2W. That is if you consider doing the most dmg or being the strongest in a pve game as “winning”.

Cons:
-New Player Unfriendliness. Playing the first 300 or so hours (if not more) of a new account will suck omega donkey balls. Unless you only play for the horizontal content.
-Gatekeeping. Parties only want the most geared characters, so unless you’re a standout it will take longer to get into lobbies.
Can’t get into a lobby cause your character is average? Well, luckily RMTing has you covered. It’s a really vicious cycle of: Gatekeeping > Frustration > RMT (More Bots)> No serious ban > Gatekeep/Frustration > RMT…
Support Meta and Shortage: Think holy trinity but without the tank. A support is mandatory for every Lost Ark raid.

-Grind/High time commitment. If you're a F2P player trying to playtime your way to the newest raids (if you're not already there), it can be a suffering experience.

-Alternate Characters. Playing a maximum of 6 characters will maximum gold income per week. I would rather just play my main more.

+-RNG Power Systems. Every power system in the game is RNG-based. I like RNG power systems, but I think a majority of people would think hitting 1% odds for an upgrade to be an awful system.

Closing Review: Top-tier MMORPG 9/10, for me at least. There is so little "homework" required of me every day/week that I could uninstall the game for 6 months, come back, and still be fighting the newest raids. However, this isn't the case for everyone and those who continue to grind 6 characters will most likely burn out at some point (similar to what happened to me a while back).

I don't care much about being the strongest in the server so P2W aspects don't bother me much. Bots, however, do since they inflate gold prices to places that regular F2P are struggling to buy from. This has a direct effect on Pheons (which I normally do not mind) as the price of them gets too extreme.

Lost Ark isn't dead and will not be dead for a long long time as it does a good job at retaining existing players, but I do not see a rise in player count ever happening unless something radical happens.

Lost Ark Review

Lost Ark was genuinely a lot of fun when it first released, especially while playing with friends. Over time, though, my friends gradually dropped off, and as the game progressed, so did my sanity.

I only played Bard, with a roster of six: Featherfox(i/ii/iii/iv/xxv). I was basically a Heavenly Tune fanatic.

Coming from first-person shooters, I really liked Lost Ark’s combat. It felt fresh and innovative to me. The raids were challenging, but they were also rewarding because, as a support, I could contribute a lot of aggregate utility while playing with friends and tackling difficult content together over repeated attempts.

I think I avoided some of the worst frustration compared with my friends who played damage dealers. As a Bard player, I probably experienced less of the toxicity, prejudice, and discrimination that they dealt with, which may be part of why I lasted longer.

At this point, I think it is already well established that the game’s design helps propagate discriminatory and unhealthy player behavior. The community seems to be behaviorally pushed into a kind of collective action problem, where raids in public lobbies are treated more like “homework” than recreational challenges. Because the game is such a massive time sink, and because most people have limited free time, that pressure seems to encourage toxic elitism. That raises the sanity cost of playing and lowers the aggregate enjoyment people get from the game overall. New, casual, and part-time players seem to suffer the most from this.

On a more personal level, one thing I disliked was how new content and limited-time events were sometimes released at awkward times, like during exam weeks or exam months. During those periods, I could not realistically or ethically justify spending time on the game instead of studying, whether that meant learning raid mechanics or just grinding events. I also suffer from pretty severe raid anxiety, and that only got worse as more of my friends quit. On top of that, the newer power systems felt increasingly convoluted and grindy as the game went on, which made the game demand more effort and sanity for the same, or even less, aggregate enjoyment.

Overall, Lost Ark started as an exciting and innovative MMO for me, especially with friends, but over time the social pressure, time demands, anxiety, and increasingly convoluted progression systems made it much harder to enjoy.

The campaign is a walking and talking simulator. Killing things during the campaign gives very little XP so you spend all your time walking past enemies from NPC to NPC doing nothing but talking and doing little 2 minute quests. I'm not sure if this improves later in the campaign as I got so bored after a few hours of playing that I had to stop.

I then used the powerpass to instantly arrive in the endgame, which was actually kind of nice that they have this. Upon arriving in endgame I discovered that there are really just two main builds per class which are endgame viable, so you're basically locked into one of those builds. The amount of systems and items in the game are unnecessarily numerous and complex. Other ARPGs are able to accomplish this same level of depth with far fewer systems. A lot of these systems feel like they were thrown on just so that there's yet another type of currency that you need, to further increase the chances that you're going to pay money to buy some. None of these extra systems really bring anything interesting to the game, other than maybe the cards system, which was interesting.

I then started doing some content. I enjoyed Chaos Dungeons enough but it only lets you do one per day. The daily event gating is garbage (I want to be able to run the content that I want to run). Then I attempted one of the solo raids because it was one of the few daily event types that I was able to still do at that point.

The boss mechanics are terrible. There are these timed mechanics where the boss performs a particular action and you have to do something specific to counter it, but it doesn't explain what you need to do, and if you miss it it's an unavoidable insta-death no matter where you stand. So you need to go look it up online to understand what you need to do for each of these mechanics, of which there are several.

I didn't find that they were particularly well telegraphed either (a slight change in the color hue of the boss for instance). Some counters are literally just a matter of mashing a key at a certain phase and hoping you time it right. Others are using a specific type of grenade at a specific point during the battle. One miss and you're toast. It's a frustrating, boring, and lazy way to do boss mechanics. The bosses in PoE2 have equally challenging mechanics, but without being boring and frustrating like these, plus you actually know what you're supposed to do by just looking at the fight in PoE2, which is not the case here. 

After I encountered that that was pretty much it for me in terms of playing. Insta-kill boss mechanics that you need to look up the counters to on a wiki is not my cup of tea. This could have been a great ARPG but they've made too many design mistakes and overcomplicated the heck out of it. I'm sure this will appeal to a particular type of gamer, but it's definitely not going to appeal to most players.

This isn't even counting the other bad systems like the micro-transactions, which offer "pay to win" style rewards for purchases and subscriptions, which is a lame approach to free game monetization. It's a shame that a game that has so much potential ended up becoming an uninspired cash grab like this. I really wanted to like this game but it just rubs me the wrong way in too many ways. I heard they are working on a Lost Ark 2 and I hope that they improve on this stuff. If it ends up just being a clone of this then it's not going to attract many players. There are already far better ARPG games out there right now. PoE2 is about to completely revamp their endgame in a few days, and D4's new expansion will be dropping around the same time.

[h1]⚔️ [i]Lost Ark[/i] - Beautiful Combat, Brutal Monetization[/h1]

[b]What I Played:[/b] 232 hours across multiple classes, pushed through the main story, hit endgame, ran my share of Abyssal Dungeons and Legion Raids, and spent way too many evenings staring at honing screens watching my materials evaporate. I came in expecting a solid action RPG MMO and got exactly that — wrapped in one of the most aggressive monetization structures I've seen in a free-to-play game.

[b]The Good:[/b]
[list]
[*]The combat is genuinely top tier. Every class feels impactful and flashy, and pulling off a perfect raid mechanic with your team hitting abilities in sync is chef's kiss. This is where Lost Ark absolutely shines and it's the reason I kept logging in.
[*]The sheer amount of content is impressive. Between the continent exploration, collectibles, sailing, islands, and all the endgame raids, there's a ridiculous amount of stuff to do.
[*]Legion Raids are some of the best MMO raid content I've experienced. Valtan and Vykas had my group wiping for hours and it never stopped being fun to learn.
[/list]

[b]The Bad:[/b]
[list]
[*]The honing system is soul-crushing. Watching upgrade after upgrade fail at 10-15% increments while your gold and materials disappear feels deliberately designed to push you toward swiping. After 232 hours I still felt like I was behind.
[*]Time gating is everywhere. Daily chaos dungeons, daily guardian raids, weekly lockouts — miss a day and you're falling behind. It stops feeling like a game and starts feeling like a job you forgot to clock into.
[*]The cash shop is aggressively in your face. Between skins, battle passes, and the ability to essentially buy progression, the whole thing reeks of "spend money or suffer." It's technically free to play but the grind without paying is brutal by design.
[*]The early game story is a slog. Hours of generic fantasy questing before the game actually opens up.
[/list]

[b]Verdict:[/b] [b]Not Recommended[/b] - Look, Lost Ark has some of the best combat in any MMO and genuinely great raid content. But after 232 hours I can't in good conscience recommend something that respects your wallet less than it respects your time — and it barely respects your time either. If you can treat it as a purely casual experience and ignore the FOMO, there's fun here. But the game doesn't want you to be casual. It wants your credit card. Decent game buried under a cash grab framework.

17,260 hours... I think that tells you everything about how I feel about this game, and yet here I am, equally ready to recommend it and to warn you about every single thing that will make you want to uninstall it.

The Good Stuff
When Lost Ark launched in the West, there was nothing quite like it. The hype was real and it was earned. The combat feel, the class variety, the story, the sheer visual spectacle of it all, it was something else. But the crown jewel of this game, the thing that makes it truly unique, is the Legion Raid system. Beautifully designed boss mechanics, environmental hazards, movement patterns you actually have to study and master. When a raid clicks and your group executes a perfect clear, there is no feeling like it in any other MMORPG. Nothing comes close.
The community that formed around this game is also something special. Guide creators, Discord groups, theorycrafters who probably put more hours into understanding this game than the developers themselves. The Inferno raid crowd especially, a genuinely elite and passionate group of players who pushed the content to its absolute limits. I cleared several raids on Inferno difficulty myself, and the friendships I made through this game are ones I still carry today, long after logging off for the last time.

Now Buckle Up
From literally day one, the game was drowning in bots. Bot farms everywhere, gold selling operations running openly, and the economy was poisoned from the very start. Smilegate banned millions of accounts over the years but never truly solved it. The RMT ecosystem that grew out of this was tolerated for the first two to three years with barely any punishment, because the in-game store prices were so absurd compared to just buying gold from bot sellers that basically everyone was doing it. Smilegate looked the other way.
The content that actually made this game worth playing, the Legion Raids, came way too late to the Western release. By then, players had already been buried under an avalanche of daily and weekly homework that turned the game into a second job. And not a light one. You needed up to six alts to stay competitive, and every single one of them needed a full rotation of dailies, weeklies, time-gated world bosses and island events that required you to drop everything and be online at a specific moment. They eventually shortened the dailies three years in, which is basically an admission that they knew it was unbearable all along.
The tier system is a treadmill that never stops. Every previous tier becomes irrelevant almost instantly, yet the grind to stay current in the latest tier demands either an enormous amount of your time or an enormous amount of your money. Those are your two options.
And if you ever dared to take a break, good luck coming back. Returning to Lost Ark after any significant time away meant either opening your wallet wide or hoping your friends cared enough to carry you back up to relevance. In the early years especially, returning players were practically starting from scratch in terms of the meta, the economy, and the gear gap. It may be somewhat more forgiving these days, but for a long time the game actively punished you for having a life outside of it. I do not play Lost Ark anymore, and for the first time in years I actually play games on my own schedule. When I was playing Lost Ark, I was not playing games whenever I wanted. I was playing Lost Ark, on Lost Ark's schedule, every single day.
This created a brutal gatekeeping culture. Even the weekly homework raids, which should have been accessible content, were treated like high-stakes prog sessions. Groups only wanted the most geared, most experienced players. Everyone else got left out. And then you had the bus system, players literally paying to be carried through raids without learning any mechanics, collecting achievements and gear, and then showing up to PUG groups as a complete liability. Trust in random groups collapsed completely, which pushed everyone into static teams, and static teams came with their own universe of interpersonal drama that I can only describe as a Brazilian soap opera.
Class balance for the first two to three years was genuinely rough. New classes would release slightly overtuned for obvious commercial reasons, while older classes would get left behind so badly that showing up with one would get you visibly judged.
PVP exists in this game the same way a potted plant exists in an office. It is there. No one asked for it. No one waters it.
And yes, the armor design for female characters follows the proud Korean MMORPG tradition of providing maximum combat effectiveness through minimum fabric coverage. Make of that what you will.

So, Recommended?
Sadly, with a bruised heart, no. BUT;
If you love deep raid mechanics, satisfying combat, and the kind of community that genuinely cares about the game, there is nothing else that delivers what Lost Ark delivers at its best. Go in knowing that the game will ask a lot from you, sometimes more than it has any right to, and that many of its worst problems were self-inflicted wounds that never fully healed.
I gave it 17,000 hours of my life. I regret nothing. I am also never getting those hours back.

I have finally reached the point in this game where I've gotten all the mandatory collectables and now only have to look forward to the raid treadmill. I'm not sure if that makes me qualified to discuss endgame-endgame, but let's be real, unless you're a content creator or you're okay setting your hard-earned money on fire, you'll probably get bored of the game before then anyway. Note that my play hours are a little inflated because I leave the game running instead of waiting 10 minutes for it to start up again (that's not a joke, either).

Personally, I had a blast playing the game and still do (though I'm about personally 'finished' with the game because I only have one non-hardmode raid left to clear and the most recent hardmode is always essentially inaccessible to non-whales), but their business strategies and adaptations to keep the game relevant are frustrating at best and downright predatory at worst. I played this entirely f2p (besides a character slot I bought bc I didn't want to delete any of my previous toons in order to play another class, but ultimately I still only played 6 characters so it wasn't required for any strategies I did), and I was at a point of time in my life where I had a bunch of time to burn and needed to stay busy, so Lost Ark was actually a great fit. I think if you play it at your own pace and keep your blinders on to what's going on at the top-top-tier of raiding and whatever is going on in Korea, you'll really enjoy the game.

There's a ton to do, but if you stress over trying to rocket straight into the endgame, you'll quit. If you've played Old School Runescape, the progression is very similar. The problem is everything in this game tries to force you into doing the newest, shiniest raid before you're ready instead of letting you savor the journey because you don't need to spend money to enjoy older content. The situation LOA is in reminds me a lot of when Runescape tried to copy WoW's combat, and everyone quit. Instead of embracing long-form character progression which I really personally enjoyed, they throw you into the final area of the game where you're flooded with systems upon systems just so you can get into the newER raids faster. I have yet to have a single friend that used the powerpass to jump into raiding and stuck around, and unfortunately, every single update forces everyone further into this situation. One of their most recent updates completely removed Tier 3 progression and made that entire content completely meaningless, which is a shame because, as someone who started a couple months ago, it was really the best content the game had to offer (solo raids). This is an update they had to make because they've been bleeding players since launch years ago, and they unfortunately now have to cater to all the whales not wanting to wait an extra lockout to gear up their 16th alt, but this butchers the experience for any new players wanting to try it out because of how quickly it pushes you through.

All that being said, though, if you have the discipline not to let that pressure you into rushing into the latest raid, this game actually has really good and rewarding character progression and lots of extra horizontal content to do that contributes enough to your power to where you notice it but not so much that you can't do the content. It also boasts the best and most rewarding combat in any MMO, both in solo mode and group raids (but you have to be resilient because the first couple tries you'll probably mess up mechanics and die).

People constantly complain about the community but honestly everyone I've interacted with has been very friendly and helpful. Even when I wipe the raid like a noob, people are usually pretty patient and explain how I can fix it. Maybe if you argue with people and are rude then that might be different, but I usually just eat crow and do my best to learn from my mistakes (though there are a few times I've had to take off my gear and get carried by the group if I'm still not getting it).

If you're patient and like engaging with/mastering a bunch of gear/progression systems, I'd definitely recommend giving it a try. I've had a blast, and since I don't spend money on it, I don't have any pressure to keep playing once I stop enjoying it.

I sank 10,000 hours into Lost Ark over three years. A lot of those hours is AFK while multi-task working from home. 

The combat is a literal 10/10 – the most fluid, responsive, and skill-expressive action combat ever shipped in an MMO. Every other system exists to gatekeep it.

To earn gold you raid.
You can only do a few raids each week per character.
There is no, "farming to make gold"
You make alts to do more raids, to make more gold.
To raid with pugs you need titles.
To earn titles you need gold → gear → engravings → gems high enough that party leaders actually accept you.
To become a party leader yourself you must have title, gear, engravings, and gems good enough for players to want to join you for the social proof. Then you also need to be able to lead the raid by running the sidereals. 

The loop is engineered to pressure Pay-to-Win from the in-game shop. RMT sites always stay one step ahead of bans, so most players I played with swiped that way. Credit-card swiping the cash shop is possible but hilariously inefficient. I watched players drop $50k only to see every single purchase handed out in a new-player pass six months later.

F2P route: maintain six alts, run every single raid on all of them, funnel 100 % of resources into one main. Miss a single week and your character falls behind the ilvl curve, groups won't accept you, and the cycle resets. 

I mained Pistoleer when it was universally called a troll spec. Built a partnered YouTube channel around raid nights and Pistoleer gameplay. The eventual buff felt like vindication toward the end before I quit playing.

The deeper problem is systemic burnout by design.

• Novelty-first philosophy: cutscenes and long animations you cannot skip after the first time.
• 12-month patch lag: community screams, developers “listen” exactly one year later.
• FOMO layered on FOMO: cash shop, title gates for pugs, new content dropped exclusively on holidays when normal humans are with family.

Every design decision screams “make it fresh for the first playthrough, make it painful for the 999th.” Replayability was never the goal; retention-through-grind was.

Take Lost Ark’s combat, drop it into a League-of-Legends-story arch & universe that rewards replayability, removes all P2W vectors, and you would have the greatest MMORPG ever made.

What we actually have is a Korean grind factory with god-tier raids and the single best combat engine in the genre, deliberately crippled by monetization, title politics, and anti-replayability systems. Every decision they make feels out of touch, and makes you wonder if anyone designing the game actually plays the game. Also, the stories and scripts are 100% done by AI.

After spending 115 hours in Lost Ark, I can’t help but feel disappointed by the game’s overall experience. While the game has a lot of promise, it falls short in several key areas that leave it feeling repetitive and frustrating rather than rewarding.

First off, the combat system starts off feeling fun, but it quickly becomes mind-numbing. While the flashy abilities and skill combos are initially exciting, they lose their charm over time. The problem isn’t that the combat is bad – it’s just incredibly repetitive. I found myself going through the same motions over and over again, battling waves of enemies without much challenge or variety. Boss fights, which should be a highlight, often feel like a chore, with predictable patterns and little-to-no meaningful strategy involved.

The story is another letdown. The game’s narrative feels like an afterthought, offering little in terms of emotional investment or character development. The writing is bland, and the dialogue often comes off as forced or generic. Even though the world of Lost Ark has some potential, the story doesn’t do enough to keep me engaged or invested in the world.

The grind is where Lost Ark really starts to wear thin. After a few dozen hours, it becomes painfully obvious that the game’s design is built around making you repeat content ad nauseam. Whether it’s grinding for gear, upgrading items, or taking on repetitive dungeons, the game doesn’t feel rewarding – just a time-sink. The constant push to spend money on progression (via microtransactions) becomes more and more apparent, and the game’s monetization strategies feel intrusive, especially for those not looking to invest in the cash shop.

The lack of meaningful endgame content also becomes evident after a while. After the initial story and progression, you’re left with little to do other than grind for incremental rewards. The raids, dungeons, and events start to feel like they’re there just to pad out playtime, and it’s hard to shake the feeling that the game is more about keeping you hooked long enough to spend money rather than offering satisfying, long-term gameplay.

While Lost Ark is visually impressive and the world is well-designed, it’s not enough to overcome its repetitive gameplay, lackluster story, and constant grind. For those who enjoy mindless farming and don’t mind spending money to progress, Lost Ark may still hold some appeal. But for me, after 115 hours, it’s clear that the game’s flaws outweigh its strengths.

Overall, I can't recommend Lost Ark to anyone looking for a deep, engaging MMORPG experience. If you’re looking for a game with meaningful progression, a rich story, and content that feels worth your time, there are better alternatives out there. Unfortunately, Lost Ark ends up feeling more like a cash grab than a truly fulfilling MMORPG.

Lost Ark is an unusual beast: a Korean-developed MMOARPG that blends the frenetic, loot-driven combat of Diablo with the persistent world and social systems of traditional MMOs. The result is overwhelmingly dense, occasionally frustrating, and surprisingly compelling once you surrender to its rhythm.

The Currency Conundrum
Let's address the elephant in the room immediately: Lost Ark has a currency problem. Silver, gold (two types), pirate coins, crystals in multiple hues, and more tokens than a county fair—all exchangeable for other currencies or goods in ways that feel deliberately obfuscated. It's indicative of the game's primary issue: Lost Ark is as dense as a block of lead and roughly as good at explaining itself. Nearly 60 hours in, my storage box remains full of items I don't understand and will probably never use.

Combat That Sings
Thankfully, everything else sings. The combat is immediately cathartic—frenetic, impactful, and designed to make you feel overpowered in the best way. With 15 classes spread across five main archetypes (Warrior, Martial Artist, Gunner, Mage, Assassin), each plays distinctly enough to warrant multiple playthroughs. Playing as a Deathblade Assassin, every skill found purpose; modifiers unlock as abilities level, creating meaningful customization without the paralysis of getting it wrong.

The game thoughtfully starts you at level 10 with a full skill bar—a change from earlier builds that streamlines the experience. While veteran players might mourn the lost introductory levels, the adjustment demonstrates developer Smilegate's willingness to learn and improve.

Structure and Story
Quests follow familiar paths: kill quests, fetch quests, more fetch quests. The menial tasks can feel beneath your station as the Champion of Luterra, and the lack of quest stacking means you're rarely leaving hubs with a full log. But Lost Ark cleverly structures each new continent as a self-contained story arc. One region channels Final Fantasy VII's Midgar with steampunk aesthetics; another requires shrinking potions to fight monstrous insects. This creativity keeps the busywork tolerable.

The overarching plot—hunting seven pieces of the titular Ark to banish darkness—takes a backseat to these regional tales. Characters are likeable, writing cheesy in that JRPG way but sprinkled with genuine pathos. The first major arc involving Prince Thirain's kingdom is genuinely engaging.

World and Systems
This is where Lost Ark reveals its true ambition. Beyond the main quest lies staggering depth:

Chaos Dungeons offer procedural horde-mode fights

Guardian Raids and Abyssal Dungeons provide challenging group content

Your Stronghold functions as a customizable base for crafting and research

Trade skills cover foraging, hunting, fishing, mining, and treasure hunting

The Adventurer's Tome tracks collectibles across continents, rewarding completionists with mounts, skins, and stat boosts

Mokoko Seeds number in the thousands for those who must find everything

Each new continent (with three added for Western release) contains hidden stories, secret bosses, and rare discoveries. It's designed for hundreds of hours.

Solo vs. Multiplayer
Playing pre-release on an under-populated server meant experiencing much of Lost Ark solo—not ideal for an MMO. The 20-hour journey to level 50 works fine alone, but the endgame content demands cooperation. Once you reach Vern and unlock the good stuff, the game transforms. A free level 50 boost for a second character after your first max-level run is a welcome quality-of-life touch.

Presentation and Customization
Character creation offers surprising depth—easily 15 minutes vanished before my first adventure. The zones remain consistent rather than procedurally generated, making subsequent playthroughs feel familiar and efficient. Visuals are vibrant, and the world feels alive in ways procedurally generated ARPGs often don't.

Shortcomings
Beyond the currency confusion and fetch quest fatigue, a few issues persist:

Generic side quests rarely advance story or interest

Limited quest stacking means constant back-and-forth travel

Traditional MMO roles (tank/healer/DPS) don't really exist—adjust expectations accordingly

The endgame mountain requires months to properly evaluate

Verdict
Lost Ark is a lot. A lot of currencies, a lot of systems, a lot of content, a lot of hours. Approach it for what it is—an Action-RPG with MMO trappings, not the reverse—and there's a sprawling world of adventure to discover. The combat is excellent, the class variety genuine, and the density of things to do borders on overwhelming.

It's the kind of game that connects people across distances, the way MMOs have always done best. I can't wait to play it with friends.
There's a server maintenance, for what feels like every 4 days. Fun MMO experience regardless.
I just like and enjoy the overall gameplay of this title.

Lost Ark has the best combat system in any MMO I've ever played.[b] Unfortunately[/b], it's wrapped in so many layers of predatory systems, FOMO mechanics, and terrible new player experience that I can't recommend it unless you hate yourself or have unlimited free time.

[h1]The Good (Yes, There Is Some)[/h1]

[h2]Combat: 10/10[/h2] - No joke, the raid fights and combat mechanics are chef's kiss. This is what keeps people playing despite everything else. The boss encounters are challenging, rewarding, and genuinely fun. If you could extract just the combat and raids, this would be a masterpiece.

[h2]Visuals: 8/10[/h2] - Game looks gorgeous. The particle effects, character designs, and animations are top-tier. You'll look cool while suffering.

[h2]Content Volume: 9/10[/h2] - There's an insane amount of stuff to do. Whether you should do it all is another question entirely.

[h1]The Bad (Oh Boy, Here We Go)[/h1]

[h2]New Player Experience: 2/10[/h2]

Imagine walking into a library where every book is written in a different language, the Dewey Decimal System was replaced with hieroglyphics, and the librarian just screams FIGURE IT OUT before running away. That's Lost Ark for new players.

You'll be bombarded with:
47 different currencies (I counted)
Systems within systems within systems
Pop-ups that make early 2000s malware look subtle
Events you can't do
Guides that are already outdated
That nagging feeling you're doing everything wrong (you probably are)

[h2]The Grind: 3/10[/h2]
Korean MMO grind is expected, but Lost Ark takes it to another level. Everything is time-gated, ticket-gated, RNG-gated, and paywall-gated. Miss your daily/weekly stuff? Congrats, you're now permanently behind forever.

[h2]P2W Elements: 4/10[/h2]
"It's not P2W, it's pay-to-progress-faster!"... Sure BRO, while you can technically do everything as F2P, whales will reach endgame content months before you. The game constantly reminds you that your life would be easier if you just opened your wallet

[h2]Story: 1/10 [/h2]
The story is so bad it's almost impressive. You're supposedly the chosen one, but you feel like an NPC in your own adventure


[h1]The Ugly[/h1]

Returning Player Experience: 0/10

Took a break? Cool, the game changed completely, your guides are worthless, and there's zero help to catch you up. Hope you enjoy feeling lost in a game called Lost Ark (maybe that's the joke?).

FOMO Mechanics: 0/10

This game wants you to feel bad about having a life. Limited events, daily lockouts, weekly resets, seasonal content - it's all designed to keep you anxious and logging in. It's exhausting.

Customer Service: 1/10

Amazon Games customer service is about as useful as a chocolate teapot. Lost items? Bugs? Good luck.


[h1]Who Is This Game For?[/h1]

[h2]Yes if[/h2]
You enjoy Korean MMO grind culture and know what you're signing up for 
You have 4-6 hours daily to commit 
You love spreadsheets, wikis, and external guides 
You either started at launch or you're a masochist 
You have a guild/friends to carry you through the learning curve
You don't mind P2W elements

[h2]No if[/h2]
You have a job, family, or literally any other hobby 
You want to play casually 
You value your mental health 
You expect games to teach you how to play them 
You took a break and want to return 
You're new to MMOs


[h1]Final Thoughts[/h1]

I have almost 1,2k hours in this game. That should tell you something about how good the core combat is. But it should also tell you something that despite loving the raids, I still can't recommend this to anyone. The combat is a 10/10 trapped inside a 4/10 game.

Wow, what a mess this is. While it has potential fundamentally, it just tries to be too many things at the same time, totally losing any identity and watering down every aspect.
The game is solid from a technical perspective. While it doesn't do anything mind-blowing, it mostly runs well and looks good. I never encountered any major bugs, crashes or freezes. It features a vast, mostly beautifully designed world and an interesting premise for a good narrative. Enemy encounters and set pieces are sometimes spectacular. 
But... it just throws such a huge pile of mechanics and systems at you, that it all ends up being a complete chaos fest. Whenever you start the game, you are greeted by windows upon windows of this and that. Some of the stuff is even totally irrelevant for you, but it is still thrown at you. Thousand of packs, items, events, rewards etc. Here is [insert random thing]. OK. And here is [insert another random thing]. OK.
20 minutes later I am done just clicking through that stuff, and by then I sometimes lost all interest in even playing the game, because each start of it is just exhausting.
The UI is incoherent and unintuitive, there is no clear design to all the windows, and functions, as if each one was designed by a different person and just thrown into the game to have "more stuff". 
Of course you have more skills, buffs, levels, gear, equipment, enchantments etc. than you could ever keep track of. Of course you can build up a whole island and have a game within the game there. Of course you complete a bazillion stupid fetch quests which are basically identical. Of course you can have emotes, play music and cook. Of course there are thousands of character cards and hidden collectibles, which give tiny bonuses. Of course you can have a huge number of pets and mounts. It. Is. Just. Too. Much. Of. Everything.
And the problem with the sheer amount of stuff is that most of it is half-baked and poorly explained.
Why the hell is only the very first sentence of each conversation voiced?
Why the hell are some items forever stuck in my inventory without any way to get rid of them?
Why the hell is is such a pain to play in a party with friends? 
Why the hell aren't there more well written quests instead of all the slop?
I could go on and on... and I plan to at least finish the main questline, as I generally hate stopping midgame. But never have the words "less is more" been more fitting than in this case.

tl;dr: Temper your expectations. Devs will never stop adding vertical progression systems. FOMO will be the end of you. If you do not have an active guild, static, or are not on a Discord server that organizes raids, you're going to have a very bad time. Alternatively, pay ~$100k USD to immediately max your character out.

I wish there was a "Neutral" option instead of straight up having to recommend or not recommend a game. At it's core, Lost Ark is a fantastic isometric ARPG with some of the best combat, boss design, and raids in the genre. Of course, this is a Korean MMO, so you have two options if you want to be viable in endgame raids (which are the main selling point and attractions of the game). You can either shell out a ridiculous amount of money in order to bypass the relentless, nonstop grind for character power, or you can play this game like a second job, raiding on multiple characters on multiple rosters in order to maybe be strong enough to be accepted into endgame raids. There is also a third, less popular option that I recommend, which is to not give in to FOMO and simply play at your own pace. 

Lost Ark is the definition of a "marathon, not a sprint" game. The devs here are not completely clueless (unlike some other KRMMOs *cough* Blade & Soul *cough*) and frequently host catch-up events that new players can take advantage of to quickly and relatively painlessly progress to almost endgame levels. 

However, this only shifts the problem from being eligible for participating in endgame raids to having nobody accept you for raids because people can easily tell from a glance if you are new to the game (low roster level is an immediate giveaway, not having requisite achievements that can only be gotten from playing the raids you are trying to apply to is also a giveaway). Truly, the only way a new player will be accepted into raids is if you go out of your way to find a static, guild, or join a community Discord that organizes raids. Pugging will absolutely destroy your sanity, and carries the extreme risk of being "jailed" in raids (the game will only let you progress through gates in a raid with people with the same gate completion, so if your party disbands mid-raid, you are SoL).

All in all, if you have a static, friends to play with, or are in a Discord that organizes raids, then you'll probably have a great time with this game. If you're a solo player that wants to experience the endgame, you probably won't have trouble getting to endgame due to the existence of solo raids, but you are going to have a VERY bad time in party finder trying to persuade pugs to let you join them. 

Some other things to note for prospective players that don't quite fit anywhere else in this review: 

(1) Classes are gender-locked - this might be a dealbreaker for a lot of people - and there is a strong bias towards female classes. 
(2) Raids are limited entry - you can only enter a raid once per character per week, and you can only enter 3 different raids per character per week. Meaning you will have to play alts if you want to make any meaningful income.
(3) Raids are difficult, and personal responsibility is high - a single person can wipe the entire raid with certain mechanics, and it is expected that you study raid guides thoroughly before joining raids. Some of these guides can be hours long. Expect to prog for dozens of hours on endgame raids if you have no experience.
(4) RNG upon RNG upon RNG - upgrading ANYTHING involves copious amounts of RNG. You WILL get frustrated with honing and rolling for stats and lines on accessoires. On the flipside, you CAN get lucky and save millions of gold with a lucky tap or roll.
(5) There is a story. Is it good? Eh. Is it voiced? Sometimes? Should you care about it? Maybe, if you're into it. Don't expect something magnificent is what I'm getting at.

I’ve been playing Lost Ark since the Western beta. At the time, I was working at Amazon in the IT department and wanted to be part of something different outside of my 9–5. I played the game pre-release and post-release, and in the beginning it genuinely felt exciting and fun.

Progressing through the story, exploring the world, and learning the systems was enjoyable—especially because I was playing alongside my best friend. Early on, the game felt rewarding and social, and there was a real sense of momentum as you moved forward.

However, once progression became heavily tied to gear honing, resource grinding, and item level requirements, the experience changed completely. The grind to increase item level became incredibly frustrating and time-consuming, to the point where it felt almost impossible without extreme dedication or spending. This is ultimately what caused my best friend to stop playing altogether.

On top of that, gatekeeping became a major issue. Endgame content increasingly revolves around strict requirements—high item levels, perfect engravings, optimal card sets, and specific classes—making it extremely difficult for returning, casual, or unlucky players to participate. Even when you meet the basic requirements, it’s common to be declined repeatedly from groups unless you vastly overgear the content.

This creates a cycle where:

You need raids to progress

But you can’t get into raids without already being over-progressed

Which pushes players toward burnout, bussing, or quitting entirely

I continued playing for longer—partly due to my connection with the company—but over time it became clear that Lost Ark feels less like a game and more like a second job. Daily chores, time-gated content, and FOMO-driven systems don’t respect the player’s time, especially for anyone with real-life responsibilities.

This sentiment is widely shared in the community. While Lost Ark has excellent combat, beautiful visuals, and some of the best raid designs in the genre, it relies heavily on:

Excessive daily and weekly homework

RNG-based progression that can feel punishing

A gatekeeping-heavy endgame culture that discourages new or returning players

Eventually, burnout becomes inevitable.

Now, I mostly log in only for new content, events, or free rewards, rather than playing consistently. The core gameplay is still impressive, but the overall progression and social systems make it hard to enjoy long-term unless the game becomes your main focus.

Lost Ark is a great game at its core—but one that struggles to balance ambition, accessibility, and community health. If you have unlimited time, you may love it. If not, it can quickly become exhausting.

Lost Ark has several fundamental issues that make it impossible for me to currently recommend.

The first and foremost problem is that if you didn't play since launch, or even just took a break for as much as a week, you have permanently fallen behind in progression and the only thing you can do to catch up is to swipe. Reward and progression is based on a system of dailies and weeklies - skip them once and you fall behind. Updates extend the power ceiling faster than you're able to keep up even if you play actively and skipping even a week can be crippling.
Game is in practice a treadmill and it traps you with fear of falling behind. You can't slowly catch up and do things later - aside from average player strength constantly going up, if you don't get the relevant achievement for clearing a raid within 2 weeks of its release, people will not accept you to many lobbies for it as you'll be a risk factor to clearing their weeklies fast as obviously everyone wants to reclear their homework raids smoothly with people who know what to do, rather than risk taking potential first timers that will cause wipes for hours before they disband. Old raids are no longer being run as only 3 raids per character per week give gold rewards, meaning players only really run the latest 3, so until you catch up, you're basically playing single player. To compensate for that, older raids have been getting solo modes, but they're easy to the point of being boring. Events and catch up systems will allow you to start being only 6-12 months behind relative to the veterans, rather than years that passed since release, for what it's worth.
The "having to swipe to catch up" problem also results in game hemorrhaging players as people who took a break oftentimes simply don't come back as they'd have to spend the equivalent of hundreds of $ to compensate for even a few weeks.

Second issue is the RNG nature of the various progression systems. Combined with rewards being daily/weekly, this means some players will naturally be weeks or months ahead of others. Some people will be done with a progression system after a month, others after half a year. Of course you can also swipe if you get unlucky, and you'll be especially compelled to do so if bad RNG causes you to fall behind and be unable to keep up with friends you play with. Effectively, systems are designed to create inequality to make people feel bad and compel them to spend money to catch up if they get unlucky.

The third major problem isn't related to the game itself, but to the publishing contract between the Korean developer (Smilegate) and western publisher (Amazon), specifically it expiring next year.
There's been complete radio silence about the topic. We don't know what will happen when it expires, especially given how Amazon Game Studios was scaled down to a skeleton of what it was in recent years. Are they planning to extend the contract? Will there be no more updates and game will stay on life support? Is there a risk of end of service? Is a new western publisher planned? If so, will characters transfer? It's pure guesswork and unfortunately it's a topic that's impossible to ignore as you really don't want to play a time and money consuming game that may be sunset in the west within a year.

Now, if you're willing to ignore said problems - possibly having to swipe to catch up, progression being slow and RNG based, having to diligently do dailies and weeklies or swipe regularly to make up for missed homework, game's future being uncertain - game offers some of the best raid gameplay out there and really good, if inconsistently translated, story and has an amazing soundtrack.

A Beautiful Disaster Wrapped in RNG and Outdated Design

Lost Ark is, without exaggeration, one of the most frustrating MMORPG experiences I’ve ever had. It’s a game built on stunning visuals and flashy combat, yet completely suffocated by some of the most predatory, toxic, and exhausting systems seen in the genre.

Let’s start with the core progression: everything is RNG. Every upgrade, every attempt at progress, every step forward is locked behind layers upon layers of randomness. Instead of feeling rewarding, progression becomes a coin flip simulator where your time, effort, and materials can simply evaporate because the game decided today isn’t your lucky day. It’s not skill-based, it’s not engaging—it’s just maddening.

And if you think you can power through it by focusing on one character, think again. Lost Ark practically forces you into maintaining 10+ alts just to funnel resources into your “main.” This isn’t optional; it’s a design choice that turns the game into a second job. The daily checklist alone feels like punishment, not entertainment.

But what really pushes Lost Ark into “unplayable” territory is the community behavior surrounding it. The obsession with gatekeeping players based on titles, achievements, or content cleared during the first week of a new patch is absurd. If you didn’t no-life the game the moment new content dropped, expect to be blacklisted, kicked from groups, or straight-up ignored. Instead of encouraging growth, the community often acts as a prison guard enforcing elitist, unrealistic standards.

In the end, Lost Ark could have been great—but its own systems are working overtime to make sure you never get to enjoy it. Between the endless RNG, the alt-character grind, and a community that punishes anyone who isn’t already at the top, the game ends up feeling less like an MMORPG and more like a chore wrapped in flashy animations.

Verdict: Beautiful on the surface, absolutely miserable underneath.

+++ If you value your time, sanity, or the concept of fun, there are far better games out there.
