It must be fate that Chris Wilson's video about Dark Patterns in games was in my recommended feed on the last day before the big update of Act 4 & The Final Day raid. I'm getting off the hamster wheel.

This game's raid combat and different classes were the only saving grace for me. In the last few weeks, I found myself enjoying solo raids on my rat alts because playing them was a breath of fresh air compared to running the same 6 gold earners for the 9000th time. I enjoyed my time with the game playing with my friends and random people but if there's one sentence I can use to described this game is "It's as wide as the ocean and as deep as a puddle." Every older raids or activities they've introduced is abandoned because people only interact with the few latest content.

Almost every system in this game is debilitating and riddled with layers of RNG: it's by design to time gate slowing down progression. It uses so many predatory psychological manipulation like FOMO to keep you playing in the hopes that you get lucky: if you just get one good Frost/Flame Hell Key run, you'd save millions of gold from just getting a few Grudge, Keen Blunt, Cursed Doll, Raid Captain or Adrenaline books. But at the end of day, it's not going to happen. When you succeed, you don't feel good and want to do it again. You feel good that you never have to interact with that system ever again (like Transcendence or Elixirs). Designing progression systems like that makes it inevitable that your game will lose players. Old systems (Elixirs) get reworked to be easier to min-max because there's a new system that will make more money (Ark Grid). The game's reward system with the raids encourages gatekeeping by design because you want to finish your three gold earning raids ASAP so you can move on to the other 5 gold earning characters. The mokoko bootcamp event doesn't really help new players learn the raid, it only helps new players finish a raid by getting carried.

At the end of it, this game is just a predatory mobile game with a good combat/raid design. The game controls how much you get to play: everything is time-gated. It's heavily pay-to-win and has gotten worse with new content like Ark Grid and Paradise. The RNG is so egregious that it's impressive to say the least: one tapping/free tapping a weapon to +25 compared to the average cost is several millions of gold and compared to pity is probably in the tens of millions. When I found out about the Ark Grid system, I realized that this game isn't going to change. Smilegate will just nerf old systems (because it doesn't make a lot of money anymore) and introduce new systems to keep the hamsters on the wheel.

I, too, have seen the light; I've escaped and gotten off the hamster wheel. Stay away from this game and every predatory games like it. Remember that games are there for your enjoyment and played on your schedule. If you're playing on the game's schedule, it's just another job.

Not because the combat is bad (it’s actually fantastic), but because the entire structure is a masterclass in psychological predation. I actually didn't write a negative review like 2 years ago when I stopped playing because I was just so impressed by how impressive the psychological tactics were that it honestly should be a positive review. 
This game is a brilliantly toxic product that targets its audience who are pretty much all basement-dwelling rats with non existent awareness, tricking them into believing that running the same meaningless chore on twelve alt-characters is a valuable life contribution to their imaginary community. It makes you feel valuable surviving on welfare checks by convincing you that maintaining your roster level just to find a group for a raid is some sort of a noble calling of you leading some sort of heroes that give you the imaginary perception of being better than other people when in reality you’ve just built a sweatshop for yourself. Every day you feed them Chaos Dungeon rations, send them to do your busywork, and somehow convinced yourself that funneling mats into your main is real life progress.
The monetization is the final humiliation: your 400 hours of grinding for an upgrade, thinking it was all worth it for that +1 honing success only to instantly fail and having all your gold evaporate when one bored banker by swiping his Amex on a lunch break gets his cartoon sword shinier than you. And the worst part? You know this, but you still log in the next day and whisper to yourself "one more try". That’s the level of psychological brilliance of exploiting FOMO we're dealing with, disguised as fantasy. You’re chasing timers like they owe you rent. You log in out of guilt, collect your daily “rewards,” and tell yourself it’s self-care. It’s the first game where burnout is an official feature, and logging off feels like quitting your job without notice.
It’s addictive and fundamentally rotten. The perfect mix of dopamine, despair, and denial is a monument to how far humanity will go to feel “productive” while achieving absolutely nothing.

Hello everyone,

Having over 3,500 hours of play, I think I'm legitimate enough to write a review.

I'll try to structure my reasoning by starting with the negative points:

The two biggest red flags are the publisher's development team, AGS, and the community.
AGS started to listen to its players a little when the game's population declined by 20.
Unfortunately, over the past few months, they decided there were still players to drive away, and they decided to remove French and German from the game. They also removed the portability of many keyboards such as AZERTY, QWERTZ, etc. For those who play with keyboards removed, you will be penalized because there are certain fights that require QTEs.
The community is also very, very toxic. Being a P2W, there are a lot of egos, and instead of helping each other with a relatively low playing population, they prefer to continue to sink each other. There are still some people who want to help old returners and new players, but the vast majority prefer that they play in their corner in solo raid (the height of it for a game that calls itself Massive Multiplayer Online) so as not to bother them.

regarding positive points, having played several MMO RPGs, Lost Ark's graphic style and combat are unparalleled. The soundtracks for the encounters enhance the combat. The story is very interesting and very long. You'll need dozens of hours to complete the main quest (still ongoing), featuring one of the best antagonists ever created in a game: Kharmine.
There are some areas for improvement regarding the daily workload. They reduced the number of Chaos Dungeons and Guardians to one per day per character. But unfortunately, they implemented a new seasonal feature: Paradise, which, despite all the rewards it provides, once again requires a considerable amount of time to dedicate to this activity.
There are regular events to try to catch up on the released content. In any case, all the Legion raids are obsolete, as are the beginnings of the Kazeros raids. With only 10,000 players connected simultaneously, raids outside of the four most recent ones are practically impossible to do due to the lack of groups (except for solo raids).
Make no mistake, if you want to join the latest raid, which will be released in November, you have two choices: Either have picked up the game several months ago, or pay up your credit card and spend thousands of euros.
In conclusion:

Lost Ark is a unique game with great qualities, but unfortunately it's been undermined by its evolution curve, which resembles a Las Vegas casino, as well as its toxic community.

The game encapsulates everything that makes an MMO completely terrible. 
- Time limited content (Dailies). A complete disrespect to the players time, while also nudging the players to log out of the game once they are done
- RNG based gear upgrades (why not make the gear itself a drop chance to be hype over, instead of your resources maybe being useful or wasted). 
- Every server is a separate account, meaning you have to do all of your roster and character progress from scratch, if you need to switch server to play with a friend. And btw, you cannot move a character to another server or matchmake between servers, which almost kills the MMO aspect
- Heavy P2W. What makes what a player has accomplished special, if you can simply pay your way to it? What proves to others and yourself, that your achievements and gear are the result of skill, knowledge and time?

The combat and the world design is amazing, visual effects and class identity is almost peak, but it is wrapped around a turd of horrible game design that does everything perfectly horrible.

My suggestion: 
-Make Lost Ark monthly subscription, scrap the entire microtransaction shop and make cosmetics a result of gameplay and achievements instead, exactly like titles and collection. 
- Get rid of all daily, weekly, general time limited stuff, when the player has the time they should be able to play as much as they want under the same conditions. 
- Introduce non-raid based gear progression and remove the entire honing system. Swap it out for gear drops across various activities, where the uses of different gear have different uses throughout different content (horisontal progression).
- Suggest potential new content to the player base, make them have a say and what they would like, since they will be paying monthly.
- Make roster progress tied to your account, so it is shared across all servers. 
- Make cross server matchmaking possible
- Make character server migration possible, maybe with a cooldown to reduce server stress
- When adding new content, make sure it acts as an alternative and in very rare cases a direct upgrade

With all this you can even slow down overall progression, because it would respect the players' time, and not render their progression obsolete should they take a brake from the game.

After almost 3000 hours in Lost Ark, I can confidently say it’s one of the best MMOs if you enjoy challenging PvE content. The raid design and combat system are unmatched — every boss fight feels unique, and clearing hard content is an unforgettable experience.

There’s also a huge amount of horizontal content. Even with all my playtime, I’ve barely completed half of the available achievements and collectibles. On top of that, the cinematics, soundtrack, and story presentation make exploring Arkesia truly immersive and memorable.

That said, the game isn’t perfect. The community leans hardcore, which can create gatekeeping and raid anxiety, especially in the latest raids at the highest difficulties. However, this is much less of an issue now thanks to solo mode content, which lets you progress at your own pace without depending on others. Plus, if you make friends or join a guild, there are plenty of friendly communities willing to help new and returning players.

The weekly raid cycle can sometimes feel like repetitive “homework,” and the layered RNG systems can be frustrating. Also, the time you can spend on your main character is limited — dailies are short, raids are weekly-locked, and events don’t last long, so alts are almost mandatory if you want more playtime. On top of that, the learning curve for newcomers is steep, especially when it comes to engravings, gearing, and raid mechanics.

The monetization gives paying players some convenience, but F2P is completely viable, and you can enjoy all the content without spending money

That said, the game has its flaws. The community leans heavily toward hardcore players, which creates a lot of gatekeeping and “raid anxiety” for newcomers or casuals. Weekly raid rotations can turn into repetitive “homework,” and the multi-layered RNG systems can be frustrating to deal with. Another core issue is that you can’t really spend much time on your main character — daily tasks take 10 minutes, weekly raids are limited, and world events are over quickly. If you want more playtime, you’re essentially pushed into alts. On top of that, the game has a steep learning curve, making it overwhelming for new players to understand engravings, gearing, and raid mechanics.

The game’s monetization system gives paying players some convenience and advantages, but it’s still fully possible to reach endgame and remain competitive without spending a cent. 

Pros:
+ Unmatched raid design and combat feel
+ Tons of horizontal content with long-term goals
+ F2P is completely okay
+ Epic story presentation with OSTs, cutscenes, and lore
+ Clearing hard raids provides incredible satisfaction
+ Tons of classes with different playstyles

Cons:
- Community leans hardcore, leading to gatekeeping and raid anxiety
- Weekly raid cycle can feel like repetitive “homework”
- Multi-layered RNG can be frustrating
- Limited playtime with your main; alts are almost mandatory
- Steep learning curve for new players
- PvP will not satisfy you probably

I don’t usually write reviews on Steam, but the recent changes to Lost Ark are quite juicy. As a returning player who participated in Brel Hard prog and quit afterward, I genuinely believe these updates could save Lost Ark. Hear me out:

Solo Raids:
Extremely friendly for new and returning players. They’re easy, have no tight DPS checks, and are enjoyable even if you're not already familiar with the raid. You can also earn tons of honing materials for both your main and alts to catch up.

Raid Design Changes:
The newer raids have reduced difficulty—fewer wipe mechanics and one-shot attacks. You can even revive during raids now. With the Mokoko title, players are much more willing to take you along even if you haven’t cleared it before. My main is now 1660 after just two weeks (due to the powerpass), I’ve had no trouble getting into raids at my item level. ( The highest raid currently requires item level 1680.)

Daily Quest QoL:
No more daily Una Tasks—yes,Finally! Weekly Una Tasks still exist, but you can complete them just by running Chaos Dungeons three times a week. Even if you're playing six characters, it no longer feels like a second job.

Events:
There are tons of new events, and you’ll get a full set of Legendary skin jars just for logging in. A year ago, I wouldn’t have recommended Lost Ark to any of my friends. But now, I honestly think it’s a great time to return to the game.

Personally I very much enjoy this game. I say I maybe recommend it rather than fully recommend it because it's a large investment. The story from level 1-60 isn't too taxing, but once you hit 60 and get into endgame content, things can get confusing. I'll be honest, and call me a noob all you want, but I still have to look at guides to understand a lot of things. I have certain memory and processing problems, and find it difficult to retain all of the information needed to create a good character build. It can get extremely overwhelming.

Some people will get very toxic in party content if you don't know every little detail about your character build, so don't fat finger a key in your rotation during endgame raids. They mean serious business. They will kick you and be-smite your name forever.

Thankfully, the developers have kindly introduced solo endgame content for losers like me who A) Don't interact with other people well due to generalized anxiety disorder, and B) don't know our rotations and get through fights by sheer luck and button smashing (At least I'm honest). I am graeatly thankful for that.

On the positive side, there is tons of content. There are multiple different raids and dungeons that you can do daily or weekly, as well as tasks. There's the Ark tour, the sidequests, your Stronghold to keep up with, the proving grounds PvP, my personal favorite fun game: the tower, and so many events thet always give rewards. 

Lost Ark is expensive to create the best builds, but it is not entirely impossible to F2P. Events often give away special loot to help develop your character, as do endgame dungeons and raids. something extremely useful, particularly if you have alts that you don't want to level from 1-60, but don't have the gold for knowledge transfer is the powerpass. Normally you have to buy it with gems, but during a lot of events you will be given one for free, so as long as you are already knowledgeable enough of high level character building and content, or willing to spend a lot of time learning, I reccomend using them to skip some character levels.

TL;DR: Lost Ark is a great game if you can afford the time and investment. If you get overwhelmed, search for guides. If you can't avoid trolls, play solo content, it's nice and quiet. You can smash buttons and not have to know your rotation.

[h2]🧙‍♂️ Looks like Diablo, endgame feels like Depression[/h2]

[h3]📊  Objective Review[/h3]

[b]Platform:[/b] PC
[b]Performance:[/b] Good performance overall. It runs well on mid range PCs without major issues. Stability and load times are acceptable for an MMO of this scale.

[b]Gameplay:[/b] The combat is the strongest aspect of Lost Ark. Visually spectacular, fast paced, and with an immense variety of classes each with their own style, mechanics, and beautiful animations. Between raids, dungeons, events, and PvE progression, there's a lot of content to explore, especially for newcomers to the MMORPG genre. (Party finder is trash, more on this on progression category.)

[b]Graphics & Design:[/b] Outstanding for an MMO. Characters are highly customizable, environments are immersive, and the overall visual polish is very high. Lost Ark does not feel like a budget game its presentation rivals many full-priced AAA titles.

[b]Progression & Endgame Balance:[/b] This is where the cracks start to show. While early and mid game are smooth and engaging, the late game becomes a grind heavy wall. The gear enhancement system relies too much on RNG, which leads to frustration. Without a solid group, it can be a nightmare to find parties for mid to late content due to server population differences. The Party Finder is slow, unreliable, and often more time consuming than the actual content.

[b]Replayability:[/b] Technically, yes. Realistically, not so much. Progression slows down massively, improvements become microscopic and demand weeks of farming, and the community grows increasingly hostile toward new or undergeared players. Playing alone toward the end is exhausting unless you already have an established group.

[h3] Personal Experience[/h3]

As a longtime MMO player and fan of mage classes, I loved the class design and spell animations in Lost Ark. Playing solo was fine at first, but once I teamed up with friends, the entire experience became far more enjoyable mostly because it allowed me to bypass the toxic party search system and jump straight into actual gameplay.

The early and mid game content is genuinely fun. It has good pacing, engaging story beats, and a strong hook. But the endgame? Not worth it unless you’re playing with a team and you’re ready to commit a significant chunk of your life to sitting in party finder queues.

[h2]⚠️ Play it casually with friends and enjoy the early game. If you’re thinking of going solo all the way to endgame, think again. Your patience may not survive.[/h2]

While you are in your 24k queue on an EU server here's a guide on how to make pizza dough for a delicious pizza of your choice!

Ingredients:
500g '00' flour or plain flour, plus extra for dusting
1 tsp salt
½ tsp dried yeast (not fast-action)
400ml warm water
Oil, for greasing.

STEP 1
It’s easiest to make this in a standing mixer with a dough hook (otherwise mix it in a bowl and knead on your work surface). Put the flour and salt in the bowl and mix the yeast into the water. It’s always a good idea to wait 5 mins before using the liquid to see if the yeast is working – little bits will start to rise to the top and you’ll know it’s active.

STEP 2
Turn on the motor and pour in the liquid. Keep the speed on medium-high and it should come together as a ball. If the bottom is still sticking, tip in 1-2 tbsp of flour. Knead for 5-7 mins until the dough is shiny and it springs back when you press your finger into it. (If kneading by hand, it will take you about 10 mins.) Try not to add too much flour if you can. This is a slightly sticky dough, but that keeps it light and it rises beautifully.

STEP 3
Use oiled hands to remove the dough from the hook and bowl. Oil another bowl and place the dough in it. Turn it around so that it’s lightly coated in the oil. Cover tightly with cling film and then a tea towel. Place in a draught-free area that’s warm and leave until the dough has doubled in size. If it’s a hot day, it should only take 2 hrs to rise, but it could take 4 hrs if it’s cold. (If you don’t plan to use the dough for a day or two, place it in the fridge straight away; take it out 3-4 hrs before using. Punch it down first and bring it together on a floured surface.)

STEP 4
Divide the dough into 2 pieces for big pizzas or 4 for plate-sized ones, then shape into balls (see Shaping the dough in tips, below) – dust them in flour as they will be sticky. Keep them covered with a tea towel or cling film while you prepare the toppings. (you can also freeze them in sealed bags. Just thaw in the fridge on the day, then bring to room temperature 3 hrs before using.)

STEP 5
To shape the dough: If you want to get air pockets and a light but crisp dough, then don’t use a rolling pin. It flattens and pops the air bubbles. (Two days in the fridge will produce the most air bubbles – take it out three to four hours before using.) If your dough is at room temperature, you can use your fingers to gently stretch the dough out. Once it’s about 16cm, place the disc over the tops of your hands (not palm side) and use them to stretch it further, up to about 25cm. You can start pressing out the other discs, then wait to do the final bit when you’re ready to cook. Once you’ve mastered stretching the dough out, you can experiment with other shapes: rectangles, rounds or squares all look authentic.

STEP 6
To cook the pizza: An outdoor gas barbecue is best for controlling the temperature, but charcoal will give your pizza a more authentic, smoky flavour. For gas, turn the flames down to medium-low so that the bottom of the pizza doesn't burn. When cooking on a charcoal barbecue, let the coals turn grey before you pop on the pizza.

STEP 7
Place the pizza on a floured baking sheet (with no edge) or a pizza peel – this is a flat pizza paddle with a long handle, which makes it easier to get the dough on and off the grill. The flour will provide the 'wheels' for it to slide onto the grill – don’t use oil as it sticks more and won’t transfer as well.

STEP 8
Make sure the grill is hot and the flames have died back if cooking on charcoal. Slide the dough onto the grill, close the lid (if your barbecue has one) and give it three to four minutes. The dough will puff up; it's ready when the bottom has light brown stripes. Use tongs to pull the dough off and turn it upside down.

STEP 9
Assemble the pizza of your choice – see 'Goes well with', right, for topping suggestions. Remember that less is more, as the dough will stay crisper and the toppings will cook better.

STEP 10
Place the pizza back on the grill, uncooked-side down, and shut the lid. Give it another three to four minutes, then remove when the cheese is melted and the toppings are hot.

I've been playing War Thunder through the Browser Launcher rather than Steam because I originally had an Xbox account with a lot of progress, and I didn't want to start all over again. In total, I've got around 2,000 hours of playtime.

Now, I'd like to get to the main point of this post.

Germany is, in my opinion, one of the most neglected and frustrating nations to play in War Thunder. I mean, how does it make any sense that the German Leopard 2A8 is supposedly an inferior version of the Norwegian one that's being added to the game?

It genuinely frustrates me that Gaijin seems so reluctant to give Germany the equipment it deserves. And this isn't an isolated incident.

Take the Leopard 2A7V, for example. The Bundeswehr itself published data regarding the gun depression and elevation, yet apparently that wasn't considered sufficient evidence to justify a buff. Meanwhile, the Leopard 2A8 was nerfed based on what appears to be nothing more than a picture from a news article that wasn't even published by an official Bundeswehr source.

How is that supposed to make sense? Why are the standards of evidence seemingly so inconsistent when it comes to German vehicles?

Then there's the situation in Ukraine. Germany supplied Ukraine with older Leopard 2A4 tanks, some of which were already approaching the end of their service life. Yet these vehicles have demonstrated that they are still capable of taking on modern Russian equipment, including the T-90M, one of Russia's most advanced main battle tanks.

I'm not saying that real-life performance should automatically determine how a vehicle performs in War Thunder. However, it does make you wonder why certain vehicles are treated so differently when it comes to their in-game capabilities.

I've spent around 2,000 hours playing this game, and it genuinely hurts to see Germany being treated this way. As a German main, it's incredibly frustrating to constantly receive equipment that other nations have had access to for several updates already, while Germany seems to be left behind.

Maybe Gaijin is simply afraid of making Germany too powerful. But if that's the case, I think they should reconsider how they balance the nation.

My advice to anyone who wants to enjoy War Thunder at top tier is simple: DON'T PLAY GERMANY.

Play Sweden instead. At this point, Sweden feels more like what Germany's top-tier lineup should have been all along.

I genuinely hope Gaijin starts paying more attention to Germany and gives the nation the treatment it deserves.

I waited three years for a German top-tier main battle tank. What arrived is a “new” vehicle that simultaneously loses to older, lighter, and even not-yet-fully-in-service opponents in its stat card, its equipment list, and its protection logic. In just a few days on the dev server, the Leopard 2A8 turned itself into a textbook example of War Thunder’s double standards.

Start with gun depression. The Leopard 2A8’s depression was cut from the Leopard 2 family’s mechanical limit of −9° to −7.4°, based on a KNDS commercial brochure. The problem is not whether −7.4° exists in that brochure. The problem is that other data from the same brochure suddenly stopped counting. The community kept asking: if −7.4° from a brochure is enough to justify a nerf, why are the weight figures and protection claims in the same document dismissed as “marketing material”? One player put it perfectly: “They even treat data from the same manual differently, taking only the numbers that weaken the Leopard 2A8.” The more reasonable explanation for −7.4° is a software fire-control safety limit after installing Trophy APS radar and external modules, not a mechanical hard stop. The game turned it into a permanent lock and pushed a 2020s tank’s hull-down capability below that of early Leopard 2s.

Then there is equipment. Germany is the manufacturer and primary operator of the Leopard 2A8, yet the German 2A8 in-game has the worst configuration of them all. The Norwegian 2A8NO in the Swedish tree gets a laser warning system and a top-mounted machine gun; the German 2A8 gets neither. Germany receives an early trial/training configuration, Norway receives a full service configuration, and the depression nerf is justified using brochure data from a trial vehicle — the benefits are split both ways, while all the drawbacks go to German players. At 13.3, a laser warning receiver is not a “nice extra”; it is basic survival information against laser-guided weapons. Without it, you do not know you have been lased until the missile is about to hit. The missing top-mounted machine gun is just as absurd: the older 2A7V has two machine guns in-game, while the newer 2A8 is left with only a coaxial MG.

Protection is the most glaring part of the whole controversy. The Leopard 2A8’s upper glacis KE protection in-game is roughly 650 mm, while the Strv 122 series that entered service in the early 2000s has 750 mm. The same line keeps appearing on the forums, and it has become both a meme and an accusation: “The 2020s 2A7 and 2A8 actually have worse protection than a 1990s 2A5 prototype.” The Bundeswehr’s own page explicitly states that the 2A8’s physical armor was “strengthened” compared with previous models; KNDS materials also indicate that its armor package includes heavy tungsten alloy, with KE protection expected to improve by 50–100 mm. Yet armor reports submitted again and again are met with “insufficient evidence” or simply closed. Meanwhile, the depression nerf report went through at lightning speed. Players summed it up precisely: to get a buff, “you need 182 original documents signed by world leaders”; to get a nerf, one brochure is enough.

There is also inherited laziness at the mechanical level. The 81° forced ricochet fails on the upper glacis, and the gun mantlet weakness was carried over from the 2A7V to the 2A8 unchanged. These are not “teething problems” for a new vehicle; they are known bugs from older vehicles packaged and ported over. The dev team explains the rushed release with “Work in Progress,” but the 2A7V’s armor issue was “accepted” three years ago and still has no substantive fix. WIP cannot be an excuse for copying known defects onto a new vehicle.

What turns this review from “stat dissatisfaction” into a trust issue is the asymmetrical standard running through everything. When a brochure hurts Germany, it is “sacred text”; when it helps Germany, it is a “marketing lie.” Sweden gets the more complete 2A8; Germany gets the trial configuration. Nerfs are executed immediately; buffs are shelved indefinitely. This is not a discussion about whether one tank is “strong enough.” It is about a German tank being systematically turned into the worst version among its manufacturing country’s own tree. If “historical accuracy” is a switch that can be selectively flipped depending on the nation and the direction of the change, then it is no longer a standard — only an excuse.

The Leopard 2A8 is allowed to have weaknesses. The problem is that its current weaknesses come neither from the physical limits of the real vehicle nor from a balancing logic applied equally to all nations, but from a set of realism rules that only work in one direction. Until that is addressed, putting this vehicle into the game under the title “Europe’s most advanced tank” is itself an irony.

I really enjoy War Thunder. I think it's one of the very few games that can scratch that itch of vehicular combat. Whilst not always realistic, it's definitely one that's up there. I suck (biggest skill issues), but it is a lot of fun.

That being said, I cannot recommend War Thunder, or review it positively, in its current state. The game has some gripes that, I think, need addressing to make it a great game.

[h2]The Good Bits[/h2]

[b]Looks[/b] - War Thunder is a great looking game. Regardless of settings, it looks fantastic. I like to play on "Movie" settings and it looks incredible. The vehicles are fantastically modeled (physically/externally) and the attention to detail on the exterior shows. The terrain also looks fantastic, and the weather effects are impressive.

[b]Gameplay[/b] - The core gameplay loop is fun, if a little stale with the limited game/match modes available. Driving around, firing a shell at another tank and having a funky X-Ray of what you did to the tank is oddly satisfying. I also enjoy the grind, to a degree. It's rewarding to unlock a new vehicle, especially if it's one you really want.

[b]The Early Game[/b] - Peak War Thunder. Smooth progression, even fights. This is where it really shines before the top tier pain.

[b]Variety[/b] - There is a plethora of vehicles and nations to play in War Thunder, from WWII to the modern age, there's something in there for everyone. And (for the most part) vehicles behave how you'd expect. War Thunder likes to say it's "realistic" and I agree, to a point. There are certainly aspects that are not, but relatively? It's not the most heinous thing out there claiming realism.

[h2]The Not So Good Bits[/h2]

[b]The Grind[/b] - I know right? I said I enjoy the grind. And I do. But it's deliberately made to be a [i]snail's pace[/i] (see what I did there?). It is savage and, win or lose, you lose a portion of your Silver Lions and suffer a loss in earned Research Points for losing, even if you played well. That can sting. In addition, the disparity between Premium and Standard accounts is massive. It's deliberately frustrating to try and force you to pull your wallet out to stop seeing the "Here's what you could have got, if you weren't so tight with your money. Loser."

[b]Premium/Event Vehicles[/b] - This is a big one for me, and I see it in forums a lot. Not because they can be released over/under tuned (although the majority seem to perform well above what they should), but the fact that some of them cost the same as a AAA game at full price. For a single vehicle. I admit, I have purchased a couple, and one for purely nostalgic reasons of playing the [i]Comanche[/i] helicopter games when I was younger, but that stung the wallet a little bit. Several premium and event vehicles have also, as soon as the events they were released in end, been nerfed into the ground, or (as was the case with the Scimitar Mk2) received better rounds/mods once the event to unlock it was over and now the vehicle is behind a paywall. Either make them unlockable, but you really have to grind it, or don't update/upgrade them when they can no longer be ground for and require a AU$90+ purchase.

[b]CAS/Helicopters[/b] - This is a nightmare as soon as fire and forget or remote guided weapons become a thing. Most of them have absolutely bonkers range, and pilots can yeet them from relative safety into your spawn. So just stay still and keep your spawn protection, right? Wrong. They're so far away, it takes long enough in some cases that your spawn protection just runs out, or you don't know one is coming so you move. Helicopters at high tier are particularly egregious for this. The helicopter loop is: Take off. Fire a bum-fucking amount of guided missiles downrange whilst barely visible. Land. Rearm. Repeat. CAS (Close Air Support) isn't much better, especially with the "crash land" strat that seems very popular to rearm faster.

[b]Selective Realism[/b] - A lot of people scream "Russian Bias!" and start pointing out specific things which, granted, are a little bit off. But it feels more like a "rock, paper, scissors" balancing act. You have ERA and an autoloader? Awesome. Your reverse speed is terrible. You have decent thermals, are fast, and a 20x zoom? Fantastic. Here's a 20mm round that will punch through your thickest armour and melt your crew. Where it gets frustrating is when the detail of available information gets applied. Certain vehicles are given the absolute best theoretical performances based on commercial brochures. Others get not a lot or information that is completely wrong (but please don't leak secret material, that's silly). I understand it's more likely to be a balancing thing to keep the game fun for everyone, but that means you can't claim to be "realistic" if certain vehicles get stat card levels of detail and others suffer horribly.

[b]Naval Mode[/b] - I played some Naval RB many moons ago. It's fun, but there isn't a lot of love or reasons for people to switch to it. In its current state it's just grim. There's no enticement, no grand scale, nothing that really draws people in.

[h2]The Really Not Good Bits[/h2]

[b]Map Size[/b] - Oh. Boy. Where do I begin? The maps are [b][i]TINY[/i][/b] for anything beyond early Cold War vehicles. The four "large" maps are large by the grace of having bits of terrain blocking you from just smashing each other from the other end of the map, and even then when you're in vehicles designed to engage targets at 3-4km away, having a map that has a maximum of 2km is a bit rich. It makes most engagements feel like a knife fight, and directly contradicts the doctrines of certain nations. Now, I'm not saying the game needs to be a boring long range duel of boringness, but opportunities to flank properly, plan out attacks and then engage targets at a variety of ranges, not just between 500m-1km would only be a benefit. In addition to that, bigger maps mean further aerial spawns, making pilots actually have to close in and engage targets with some form of risk, not just hide in or near the spawn and fire a volley, then duck back into cover chuckling because they can't be hit whilst blowing up 5 different players. As they are though, as soon as you leave WW2 and start getting stabilisers/autoloaders/thermals/ATGMs, the maps are far too small for the engagement ranges of both ground and aerial vehicles.

[b]The Economics of Playing[/b] - This is, in my opinion, the worst part about War Thunder as it stands. When you drop into a match you are in a team. Your team is then further broken down into squads. These elements give a [b][i]massive[/i][/b] indication that it is a [b]team[/b] game and that your actions should be for the benefit of your team. The economy throws that completely out the window. You want maximum Silver Lions and Research points? You need to kill the fuck out of people, whilst not dying. You die? You lose Silver Lions to repairing and rearming your vehicle. The only aspect of "Teamwork" in War Thunder is a little in game boost for being within a certain distance of your squadmates. It rewards working as a team in the loosest sense. Why is this an issue? Combined with tiny map designs and wonky sightlines, you have players who actively ignore capturing objectives to push obscure angles so they spawn snipe you into oblivion to maximise their winnings. I am not "anti" spawn killing. If you, as a team, have not secured objectives and refuse to leave your spawn, expect to have the other team roll in to say hi. But to be able to ignore objectives and get somewhere that enables spawn sniping with minimal repercussions is infuriating. And this playstyle is only getting worse and more common.

As mentioned, I enjoy War Thunder. I want it to be a great game and I want others to enjoy it. But I cannot recommend people start playing the way it is right now.

I like War Thunder. I like its concept, gameplay, atmosphere, and the thrill of immersing myself in the world of military vehicles. It has a lot of potential, but after 1,000+ hours, its major issues keep me from recommending it.

The grind is horrible. Researching an entire nation's tech tree takes far too long, especially for players who don't spend money. The grind becomes repetitive and turns the game into a chore. The pay-to-progress model needs to end, and the grind needs to be significantly reduced. A player-friendly game naturally makes people more willing to spend money on it.

Matchmaking is inconsistent and often feels unbalanced, with huge skill gaps between players on opposing teams. Long-standing bugs and balance issues remain unresolved, and some premium vehicles feel far more forgiving or effective than their standard versions.

Despite everything, War Thunder is still an incredible and fun game. The constant addition of new content and events shows just how much potential it has. I just wish Gaijin would focus more on making the game enjoyable and less on making it feel like work.

After 2,000 hours in War Thunder, I had finally reached top tier in the two nations I wanted to play. Three years of grinding, hundreds of hours spent unlocking vehicles, farming research points and accumulating Silver Lions.

I think this game is really what you make of it- you shouldnt race to the newest shiniest tanks and planes in the same way you shouldn't drive a car or ride a bike before you learn how to walk. The most important thing i've learned is that every battle rating has a place- lower battle ratings are silly and fun and lighthearted, and higher battle ratings (often called the sweaty areas) are more focused on advanced tactics and coordination with teammates. Similarly, arcade and realistic are both fantastic modes in their own rights, and I believe that everyone should try every facet of this game at their own pace.

The most important advice i have for this game is to not rush your progression, and to be focused more on improving rather than winning. You can do everything right in your situation and still lose- such is the reality of playing pvp with other living humans. If you moderate yourself this game can and will be lots and lots of fun.

Also: dont buy a premium rank IX plane until you know how missiles work, it wont end well for you, you'll be sad and have a 30 dollar plane that you dont know how to use. you should buy your premiums at levels of the game that you already know how to play, which will yet again be much more fun for you!

It loves your wallet, and it only texts when there’s a new major update, full of shiny new vehicles I’ll unlock in roughly three years, unless I hand over my entire salary, which, let’s be honest, I’ve considered. Every time I come back, it swears it has changed. “We’ve decompressed the BRs.” “We’ve fixed the economy.” “We hear you.” It has never once heard me. It heard the review bombing in 2023, panicked like a man caught on his phone at 3am, gave back the repair costs, and two months later was already doing the same thing.

For years I played the West, and for years I watched Soviet tanks do things that would make a physicist file for early retirement. I watched an IS-2 HE round hit the side of a hill and somehow give my entire crew emotional damage. I watched Soviet ammo racks take a direct APFSDS hit and do nothing, like a man who took a hammer to the face and just said “nyet.” Every time I typed “Russian bias” in chat, a forum guy materialized out of thin air within 0.3 seconds, as if summoned, to explain with 47 paragraphs and a cropped spreadsheet that I’m just bad.

So I did the only reasonable thing. I switched to Russia.

I now own 141 Soviet vehicles. One hundred and forty-one. More than the USA, Germany and Britain combined, almost. If Russian bias were real, I should be a god. My Realistic Battles win rate is 53%. Fifty-three. I have bought the entire Soviet arsenal and the bias has given me a 3% edge over a coin flip.

The bias is real. I’ve just come to understand it moves to whatever nation I stopped playing. The day I unlocked the T-80BVM, it turned out to be made of wet cardboard and good intentions. The moment I left the US tree, the F-14 started printing kills in someone else’s hands. The game has an anti-bias system, and that system is me.

Some numbers from my medical file:

13,551 deaths. I have died more times than most medieval villages had people.
Over 109 million Silver Lions earned, every single one of which went straight back to the Snail in repair costs, like paying child support to a mollusc.
4,907 air kills in Air RB, and I still can’t land.
12,324 ground targets destroyed in RB, and somehow Gleb is still alive.
6 wins in Simulator. Six. I tried Sim exactly once like a guy trying a sex thing his ex suggested, and we never spoke of it again.
113 naval kills, because once in a while I go to the navy the way people go to their hometown bar to feel something.
84 Swedish vehicles, because when the Russians hurt me I need somewhere to cry and the Strv people never ask questions.
“Fire Arrows: destroy 1000 player vehicles with guided missiles.” Yes. I am that guy now. I became what I hated.

Every match is the same. You spawn. You feel strong. You push. You think “Holy shit, maybe this is my game.” Then a 2S38 piloted by Gleb (Gleb has 41,000 battles, a 9% win rate, and still somehow kills you every single time) pops up behind a pixel-thin fence and turns your crew into a historical footnote. Your team’s response: five players J-out instantly, two bots drive into the ocean, and one guy named xX_SturerEmil_Xx types “skill issue” while sitting in spawn in a Ho-Ri.

And yet I keep coming back.

Because somewhere, under the economy designed by a slot machine that went to business school, under the matchmaker that thinks 9.7 vs 10.7 is “balanced,” under eleven years of patches that fix one bug and add four, there is the greatest military vehicle game ever made. Every once in a while you get that one match. Three kills off a single flank, your shells finally obeying physics, the enemy team panicking in chat. You feel like a god. You feel like Kurt Knispel. You start thinking maybe the Snail loves you after all.

Then you check your rewards: -2,400 SL.

The players of this game have literally leaked classified military documents onto a public forum just to win an argument about tank armor. Multiple times. That’s the mental state this game puts you in. I haven’t leaked anything yet, but I’d be lying if I said I haven’t looked at my uncle’s old army binder and thought about it.

My girlfriend asked me why I keep playing a game I clearly hate. I told her it’s complicated. She said that’s what she said about her ex. We both went quiet.

11/10. The only relationship I’ve had that lasted eleven years. It has never once said sorry. See you next November. Feed the Snail.

– Mr_Suits, 47 days of my life I will never get back (Fuck you Gleb)

The mistel knows where it is at all times. It knows this because it knows where it isn't. By subtracting where it is from where it isn't, or where it isn't from where it is (whichever is greater), it obtains a difference, or deviation. The guidance subsystem uses deviations to generate corrective commands to drive the mistel from a position where it is to a position where it isn't, and arriving at a position where it wasn't, it now is. Consequently, the position where it is, is now the position that it wasn't, and it follows that the position that it was, is now the position that it isn't.

In the event that the position that it is in is not the position that it wasn't, the system has acquired a variation, the variation being the difference between where the mistel is, and where it wasn't. If variation is considered to be a significant factor, it too may be corrected by the GEA. However, the mistel must also know where it was.

The mistel guidance computer scenario works as follows. Because a variation has modified some of the information the mistel has obtained, it is not sure just where it is. However, it is sure where it isn't, within reason, and it knows where it was. It now subtracts where it should be from where it wasn't, or vice-versa, and by differentiating this from the algebraic sum of where it shouldn't be, and where it was, it is able to obtain the deviation and its variation, which is called error.

The game is well-made, but in the long term, it’s designed to foster frustration rather than enjoyment.

I recommend titles that aren't free-to-play but offer a far more satisfying experience—specifically the new *HEAT* (or similar titles), as well as the well-established *DCS World* and the *IL-2 Sturmovik* series. These are similar to *War Thunder* but lack the frustration caused by ruthless, rigged battle ratings.

# To all War Thunder players: Reject double standards and division. Let’s unite again this Christmas

If you are a military vehicle enthusiast who values historical authenticity in War Thunder, whether you are a veteran tanker or a new player, please take a moment to read this.

Recent discussions on the Xiaoheihe community are not about the balance of a single vehicle. Instead, they reveal Gaijin’s increasingly obvious **dual standards for stat implementation**. Multiple cutting-edge vehicles across different tech trees have been adjusted against publicly available technical documentation. The upcoming F-15EX for US and Israeli tech trees has been gimped in the test server. The ZBD04A shares the same weapon station concept as the BMD-4, yet only the ZBD04A’s autoloader speed has been nerfed. All NATO MBTs armed with the L55A1 gun have had their gun depression capped to levels similar to the T-90M, ignoring official design specifications. These issues affect vehicles from Chinese, US, Russian and NATO tech trees alike. This is never a complaint from players of just one nation tree.

What makes things worse is how the developers respond. When players submit manuals, official reports and credible technical sources, Gaijin selectively picks evidence without establishing a transparent, consistent standard for vehicle modelling. Instead of addressing the evidence, the studio allows toxic narratives to spread, deliberately stoking factional conflict. Criticism of inconsistent historical modelling is twisted into “one nation tree asking for buffs”, pitting player groups against each other to distract from arbitrary, evidence-light changes to real-world vehicle performance.

War Thunder drew us in with its promise of hardcore simulation and historical accuracy. If vehicle parameters can be altered arbitrarily and rules shift between updates, that “realistic simulation” claim becomes nothing more than marketing copy. The vehicles getting adjusted now are the F-15EX, ZBD04A and L55A1-equipped NATO tanks. Tomorrow, the vehicle you main could be modified without solid supporting documentation. This harms every player who trusts the game’s premise and invests their time and money here.

Veterans will remember the May Strike of 2023. Back then, Gaijin pushed through hasty economy changes while ignoring community feedback. Players worldwide set aside nation-tree rivalries and staged a coordinated boycott, forcing Gaijin to roll back the controversial changes. That action proved one thing: players are not disposable metrics. When we stand united, our voices cannot be ignored.

That same arrogance and unilateral decision-making is returning. Gaijin appears to rely on dividing the community to break our consensus, trapping us in endless infighting so they can avoid questions about consistent historical modelling standards. To push back, we need to recreate that unity and organise a coordinated action: **a game and spending boycott this Christmas**.

This movement does not belong to any single tech tree. It does not matter if you play Chinese, Russian, American, German vehicles, or whether you are new or experienced. You do not need to argue or flame online. There are only two simple asks: do not log into the game over the Christmas period, and make no purchases — no Golden Eagles, no bundles, no store transactions of any kind. Our demands are clear and reasonable: adopt an open, stable and unified set of historical modelling rules; properly review credible technical sources submitted by the community; end double-standard stat changes; stop intentionally stirring conflict between player groups; uphold the core promise of historical simulation and respect every player.

A note for new players: do not fall for divisive talking points. Do not accept the idea that nerfs are justified just because other vehicles are strong. Balance should be built on documented real-world performance, not selective nerfing to force artificial parity. If this double-standard practice continues unchecked, any vehicle you enjoy may have its value undermined by arbitrary developer decisions in the future.

We love the aircraft, tanks and ships of War Thunder, and we are willing to support a well-made military game. But our passion should not excuse unfair treatment. The May Strike showed what united players can achieve, and now it is our turn. Set aside faction bias, stop turning on each other, and combine our scattered frustrations into one clear message.

This Christmas boycott is not meant to destroy the game. It is an effort to save the core promise it was built upon. Please share this with every tanker you know and stand with us. Tell Gaijin: we accept well-reasoned, evidence-based balance adjustments, but we will not accept double standards, disregard for historical data, or deliberate community division.

If the developers continue to ignore the community’s legitimate concerns, we will hold our ground. All we want is a War Thunder with consistent standards, respect for real-world vehicle data, and respect for its playerbase.

The most disappointing thing about War Thunder isn't even the grind or the pay-to-win aspects—it’s the long-standing double standard the developers apply to the Soviet tree versus non-Soviet trees. It’s becoming hard to believe this is still a fair, multinational vehicle combat game.

The disparity in update speed is obvious. The Soviet tree keeps getting stacked with overpowered additions like 4.5-gen fighters, modern air defense, and tank support vehicles. Units like the BMPT, BMPT-72, Pantsir-S1, and Pantsir-SM SV are glaringly imbalanced; even after BR (Battle Rating) adjustments, the match experience remains terrible. Meanwhile, non-Soviet vehicles are constantly getting nerfed—armor, radar, missiles, and traverse speeds are all fair game. We’re seeing absurd mechanics like "floating breech blocks," "leaky armor," and composite armor magically turning into spaced armor.

Even worse is the double standard in the Issue Section and data sourcing. Soviet data is often accepted loosely, while valid feedback for non-Soviet vehicles is frequently dismissed or closed. When players provide third-party data, simulations, or gameplay footage, the devs reject it for "not meeting standards," yet their own sources remain opaque. From ammo models and armor penetration to reload times, AD, and CAS efficiency, the Soviet tree seems to enjoy hidden advantages, while everyone else gets repeatedly "filed down" by the nerf bat.

If the developers continue using "selective realism" to favor the Soviet Union without transparent data sources, unified balancing standards, and fair Issue handling, the game will only continue to drive away non-Soviet players.

Gaijin's Double Standards and Selective Realism: Three Years of Waiting, Only to Be Betrayed

First of all, I want to make one thing clear: the core gameplay and combat mechanics of this game are absolutely worth trying. However, the sheer level of bias, prejudice, and discriminatory treatment demonstrated by the developers at Gaijin is simply unacceptable.

On December 14, 2023, the Air Superiority update was released, introducing the Leopard 2A7V as Germany's top-tier main battle tank. At the time, we believed this was merely the beginning of Germany's modern top-tier lineup.

On October 30, 2026, the development blog for the Shadow of the Eagles update was finally published. The Leopard 2A8 was finally coming to the game. From the Leopard 2A7V to the Leopard 2A8, we had waited nearly THREE YEARS.

And what exactly did we get after all that waiting?

The 81-degree ricochet mechanic? Apparently, it no longer applies to the Leopard 2A8

According to the game's own mechanics, APFSDS rounds are supposed to automatically ricochet at impact angles of 81 degrees or greater. Yet, when it comes to the Leopard 2A8, this rule suddenly stops applying. The projectile simply penetrates the upper frontal plate as if the ricochet mechanic did not even exist.

A tank from the 2020s, with armor protection from the 1990s

The Leopard 2A8's upper frontal armor is modeled at just 650 mm KE protection in-game, while the Strv 122 series, which entered service in the early 2000s, enjoys 750 mm KE protection.

As one forum post put it: "The 2020s tanks like the 2A7 and 2A8 literally have worse protection than a 1990s 2A5 prototype."

Armor improvement reports have been submitted time and time again, only to be rejected repeatedly under the same excuse: "Insufficient evidence."

This is NOT balance. This is SELECTIVE REALISM.

Whenever accurate modeling would benefit German vehicles, Gaijin hides behind the convenient excuse of "insufficient evidence." But whenever there is an opportunity to nerf them, suddenly the evidence is good enough, the mechanics are flexible enough, and the changes go through at lightning speed.

Let's look at this absolute farce.

We waited THREE YEARS for this tank, yet before it has even reached the live server:

Its advanced configuration is already being handed to other nations.
The Leopard 2A8 with a 12.7-caliber weapon station wasn't given to Germany but went to Sweden instead.
Its gun depression and elevation angles are nerfed at lightning speed.
An issue report based on a document that has not even been conclusively verified as being substantially identical to the Leopard 2A7NOR promotional brochure was apparently enough to get the change approved almost immediately.
Its combat weight is increased almost overnight.
A single photograph from a European defense exhibition was apparently sufficient evidence to push through an issue report increasing its combat weight.
But what about its maximum speed? The very same photograph contains information indicating a maximum speed of up to 65 km/h. Yet when players submit this information to support the Leopard 2A8's mobility, suddenly it becomes "insufficient evidence."

Do you see the pattern here?

One photograph is enough to justify a nerf, but somehow not enough to support a performance characteristic. One set of claims is accepted immediately, while another is dismissed without proper consideration.

How convenient.

This is not historical accuracy. This is not game balance. This is a blatant double standard.

We are not demanding that German vehicles must always be superior to everyone else's. We are not asking for preferential treatment, nor are we asking Gaijin to make Germany the strongest nation in the game.

ALL WE WANT IS FAIRNESS.

If Gaijin insists on using real-world documentation and historical accuracy as the foundation for vehicle performance, then apply those standards consistently to EVERY nation, not just when it suits your agenda.

Three years of waiting should not end in disappointment, double standards, and selective nerfs.

Title: Burning your cash in a fire is more rewarding than spending a dime on this game — The ultimate digital gulag.（文末有中文版）

If you haven't started playing yet, congratulations, RUN! Do not touch this industrial trash wrapped in a "hardcore realistic" facade. If you are currently playing, take my advice: uninstall immediately, save yourself, and go do literally anything else. Even sleeping is a better use of your time than being a digital slave in this cyber-prison.

This game is a textbook example of how NOT to run a live-service game. Its continued existence is an insult to the modern gaming industry.

1. Disgustingly Fake "Realism" & "Historical Accuracy"
The devs brag about "historical research" and "hardcore physics," but I've tested it, and the illusion shatters instantly. The so-called ballistic physics is just a pre-calculated horizontal firing table! Laser range a target at 1000m, and your point of impact is exactly the same whether you are shooting flat or at a -5 degree depression. The theoretical 1-meter deviation doesn't exist because the game simply doesn't calculate vertical angle corrections. It's just a table-lookup simulator. The visual trajectory of the shell doesn't even tilt; Battlefield 5 had better real-time ballistic logic a decade ago.
The "research" is blatantly double-standardized: when players submit real military data to buff Western vehicles, Gaijin rejects it with a simple "source is not authoritative." Meanwhile, Soviet vehicles get magic, made-up stats based on "reasonable speculation." Players are now trolling the Issue Tracker with masterpieces like: "There is no document proving the Leopard 2A8 can fire DM53, so it should only be able to fire potatoes," and "Gorbachev never provided official documents with a cover page proving the dissolution of the USSR, so the Soviet Union cannot dissolve." Gaijin's logic: "Unless you leak classified documents, your tank gets no armor."

2. Pay-to-Suffer, Grinding is a Prison Sentence
War Thunder's monetization is a terrifying mix of a Skinner box and psychological manipulation. In other games, leveling up makes you stronger; in WT, "grinding" is just buying an entry ticket to the next tier of suffering. Want to play top-tier MBTs? Spend hundreds of hours in WWII vehicles first. Bought a premium pack? Congratulations, you just bought a "less suffering" accelerator. You still have to endure the stock grind and research parts. You aren't buying fun; you're buying a heavier digital shift-schedule and a massive dose of anxiety.

3. Disastrous Servers & "Not a bug"
Veterans know this all too well: the netcode and physics synchronization are atrocious. "Trade kills" (both players firing and dying simultaneously) are almost non-existent here because WT uses serial event processing. Whoever the server registers as dying first wins; the other shell gets eaten or vanishes. Vehicles teleport, shots get swallowed. Even the 3-axis stabilizer on the Turm III is broken—the server can't even synchronize the turret's spatial posture, so you aim at the head, but the shell flies into the Nth dimension. The most hilarious part? You submit a bug report, and you get the cold, automated response: "Not a bug."
I heard they are using this outdated Dagor engine—which can't even synchronize 30 vehicles properly—to build a 128-player infantry mode? That's not innovation; that's digging their own grave while Battlefield and Delta Force sit right at the front door.

4. A Toxic Community & Arrogant Devs
The ecosystem is a literal snake pit. You have faction fanatics, armchair historians, and doxxers everywhere. The devs use double standards to silence players on the Issue Tracker while their business model relies entirely on copy-pasting. It's 2026, and they refuse to make new models. Everything is just a new turret or a reskin slapped onto an old chassis, sold as a new premium. Why? Because they can't fix the bugs that come with new models, and reskins print money.

Conclusion:
This game is like an expensive pre-packaged meal falsely advertised as "freshly cooked." You take a bite, realize it's spoiled, and customer service tells you, "This aligns with our balance settings."
Let me give you a piece of advice: Burning your money in a fire is a physical loss, but at least you hear the crackle. Giving it to Gaijin is a triple-reaping of your money, time, and mental health. It won't just refuse to make you happy; it will strap you to a treadmill and drain you dry. Run away. As far as you can.


如果你还没入坑，恭喜你，快跑！千万别碰这坨披着“硬核拟真”外衣的工业垃圾；如果你正在玩，听我一句劝，立刻点击卸载，放过自己，去干点啥都好，哪怕是去睡觉，也比在这个赛博牢房里当黑奴强。

这游戏现在完全就是个长线运营的反面教材，能活到现在简直是对现代游戏工业的侮辱。

1. 虚假到令人作呕的“拟真”与“考据”
制作组天天吹自己“历史考据”、“硬核物理”，我实测下来，这游戏底裤早就漏了。所谓的弹道物理，说白了就是套了一个水平射表！ 你拿激光测距仪测个1000米，水平射击和负5度俯角射击的弹着点一模一样，理论上该差出的一米根本不存在，因为它底层压根没算俯仰角修正。这就是个查表模拟器，炮弹连视觉上的弧线姿态都不调，战地5十年前的实时计算逻辑都按着它的头打。
所谓的考据更是双标到了极点：玩家拿真实军事资料去加强西方载具，官方一句“资料不权威”直接驳回；苏系载具随随便便“合理推测”魔法起飞。玩家甚至在Issue区整出了“没数据不能证明豹2能发炮弹，只能发射土豆”、“戈尔巴乔夫没提供解体苏联的官方数据，所以苏联不能解体”的神仙段子。官方这波叫“只要你拿不出涉密的绝密文件，我就当你的坦克没有装甲”。

2. 付费买罪受，开线如坐牢
战雷的付费逻辑简直是斯金纳箱和心理学的究极缝合。别的游戏升级是变强，这游戏的“开线”就是解锁下一个受虐分房的入场券。你想玩顶级坦克？先肝几百个小时二战车。你充钱买礼包？恭喜你，只是买了个“少肝一点”的加速器，白板期照样坐牢，配件照样要肝。花钱买不到快乐，只能买到一套更沉重的电子班表和更浓烈的焦虑。

3. 灾难级的服务器与“Not a bug”
作为老玩家，大家应该都有体会，这游戏的网络同步和物理结算烂得发指。战地五里的“同时开枪同时暴毙”在这里几乎绝迹，因为战雷的服务器是串行事件结算，谁先死服务器说了算，吞子弹、吞炮弹、载具瞬移是常态。三稳豹这种带第三轴稳定的车，服务器连姿态都同步不明白，你瞄着头，炮弹飞去了异次元。最滑稽的是，你提交Bug报告，得到的永远是那冰冷的三个字：“Not a bug”。听说他们还要拿这个连几十人载具同步都做不好的Dagor老引擎，去硬做128人大战场的步兵模式？这不是创新，这是自掘坟墓。

4. 养蛊的社区与傲慢的官方
游戏生态乌烟瘴气，系别魔怔人、资料考据狂、开盒挂人的神仙满天飞，官方在Issue区双标堵嘴，在商业上疯狂换皮。2026年了，连个新模型都舍不得做，全是在原来的底盘上换个头、换个皮就拿出来当新礼包卖。因为新模型有Bug他们修不明白，更因为换皮来钱快。

总结：
这游戏就像一盘包装精美、打着“现炒”招牌的预制菜。吃了一口发现是馊的，找客服退货，客服说“这符合我们的平衡性设定”。奉劝各位：把钱撕了，那是物理消耗，你还能听个响；把钱充给Gaijin，那是精神、金钱、时间的三重收割，它不仅不让你爽，还要把你挂在战雷的跑步机上榨干。 赶紧跑，越远越好。

First and foremost I'm a life long and very absorbed student of weapons and war - both by education and passion. For absolute breadth there is no game like it and it's absorbed me for countless hours. It's an addictive hobby, but no more so than most others military history nuts come into. The vehicles are amazing and it's a gorgeous game. For sheer cinematic value on average hardware nothing can beat it.

That said War Thunder is far from perfect - the attention to crafting the vehicles and weapons is immersive. The battlefields might as well come from Star Fox or Battletech and the community can be more than a little toxic as it includes a lot of youngsters with out any supervision. 

Arcade mode is just that, and can be a blast - air arcade has some of the most imaginative battlefields and landscapes out there but it's also nuts and you have to just laugh when you get taken out. Ground arcade is just a simplified mode of ground 'Real Battle' with easier aiming and quicker game play. For old eyes like mine it's a go to. If you're not someone who needs a million miles a minute and can cope with slower gameplay, Naval is awesome - and some of the extended conflict matches (bigger maps ~ 2hr games, but you can duck out whenever) are the best game modes War Thunder devs have ever made. Depending on the state of the game it's possible for opposing spawn points (your choice to spawn there) to occur with in less than 5km of one another. For battleships this can be a thrilling point blank 'broadside' fight that is as much a test of fortitude as it is skill.

Calling a mode 'Real Battle' is a bit of a farce as well - air consists of a map for ~ 60 aircraft, 30 per side, lined up at 70km distance for jets, and a line of 'ground targets' (very simple firebases)  There are 'supply bases' that can be bombed, but both Air Arcade and air 'RB' are filled with dogfight obsessed players, many of whom cannot comprehend why aircraft are included (now to include strategic bombers) that cannot dogfight. High tier featuring many of the slick, modern aircraft featured in promos is nothing but 'missile spam.' Missiles begin flying like a medieval arrow storm at anywhere from 50km on in, and though some claim one can be skilled enough to avoid or dodge (and there is much insulting and name-calling if one cannot dodge how other players think it should be done.) At lower levels air RB can be fun but it gets repetitive. You have no choice of what map you're flying in and you must have your battle lineup selected before time. There is less focus on fighters only but bombers almost always fly alone as there is no real insentive to do otherwise. 

As a matter of fact there is no real reason to play the game according to militarily accurate tactics at all. Other than a voice comms linked group of up to four can utterly dominate air or ground if the players are adequate and good at covering one another. People from some areas in the world are accused at length of cheating because their gaming culture is competitive and collaborative - there are highly developed 'clans' or squadrons that have extremely well thought out and coordinated 'battle nets' allowing even randomly spawned 'allies' to coordinate and work efficiently. For lone wolf players this can be frustrating to the point of infuriating and cause...again...toxic behavior and words of team chat.

Sim is the 'redheaded stepchild' of War Thunder and only Air Sim is worth mentioning. Play is strictly first person (from the cockpit) and the maps range from 64 x 64km to 128 x 128km. Battles are long, and there is bigger balance between strike & bomber players, and fighter pilots. Flight models can vary radically from RB and often planes that are dogs in that mode shine in Sim. 90% of content creators, especially those famous for rating vehicles, ignore this mode as the younger crowd looking for short games considers it 'boring.' For the most part the sim community is small enough that you get to know other regular players - the best part being you aren't restricted to a random map and bunch of players. If you don't like a particular map, choose another. If you find someone you detest in the lobby, go to another one. 

Gaijin, War Thunder's developer, has a very puzzling if straight forward business model...and they also listen way too much to 'the mob' on their forums. Besides their ability to take any new game mode and ruin it: a new 'nuclear escalation' mode is populated by respawning and rage-inducingly accurate SAM sites that are very difficult to eliminate thanks to a unrealistic mechanic where something like 90% of the weapons launched at them are successfully intercepted. One of the main marketing tools is 'snail rage' (Gaijin's logo is a snail) where players end up so angry at the game they either uninstall...or buy a premium vehicle. Which used to help for a while as they tend to be more powerful, but not so much anymore. 

Further, today's 'top gun' will eventually get either raised in battle rating so it's operating against far tougher (to the point of invulnerable) opponents or have weapons 'nerfed.' Always claiming some new data, game devs routinely take a weapons system that preforms reliably better than others and make it worse. Sometimes it's because the hue and cry of the mob of players (most who are young and often toxic) sometimes it's to sell a new premium vehicle.

Last, a word of advice: Free to Play is wholly misleading. Some players pride themselves on climbing the ranks with out paying a dime. They cry about 'pay to win' players but often this is because they don't have a job and don't comprehend that the game is developed as a business. For those playing in places with depressed economies, there is no scaling of costs however and for someone somewhere else in the world paying $80 for a premium vehicle is insane, where as here it's less than a day's wages.

This game's quite fun once you find a mode and BR where you enjoy the match dynamics and a vehicle that suits your style. If you happen to be a WW2 enjoyer you'll probably have a good time and have a wide selection of planes and the opportunity to play several countries without investing time or money heavily into the game, while if you're into jets or modern tanks you may have to suffer through the grind to even get a chance to see if you like the gameplay at all.

The potential issues come from the fact that you cannot really find that information out until you've grinded long dark hours in the abyss of the salt mines to unlock a vehicle you like, which if you don't already know what it'll be playstyle and balance wise, means grinding at least one full tree. It's also not enough that a vehicle is nice itself, but the matchmaking of the BR system heavily affects some of them negatively.
For example many vehicles that were the apex predators of their historical eras end up in a higher BR bracket often, facing technology from future conflicts with technology sometimes decades ahead of their own, and thus an otherwise very good vehicle ends up being absolutely miserable to play. The matchmaking algorithm is the game's biggest caveat and the major reason why test driving/flying a vehicle is insufficient information whether you'll actually enjoy it.

There's nothing really majorly wrong with the game itself in my opinion, the BR system is its biggest problem followed by a lack of gamemode variety, both of which have gotten recent dev attention (Nuclear Escalation is an excellent gamemode despite its imperfections, and dynamic BR is coming in the near future), so the only thing really left to critique is the amount of grind, which really encourages getting premium time or a premium vehicle. So let's talk about that a bit.

Premium packs in this game are absurdly expensive unless they're on sale, and by default I would highly recommend against all of them. The game regularly has sales though, and at least once a year you're guaranteed a 50% off sale on everything in the store including all the packs, vics and premium time. If you're okay investing the price of a regular game into this free game, then you can guarantee a much more tolerable progress curve for a single whole nation's progress tree, and a reliable source of in-game money to purchase tech tree vehicles and modifications as you unlock them.

If you're a WW2-era player you can probably make do without premium time, but otherwise I strongly suggest either: buying 90d/180d premium time at -50% off to bash out one of the nations' research tree, or getting a single higher-BR premium vehicle at -50% for the nation you wish to grind the research tree for. Do your research online before investing money into any of the premium vehicles as they offer various playstyles and some are notoriously more complicated or appeal to very different players or excel at very different game modes, and don't mix these easily. For example, buying any premium plane above 12.0 battle rating risks throwing you directly into modern radar-driven BVR missile combat with FOX3's and notching and multipathing and all that requires you to know a lot of information and positioning. The plane isn't "better" by having higher BR, because your opponents will be "better" too, including lots of experienced players.

(For context, for me, my sweet spot is BR 9.3-12.3 air realistic battles. It took me until my 12.0 Phantom in the British tree to figure that out, as literally everything before that was a slog for me regardless whether I was doing well or not. I purchased the Wyvern turboprop ground attacker craft and used it to progress through a big chunk of the British air tree and realized I really enjoy the era of jets where things start having missiles and afterburners, but before radars and radar missiles take over and make BVR the default form of combat. Now that I've branched out and obtained a couple more premiums to unlock trees from other nations, I've come to find a lot of enjoyment in flying MiG-21/J-7 variants, F-4 Phantom variants, F-5 variants, Harrier variants and the Yak-38 and the Draken.)

TL;DR: The community's kinda salty sometimes but the game's honestly fine, but do expect to spend 30-60 bucks on the game to fully enjoy it if you want to play battles with modern vehicles. It's not a simulator but it's much closer than any non-flightsim game, to make a racing game comparison this is like Gran Turismo instead of iRacing. Real knowledge will greatly help you (especially knowing on average what each vehicle excels at), but is not required to play. The mouse controls combined with the good damage models are honestly WT's best selling point, and make for a very addicting game where you click on stuff and occassionally get mad that the enemy had the better shell/missile. :^)

Don’t play this if you’re new. I’ve been playing this game since release. While I have in the past enjoyed it, that’s changed recently. It’s so horrible to play if you are thinking of starting now. Wait a few patches till they either decide to fix their multitudes of issues, or just don’t play.

If you don’t care about endgame content or story, which is about 90% of the game, then I guess you’ll probably be completely content with the current state of the game.

I love the turn based combat system, but the shill and powercreep has gotten out of hand and is borderline unplayable for free-to-play and new accounts. The bosses that were designed to shill the new elation path are still somewhat difficult to beat with an elation team. That shouldn’t happen. There is supposed to be a boss coming out that takes 75% reduced damage from non-elation units apparently. It’s annoying to deal with the constant shill. 

The hit point inflation is also getting out of hand, to the point that bosses are literally double their hit points from when they were last in endgame. They have also introduced a new mechanic called voracity that will basically revive the enemy if you don’t do enough damage. It was introduced because of a current quest plotline, but is not tied to the quest itself. If you are early game, you are still affected by it. This becomes an issue with newer players who may already be struggling with fights, and now those fights are much longer and more difficult. While I like the mechanic in concept, it shouldn’t be affecting the fights across the entire game in my opinion, and it has NO place in endgame content. 

This current Apocalyptic Shadow is possibly the worst one we’ve ever had and I think the voracity mechanic effecting apoc is a large factor in that (along with the horrid HP inflation.) Despite having the teams that the apoc nodes were specifically designed to shill, it was still a hassle to clear. I’m not asking for endgame to be easy— I’d prefer a challenge, but this is getting out of hand. They already have an entire endgame designed around the players who will spend money on getting lots of eidelons. They don’t need to turn Apoc and MoC into Anomaly Arbitration. The new pure fiction isn’t currently out yet, but I’ll bet it’s gonna be just as bad. 

As for the story, it’s been rushed and a bit of a mess. I know some of it was because they had to change things last minute due to reasons outside the game, but they should have pushed back the schedule or something if that was the case because planarcadia is messy. No one gets much character exploration at all even when they get an entire SP and Evanescia was so irrelevant it was almost impressive how little would have to be changed to write her out of the story entirely. It hasn’t been horrible by any means, and in all honestly I liked planarcadia for the most part, but most people I’ve seen talk about it were decidedly not fans of it. 

The character designs have become somewhat repetitive and a third of the planarcadia cast has the same exact color palette. 

The rewards are abysmal. You get enough for maybe 50-60 wishes per patch, but that’s assuming you do every single daily check in, event, weekly DU/CW points, and that you are able to fully clear every endgame. Most people can’t/don’t do all of them. That isn’t enough for a singular 5 star, and it’s not even guaranteed to be the one you want. Again, they give you 50-60 pulls over the span of 6 weeks, during which there are anywhere between 8 and 16 banners during those weeks, and that’s not including the 8 fate stay night collab banners. They do maybe 1 event a patch (which again is usually around SIX WEEKS LONG) and these events can almost always be done in an afternoon and give usually less than a full 10 pull. 

None of this has even mentioned the blatant racism, either. There are so few people of color in this game and the ones that are there are either racist caricatures or are basicially grey. It’s like hoyoverse is allergic to color. Arlan is incredibly grey and his kit names are centered around things like breaking chains…. It’s really odd quite frankly. There’s also a black man with “donut lips” in robins trailer. It’s straight up racist. 

The game in its current state is a mess and the people at hoyoverse don’t care about their playerbase or its opinions so long as they can still milk them for money.
